edits.html:
Polymyalgia Rheumatica

aching with normal strength · sedimentation rate and creatine kinase · giant cell arteritis overlap · prednisone responseIs this pain and stiffness with normal strength after 50, and does low-dose prednisone clear it within days?

The decision point

Polymyalgia rheumatica presents at age >50 with bilateral proximal girdle aching with morning stiffness, systemic symptoms and ESR ≥50 (erythrocyte sedimentation rate). There is no true weakness and no muscle tenderness. "Can't get out of bed" here reflects pain and stiffness, not weakness; weakness points to myositis. Treatment is low-dose prednisone ~15 mg. A dramatic response within days is nearly diagnostic.

Defining criteria Diagnosis – age >50, bilateral proximal girdle aching with morning stiffness, ESR ≥50, with normal strength and no muscle tenderness · Response criterion – dramatic improvement on prednisone ~15 mg within days is nearly diagnostic · Rules out polymyositis – PMR is pain with normal CK; polymyositis is weakness with elevated CK
Proximal pain & stiffness – the differential
DiagnosisKey discriminatorLabsTreatment
Polymyalgia rheumaticaProximal pain/stiffness, strength normalESR/CRP ↑, CK normalLow-dose prednisone
Giant cell arteritis EmergencyHeadache, jaw claudication, vision loss; coexists with PMR in ~50%ESR often >50–100High-dose prednisone; don't wait for biopsy if vision is threatened
PolymyositisProximal weakness > painCK ↑, anti-Jo-1High-dose steroids
Elderly-onset RASmall-joint synovitis (MCP/PIP), erosionsRF / anti-CCP +Methotrexate
FibromyalgiaDiffuse tender points, younger womenNormal ESR/CRPExercise, duloxetine, amitriptyline
Hypothyroid myopathyFatigue, weight gain, bradycardiaTSH ↑, CK ↑Levothyroxine
Statin myopathyStatin exposureCK ↑Stop the statin
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
ESR and CRPFirstESR elevated, typically 50 or higherSupports PMR in the right clinical picture; normal values point toward fibromyalgia or another cause
CKFirstNormal CKPain without muscle injury; excludes polymyositis and statin myopathy
TSHFirstNormal TSHExcludes hypothyroid myopathy, which can mimic proximal aching
RF and anti-CCPBy branchNegative in PMRSwollen MCPs or PIPs: consider elderly-onset RA
Temporal artery biopsyBy branchGranulomatous arteritisHeadache, jaw claudication or vision change: GCA; start high-dose prednisone before biopsy
Response to prednisone about 15 mg (clinical diagnosis)ConfirmsDramatic improvement within daysPMR; no response after a week means reconsider the diagnosis
EMG and muscle biopsySkipNormal in PMR; strength is 5/5Reserved for true weakness with high CK (polymyositis)
Scenario bank
  1. 72 yo F, bilateral shoulder and hip girdle aching, morning stiffness 90 min, ESR 62, strength 5/5 → Polymyalgia rheumatica → prednisone 15 mg daily
  2. 72 yo F with known PMR, new jaw claudication and temporal tenderness → Giant cell arteritis → high-dose prednisone immediately, biopsy after
  3. 68 yo M, progressive proximal weakness, CK 4,000, normal ESR → Polymyositis → EMG and muscle biopsy
  4. 70 yo F on atorvastatin, proximal aching, CK 900 → Statin myopathy → stop the statin and recheck CK
  5. 66 yo F, proximal aching, ESR 12, TSH 14 → Hypothyroid myopathy → levothyroxine
  6. 74 yo F with presumed PMR, no response after a week of prednisone 15 mg → Reconsider the diagnosis – PMR responds within days
  7. 63 yo F, widespread pain, non-restorative sleep, normal ESR and CK → Fibromyalgia
Pearls PMR (polymyalgia rheumatica) = pain with normal CK (creatine kinase); polymyositis = weakness with high CK · PMR responds to low-dose steroids, GCA (giant cell arteritis) needs high dose · every PMR diagnosis gets a GCA symptom screen, and ~50% of GCA patients have PMR · NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) fail in PMR; they are a close but inadequate therapy.
Sequencing trapTreat-the-number

edits.html:
Osteoarthritis

pharmacotherapy ladder · class right, member wrong · ketorolac's 5-day maximum · excluding inflammatory arthritisIs the offered drug the right member of the right class for a chronic condition in this patient?

The decision point

A drug class can be correct while the offered member is wrong. An NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug) is first-line for knee OA (osteoarthritis). The NSAID ketorolac has a hard 5-day maximum because of GI (gastrointestinal), renal and bleeding risk. If it is the only NSAID offered, it is ruled out for a 6-month condition in a 72-year-old, and acetaminophen is the default choice.

Guideline currency The ACR/Arthritis Foundation 2019 (ACR: American College of Rheumatology) guideline strongly recommends topical NSAIDs for knee OA (upgraded from conditional in 2012). It also strongly recommends oral NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs). In the same guideline, acetaminophen was downgraded to conditional. It is framed for patients unable to take NSAIDs, and its effect sizes in trials are small. Older NBME (National Board of Medical Examiners) items still key acetaminophen. This patient's factors also favor it: age 72, with its GI (gastrointestinal), renal and CV (cardiovascular) risk, and pain rated 3/10.
Osteoarthritis pharmacotherapy ladder
TierIntervention
AlwaysExercise (strongly recommended) · weight loss – with BMI 35, the highest-value intervention · self-management programs
First-line drug, kneeTopical NSAIDs – preferred in the elderly, minimal systemic exposure
NextOral NSAIDs – lowest effective dose, add a PPI if GI risk
ConditionalAcetaminophen (limited efficacy) · duloxetine · topical capsaicin
AdjunctIntra-articular glucocorticoid injection
Recommended againstOpioids · hydroxychloroquine and methotrexate (strongly against) · glucosamine · oral glucocorticoids (strongly against)
DefinitiveJoint replacement for refractory disease
Excluding inflammatory arthritis No fever, no morning stiffness, no synovitis, crepitus present: this pattern is mechanical, not inflammatory. It excludes hydroxychloroquine and prednisone. Oral steroids are strongly recommended against in OA (osteoarthritis); the accepted steroid route is intra-articular.
Scenario bank
  1. 68 yo F with knee osteoarthritis still limited by pain despite exercise and weight loss → Topical diclofenac → the first-line drug for knee OA
  2. Knee OA with CKD or prior GI bleed → Topical NSAID or acetaminophen, avoid systemic NSAIDs
  3. Refractory pain despite NSAIDs and PT → Intra-articular glucocorticoid
  4. Morning stiffness >1 hour with symmetric MCP/PIP synovitis → Rheumatoid arthritis → RF/anti-CCP, DMARDs
  5. Acute monoarticular knee with warmth and effusion → Arthrocentesis before any pharmacotherapy
  6. End-stage disease, failed all conservative measures → Joint replacement
Transferable rule When choosing initial pharmacotherapy, read which specific agent represents each class. A class can be right while the offered member is wrong: ketorolac for chronic OA (osteoarthritis), gentamicin for simple cystitis, chloramphenicol for otitis. Check the offered drug rather than rejecting the guideline.
Class-vs-member

edits.html:
Brachial Plexus Injury at Birth

upper vs lower plexus vs fracture · Moro, biceps and grasp by lesion · Horner syndrome rides with T1 · prognosisWhich of Moro, biceps and grasp is lost, and are ptosis, miosis or crepitus present?

Source vignette Pt – 1-day-old boy, 4.4 kg, 39 wk forceps delivery complicated by shoulder dystocia, mother with insulin-treated gestational diabetes and obesity; right hand barely moves, held with the wrist extended, MCP joints hyperextended and IP joints flexed; grasp absent, Moro and biceps reflexes intact; no crepitus; slight right ptosis and a smaller right pupil · Q – the most likely cause; options spanned clavicle fracture, humerus fracture, C5-C6 injury, C8-T1 injury, perinatal asphyxia and perinatal ischemic stroke
The decision point

Three reflexes localize a weak newborn arm. The Moro reflex needs shoulder abduction and elbow extension (C5-C6) and a pain-free arm. The biceps reflex runs through C5-C6, and the grasp runs through C8-T1. Here the grasp is absent while Moro and biceps are intact. The hand is clawed, and the same side has ptosis and miosis. This is a lower plexus (Klumpke, C8-T1) injury. Horner syndrome occurs because the sympathetic fibers to the eye leave the cord with T1.

Erb palsy (C5-C6) is the most common birth palsy and shows the reverse pattern: Moro and biceps lost, grasp kept. A clavicle or humerus fracture lowers the Moro only through pain. It keeps biceps and grasp and has crepitus.

Newborn arm weakness: reflexes by lesion
MoroBicepsGraspPosture and other tellInjury
Decreased (pain)IntactIntactCrepitus or a bony step over the clavicle; a callus lump laterClavicle fracture
Decreased (pain)IntactIntactCrepitus and swelling of the upper armHumerus fracture
DecreasedDecreasedIntactWaiter's tip: arm adducted and internally rotated, elbow extended, forearm pronated, wrist and fingers flexedErb-Duchenne palsy, upper plexus (C5-C6)
IntactIntactAbsentClaw hand (wrist extended, MCP hyperextended, IP flexed) with ipsilateral Horner (ptosis, miosis)Klumpke palsy, lower plexus (C8-T1)
AbsentAbsentAbsentFlail arm, often with HornerTotal plexus palsy (C5-T1)
VariablePreserved or briskPreservedFocal seizures and later upper motor neuron signsPerinatal ischemic stroke
Depressed on both sidesDepressed on both sidesDepressed on both sidesAltered mental status, poor tone, poor feeding or breathing, seizuresPerinatal asphyxia
Scenario bank
  1. 1-day-old boy, 4.4 kg, delivered with forceps after shoulder dystocia; mother has insulin-treated gestational diabetes; the right hand is held with the wrist extended, MCP joints hyperextended and IP joints flexed; grasp absent; Moro and biceps reflexes intact; no crepitus; mild right ptosis and a smaller right pupil → Lower brachial plexus (C8-T1) injury → Klumpke palsy
  2. 1-day-old girl, 4.6 kg, after shoulder dystocia; the left arm lies adducted and internally rotated with the elbow extended, forearm pronated and wrist flexed; left Moro and biceps reflexes absent; left grasp strong; no crepitus; pupils equal → Erb-Duchenne palsy → Physical therapy with gentle range of motion
  3. 2-day-old boy, 4.2 kg, after shoulder dystocia, moves the right arm less; right Moro diminished and he cries when the arm is moved; biceps reflex and grasp present on both sides; crepitus over the midshaft of the right clavicle → Clavicle fracture → Gentle handling and pain control
  4. 3-week-old girl with an Erb palsy from a shoulder dystocia delivery; she has begun to flex the elbow a little; no crepitus; radiographs of the clavicle and humerus are normal → Range-of-motion exercises with physical therapy → Upper brachial plexus (C5-C6) injury
  5. 7-month-old boy with a left upper brachial plexus injury from birth who has had physical therapy since the first weeks; he still has no elbow flexion or shoulder abduction on the left → Referral for surgical nerve repair → Upper brachial plexus (C5-C6) injury without recovery
  6. 3-day-old girl with weakness of the right arm after a difficult vaginal delivery → Ipsilateral ptosis and miosis → Horner syndrome from a T1 injury
Management and prognosis Gentle massage and range-of-motion exercises with physical therapy to prevent contractures; most infants recover within months. No improvement by 3 to 9 months: refer for surgical nerve repair. Horner syndrome marks a T1 injury and predicts a poorer outcome. A clavicle fracture needs only gentle handling and pain control.
Pearls Risk factors: macrosomia, shoulder dystocia and maternal diabetes, with obesity and instrumented delivery adding to them · Traction on the head and neck during shoulder dystocia stretches the upper roots (Erb); traction on a raised arm, as in delivering the posterior arm, stretches C8-T1 (Klumpke) · An intact, symmetric Moro does not exclude a plexus injury, because Klumpke spares the shoulder; check the grasp
Pairs with Arm Injury in a Young Child: its pediatric elbow neighbors line names these palsies; this brief covers the reflex split. Torticollis and Plagiocephaly in an Infant: the other birth-position injury; it lists clavicle fracture only as a neck-mass mimic, and the clavicle question is in this brief. Stroke in a Child or Adolescent: perinatal stroke presents with focal seizures and upper motor neuron signs, not a limp arm with one lost reflex. Ask: are the signs upper or lower motor neuron?
Transferable rule When a newborn will not move one arm, read three reflexes before the posture. A lower Moro alone with crepitus is a fracture. Lost Moro and biceps with a kept grasp is C5-C6. A lost grasp with Moro and biceps kept is C8-T1. In C8-T1 injury, ptosis and miosis confirm T1 and predict slower recovery.
Mirror twinC5-C6 injury is the commonest birth palsy and shares the shoulder dystocia, but it loses Moro and biceps and keeps grasp, the reverse of this infant.
Salient decoyClavicle fracture: suggested by a 4.4 kg infant after shoulder dystocia. It lowers the Moro from pain, keeps the grasp and gives crepitus; none of these is present.
True-fact-wrong-slotPerinatal ischemic stroke causes one-sided weakness, but with seizures and upper motor neuron signs, not a clawed hand with Horner.
Unchecked attributePerinatal asphyxia is global and bilateral, with altered mental status and poor tone; this infant has one weak hand.

edits.html:
Developmental Milestones and Normal Growth

birth weight rules · four developmental laws · milestones at 2, 4, 6, 9 and 12 months · delay by domainDo the weight and milestones fit the age, and if not, which domain is delayed?

The decision point

Birth weight is regained by 10–14 days, doubles by 4–6 months, triples by 1 year and quadruples by 2 years. When the numbers match a milestone rule and the exam is normal, management is reassurance; any other intervention is unnecessary.

The four developmental laws
  • Motor descends the body – 2 mo lifts head · 4 mo head steady + forearms · 6 mo rolls / props on hands · 9 mo sits alone · 12 mo pulls to stand and cruises
  • Grasp moves pinky-side → thumb-side – 4 mo midline · 6 mo whole-hand reach · 9 mo raking · 12 mo pincer
  • Language: vowels → consonants → meaning – 4 mo "ooo" · 6 mo raspberries/squeals · 9 mo "mamama" · 12 mo "mama" meaning mama
  • Social: everyone → someone – 2 mo social smile at anyone · 6 mo familiar faces · 9 mo stranger and separation anxiety · 12 mo social games, object permanence
Age anchors
AgeImageHook
2 moThe Greeter – lifts head, tracks you, smiles, coosTWO eyes track, TWO lips smile
4 moThe Sphinx – head steady on forearms, hands to midline and mouthFOUR = everything to the FORE
6 moThe Roller – rolls, sits propped, mouths toys, laughsSIX: Sits, Squeals, raSpberries
9 moThe Anxious Sitter – sits alone, rakes, babbles, cries at strangersNINE = "No! Not you!"
12 moThe Little Person – cruises, pinches a Cheerio, first wordONE year = ONE word, ONE-finger pinch
Scenario bank
  1. 4 mo M, birth weight 3.2 kg, now 6.6 kg, normal exam → Normal growth – weight doubles by 4 to 6 months → reassurance
  2. 12 mo M whose weight has tripled since birth → Normal growth → reassurance
  3. 10 day M who has not yet regained his birth weight → Normal weight loss – birth weight is regained by 10 to 14 days → reassurance
  4. 2 mo M who lifts his head and smiles socially → Age-appropriate development
  5. 9 mo M who cannot sit without support → Gross motor delay → developmental evaluation
  6. 6 mo M who does not babble and does not respond to sound → Audiology evaluation
  7. 18-month-old with a 12 to 15 word vocabulary understood mainly by family, frequent jargon, single words without phrases, who scribbles, follows a one-step command without gesture and shows stranger anxiety, but pulls to stand and only cruises → Gross motor delay → walking easily is expected by 18 months
  8. 18-month-old with isolated gross motor delay and otherwise normal development → Refer for early intervention services → under age 3 the referral is the pathway
  9. Why an 18-month-old’s language is normal although strangers understand few of his words → Speech is expected to be intelligible mainly to family at this age, with jargon normal → intelligibility milestones come later
  10. 4-year-old boy at a well-child visit who imitates a straight line but cannot copy a circle, jumps but cannot balance on one foot, and combines words with only half his speech understood; normal examination → Delayed gross motor, fine motor and language → global developmental delay: evaluate for a cause and refer to the school district for a preschool special education evaluation (early intervention is for children under 3)
  11. 4-year-old girl who hops on one foot, copies a square, draws a stick figure and plays cooperatively, but speaks in two-word phrases that strangers rarely understand → Isolated language delay → one delayed domain; obtain a hearing evaluation
  12. 4-year-old boy who speaks in sentences strangers understand and plays cooperatively with friends, but cannot hop on one foot and cannot copy a circle → Global developmental delay → two domains delayed: gross motor and fine motor
Red flags No social smile by 3 mo · no babbling by 9 mo · no words by 15 mo · not walking by 18 mo · hand preference before 12 months (suggests hemiparesis) · loss of any acquired milestone at any age; regression is always pathologic (Rett, autistic regression, metabolic disease, leukodystrophy).
Primitive reflexes must leave before the skill arrives Palmar grasp gone 3–6 mo (enables voluntary grasp) · Moro by 6 mo · rooting by 4 mo · ATNR (asymmetric tonic neck reflex) by 4–6 mo · parachute appears 6–8 mo and stays for life · Babinski normal until 12–24 mo. Persistence beyond these windows indicates a UMN (upper motor neuron) lesion or cerebral palsy. Note: the CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) 2022 revision moved milestones from the 50th to the 75th percentile. As a result, "sits without support" is now listed at 9 months, where older sources say 6.
The 18-month set, and the ages that neighbour it Walks easily and climbs – the gross motor item · Scribbles – fine motor · At least 3 words beyond mama and dada, with frequent jargon – language; intelligibility to strangers is not expected yet · Follows a one-step command without gesture – cognitive · Two-word phrases belong to 24 months and 75% intelligible speech to age 3; neither is expected at 18 months · Stranger anxiety is normal from 6 to 9 months to about age 2 and supports intact social development
The 4-year set, and global delay Hops on one foot and throws a ball overhand – gross motor · Copies a square and draws a simple stick figure – fine motor · Speaks in sentences that strangers understand and tells stories – language · Plays cooperatively with friends – social · Jumping, imitating a line and combining words – younger skills; having them does not make a 4-year-old normal in that domain · Global developmental delay – significant delay in two or more domains; evaluate for a cause; under age 3, refer for early intervention; from age 3, refer to the school district for a preschool special education evaluation, with speech, physical and occupational therapy. How NBME framed it: the stem gives one skill present and one missing in each domain, and the options grid normal or delayed across three domains.
Pairs with Part I Feeding an Infant or Toddler covers the case where growth falters because of how the child eats rather than how much.
Salient decoyNormal in all three domains: jumping and combining words are skills of a 2-year-old, so having them does not make a 4-year-old normal
Unchecked attributeGross motor marked normal: he can jump, but a 4-year-old hops on one foot and this boy cannot balance on one
Unchecked attributeFine motor marked normal: imitating a line is not copying a shape; a 4-year-old copies a square, and this boy cannot copy a circle
Unchecked attributeLanguage marked normal: he combines words, but only half his speech is understood; a 4-year-old speaks in sentences strangers understand

edits.html:
School Difficulty in a Child

behavior confined to school · the child's private interview · learning vs behavioral disorders · hearing and visionDoes the behavior stay at school, and what does the child say when interviewed alone?

Source vignette Pt – 9 yo M, irritable and fighting at school since third grade began, with school refusal; privately reports classmates call him a baby because he counts on his fingers and reads slowly; behavior normal at home · Q – the most likely diagnosis; options spanned specific learning disorder, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, social anxiety disorder and oppositional defiant disorder
The decision point

The mother's chief complaint is irritability, a fight and school refusal. In a private interview, the child says his classmates call him a baby because he counts on his fingers and reads slowly. This private disclosure identifies the diagnosis. Each behavioral disorder in the differential explains the behavior, but only specific learning disorder also explains the failing grades.

Onset coincides with an academic transition: third grade, where learning to read becomes reading to learn. The symptoms are confined to school, with normal behavior at home.

Defining criteria Specific learning disorder – achievement below intellectual potential in reading, writing or math for at least 6 months despite support · ADHD – symptoms in at least 2 settings with onset before age 12, so school-only behavior excludes it · Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder – severe outbursts at least 3 times weekly for at least 12 months with persistently irritable mood between them · Oppositional defiant disorder – a pattern of defiance, argumentativeness and vindictiveness toward authority for at least 6 months · Social anxiety disorder – fear of scrutiny across situations, and not diagnosed when better explained by another disorder
The school-age child with behavior change – the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Specific learning disorderBehavior downstream of an academic skill deficitThe child names the deficit himself when interviewed privately
ADHDInattention and hyperactivity carried everywhereSchool and home both complain
Disruptive mood dysregulationChronic angry mood between frequent outburstsOutbursts three times weekly for a year; explains no academic decline
Oppositional defiant disorderDefiance toward authorityArgumentative and vindictive, not avoidant
Social anxiety disorderFear of scrutiny generallyFear of eating, speaking or performing anywhere, not only where a weakness shows
Absence seizuresBrief lapses many times dailyStaring spells provoked by hyperventilation
Hearing or vision impairmentSensory barrier misread as inattentionSits close, turns the head, mishears
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Private interview with the childFirstChild names the deficit: slow reading, counting on fingersBehavior is downstream of an academic problem
Hearing and vision screeningNextAbnormal screenSensory barrier, not a learning disorder: audiology or eye referral
Parent and teacher ADHD rating scalesBy branchSymptoms in two or more settingsADHD; behavior confined to school argues against it
EEGBy branch3 Hz spike-and-wave provoked by hyperventilationAbsence seizures behind staring spells and falling grades
Psychoeducational testing (cognitive and achievement)ConfirmsAchievement below age and intellect for 6 months despite supportSpecific learning disorder: school-based support
Scenario bank
  1. 9 yo M, irritable and fighting only at school since third grade began, reads slowly and counts on fingers, normal behavior at home → Specific learning disorder → educational testing
  2. 9 yo M with suspected specific learning disorder, initial evaluation → Educational testing plus hearing and vision screening → rule out psychiatric and medical causes
  3. 8 yo M, inattentive and disruptive at school and at home, loses things, since age 5 → Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
  4. 10 yo M, argumentative and vindictive with all adults for a year, grades normal → Oppositional defiant disorder
  5. 9 yo F, severe temper outbursts 4 times weekly for 18 months, persistently angry between outbursts → Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder
  6. 12 yo F, fear of speaking or eating in front of others in every setting, blushing and trembling → Social anxiety disorder
  7. 7 yo F, brief staring spells many times daily, declining grades, provoked by hyperventilation → Absence seizures → electroencephalogram
  8. 8 yo M, declining grades, turns his head to listen, frequently says what → Hearing impairment → audiology evaluation
  9. 13 yo M refuses to attend school, stomachaches on school mornings that resolve on weekends → School refusal
Behavior is a symptom, not a diagnosis Before naming a behavioral disorder in a school-age child, ask what the child is avoiding. Learning disorder, hearing or vision loss, absence seizures, bullying and abuse all present as acting out.
Pearls Count the settings: behavior in one setting means something about that setting; behavior in two or more settings is a disorder the child carries · Symptoms starting at a school transition point to an academic-demand mismatch rather than a primary mood disorder · Early intervention improves self-esteem and social skills as well as grades · Social anxiety is explicitly not diagnosed when the avoidance is better explained by another disorder
Pairs with Related conditions without their own brief: ADHD (attention deficit hyperactivity disorder) diagnosis and stimulant management.
Transferable rule In a child with a behavior problem, the parent's history gives the chief complaint and the child's private disclosure gives the diagnosis.
Class-vs-memberSocial anxiety is a real disorder whose own criterion excludes it when another disorder explains the avoidance.
Mirror twinOppositional defiant disorder is the defiant version of the same complaint; he is avoidant.

edits.html:
Suspected Child Abuse

fractures that mean abuse · red flags · the bone-disease mimics · a risk factor is not a findingDoes the fracture need a pull, twist or squeeze, and does the film or exam give a bone disease its own sign?

Source vignette Pt – 13-month-old boy brought by an aunt for left leg pain; irritable, refuses to stand, cries when the leg is touched; born at home without prenatal care, exclusively breastfed without vitamin D, no routine care; his mother broke her forearm and wrist as a child · Exam – weight 5th percentile, height 50th; swelling and point tenderness of the distal left thigh; no bruises; beefy red diaper plaques with satellite papules · Imaging – medial metaphyseal corner fracture of the distal femur · Q – the most likely cause of the x-ray findings; options spanned abuse, two metabolic or genetic bone diseases, an infection and a histiocytic disorder
The decision point

In a young child, three fractures are abuse until proven otherwise. A metaphyseal corner (bucket-handle) fracture needs a forcible pull or twist of the limb. A posterior rib fracture comes from squeezing the chest. The third is a femur fracture in a child who does not yet walk. The bone-disease mimics each need their own finding on the film or exam. Rickets needs osteopenia with cupped, frayed metaphyses. Osteogenesis imperfecta needs blue sclerae and many low-energy fractures. Langerhans cell histiocytosis needs a punched-out lytic lesion.

A risk factor in the history (breastfeeding without vitamin D, no prenatal care, a parent's single childhood fracture) is not that finding. A film with normal bone density and a classic abuse fracture outweighs that risk factor; the fracture stays abuse until proven otherwise.

Red flags for abuse History – injury inconsistent with the child's developmental stage, delay in seeking care, a story that changes or conflicts between caregivers · Bruises – patterned (belt, buckle, hand), any bruise in an infant who is not yet mobile, or bruises over the ears, neck or trunk rather than shins and forehead · Burns – linear or sharply demarcated, such as immersion burns with a clean line · Fractures – metaphyseal corner, posterior rib, femur before walking, multiple in different stages of healing, skull · Head – subdural and retinal hemorrhages
Fracture in an infant or toddler: the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellWhy less likely here
Child abuseHistory that does not fit the injury or the child's development; delay in careMetaphyseal corner, posterior rib, or femur fracture before walking, on a film with normal bone densityThe key: a pull-or-twist fracture with no sign of bone disease
Osteogenesis imperfectaType I collagen defect, usually autosomal dominant; fractures with minimal traumaBlue sclerae, easy bruising, short stature, hearing loss, a family history of many fractures; osteopenia on filmNo blue sclerae, normal height; a parent's single childhood fracture is not that history
RicketsVitamin D deficiency in an exclusively breastfed infant without supplements; X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets looks similar on filmFilm: osteopenia, cupped and frayed metaphyses, widened physes; exam: bowed legs, widened wrists, rachitic rosaryRisk factor present, film findings absent; the metaphysis is fractured, not frayed
Congenital syphilisUntreated maternal infection; early (under 2 years): snuffles, palm and sole rash, hepatosplenomegaly, periostitis; late: saber shin, frontal bossing, saddle noseRash, snuffles, big liver; later saber shinNone of its findings; it does not cause corner fractures
Langerhans cell histiocytosisA rash that looks seborrheic or candidal but is petechial or crusted and persists; sometimes diabetes insipidusPunched-out lytic skull or long-bone lesionThe film shows a fracture, not a lytic lesion
Toddler's fracture (accidental)A child who has started walking; new limp after a minor, often unwitnessed twistNondisplaced spiral fracture of the distal tibiaWrong bone and wrong pattern
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Radiograph of the painful limbFirstCorner fracture, normal bone densityA pull-or-twist injury: suspect abuse
Skeletal surveyNextOccult fractures: multiple, different ages, posterior rib, skull, metaphysealRequired for suspected abuse under age 2
Head CTNextSubdural hemorrhage or skull fractureAbusive head trauma, which can be silent on exam in an infant
Dilated funduscopic examNextRetinal hemorrhagesAbusive head trauma
CBC, PT and aPTTBy branchNormalWhen bruising is present: excludes a bleeding disorder before calling bruises inflicted
Calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, PTH, 25-hydroxyvitamin DBy branchLow phosphate, high alkaline phosphatase; high PTH and low vitamin D in nutritional ricketsOnly when the film shows osteopenia, cupping or fraying: rickets
Genetic or collagen testing for osteogenesis imperfectaSkip Not needed without blue sclerae, osteopenia, hearing loss or a family history of many fractures
Scenario bank
  1. 13-month-old boy brought by an aunt for 1 day of left leg pain; irritable, refuses to stand, cries when the leg is touched; born at home without prenatal care, exclusively breastfed without vitamin D supplements, no routine medical care; his mother broke her forearm and wrist as a child; weight 5th percentile, height 50th; swelling and point tenderness of the distal left thigh; no bruises; beefy red diaper plaques with satellite papules; radiograph shows a medial metaphyseal corner fracture of the distal femur → Child abuse → a corner fracture needs a forcible pull or twist of the limb; admit for safety, report to child protective services, and obtain a skeletal survey, head CT and funduscopy
  2. 4-month-old boy with a swollen right thigh; his father says the leg got caught in the crib rails while he was out of the room; the infant cannot yet roll over; no bruises, white sclerae, normal growth; radiograph shows a midshaft femur fracture with normal bone density → Skeletal survey → a femur fracture in a child who does not walk is abuse until proven otherwise; head CT, funduscopy and a report to child protective services go with it
  3. 7-month-old girl brought in for fussiness; exam shows bruises on both ears; skeletal survey shows two healing posterior rib fractures; the parents say she bruises easily and ask to take her home tonight → Discharge home with outpatient follow-up → safety comes first: admit, report to child protective services, and complete the head CT and funduscopy
  4. 8-month-old boy with his third fracture, a humerus fracture after being lifted from his crib; blue sclerae; length 5th percentile; his father has hearing loss and had many fractures as a child; radiographs show diffuse osteopenia and several healed long-bone fractures → Osteogenesis imperfecta → type I collagen defect: blue sclerae, hearing loss, osteopenia and a family history of many low-energy fractures
  5. 14-month-old girl, exclusively breastfed, no vitamin D supplements, with bowed legs, widened wrists and beading along the costochondral junctions; wrist radiograph shows osteopenia, cupped and frayed distal radial and ulnar metaphyses and widened physes, with no fracture; phosphate low, alkaline phosphatase high, PTH high → Nutritional rickets → vitamin D deficiency: treat with vitamin D; X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets looks the same on film but runs in families and does not respond to vitamin D
  6. 18-month-old boy with a crusted, petechial rash in the diaper area and scalp that has not cleared with 4 weeks of topical nystatin; new polyuria and polydipsia; skull radiograph shows a well-defined punched-out lytic lesion → Langerhans cell histiocytosis → a punched-out lytic lesion with a treatment-resistant rash and diabetes insipidus; biopsy confirms
  7. 6-month-old boy seen for cough; chest radiograph shows a healing posterior rib fracture; the mother says he has never been injured; a small bruise is on the left ear; the physician is not certain the injury was inflicted → Report to child protective services → physicians are mandated reporters on reasonable suspicion, not proof; admit and obtain the skeletal survey, head CT and funduscopy alongside the report
Management Safety first – admit the child to the hospital rather than discharge to the suspected caregivers while the workup runs · Report – to child protective services on reasonable suspicion; physicians are mandated reporters and do not need proof, and the report is not delayed for the skeletal survey or other results · Evaluate – skeletal survey, head CT and funduscopy, plus the by-branch labs above
Pearls Abuse also presents as a posterior rib fracture or a femur fracture before walking, or with an added bruise on the ear or trunk · A walking toddler with a spiral distal tibial fracture after a minor twist has an accidental injury. The same child with a corner fracture does not · Caregivers who were themselves abused or neglected, an unstable home and a child with chronic medical problems raise the risk. The diagnosis rests on the fracture pattern
Pairs with Aquifer Bruising and Purpura in a Child covers bruising. Ask: is the bruise somewhere a child of this age could bump, and are the platelets normal? Part I The Limping Child master table covers the toddler's fracture. Ask: does the child walk, and is it a spiral tibial fracture or a corner fracture? Part II Vitamins and Nutritional Deficiencies covers vitamin D deficiency rickets and the 400 IU supplement for breastfed infants. Part I Bone Lesions in a Child covers the lytic lesion. Ask: is the bone destroyed, or broken?
Transferable rule Some fractures in a young child need a force the child could not generate. Treat these as abuse until the film or exam shows a sign specific to a bone disease. A risk factor in the history is not that sign.
Unchecked attributeRickets: exclusive breastfeeding without vitamin D is a real risk factor, but the film never showed osteopenia, cupping, fraying or widened physes.
Salient decoyLangerhans cell histiocytosis: the beefy diaper rash with satellite papules is ordinary candida; Langerhans cell histiocytosis causes punched-out lytic lesions, not corner fractures.
Salient decoyOsteogenesis imperfecta: the mother's one childhood forearm fracture is common; without blue sclerae, short stature, bruising or many fractures, this is not osteogenesis imperfecta.
True-fact-wrong-slotCongenital syphilis: no prenatal care is a real risk, but saber shin, frontal bossing and saddle nose are late findings, and none of its signs is a corner fracture.

edits.html:
Shock in Children

four categories by mechanism, not appearance · cold shock in children · perfusion before pressure · septic shock ladderIs perfusion abnormal, and what is wrong with the circulation rather than with the skin?

Source vignette Pt – 4 yo F, fever to 40 C, petechial rash, obtundation, capillary refill 4 seconds, no response to three fluid boluses; no blood pressure reported · Q – the category of shock; options spanned distributive, cardiogenic, hypovolemic and obstructive
The decision point

Fever, a petechial rash and shock in a preschooler indicate septic shock. Septic shock is by definition distributive. Inflammatory mediators produce vasodilation and capillary leak, so blood is maldistributed rather than absent, inadequate or obstructed.

She does not look vasodilated. Capillary refill of 4 seconds is cold shock, which is how children usually present. Children compensate by vasoconstricting and raising the heart rate, so the bedside picture mimics hypovolemia. The vignette gives no blood pressure, because in children hypotension is a late, pre-arrest finding.

Defining criteria Distributive shock – vasodilation and capillary leak with maldistributed flow despite normal or high cardiac output · Shock in a child – a perfusion diagnosis: mental status, capillary refill above 2 seconds, weak pulses, urine output under 1 mL/kg/h · Hypotension – not required, and marks decompensation when present · Fluid-refractory shock – persistent after 40 to 60 mL/kg, the trigger to start a vasoactive infusion
The four categories of shock – what to look for
CategoryMechanismThe NBME tell
DistributiveVasodilation and capillary leakFever with a source, urticaria, or a spinal injury; wide pulse pressure when warm
HypovolemicVolume loss – gastrointestinal, hemorrhage, burns, ketoacidosisA stated route of loss, dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes
CardiogenicPump failure – myocarditis, arrhythmia, congenital lesionGallop, hepatomegaly, crackles; worsens with fluid
ObstructiveMechanical block – tamponade, tension pneumothorax, ductal-dependent lesionDistended neck veins with clear or asymmetric lungs, muffled sounds
Anaphylactic distributive subtypeIgE-mediated vasodilationUrticaria, angioedema, wheeze within minutes of exposure
Neurogenic distributive subtypeLoss of sympathetic tone above T6Hypotension with bradycardia, warm dry skin
Management ladder – pediatric septic shock
TierInterventionEscalate when
1Recognise, obtain access, balanced crystalloid 10 to 20 mL/kg per bolus up to 40 to 60 mL/kg in the first hour, reassessing after eachShock persists after 40 to 60 mL/kg, or rales or hepatomegaly appear, which stops the fluid
2Start a vasoactive infusion – epinephrine or norepinephrineCatecholamine-resistant shock
3Hydrocortisone for catecholamine-resistant shock or suspected adrenal insufficiencyNo response; consider extracorporeal support
ParallelAntimicrobials within 1 hour for septic shock, cultures first only if they cause no substantial delay –
Scenario bank
  1. 4 yo F with fever to 40 C, a petechial rash, obtundation, capillary refill 4 seconds and no response to three fluid boluses → Distributive shock → septic shock, cold phenotype
  2. 4 yo F in septic shock still hypoperfused after 60 mL/kg of isotonic fluid → Start a vasoactive infusion → fluid-refractory septic shock
  3. 4 yo F with septic shock whose blood cultures are pending → Give antimicrobials within 1 hour → cultures first only if they cause no delay
  4. 9 mo M with 5 days of vomiting and diarrhea, sunken eyes, capillary refill 3 seconds and tachycardia → Give a 20 mL/kg isotonic fluid bolus → hypovolemic shock
  5. 8 yo M with viral myocarditis, a gallop, hepatomegaly, crackles and capillary refill 4 seconds → Give small 5 to 10 mL/kg fluid aliquots with an inotrope → cardiogenic shock
  6. 16 yo M with a penetrating chest wound, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds and hypotension → Pericardiocentesis → obstructive shock from tamponade
  7. 5 yo F with meningococcemia who remains shocked on an epinephrine infusion → Give hydrocortisone → Waterhouse-Friderichsen adrenal insufficiency
  8. 16 yo M with urticaria, wheeze and hypotension minutes after eating peanuts → Anaphylactic shock → a distributive subtype
  9. 17 yo M after a cervical spine injury, hypotensive with bradycardia and warm dry skin → Neurogenic shock → also a distributive subtype
Exceptions Where intensive care is not available and the child has sepsis without hypotension, bolus fluid is recommended against. This is a strong, high-certainty recommendation. Also, adolescence is never itself a reason to admit; the same hospitalisation thresholds apply as for adults.
Pearls Hypotension is a late sign in children; they defend pressure with tachycardia and vasoconstriction, then decompensate abruptly · Children get cold shock and adults get warm shock; a vasoconstricted child's shock is still distributive · Anaphylactic and neurogenic shock are distributive subtypes, so classify the shock as distributive, not as the subtype, unless the subtype's trigger is present · Neurogenic shock is the one form of shock with hypotension and bradycardia; all other shock is tachycardic · Fever plus petechiae plus toxicity is meningococcemia until excluded; petechiae in a well child point instead at immune thrombocytopenia
Pairs with Part I Bacterial Meningitis covers the CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) grid and meningococcal disease; this brief covers only recognition and resuscitation. Ask: is perfusion abnormal? If yes, resuscitate before you investigate.
Transferable rule Shock is classified by mechanism rather than appearance, so ask what is wrong with the circulation instead of what the skin looks like.
True-fact-wrong-slotFluid refractoriness in sepsis reflects leak and vasodilation, not pump failure.
Class-vs-memberAnaphylaxis: it is in the right class but is the wrong member, with no exposure and no urticaria.

edits.html:
Follow-Up of the Preterm Infant

corrected age · milestones at corrected age · growth faltering thresholds · vaccines at chronological ageWhat is the corrected age, and do growth and milestones fit it?

Source vignette Pt – 18 mo F, former 26-week preterm infant, just walking, 10 words, imitates and scribbles; height, weight and head circumference all at the 15th percentile · Q – the most likely assessment; options spanned normal growth and development for corrected age, global developmental delay and failure to thrive
The decision point

Calculate the corrected age first. Born at 26 weeks, she was 14 weeks early. At 18 months chronological age, her corrected age is about 14 and a half months. Judge every milestone against that age. She has just started walking, which is on time. Her vocabulary of 10 words is ahead of the three to five words expected at 15 months. Following a call, imitating and scribbling are age-appropriate.

All three parameters sit together at the 15th percentile. They are proportionate, symmetric and well within normal. Faltering growth requires a parameter below about the 2nd percentile or a downward crossing of two major lines, and she has neither.

Defining criteria Corrected age – chronological age minus the weeks born before 40 weeks · How long to correct – through 24 months for growth and development; newer data support 36 months in extremely and very preterm children · What is never corrected – immunizations, given at chronological age regardless of gestational age or birth weight; the one weight rule is the birth hepatitis B dose at 2 kg or more, and it is a weight threshold rather than an age correction · Normal percentile range – the 15th percentile is normal; faltering growth needs under about the 2nd percentile or a crossing of two major lines
Assessing the former preterm infant – the differential
AssessmentIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Normal for corrected agePreterm child meeting milestones and tracking a normal percentile once correctedCorrected-age milestones met, parameters proportionate above the 2nd percentile
Global developmental delaySignificant delay in two or more domains at corrected ageNot walking or no words at 18 months corrected, often with a falling head circumference
Isolated growth falteringWeight crosses percentiles downward with intact developmentWeight disproportionately low with length and head preserved
Failure to thriveInadequate calories, malabsorption or increased demandParameter below the 2nd percentile or crossing two major lines
Constitutional smallnessSmall but healthy child on a low-normal curveNormal growth velocity along their own percentile
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Growth plotted at corrected ageFirstAll three parameters together, above the 2nd percentileNormal growth; weight alone low points to inadequate calories
Developmental screen at corrected ageNextMilestones met for corrected ageNormal; delay in two or more domains needs early intervention referral
Retinopathy of prematurity exam and hearing screenScreenRetinopathy or failed hearing screenRequired by gestational age and birth weight, however well the infant looks
Cranial ultrasound, all born under 32 weeksConfirmsGerminal matrix or intraventricular bloodIVH; screen at 1 to 2 weeks, repeat to follow progression
CBC with reticulocyte countBy branchNormocytic anemia with no reticulocytosis for its degreeAnemia of prematurity; microcytosis or brisk reticulocytes point elsewhere
Failure-to-thrive laboratory workupSkipThe 15th percentile is normalProportionate, steady growth needs routine surveillance only
Scenario bank
  1. 18 mo F, former 26-week preemie, just walking, 10 words, imitates and scribbles, with height, weight and head circumference all at the 15th percentile corrected → Normal growth and development for corrected age → corrected age about 14 and a half months
  2. Former 26-week premature infant now 12 months chronological, how to plot her growth → Plot at corrected age until 24 months → chronological plotting overstates the deficit
  3. 6 mo old former 28-week premature infant due for routine immunizations → Immunize at chronological age on the standard schedule → prematurity is never corrected for vaccines
  4. 18 mo F, former 26-week preemie, not sitting, no words, head circumference below the 2nd percentile → Refer for developmental evaluation and early intervention → delay across multiple domains at corrected age
  5. Former 26-week premature infant at neonatal intensive care unit discharge, required screening → Retinopathy of prematurity screening – plus a hearing screen → screening driven by gestational age and birth weight
  6. 18 mo former premature infant with all growth parameters at the 15th percentile and tracking steadily → Continue routine surveillance → the 15th percentile is normal
  7. 15 mo M, former 30-week preemie, weight at the 2nd percentile with length at the 25th and head circumference at the 30th, corrected → Inadequate caloric intake → not explained by prematurity
  8. Why growth and development in a preterm child are assessed at corrected rather than chronological age → She has had fewer weeks of growth and brain development → uncorrected assessment falsely labels delay
  9. 24 mo former 26-week premature infant with normal growth and development → Stop correcting for prematurity → plot chronologically from here
  10. 6 wk old former 31-week infant, medically stable and gaining weight, parents asking about the 2-month vaccines → Give them at 2 months of chronologic age on the standard schedule → prematurity is never corrected for vaccines
  11. Why medically stable preterm infants are vaccinated on time rather than deferred → They are at high risk from vaccine-preventable disease and mount an adequate antibody response → immature is not immunocompromised
  12. Preterm infant weighing 1.8 kg at 12 h of life, mother hepatitis B surface antigen negative, due for the birth dose → Delay until the weight reaches 2 kg → the only weight-gated vaccine
  13. 1 wk old girl born at 29 weeks, birth weight 1.51 kg, tolerating feeds, normal vital signs, nondysmorphic, soft anterior fontanelle, moving all four limbs → Screening head ultrasound → all preterm infants under 32 weeks, at age 1 to 2 weeks
  14. Why prematurity under 32 weeks is the threshold for intraventricular hemorrhage screening → The germinal matrix involutes by 32 weeks → before then its thin-walled vessels rupture with swings in cerebral perfusion
  15. 3-day-old born at 28 weeks, 1.04 kg, Apgar scores 8 and 9, afebrile, no maternal fever, membranes ruptured 3 hours before birth; an hour of lethargy and hypotonia, apnea with bradycardia, a tense fontanelle, head circumference up 3 cm since yesterday, then a generalized seizure → Intraventricular hemorrhage → germinal matrix bleed; confirm with cranial ultrasound
  16. Neonate born at 29 weeks who on day 2 develops apnea, lethargy and a bulging anterior fontanelle → Cranial ultrasound → sees blood in the germinal matrix and ventricles through the open fontanelle
  17. 7 wk old born at 32 weeks, feeding and gaining well on fortified formula and ferrous sulfate, pulse 150 with a soft systolic flow murmur; hemoglobin 8, reticulocytes 1.4%, normal platelets and white count, normocytic normochromic smear → Impaired erythropoietin production → anemia of prematurity; the marrow is not asked to respond
  18. 10 wk old term infant, thriving and asymptomatic, hemoglobin 10 with a normocytic smear and normal platelets and white count → Physiologic anemia of infancy → the normal erythropoietin nadir at 2 to 3 months
  19. 6 wk old former 28-week infant with new apnea spells and flat weight gain; hemoglobin 6.5, low reticulocytes, no hemolysis → Red cell transfusion → symptomatic anemia of prematurity
Reading the neonatal history Former 26-week premature sets the age correction; it is not the problem. Mild bronchopulmonary dysplasia with normal head ultrasounds looks like a list of morbidities but is reassuring. Normal cranial imaging excludes the intraventricular hemorrhage and periventricular leukomalacia that drive adverse neurodevelopmental outcome at this gestational age.
Intraventricular hemorrhage Mechanism – fragile germinal matrix vessels rupture with swings in cerebral perfusion (hypotension, hypoxia, hypo- or hyperventilation), and the blood can extend into the lateral ventricles · Who – under 32 weeks gestation or under 1500 g · When – the first few days of life, and often asymptomatic · Symptomatic signs – lethargy, hypotonia, seizures, apnea, bradycardia, a bulging fontanelle, a rapidly rising head circumference, acute anemia · Diagnosis – cranial ultrasound, repeated to follow progression; routine screening under 32 weeks · Versus hypoglycemia or hypocalcemia – lethargy, hypotonia and seizures, but never a growing head · Versus hypoxic ischemic encephalopathy – needs perinatal asphyxia and acidosis, not a day-3 onset after Apgar scores of 8 and 9 · Versus meningitis – needs fever or risk factors such as maternal fever or prolonged rupture of membranes
Anemia of prematurity Mechanism – oxygenation at birth (breathing, ductus closure) switches off erythropoietin; a preterm infant has also missed the third-trimester shift of erythropoietin production from liver to kidney · Why worse than term – lower hematocrit at birth, shorter red cell life span, frequent NICU (neonatal intensive care unit) blood draws, iron depletion · Timing – term physiologic anemia bottoms out at 9 to 11 g/dL at 2 to 3 months; the preterm nadir is deeper (about 7 g/dL) and earlier (1 to 2 months) · Presentation – often asymptomatic; tachycardia, a flow murmur, apnea, poor weight gain · Labs – normocytic, normochromic, normal platelets and white count; the absolute reticulocyte count may be normal for age, but there is no reticulocytosis for the degree of anemia · Management – iron supplementation and fewer blood draws; red cell transfusion if severe or symptomatic · Versus thalassemia – microcytic and hypochromic with target cells · Versus hemolysis – erythropoietin rises and the reticulocytes climb · Versus iron deficiency – microcytic, and unlikely on fortified formula with ferrous sulfate · Versus anemia of chronic disease – iron trapped in macrophages by chronic inflammation, infection or malignancy, in older children and adults
Pearls Head circumference is the parameter that predicts neurodevelopment, so preserved head growth in a former preemie is the most reassuring single measurement · A percentile by itself is not a pathology; the concerning patterns are crossing lines downward and disproportion between parameters · Retinopathy of prematurity and hearing screening are required by gestational age, however well the infant looks · A preterm infant is more vulnerable to vaccine-preventable disease, so the vaccine schedule is never delayed
Pairs with Part II Abnormal Growth in a Child covers the contrasting case. Ask: are the three parameters together or apart? Parameters that are together and steady are normal. Parameters that are apart, with weight lowest, indicate inadequate calories. Part I Cerebral Palsy covers the imaging diagnosis when the delay does not resolve with corrected age. Part I Lung Disease in the Newborn and Preterm Infant covers apnea of prematurity, the diagnosis for the spells once intraventricular hemorrhage and anemia are excluded. Ask: did the spells start on day 2 to 3 in an infant who is well between episodes?
Transferable rule When a gestational age is given, do the arithmetic before interpreting anything. An option claiming that assessment is impossible is almost always wrong.
Uniform-answer doubtDeclining to assess is not caution; correction exists to make the assessment possible.
Treat-the-numberThe 15th percentile sounds low only against an unexamined assumption that normal means the 50th.
Class-vs-memberGlobal delay is a valid framework, but here it is judged against chronological rather than corrected age.

edits.html:
Hypotonia in an Infant

brain, anterior horn cell, neuromuscular junction or muscle · strength and reflexes · genetic confirmation · Down syndrome careIs the infant floppy but strong, or weak with absent reflexes, and which test confirms the level?

Source case Pt – infant with low tone, Aquifer Pediatrics 29; the case works from the hypotonia differential to Down syndrome, its confirmation and its health supervision · Q – decide whether the low tone comes from the brain or from the motor unit, confirm the chromosomal cause, then plan the child’s care for the first years
The approach

Hypotonia is a finding, not a diagnosis. Localize where it starts. Causes in the brain include Down syndrome, Prader-Willi syndrome, congenital hypothyroidism and hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy. Other levels are the anterior horn cell (spinal muscular atrophy), the neuromuscular junction (infant botulism) and the muscle (congenital myotonic dystrophy, congenital myopathies). A central cause produces an infant who is floppy but strong for the tone, often dysmorphic or sleepy, with normal or brisk reflexes. A peripheral cause produces a weak, alert infant with low or absent reflexes. Check breathing and feeding first. Send the confirmatory test, usually genetic, once the level is known.

Red flags: act before the full history
FindingWhat it points to
Weak cry, pooled secretions, belly breathing, falling saturationRespiratory or bulbar failure: circulation, airway, breathing first
Seizures or a sleepy infant after a hard deliveryBrain injury: glucose, then imaging
Ptosis, weak suck and constipation in a previously well infantInfant botulism: admit and watch the airway
Tongue fasciculations with absent reflexesSpinal muscular atrophy: breathing fails next
Infant with hypotonia: the differential
DiagnosisLevelWhat it looks likeFirst clue
Down syndromeBrain: extra chromosome 21Floppy from birth, upslanting fissures, flat midfaceDysmorphic features on the first examination
Prader-Willi syndromeBrain: chromosome 15Severe hypotonia, poor suck, almond-shaped eyesSmall genitals, undescended testes
Congenital hypothyroidismBrain: thyroid hormoneNormal at birth, sluggish weeks laterAbnormal newborn screen; big tongue, constipation
Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathyBrain: injuryFloppy, lethargic, seizures on day 1Hard delivery, low Apgar scores
Spinal muscular atrophyAnterior horn cellWeak but alert; frog-leg postureTongue fasciculations, absent reflexes
Infant botulismNeuromuscular junctionDescending weakness, ptosis, weak suckWell for weeks; constipation first
Congenital myotonic dystrophyMuscleWeak face, tented upper lip, clubfeetPolyhydramnios; an affected mother
Congenital myopathy or muscular dystrophyMuscleWeak from birth, low reflexesHigh creatine kinase (CK) in the dystrophies
History: what each answer points to
ClueWhat it points to
Floppy from the first hourCongenital: chromosomal, brain or muscle
Well for weeks, then floppyAcquired: botulism, missed hypothyroidism, metabolic
Hard delivery, low Apgar scores, seizuresHypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy
Polyhydramnios, reduced fetal movementWeakness before birth: neuromuscular disease or Prader-Willi
Parents related by bloodAutosomal recessive disease; ask whether the grandparents are siblings, with sensitivity
Mother with a grip she cannot quickly releaseMyotonic dystrophy, passed from the mother
Mother under 35Most Down infants have younger mothers, so it separates nothing
Examination: what each finding points to
FindingWhat it points to
Slips through the hands when held under the armsHypotonia; it says nothing about the level
Moves limbs against gravity, reflexes normal or briskCentral cause
Weak, reflexes absent, bright alert faceAnterior horn cell: spinal muscular atrophy
Ptosis, sluggish pupils, weak suckNeuromuscular junction: botulism
Upslanting fissures, flat midface, small ears, single palmar creaseDown syndrome; hypotonia is its most consistent infant finding
Almond-shaped eyes, small penis, undescended testesPrader-Willi syndrome
Tented upper lip, weak face, clubfeetCongenital myotonic dystrophy
First tests
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Bedside strength and reflex examinationFirstStrong for the tone, reflexes normal or briskCentral: karyotype, thyroid tests, imaging by story
Weak, reflexes absent, alertAnterior horn cell or muscle: CK and gene testing
Descending weakness with ptosis, previously wellJunction: stool toxin
Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and free thyroxine (T4)By branchHigh TSH, low T4Congenital hypothyroidism
Serum creatine kinaseBy branchHighMuscular dystrophy; normal or near normal in spinal muscular atrophy and botulism
Brain MRIBy branchWatershed or deep gray matter injuryHypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy
Chromosomal microarrayBy branchSmall deletion or duplicationDysmorphic infant with a normal karyotype
Lymphocyte karyotypeConfirms47,+21, a translocation, or mosaicismDown syndrome; a translocation means karyotypes for both parents
DNA methylation of 15q11-q13ConfirmsMaternal pattern onlyPrader-Willi syndrome
SMN1 deletion testingConfirmsNo functional copiesSpinal muscular atrophy
DMPK repeat testing, infant and motherConfirmsExpanded CTG repeatCongenital myotonic dystrophy
Stool botulinum toxin or organismConfirmsPositiveInfant botulism; treat before the result
Rapid fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) for chromosome 21Skip as the final testThree signalsFast, but has not replaced the karyotype and cannot show a translocation
Head MRI in Down syndromeSkipNo consistent findingNot indicated
Finalists
On arrivalBedside examinationNextConfirmsTreatment and follow-up
Down syndromeFloppy from birth; upslanting fissures, single palmar creaseStrength and reflexes preservedEchocardiogram and complete blood count (CBC)Lymphocyte karyotypeEarly intervention; health supervision grid below
Prader-Willi syndromeSevere hypotonia, poor suck; almond eyes, small genitalsStrength preserved, profoundly floppyKaryotype often normalDNA methylation studyTube feeding early; growth hormone; food security later
Spinal muscular atrophyAlert, frog-legged, belly breathingWeak, areflexic, tongue fasciculationsCK normal or near normalSMN1 deletion testingGene-targeted therapy; respiratory and feeding support
Down syndrome (trisomy 21) What it is – the commonest chromosomal cause of intellectual disability, about 1 in 700 US births · Who – any couple; risk climbs from the mid-30s, but most affected infants have mothers under 35 because younger women have more pregnancies · Mechanism – extra chromosome 21 material: free trisomy (most likely at any maternal age), an unbalanced translocation (relatively likelier with a younger mother), or mosaicism, with features from classic to almost none · Features – hypotonia, upslanting fissures, epicanthal folds, flat midface, small ears, loose nuchal skin; Brushfield spots, single palmar crease, clinodactyly, sandal gap; intellectual disability usually mild (intelligence quotient (IQ) 50 to 70) or moderate (35 to 50) · Diagnosis – prenatal serum analytes, nuchal ultrasound and cell-free DNA estimate risk; CVS (chorionic villus sampling) or amniocentesis diagnose; after birth a lymphocyte karyotype · Treatment – early intervention at diagnosis; an IEP (individualized education program) at school entry, with parents as advocates · Complications – heart disease in about half, some silent; duodenal atresia and Hirschsprung disease; hypothyroidism at any age; hearing and vision loss; transient myeloproliferative disorder and leukemia; atlantoaxial instability · Follow-up – the grid below · Return for – neck pain, head tilt, a change in walking, new weakness or wetting; pallor, bruising or fever; poor feeding or weight gain
Down syndrome: health supervision
CheckWhenWhy
CBCFirst 3 days, then yearlyPolycythemia, leukemoid reaction, transient myeloproliferative disorder; later iron deficiency
EchocardiogramFirst month, read by pediatric cardiologyHeart disease in about half, some not heard on auscultation
HearingNewborn, then repeatedHearing loss is more common
EyesCataract check from birth; ophthalmology at least yearlyCataracts and other vision problems
TSHNewborn screen, then yearlyHypothyroidism can appear after a normal screen
Early interventionAt diagnosisTherapies before delay shows
NeckHistory and examination every visit; positioning precautions discussed at least every 2 yearsAtlantoaxial instability; imaging for symptoms, not routinely
Gut and growthPediatric gastroenterology for feeding or weight problems; celiac serology for symptomsStructural anomalies, celiac disease
SleepSleep study for all at ages 3 to 4Obstructive sleep apnea
ImmunologyIf infections recurImmunodeficiency
Head MRINot indicatedNo consistent finding
What sets it apart
VersusWhat separates it
Prader-Willi syndromeAlmond eyes, small genitals, no Down facies; normal karyotype
Trisomy 18Hypertonia with clenched, overlapping fingers
Congenital hypothyroidismNormal at birth, floppy weeks later; abnormal newborn screen
Spinal muscular atrophyTruly weak, areflexic, alert, not dysmorphic
Other chromosomal and intellectual disability syndromes
SyndromeGeneticsSignature findingsIntellect
Fragile X syndromeFMR1 CGG repeat, over 200; X-linkedLong face, large ears, lax joints; large testes after pubertyIntellectual disability in boys; girls variable
Turner syndrome45,XWebbed neck, puffy hands and feet; coarctation in about 20%Usually normal
Klinefelter syndrome47,XXYNormal at birth; small testes, infertility, gynecomastiaLow normal
Trisomy 1347,+13Cutis aplasia, microphthalmia, cleft lip, polydactylySevere disability
Trisomy 1847,+18Overlapping fingers, prominent occiput, rocker-bottom feetSevere disability
When to send chromosome studies Features of a known chromosome disorder or an unrecognized malformation syndrome · developmental disability with other unusual findings · a stillborn infant with multiple malformations · some tumors, including leukemia · in adults, recurrent pregnancy loss · submicroscopic deletions need FISH or a microarray · Fragile X needs FMR1 repeat testing, not a karyotype; mothers of affected sons carry at least a premutation · Sharing the diagnosis: in person, privately, both parents present; ask what they know, give a warning and a short headline, respond to emotion, then plan the next visit; this sequence is SPIKES (setting, perception, invitation, knowledge, emotions, strategy and summary)
Scenario bank
  1. 1-day-old boy, floppy since birth and slow to feed; upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, a flat midface, small ears, loose skin at the back of the neck, a single transverse palmar crease and a wide gap between the first and second toes; strength and reflexes are preserved; the parents ask whether a future child could be affected → Lymphocyte karyotype → Down syndrome; only the karyotype shows free trisomy, a translocation or mosaicism, which sets the recurrence risk
  2. 5-week-old girl who slips through the examiner's hands when held under the arms; she lifts her arms and legs against gravity and kicks vigorously; knee reflexes are 3+; no fasciculations; flat midface and upslanting palpebral fissures → Brain → Central hypotonia: strong for the tone, reflexes preserved; chromosomal cause likely
  3. 3-month-old girl, born at term after a normal pregnancy, whose parents are first cousins; over 6 weeks she has stopped kicking and now lies with her legs flopped outward; alert and follows faces; fine quivering movements of the tongue; knee and ankle reflexes absent; the chest sinks as the belly rises with each breath; no ptosis, pupils react briskly, stools normal → Spinal muscular atrophy → Anterior horn cell loss; autosomal recessive, so consanguinity raises the risk
  4. 3-month-old with progressive symmetric weakness of the limbs, absent reflexes, tongue fasciculations and paradoxical breathing; face and eye movements normal; alert and social → SMN1 deletion testing → Spinal muscular atrophy; CK is normal or near normal
  5. Newborn boy, pregnancy with polyhydramnios and reduced fetal movement, intubated at birth for weak breathing; weak face with a tented upper lip, poor suck, bilateral clubfeet and low reflexes; his mother has a long thin face and cannot quickly let go after a handshake → Congenital myotonic dystrophy → Muscle; DMPK CTG repeat expanded, passed from the mother
  6. 2-day-old boy, profoundly floppy since birth with a suck too weak to feed without a tube; almond-shaped eyes, a small penis and bilateral undescended testes; palpebral fissures and palmar creases normal; standard karyotype normal → DNA methylation analysis → Prader-Willi syndrome; methylation detects deletion, uniparental disomy and imprinting defects
  7. 5-week-old girl born at home with no newborn screen; increasingly sleepy, feeds poorly, constipated, still jaundiced; large tongue, umbilical hernia, wide posterior fontanelle; tone low, face otherwise typical, reflexes present → TSH and free T4 → Congenital hypothyroidism; start levothyroxine without waiting for imaging
  8. Newborn girl with trisomy 21 confirmed on karyotype, floppy but feeding with support; the parents ask which tests she will need in the coming weeks → Brain MRI → No consistent finding in Down syndrome; not indicated
  9. Newborn boy with the features of Down syndrome born to a 24 yo mother; karyotype shows 46 chromosomes with the extra chromosome 21 material joined to chromosome 14 → Karyotype of both parents → Translocation Down syndrome; a balanced carrier parent changes the recurrence risk
  10. 2-week-old with Down syndrome, feeding well and gaining weight; no murmur; pulse oximetry 98% in the right hand and in a foot → Echocardiogram now → Heart disease in about half, some silent; echo in the first month
  11. 3 yo boy with Down syndrome at a well visit; normal newborn screen, growing along his curve, no symptoms, normal examination → TSH level → Hypothyroidism can develop after a normal newborn screen
  12. 7 yo girl with Down syndrome and 3 weeks of neck pain, holding her head tilted, falling more often and new daytime wetting; brisk knee reflexes, sustained ankle clonus and upgoing toes → Atlantoaxial instability → Cord compression at C1-C2; urgent cervical spine imaging and neurosurgery
  13. 3-day-old with Down syndrome, feeding well and afebrile; liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin; white count 45,000 with 30% blasts, hemoglobin and platelets normal → Transient abnormal myelopoiesis → Transient myeloproliferative disorder; usually resolves on its own, but later leukemia risk calls for CBC follow-up
  14. 6 yo boy with intellectual disability, poor eye contact and hand flapping; long face, large protruding ears, lax finger joints and flat feet; his mother's brother also has intellectual disability; a karyotype last year was normal → FMR1 CGG repeat analysis → Fragile X syndrome; over 200 repeats; the mother carries at least a premutation
  15. 7-week-old boy, well until 3 days ago, now constipated with a weak cry, drooping eyelids, a poor suck and weakness spreading from the face to the arms; afebrile; the team plans empiric antibiotics while cultures are pending → Gentamicin → Infant botulism; aminoglycosides worsen neuromuscular blockade; botulism immune globulin
  16. 2-month-old girl with Down syndrome, lifting her head briefly and smiling socially; the parents ask what they should do now for her development → Early intervention referral → Referral at diagnosis, before any delay appears; an IEP follows at school entry
Pairs with Part I Genetic Syndromes Recognized at Birth covers the trisomy feature map and the prenatal screen. Ask: are the hands clenched or open, and is the tone up or down? Part I Congenital Hypothyroidism covers the floppy infant found on the newborn screen. Part I Genetic Syndromes Recognized at Birth covers the malformation syndromes without an aneuploidy. Part I Cerebral Palsy covers hypoxic-ischemic injury and its imaging. Part I The Distended Abdomen in a Newborn or Infant covers duodenal atresia and Hirschsprung disease in Down syndrome. Part II Abnormal Growth in a Child covers Turner syndrome in the short girl. Part I Developmental Milestones and Normal Growth covers the early intervention referral for delay.
Transferable rule For a floppy infant, first decide whether the problem is in the brain or the motor unit. An infant who is strong for the tone with normal reflexes has a central cause, often chromosomal. A weak infant with absent reflexes has a peripheral cause. Then send the genetic test for that level.
Unchecked attributeLow tone read as weakness without testing strength and reflexes, which is the step that separates central from peripheral causes.
Salient decoyA mother under 35 argues against Down syndrome, yet most affected infants are born to younger mothers.
Mirror twinPrader-Willi syndrome is as floppy as Down syndrome from birth but has almond-shaped eyes, small genitals and a normal karyotype.
Test-overrides-findingsA positive FISH (fluorescence in situ hybridization) taken as the final answer, when only the karyotype shows a translocation that changes the parents’ recurrence risk.

edits.html:
Heart Failure

ranking interventions by outcome · blood pressure drives decompensation · lipids act over years · statins in heart failureWhich abnormal value drives this outcome, and on what time horizon does treating it pay off?

The decision point

Target the factor that drives this outcome, not simply the value that is abnormal. Uncontrolled hypertension is the direct mechanical driver of decompensation. It raises afterload, which raises LV (left ventricular) wall stress and leads to remodeling, pump failure and admission. Lipids matter for ischemic events over years. BP (blood pressure) matters for decompensations over months.

Option analysis – why each fails
ChoiceWhy it temptsWhy it fails
500 mg sodium diet"More of what's working"Impractical and not evidence-based; aggressive restriction may worsen outcomes
Potassium-rich dietAnchors on the K⁺ valueK⁺ 3.8 is normal – nothing to supplement
Blood pressure controlLooks boring –
Cholesterol / triglyceride controlThe values are abnormalReduces ischemic risk over years, not HF admissions over months
Scenario bank
  1. 68 yo M with HFrEF, BP 168/96; which intervention most reduces hospitalization → Blood pressure control
  2. 68 yo M with HFrEF; the question asks what reduces mortality → Guideline-directed therapy – ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor
  3. 68 yo M with established HFrEF and LDL 150, no clinical ASCVD → Statin per ASCVD risk assessment → statins are neither contraindicated in HF nor beneficial for HF outcomes; the indication is atherosclerotic risk
  4. 68 yo M with HFrEF who has been advised to follow a 500 mg sodium diet → Recommend 2–3 g of sodium daily → the 500 mg target is impractical and not evidence-based
  5. 68 yo M with HFrEF on an ACE inhibitor, potassium 5.8 → Stop the potassium-rich diet and recheck
  6. 68 yo M with HFpEF and uncontrolled hypertension → Blood pressure control → the primary lever in HFpEF
The statins-in-HF footnote CORONA and GISSI-HF tested rosuvastatin specifically in established heart failure and showed no mortality or hospitalization benefit. Once ventricular remodeling is the disease, lipids no longer drive it. An ACE-I (angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor), ARB (angiotensin II receptor blocker) or ARNI (angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor) reduces mortality. A beta-blocker, an MRA (mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist) and an SGLT2i (sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor) also reduce mortality. Unlike these drugs, diuretics only reduce symptoms and hospitalizations.
Transferable rule When several values are abnormal, target the one mechanistically linked to the outcome, not the most abnormal number. Match time-to-benefit to the outcome's time horizon.
Treat-the-number

edits.html:
Stable Ischemic Heart Disease

three angina criteria, not location · anginal equivalents · retired terminology · stress test choice · high-risk findingsWhat provokes the pain and what relieves it, wherever the patient points?

The decision point

Score the three angina criteria rather than judging by location. The criteria are (1) provoked by exertion, (2) relieved by rest and (3) typical substernal location. 3/3 = typical, 2/3 = atypical, <2 = nonanginal. "Epigastric burning" is a textbook anginal equivalent. Here, burning not relieved by antacids rules out the GI (gastrointestinal) explanation.

Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Resting 12-lead ECGFirstInterpretable or not: LVH with strain, digoxin, LBBB, paced rhythmDecides between exercise ECG and stress imaging
Exercise ECGBy branchST depression with exertionIschemia; for patients who can exercise with an interpretable ECG
Stress echo or nuclear imagingBy branchNew wall motion or perfusion defectUninterpretable ECG or unable to exercise; dobutamine if severe asthma
Vasodilator nuclear stressBy branchPerfusion defectChoice with LBBB or a paced rhythm
Coronary angiographyConfirmsObstructive coronary stenosisHigh pretest probability or high-risk stress findings; guides revascularization
Dobutamine stress with LBBBSkipFalse-positive septal defectsUse vasodilator nuclear imaging instead
Scenario bank
  1. 58 yo M, substernal pressure on exertion relieved by rest, interpretable ECG, able to exercise → Typical angina → exercise ECG
  2. 58 yo M with epigastric burning on exertion, relieved by rest, not by antacids → Angina pectoris → exertional, rest-relieved epigastric burning is an anginal equivalent; evaluate for ischemia
  3. 58 yo M with left bundle branch block who needs ischemia testing → Pharmacologic stress with imaging
  4. 58 yo M with severe asthma requiring pharmacologic stress testing → Dobutamine → avoid adenosine and regadenoson
  5. 58 yo M with high pretest probability and ongoing symptoms → Coronary angiography
  6. How the 2021 AHA/ACC guideline asks chest pain to be described → Cardiac, possible cardiac, or noncardiac
Guideline currency: the terminology was retired The 2021 AHA/ACC (American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology) Chest Pain Guideline discourages "typical / atypical / nonanginal" as terms. The term "atypical" was meant to signal angina without classic features, but clinicians were reading it as "not cardiac," the opposite of its purpose. The preferred descriptors are now cardiac · possible cardiac · noncardiac:
  • Cardiac – central, retrosternal, squeezing, pressure, exertional
  • Possible cardiac – stabbing, tearing, ripping, burning (epigastric burning lands here)
  • Noncardiac – pleuritic, positional, fleeting
Question banks still key "atypical angina" for a 2-of-3 presentation. Know both vocabularies: score the three criteria for the exam, and describe by probability in clinic. The shift does not change management; "possible cardiac" still gets risk-stratified and tested.
Angina classification – legacy vs 2021 terminology
Historical termCriteria met2021 equivalent
Typical anginaAll 3 – retrosternal, exertional, relieved by rest/nitroglycerinCardiac
Atypical angina2 of 3Possible cardiac
Nonanginal chest pain1 or 0Noncardiac
Stress test selection
SituationTest
Can exercise + interpretable ECGExercise ECG
Uninterpretable ECG (LVH with strain, digoxin, resting ST depression, WPW)Stress imaging (echo or nuclear)
LBBB or paced rhythmVasodilator nuclear – avoid dobutamine (false-positive septal defects)
Cannot exerciseDobutamine echo or vasodilator nuclear
Severe asthma / COPDDobutamine – vasodilators cause bronchospasm
High pretest probability, or high-risk stress findingsCoronary angiography
High-risk stress findings → cath ST depression ≥2 mm at low workload · ST elevation · hypotension with exercise · ventricular arrhythmia · large or multiple perfusion defects · drop in EF (ejection fraction).
SLE as a cardiac risk factor SLE (systemic lupus erythematosus) causes accelerated atherosclerosis. Lupus mortality is bimodal: early deaths come from disease activity and infection, and late deaths from cardiovascular disease. Chronic prednisone compounds the risk, and antiphospholipid antibodies add thrombosis. Framingham and the PCE (Pooled Cohort Equations) underestimate risk in SLE. When traditional risk factors are absent, look for one in the past medical history.
Transferable rule For chest or epigastric symptoms, the trigger and the reliever localize disease better than the location does. Pain on exertion that is relieved by rest is cardiac, wherever the patient points. Pain with meals that is relieved by antacids is GI (gastrointestinal). Pain with position or breathing is pleural or pericardial. Pain reproducible on palpation is musculoskeletal.
True-fact-wrong-slot
