edits.html:
Infective Endocarditis Prophylaxis

high-risk cardiac conditions · high-risk procedures · conditions removed in 2007 · the drug if both gates openDoes the patient have both a high-risk cardiac condition and a high-risk procedure?

The decision point

Prophylaxis requires a high-risk cardiac condition AND a high-risk procedure. MVP (mitral valve prolapse) with regurgitation, bicuspid valve, rheumatic valve disease and HCM (hypertrophic cardiomyopathy) all came off the list in 2007. A patient with MVP having a dental visit needs no prophylaxis.

Gate 1 – high-risk cardiac conditions (the whole list)
  • Prosthetic valve or prosthetic material used in valve repair
  • Prior infective endocarditis
  • Unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease; repaired with residual defect near prosthetic material; or fully repaired with prosthetic material for the first 6 months
  • Cardiac transplant with valvulopathy
Gate 2 – high-risk procedures
  • Dental work with gingival manipulation or mucosal perforation
  • Respiratory procedures breaching mucosa; procedures on infected skin or tissue
  • Not routine GI/GU procedures – that indication died in 2007 too
Scenario bank
  1. 45 yo F with mitral valve prolapse and regurgitation, due for a dental cleaning → No prophylaxis
  2. 45 yo M with a prosthetic aortic valve, due for a dental extraction → Amoxicillin 2 g one hour before
  3. 45 yo M with prior infective endocarditis and penicillin allergy, dental cleaning → Cephalexin, azithromycin or doxycycline
  4. 45 yo M with a prosthetic valve undergoing screening colonoscopy → No prophylaxis → GI and GU procedures are no longer covered
  5. 45 yo M with unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease, due for dental work → Prophylaxis is indicated
  6. 45 yo M with a bicuspid aortic valve, due for a dental cleaning → No prophylaxis → bicuspid aortic valve was removed from the list in 2007
If both gates open Give amoxicillin 2 g PO (by mouth) 30–60 min before the procedure. If the patient is penicillin-allergic, give a macrolide or doxycycline. If the patient cannot take oral drugs, give IV (intravenous) cefazolin or ceftriaxone. Clindamycin is out because of C. difficile risk. Its removal is the newest edit.
Transferable rule When a case details a patient-specific factor that only matters if the intervention is indicated (an allergy, a dose adjustment), verify the indication. The detail does not confirm the indication.
Trump-card inversion

edits.html:
Venous Thromboembolism

pretest probability governs the test · D-dimer only rules out · imaging by stability · swollen-leg mimicsHow likely is a clot before testing, and is the patient stable enough for CT?

The decision point

Pretest probability picks the testing branch, and stability picks the test. With high probability, skip the D-dimer and go to imaging. Use D-dimer only as a rule-out in low-probability patients. It is elevated in infection, malignancy, pregnancy and post-op states, so it can never rule anything in.

Defining criteria Anticoagulation duration – provoked DVT 3 months; unprovoked ≥3–6 months · D-dimer role – rule-out in low pretest probability only; never rules in · IVC filter – only when anticoagulation is contraindicated or fails
VTE testing by pretest probability
SituationNext stepConfirms, then
Low pretest probability (PE)D-dimer; negative excludes. Low + PERC negative → no testing at allA positive D-dimer confirms nothing; go to CT pulmonary angiography
High probability, or obvious DVT with PE symptomsCT pulmonary angiographyA filling defect confirms PE; anticoagulate
CTA contraindicated (renal failure, contrast allergy, pregnancy)V/Q scanA high-probability scan confirms and a normal scan excludes; a nondiagnostic scan needs leg duplex
Hemodynamically unstableBedside echo (RV strain) ± empiric anticoagulation – treat firstRV strain with hypotension: thrombolysis; CT angiography once stable
Unilateral leg swelling, moderate/high probabilityDuplex ultrasoundNoncompressible vein confirms DVT; low probability starts with D-dimer instead
The swollen leg differential
ConditionThe tell
DVTStasis/hypercoagulable risk, diffuse swelling, calf tenderness, low-grade temp
CellulitisFever, sharply demarcated spreading erythema, skin break or tinea
Ruptured Baker cystSudden calf pain with knee OA/RA; "pseudo-DVT," crescent bruise at the malleolus
Superficial thrombophlebitisPalpable tender cord along a superficial vein
Chronic venous insufficiencyHemosiderin staining, worse standing, bilateral-ish
LymphedemaPainless, non-pitting, dorsal foot, Stemmer sign
Mnemonic Virchow triad names the three routes to venous thrombosis. They are stasis (immobility, long travel), endothelial injury (surgery, trauma, a line) and hypercoagulability (cancer, pregnancy, estrogen, inherited thrombophilia).
Scenario bank
  1. 62 yo F, unilateral leg swelling with a high Wells score → Compression ultrasound → skip the D-dimer
  2. 34 yo F with pleuritic chest pain and low pretest probability → D-dimer to rule out
  3. 62 yo F with suspected PE and creatinine 3.2 → V/Q scan
  4. 62 yo F with suspected PE, hypotensive with right ventricular strain → Thrombolysis
  5. 62 yo F with a warm erythematous calf, fever, and no swelling gradient → Cellulitis
  6. 62 yo F with sudden calf pain and ecchymosis below the malleolus → Ruptured Baker cyst
Pearls The ECG (electrocardiogram) in PE (pulmonary embolism) is usually just sinus tachycardia; S1Q3T3 neither confirms nor excludes it · treatment: DOAC (direct oral anticoagulant) or heparin bridge; thrombolytics only if hypotensive/massive · provoked DVT (deep vein thrombosis) 3 months, unprovoked ≥3–6 months · IVC (inferior vena cava) filter only if anticoagulation is contraindicated or fails · the named emergencies: phlegmasia and PE · smokers ≥35 cannot use estrogen-containing OCPs (oral contraceptive pills); WHO (World Health Organization) category 4.

edits.html:
Heart Murmurs in a Child

innocent vs pathologic murmurs · one pathologic feature buys the echo · louder on standing · the continuous murmur by locationIs any single feature pathologic, and does the murmur get louder or softer on standing?

The decision point

Innocent murmurs are turbulent flow through a structurally normal heart. They are grade 1–2, early or midsystolic, musical or vibratory, and softer with standing or Valsalva. Order ECG (electrocardiogram) and echocardiography for any single pathologic feature. Pathologic features are grade ≥3, holosystolic or diastolic timing, harsh quality, persistence upright, abnormal S2, weak femoral pulses, or symptoms. A murmur that gets louder on standing or Valsalva is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy until proven otherwise.

Defining criteria Benign profile – grade 1–2, early/midsystolic, musical or vibratory, decreases with standing/Valsalva, normal vitals, S1/S2, and growth · Evaluation gate – any single pathologic feature → ECG + echocardiography · The reversal – intensity that increases with standing/Valsalva = hypertrophic cardiomyopathy until excluded
Benign vs pathologic murmurs – the screening exam
AxisBenignPathologic
HistoryAsymptomatic, normal growthInfants: poor weight gain, feeding difficulty, respiratory distress; older: chest pain, syncope, exertional intolerance
MurmurEarly/midsystolic, musical or vibratory, grade 1–2, decreases uprightHolosystolic or diastolic, harsh, grade ≥3, persists upright
Other findingsNormal vitals, normal S1 & S2, symmetric pulsesCentral cyanosis, loud/fixed/single S2, weak femoral pulses, hepatomegaly
ManagementReassuranceECG & echocardiography
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Auscultation lying and standingFirstFull benign profile: grade 1 to 2, early systolic, softer standingInnocent murmur: reassurance, no testing
Murmur louder on standing or ValsalvaHypertrophic cardiomyopathy until excluded: hold sports, ECG and echo
Femoral pulses and four-extremity blood pressuresBy branchWeak femoral pulses with arm hypertensionCoarctation
ECGNextHypertrophy or conduction abnormalityPaired with echo whenever any pathologic feature is present
EchocardiographyConfirmsStructural lesion namedAny single pathologic feature, or a benign murmur outliving its window
Echocardiography for the full benign profileSkipNormal heartReassurance alone once every benign feature is named
Scenario bank
  1. 5 yo M, grade 2 vibratory murmur at the lower left sternal border, louder supine, vanishes on standing → Still murmur → reassurance
  2. 14 yo athlete, systolic murmur that grows louder with standing and Valsalva → Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy → echocardiography before sports
  3. 6 yo F, continuous infraclavicular hum that disappears with neck rotation → Venous hum → reassurance
  4. 3 yo M, harsh grade 3 holosystolic murmur, otherwise well → ECG and echocardiography → one pathologic feature is enough
  5. Infant with weak femoral pulses and upper-extremity hypertension, continuous murmur over the back → Aortic coarctation → collateral flow murmur
  6. Well 4 yo, grade 2 midsystolic murmur at the left upper sternal border radiating to the axilla, normal S2 → Pulmonic flow murmur → innocent; a wide fixed split or ejection click would change the answer
  7. 4 yo with a soft continuous murmur under the right clavicle that fades with ipsilateral head rotation and when supine → Turbulent flow through the curved jugular and subclavian veins → venous hum, and why it is usually right-sided
  8. 3 yo with a continuous machine-like murmur under the left clavicle that does not change with head position or posture → Patent ductus arteriosus → echocardiography
  9. 9 yo with a continuous murmur heard best over the back, upper-extremity hypertension and diminished femoral pulses → Coarctation with intercostal collateral flow → echocardiography and four-extremity pressures
  10. 6-week-old with a large VSD and tachypnea with feeds, the chamber that receives the increased preload → Left atrium → left-to-right shunt increases pulmonary venous return
  11. 2 yo with a continuous machine-like murmur below the left clavicle that runs through S2, bounding pulses and a wide pulse pressure → Patent ductus arteriosus → the machine-like continuous murmur, with a wide pulse pressure
  12. 6 do M, well and thriving, a soft 2/6 holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border, normal apical impulse, 2+ equal femoral pulses, saturation 98% → A large ventricular septal defect → soft because a wide defect creates little turbulence
  13. 3 wk old, well and feeding normally, grade 2 midsystolic murmur at the upper sternal borders radiating to both axillae and the back, normal S2 with symmetric pulses → Peripheral pulmonary stenosis → resolves by 6 to 12 months
  14. 5 yo F with a continuous grade 2 hum below the right clavicle that is louder when she sits up and disappears when she lies down → Venous hum → the one benign murmur that increases upright
  15. Why a venous hum is typically louder on the right than the left → The right jugular and brachiocephalic veins are shorter and more vertical → more turbulent flow into the superior vena cava
  16. 18 mo old whose neonatal murmur radiating to the axillae and back is unchanged, with normal growth and no symptoms → Echocardiography → peripheral pulmonary stenosis should have resolved by 12 months
  17. 7 yo F, well and growing normally, with a grade 2 vibratory midsystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that softens on standing; normal S2 and pulses → Reassurance → the full benign profile is present
  18. 15 yo soccer player, asymptomatic, with a grade 2 systolic murmur that grows louder when he stands from a squat → Hold sports pending ECG and echo → louder on standing is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy until excluded
The three innocent murmurs Still murmur – vibratory, lower left sternal border, louder supine · Pulmonic flow murmur – systolic ejection, left upper sternal border, may radiate to the axilla · Venous hum – continuous, supra/infraclavicular, usually right-sided because the right jugular and brachiocephalic veins are shorter and more vertical, so flow velocity into the superior vena cava is higher; disappears with neck rotation or compression and when supine.
The continuous murmur A continuous murmur in a child has three causes, separated by location: Right infraclavicular and positional – venous hum, benign, fades with ipsilateral head rotation and when supine · Left infraclavicular and fixed – patent ductus arteriosus, machine-like, unchanged by head position or posture; runs through S2, with bounding pulses and a wide pulse pressure · Over the back with weak femoral pulses – coarctation collateral flow, with upper-extremity hypertension · Normally split S2 – a fixed split is the atrial septal defect sign, so an S2 split that moves with respiration excludes atrial septal defect.
Pairs with Part I Congenital Heart Disease covers the cyanosis and single S2 of the pathologic column. Heart Murmurs in an Adult covers the pathologic counterpart of the innocent pulmonic flow murmur. Ask: "what does standing do to it?"
The four benign murmurs Still murmur – younger children, left lower sternal border, midsystolic, vibratory or musical, louder supine and softer standing; resolves by adolescence · Pulmonic flow murmur – childhood through adolescence, left upper sternal border, may radiate to the axilla; appears or intensifies in high-output states such as fever, anemia and anxiety · Venous hum – continuous, supra- or infraclavicular, right louder than left because the right jugular and brachiocephalic veins are shorter and more vertical; the one benign murmur that increases sitting up, and it disappears supine or with ipsilateral head rotation · Peripheral pulmonary stenosis – the neonatal benign murmur, upper sternal borders radiating to both axillae and the back, from physiologically narrow proximal pulmonary arteries while fetal resistance is still falling; resolves by 6 to 12 months · Persistence past the expected age – a benign murmur that outlives its window is itself a pathologic feature · Intensity and defect size – a small ventricular septal defect is loud and a large one is soft or silent, because turbulence falls as the orifice widens
How NBME framed it A murmur new on day 3 after a normal birth examination pulls toward a ventricular septal defect or patent ductus arteriosus; its soft grade and spread to the axilla mark peripheral pulmonary stenosis. The options were the five common acyanotic lesions, so the key was the umbrella term, pulmonary stenosis.
Transferable rule In screening, reassurance requires the entire benign profile. One pathologic feature on exam, in the vitals or in the history is sufficient to start the workup.
Unchecked attributePatent ductus arteriosus: it is the right category for a continuous murmur near a clavicle. Check the side and the positional change; a ductus murmur does not change with head turning.
Unchecked attributeAtrial septal defect: the split S2 here moves with respiration, the opposite of the fixed split it requires.
Mirror twinHypertrophic cardiomyopathy: it is the dangerous mimic of the innocent murmur; the direction the murmur moves on standing separates them.
Uniform-answer doubtReassurance: accept it only after naming the full benign profile.

edits.html:
Cyanosis in the Newborn

lung, heart or airway before a lesion · work of breathing, oxygen response, two limbs · normal exam: the trigger decidesIs he working to breathe, does oxygen help, and does the cyanosis change with what he is doing?

Source vignette Pt – 32 wk, 30 minutes old, grunting and retracting, saturation 65% correcting to 92% on oxygen · Imaging – ground-glass opacities with air bronchograms · Q – the most likely diagnosis; options spanned respiratory distress syndrome, d-transposition of the great arteries and persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
The decision point

Three bedside findings settle the sort before any lesion is considered. He is working to breathe (grunting, flaring and retracting); cyanotic heart disease produces comfortable tachypnea, not distress. His saturation rises from 65% to 92% on oxygen. That cannot happen in d-transposition, where systemic flow bypasses the lungs entirely. The two limbs read the same, so nothing is shunting right-to-left across the duct. That leaves parenchymal disease. A 32-week infant with ground-glass opacification and air bronchograms has surfactant deficiency: respiratory distress syndrome.

Sometimes the examination is instead a list of normals: no murmur, symmetric pulses, equal four-extremity pressures, clear lungs, no retractions, no stridor. These normals already exclude lung and heart. The remaining finding is temporal. Ask: What brings the cyanosis on, and what relieves it? Cyanosis on latching that clears with crying is nasal obstruction, because neonates are obligate nasal breathers and crying opens the oral airway. The inverse pattern, cyanosis worsened by crying, is a tet spell.

Defining criteria Oxygen responsiveness – saturation rises substantially with supplemental oxygen in alveolar disease; it does not in d-transposition, because most systemic flow bypasses the pulmonary vasculature · Preductal vs. postductal – the right upper extremity is preductal and the lower extremities postductal; a higher preductal saturation means right-to-left ductal shunting · Ductal closure clock – the ductus arteriosus begins to constrict as early as 12 hours after birth, so ductal-dependent lesions declare after that, not at minutes · RDS (respiratory distress syndrome) risk – inversely related to gestational age, highest at ≤28 weeks; antenatal glucocorticoids reduce but do not eliminate it · Bilateral choanal atresia – incomplete canalization of the posterior nasal passage; cyanosis that worsens with feeding and improves with crying, with noisy breathing (stertor), symptomatic shortly after birth · Why crying relieves it – neonates are obligate nasal breathers; hypoxia and hypercapnia trigger crying, which opens the oral airway and temporarily bypasses the obstruction · The bedside test – inability to pass a catheter through the nares into the oropharynx, confirmed by CT (computed tomography) or nasal endoscopy · The stability gate – a cyanotic newborn whose hypoxemia does not correct on oxygen gets echocardiography, and prostaglandin E1 is added when the infant is hemodynamically unstable, because instability is what raises concern for a ductal-dependent lesion
Pertinent positives & negatives Grunting, flaring, retractions – work of breathing; this is lung disease, and it excludes the two structural cardiac options, which give tachypnea without distress · 65% → 92% on oxygen – the alveoli can be recruited; excludes d-transposition outright · Right upper and left lower extremity both 65% – no ductal gradient; argues against persistent pulmonary hypertension and against a coarctation presentation · Cyanosis at minutes of life – too early for ductal closure, which begins at about 12 hours; coarctation cannot yet have declared · 32 weeks, 1.7 kg – the base rate for surfactant deficiency; RDS incidence rises as gestational age falls · Ground-glass with air bronchograms and low lung volumes – RDS; transient tachypnea gives perihilar streaking with fluid in the fissures, and pulmonary hypertension a clear or oligemic film · Grade 1/6 systolic murmur – soft and non-specific, consistent with a physiologically open duct rather than a structural lesion · A dose of antenatal glucocorticoids – lowers the risk but never excludes the diagnosis · PPROM (preterm prelabor rupture of membranes) – raises concern for group B streptococcal pneumonia even after intrapartum penicillin; that pneumonia is clinically very hard to tell from RDS · Acrocyanosis – peripheral cyanosis of hands, feet, and circumoral area with pink mucous membranes is a normal finding in the first 24–48 hours of life; central cyanosis (mucous membranes blue) requires workup
Cyanosis in the newborn: sorting by physiology
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME (National Board of Medical Examiners) tellExcluded here by
Respiratory distress syndromePreterm surfactant deficiency; alveolar collapse minutes to hours after birthDistress plus oxygen responsiveness plus ground-glass with air bronchograms in a preterm infant(the answer)
Transient tachypnea of the newbornRetained fetal lung fluid; term or late pretermMild distress and cyanosis; perihilar streaking with fluid in the fissuresSevere distress; the film is ground-glass, not streaky
Persistent pulmonary hypertension Can't missHigh pulmonary vascular resistance; right-to-left ductal shuntPreductal saturation above postductal; film often normal, poorly oxygen-responsiveEqual limb saturations; oxygen worked; the film is abnormal
d-Transposition of the great arteriesParallel circulations; deoxygenated blood to the bodyCyanosis without retractions, and oxygen does not helpGrunting and retractions; 65% to 92% on oxygen
Coarctation of the aortaDuctal-dependent systemic flow; shock when the duct shutsPostductal saturation below preductal, presenting after ~12 hoursEqual limb saturations at 30 minutes of life
Cyanosis with a normal examination: sorting by trigger
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Bilateral choanal atresiaPosterior nasal passage fails to canalize; the obligate nasal breather obstructs whenever his mouth closesWorse with feeding, better with crying; stertor; catheter will not pass(the answer)
Tetralogy of FallotRight ventricular outflow obstruction; a spell when systemic resistance fallsCyanosis worse with crying and agitation (the inverted trigger) plus a murmurCrying makes him pink; there is no murmur
Transposition of the great arteriesParallel circulations; deoxygenated blood to the bodyConstant cyanosis unchanged by feeding or crying, unimproved by oxygenThe cyanosis comes and goes with what he is doing
Tracheoesophageal fistula with esophageal atresiaAspiration through a fistula or from a blind pouchCoughing and choking with feeds, respiratory distress, a tube that coilsHe fed well without coughing; lungs are clear
LaryngomalaciaSupraglottic collapse on inspirationInspiratory stridor worse supine and with exertion; cyanosis uncommonNo stridor at all
Transient tachypnea of the newbornRetained fetal lung fluid after deliveryTachypnea with flaring, retractions and grunting in the first hoursNo respiratory distress of any kind
MethemoglobinemiaOxidized hemoglobin iron cannot carry oxygenPersistent cyanosis that does not improve with crying or with oxygenHis cyanosis clears every time he cries
Neonatal sepsisBacterial infection with varied, nonspecific signsTemperature instability, lethargy, poor feedingNormal temperature; vigorous; blue only at the breast
Intraventricular hemorrhageGerminal matrix bleed, mainly in preterm infantsLethargy, hypotonia, apnea, seizures; found on head ultrasoundTerm infant with a normal neurologic picture
Management, in one line Support RDS (respiratory distress syndrome) with CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure). Reserve mechanical ventilation and exogenous surfactant for severe or failing cases. In the heart branch, management is instead a prostaglandin infusion to hold the duct open; in the pulmonary-hypertension branch, it is oxygen and inhaled nitric oxide. For the nasal obstruction, the first step is an oral airway with orogastric feeding to bypass the obstruction, and definitive treatment is surgical repair.
Decision spine Is he working to breathe? – Grunting, flaring, retracting → lung, not heart · Does oxygen help? – 65% to 92% → not a fixed right-to-left shunt, so not transposition · Do the limbs differ? – No → nothing is shunting across the duct · How old is he? – Thirty minutes → the duct is still open; ductal-dependent lesions have not declared · What does the film show? – Ground-glass with air bronchograms in a 32-weeker → surfactant deficiency · If every examination finding is normal – sort by the trigger: worse with feeding and better with crying is nasal obstruction; worse with crying is a tet spell; unchanged by either is a fixed shunt.
FigureApproach to neonatal cyanosisshow

Redrawn rather than reproduced. The one deliberate change from the usual published version: echocardiography and prostaglandin are shown as separate steps with the stability gate between them, because bundling them is what makes the sequencing question hard.

Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Pulse oximetry, right hand and a footFirstPreductal higher than postductalRight-to-left ductal shunt: PPHN (persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn), or coarctation after about 12 hours
Trial of 100% oxygenNextSaturation rises substantiallyLung disease; no rise means a fixed shunt such as transposition
Chest radiographNextGround-glass with air bronchograms and low volumesRDS in a preterm; streaking with fissure fluid is transient tachypnea of the newborn
Catheter through each narisBy branchCatheter will not passChoanal atresia when cyanosis worsens with feeding and clears with crying
CT or nasal endoscopyConfirmsPosterior nasal obstructionChoanal atresia; look for the rest of CHARGE
EchocardiographyConfirmsStructural lesion or high pulmonary pressuresHypoxemia that oxygen does not correct; prostaglandin E1 added only if unstable
Any testing for acrocyanosisSkipPink mucous membranesNormal in the first 24 to 48 hours: reassurance
Echocardiogram, methemoglobin level, blood cultures or head ultrasound for cyanosis only with feedsSkipNormal oximetry, pulses, heart exam and film; pink when cryingPass the catheter first; nothing in the exam points to the heart, the blood, infection or the brain
Scenario bank
  1. 32 wk, 30 minutes old, grunting and retracting, saturation 65% correcting to 92% on oxygen, ground-glass with air bronchograms → Respiratory distress syndrome → Surfactant deficiency
  2. 32 wk with respiratory distress syndrome at 30 minutes of life, breathing spontaneously → Start CPAP → Surfactant and intubation are reserved for severe disease
  3. 32 wk on CPAP with a rising oxygen requirement and worsening retractions at 6 hours → Intubate and give exogenous surfactant → CPAP has failed
  4. Term newborn at 14 hours, cyanosis with comfortable tachypnea and no retractions, clear lungs, a loud single S2, equal pulses, saturation unchanged on 100% oxygen → Obtain echocardiography → an anatomic right-to-left shunt; prostaglandin is added only if the infant is unstable
  5. Term after meconium-stained fluid, distress, right hand 95% and foot 78%, film clear with decreased vascularity → Inhaled nitric oxide → Persistent pulmonary hypertension
  6. Why an infant with respiratory distress syndrome grunts → To generate end-expiratory pressure and keep alveoli open → Flaring lowers airway resistance
  7. 2-hour-old, cyanotic when latched at the breast, pink when crying, no murmur, clear lungs, normal four-extremity pressures → Bilateral choanal atresia → Obligate nasal breathing
  8. Newborn with cyanosis that worsens with feeding and improves with crying → Pass a catheter through each naris→ CT or nasal endoscopy confirms it
  9. 6-month-old with tetralogy of Fallot, sudden deep cyanosis and inconsolable crying → Knee-to-chest positioning with supplemental oxygen → A tet spell, triggered by crying
  10. Why crying temporarily relieves the cyanosis of bilateral choanal atresia → Crying bypasses the obstructed nose→ by opening the oral airway; Neonates are obligate nasal breathers
  11. Term newborn with cyanosis unimproved on 100% oxygen and a single S2, now with weak pulses, poor perfusion and a falling blood pressure → Start prostaglandin E1 and obtain echocardiography → instability licenses the drug before the picture
  12. Why supplemental oxygen fails to raise the saturation in transposition of the great arteries → Parallel circulations bypass the lungs→ systemic blood bypasses the lungs entirely; a fixed anatomic right-to-left shunt
  13. Term newborn cyanotic from the first hours with a loud single S2 and no murmur, unimproved on oxygen → Transposition of the great arteries → mixing flow is too low-velocity to make a murmur
  14. 1-day-old boy born at 39 weeks, feeding well. Heart rate 138/min, respiratory rate 42/min, afebrile. No murmur; femoral pulses 2+. Pulse oximetry: right hand 97%, right foot 93%. One hour later: right hand 97%, right foot 93%. → Echocardiography → a foot reading under 95% with a gap over 3% on two measures an hour apart fails the screen; with no other cause of hypoxemia found, echocardiography follows, and a second retest is not part of the algorithm
  15. Newborn at 5 minutes of life, heart rate 120/min, respiratory rate 50/min, vigorous cry, flexing extremities, cyanosis of hands feet and circumoral area with pink mucous membranes → Reassurance and routine care → acrocyanosis
  16. 6-day-old breastfed M, unconjugated bilirubin 14, weight 11% below birth weight, 3 wet diapers on day 5, nursing every 4 hours, mother milk just came in → Breastfeed every 2 to 3 hours and follow up in 1 day → lactation failure jaundice
  17. 10-day-old breastfed F, unconjugated bilirubin 16, weight appropriate, 8 wet diapers daily, nursing well every 2 to 3 hours → Breast milk jaundice → continue breastfeeding and monitor
  18. 1-day-old term boy whose face turns blue within a minute of every feed and pinks up when he cries; normal heart and lung exam, pulse oximetry 97% in the right hand and 96% in the foot; a catheter cannot be passed through either naris beyond the nasopharynx → Oral airway and orogastric feeding → Bilateral choanal atresia; confirm with CT or nasal endoscopy, then surgical repair
Decoy note Antenatal glucocorticoids are genuinely protective, but they only lower the risk of RDS (respiratory distress syndrome); they do not treat it away. A grade 1/6 murmur is soft and non-specific. In a 30-minute-old it is almost certainly a physiologically open duct rather than a lesion. PPROM (preterm prelabor rupture of membranes) raises concern for group B streptococcal pneumonia even after intrapartum penicillin; that pneumonia is clinically very hard to tell from RDS, so antibiotics are started empirically pending cultures. In the normal-examination case, six normal findings each exclude one diagnosis, and the only positive finding is the timing. A primigravida with an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery, and an infant who voided and passed meconium, are inert findings. They only establish that the baby is well, which is the precondition for the sort.
Pearls Grunting with retractions that improves on oxygen is lung disease; in a preterm infant with ground-glass and air bronchograms that is surfactant deficiency. · Work of breathing is the first sort: grunting, flaring and retractions mean lung; comfortable tachypnea with cyanosis means heart. · Oxygen is diagnostic and therapeutic: it separates alveolar disease from a fixed shunt and treats RDS (respiratory distress syndrome). It is occasionally harmful: in hypoplastic left heart syndrome it lowers pulmonary vascular resistance and shifts right ventricular output to the lungs. · A lesion that depends on the duct presents when the duct closes, from about 12 hours onward. Cyanosis in the delivery room is lung disease, failed transition or transposition. · Antenatal glucocorticoids stimulate fetal surfactant synthesis and lower the risk of RDS; a dosed 32-week infant can still have it. · Hypoxia in RDS is self-amplifying. Collapse causes hypoxia, hypoxia constricts the pulmonary vasculature, and the resulting right-to-left shunt deepens the cyanosis. Shunt physiology can therefore be present without a shunt lesion. · Newborns are obligate nasal breathers. Nasal obstruction therefore gives cyanosis that worsens when the mouth is occluded by feeding and improves when it opens with crying. · The inverse pattern is the tet spell: cyanosis worsens with crying and agitation and is relieved by knee-to-chest positioning. · Pass a catheter through each naris first. It is a free bedside test, and imaging only confirms what the catheter suggested. · Choanal atresia may belong to CHARGE (coloboma, heart defects, atresia choanae, retardation of growth, genital and ear abnormalities). Unilateral disease often goes unrecognized until childhood, when it presents as chronic unilateral nasal discharge. · Tachypnea without distress points to the heart: fast breathing with no flaring, grunting or retractions, and clear lungs. Work of breathing points to the lung. · A loud single S2 with no murmur is characteristic of transposition. The absent murmur is a positive finding rather than a missing one, because flow through the mixing shunts is too low-velocity to generate sound.
Pairs with Part II Lung Disease in the Newborn and Preterm Infant covers the film-based sort among the parenchymal causes. Part I Congenital Heart Disease covers the lesion catalog once the sort points to the heart. Part II Tracheoesophageal Fistula and Esophageal Atresia covers the newborn clock (which diagnosis belongs at which hour) and includes choanal atresia in its minutes-to-hours group. Ask: is he working to breathe, does oxygen help, do the limbs differ, and does the cyanosis change with what he is doing? Part I Genetic Syndromes Recognized at Birth covers the step after a positive catheter test: which syndrome includes the choanal atresia. Part I Genetic Syndromes Recognized at Birth covers acrocyanosis as the decoy beside a trisomy 18 murmur; ask: are the lips and tongue pink?
Transferable rule When a finding has both a lung and a heart cause, sort by physiology before naming a disease. The bedside triad of work of breathing, oxygen response and a pre-to-postductal difference decides which group of diagnoses to consider. When the sort finds nothing abnormal, the pattern in time is the key finding. A trigger that runs the opposite way excludes the lesion it resembles.
Unchecked attributeContinuous positive airway pressure: a respiratory rate of 66 reads as distress, but the stem negates flaring, grunting and retractions and reports clear lungs. The rate was checked and the work of breathing was not.
Salient decoyd-Transposition of the great arteries: Transposition gives cyanosis without grunting or retractions, and oxygen does not improve it; the stem shows both the retractions and a rise to 92%
True-fact-wrong-slotPersistent pulmonary hypertension: That is a consequence of the atelectasis, not the primary disease; PPHN (persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn) gives a preductal-postductal gradient and a clear film, and neither is present
Mirror twinTransient tachypnea of the newborn: it is mild and gives perihilar streaking with fluid in the fissures; this infant has severe distress and a ground-glass film
Unchecked attributeCoarctation of the aorta: The duct does not begin to constrict until about 12 hours; at 30 minutes it is open, and coarctation would show a lower postductal saturation, not equal ones
True-fact-wrong-slotTetralogy of Fallot: its trigger is inverted. Tet spells come with crying and agitation, which is what turns this baby pink, and a murmur would be expected
Class-vs-memberTracheoesophageal fistula with esophageal atresia: Aspiration through a fistula brings coughing, choking and respiratory distress; this infant latched, sucked well, and has clear lungs
Class-vs-memberLaryngomalacia: It obstructs at the larynx and announces itself with inspiratory stridor, which is explicitly absent; cyanosis is uncommon

edits.html:
Acute Rheumatic Fever

Jones criteria · recent strep evidence · carditis on echo · a setting is not a mechanism · penicillin prophylaxisDid a sore throat come 2 to 4 weeks before, and do the findings meet the Jones criteria?

The decision point

A sore throat 2 weeks ago was followed by migratory large-joint arthritis and a new holosystolic apical murmur with fever. That is 2 major Jones criteria on a strep foundation. A travel or camping detail is a setting, not a mechanism. There is no tick bite and no rash, and the 2–4 week latency belongs to the pharyngitis.

Jones criteria – 2 major, or 1 major + 2 minor, plus evidence of strep
  • Major (JONES): Joints (migratory polyarthritis) · O carditis · Nodules (subcutaneous) · Erythema marginatum · Sydenham chorea
  • Minor: fever, arthralgia, ↑ESR/CRP, prolonged PR
Pearls Type II hypersensitivity via molecular mimicry against M protein · Aschoff bodies and Anitschkow cells on pathology · the acute attack affects the mitral valve as regurgitation; decades later the valve disease presents as mitral stenosis · treatment is penicillin plus aspirin, then monthly benzathine penicillin for years · treating the pharyngitis prevents ARF (acute rheumatic fever) but not PSGN (post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis).
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Throat culture or rapid strep testFirstOften negative by the time ARF appearsA negative swab does not exclude it; serology next
ASO and anti-DNase B titersNextElevated or rising titerEvidence of recent group A strep, required by the Jones criteria
ESR and CRPSupportsElevatedMinor criterion
ECGSupportsProlonged PR intervalMinor criterion
EchocardiographyStagingMitral regurgitationCarditis, a major criterion, even when no murmur is heard
None: Jones criteriaConfirms2 major, or 1 major and 2 minor, with strep evidenceAcute rheumatic fever; no single test confirms it
Lyme serology after a camping tripSkipNo erythema migrans or tick biteLyme gives late monoarthritis and AV block, not a new valve murmur
Scenario bank
  1. 9 yo M, migratory large-joint arthritis and a new apical holosystolic murmur 2 weeks after pharyngitis → Acute rheumatic fever → penicillin plus anti-inflammatories
  2. 9 yo M with suspected acute rheumatic fever → Anti-streptolysin O titer
  3. 9 yo M with acute rheumatic fever; which valve is most often involved → Mitral
  4. 9 yo M with arthritis 10 days after a diarrheal illness, with conjunctivitis and urethritis → Reactive arthritis
  5. 9 yo M with acute rheumatic fever and new choreiform movements → Sydenham chorea – a major criterion
  6. 9 yo M recovering from acute rheumatic fever → Long-term penicillin prophylaxis
  7. 9 yo M, migratory large-joint arthritis and a new apical holosystolic murmur 2 weeks after pharyngitis; history mentions a recent camping trip → Acute rheumatic fever → the trip is a setting, not a mechanism; no tick bite, no rash, and the latency belongs to the pharyngitis
Mimics Lyme needs erythema migrans. Its arthritis is late (months) and monoarticular, and its cardiac finding is AV block (atrioventricular block), not a valvular murmur. RMSF (Rocky Mountain spotted fever) needs headache and a rash involving palms and soles; it is a vasculitis, not an arthritis. JIA (juvenile idiopathic arthritis) needs ≥6 weeks by definition.
How NBME framed it No sore throat was mentioned, only a recent refugee camp, which also invited the travel-fever decoys; Kawasaki disease appeared as mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome, and the mitral murmur was described, not named.
Salient decoy

edits.html:
Heart Failure in a Child

the viral prodrome that is not bronchiolitis · gallop, apical murmur and weak pulses · cardiogenic shock: cautious fluidIs there a gallop or a new murmur, and are the pulses weak with a low pressure?

Source vignette Pt – 2 yo M, 4 days of rhinorrhea, congestion and low-grade fever, now tired with decreased urine output and labored breathing · Exam – T 38.2, HR 155, RR 48, BP 60/40, SpO2 91% on room air; scattered mobile subcentimeter anterior cervical nodes; gallop rhythm with a grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur at the apex; brachial and femoral pulses 1+; nasal flaring, subcostal retractions and basal rales · Q – the most likely diagnosis; options spanned acute rheumatic fever, bronchiolitis, glomerulonephritis, Kawasaki disease and myocarditis
The decision point

The respiratory findings are real, but every one of them is a consequence of the heart. Three cardiac findings decide the diagnosis: a gallop, a new holosystolic murmur at the apex, and 1+ pulses with a blood pressure of 60/40. A gallop is an S3, from a ventricle taking volume it cannot handle. In this setting, an apical holosystolic murmur is mitral regurgitation from ventricular dilation, not a primary valve lesion. Weak pulses with hypotension in a 2-year-old are shock. With basal rales and oliguria, this is acute left heart failure with pulmonary edema. That is why the lungs sound wet and the saturation is 91%. The viral prodrome is the cause, not a coincidence. The usual agents are coxsackievirus B and adenovirus. Myocyte injury is part direct and part immune-mediated.

Defining criteria Myocarditis – a viral prodrome, upper respiratory or gastrointestinal, then heart failure: respiratory distress, gallop, hepatomegaly, with or without arrhythmia, which is how it causes sudden death · Acute rheumatic fever gate – Jones criteria 2 to 4 weeks after untreated group A streptococcal pharyngitis; a concurrent viral URI is the wrong illness at the wrong interval · Kawasaki gate – fever of 5 or more days plus 4 of 5 criteria, with a cervical node over 1.5 cm; four days of fever with no criteria does not open it · Workup – troponin, ECG showing sinus tachycardia with nonspecific ST change, chest film showing cardiomegaly and pulmonary edema, and echocardiography showing diffuse hypokinesis with a reduced ejection fraction
Pertinent positives & negatives Gallop rhythm – an S3, the most specific finding in the stem for ventricular failure · Holosystolic murmur at the apex – functional mitral regurgitation from a dilated ventricle, new in a failing child · BP 60/40 with 1+ pulses – cardiogenic shock, an emergency · Basal rales with hypoxemia – pulmonary edema, not consolidation and not bronchospasm · No wheeze – argues strongly against bronchiolitis, whose classic finding it is · Decreased urine output – hypoperfusion; urine output reflects cardiac output · Subcentimeter mobile nodes – reactive to the viral illness and too small for Kawasaki, which requires over 1.5 cm · Fever 4 days with no rash, conjunctivitis or mucosal change – the Kawasaki gate fails on duration and on criteria count
Respiratory distress after a viral prodrome – the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Viral myocarditis Can't missCoxsackie B or adenovirus; prodrome then failureGallop plus new apical holosystolic murmur plus poor perfusion after a URI – (the answer)
BronchiolitisRSV; first or second year, coryza then distressWheeze and hyperinflation; heart sounds normalNo wheeze; gallop and murmur unexplained by it
Acute rheumatic feverGAS pharyngitis, then an immune sequelJones criteria 2 to 4 weeks later; migratory arthritis, choreaConcurrent viral URI and no Jones criteria
Kawasaki diseaseVasculitis of young children; can include myocarditisFever 5 or more days plus 4 criteria; node over 1.5 cmFour days of fever, no criteria, subcentimeter nodes
GlomerulonephritisPost-infectious or IgA; may follow a URIHematuria and Nephritic Syndrome, hypertension and edemaHypotensive rather than hypertensive; no hematuria
Management Treatment is supportive: diuresis, afterload reduction and inotropes. IVIG (intravenous immunoglobulin) is commonly given, but its benefit in children is not established. Do not treat the shock reflexively. This child's hypotension is cardiogenic, so a rapid large-volume bolus worsens pulmonary edema. Give fluid cautiously and in small aliquots, or not at all, while getting the echocardiogram.
Decision spine Is there a gallop or a new murmur? – Yes means the heart is the failing organ, whatever the lungs are doing · Wheeze or rales? – Rales means edema, not bronchiolitis · What is the blood pressure and what are the pulses? – 60/40 with 1+ means shock · How long has the fever run, and how many Kawasaki criteria? – Four days and none, so the gate is closed · Was the antecedent illness strep pharyngitis 2 to 4 weeks ago? – No, it is concurrent coryza, so not rheumatic fever · So what confirms it? – Echocardiography with troponin, ECG and a chest film
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
ECGFirstSinus tachycardia with nonspecific ST changesSupports myocarditis; watch for arrhythmia, the cause of sudden death
TroponinFirstElevatedMyocyte injury
Chest radiographSupportsCardiomegaly with pulmonary edemaRales are edema, not bronchiolitis or pneumonia
EchocardiographyConfirmsDiffuse hypokinesis with a reduced ejection fractionMyocarditis with heart failure; excludes a structural lesion
Cardiac MRI or endomyocardial biopsyBy branchMyocardial inflammation or lymphocytic infiltrateTissue-level confirmation when the diagnosis remains uncertain
ASO titerSkipNo pharyngitis 2 to 4 weeks earlier, no Jones criteriaConcurrent coryza is the wrong illness at the wrong interval for rheumatic fever
Scenario bank
  1. 2 yo M, 4 days of rhinorrhea and low-grade fever, now tired with decreased urine output; HR 155, RR 48, BP 60/40, gallop rhythm with a grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur at the apex, 1+ pulses, basal rales → Viral myocarditis → acute decompensated heart failure
  2. 2 yo with a 4-day viral prodrome who now has a gallop, basal rales and poor peripheral perfusion → Echocardiography with troponin and ECG → diffuse hypokinesis with a reduced ejection fraction
  3. 3 yo with suspected myocarditis, hypotensive with a gallop, rales and hepatomegaly → A rapid 20 mL/kg normal saline bolus → the shock is cardiogenic, not hypovolemic
  4. 8 mo, 3 days of coryza, now wheezing with retractions and hyperinflation; heart sounds normal with no murmur → Bronchiolitis → supportive care and suctioning
  5. 6 yo with migratory polyarthritis and a new murmur 3 weeks after an untreated sore throat → Acute rheumatic fever → Jones criteria with an antistreptolysin O titer
  6. 4 yo with 6 days of fever, bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, cracked lips, a polymorphous rash and a 2 cm cervical node → Kawasaki disease → IVIG with aspirin
  7. The organisms most commonly responsible for myocarditis in children → Coxsackievirus B and adenovirus → direct viral injury plus immune-mediated myocyte necrosis
  8. 5 yo recovering from biopsy-proven myocarditis who has a syncopal episode and an irregular pulse → Continuous cardiac monitoring → arrhythmia is the mechanism of sudden death
Pearls S3 or new murmur in any child in respiratory distress – heart failure until an echocardiogram says otherwise, however viral the story sounds · A new holosystolic murmur at the apex in a failing ventricle is functional mitral regurgitation – a consequence, not a second disease · Hypotension in myocarditis is cardiogenic: fluid loading fills the lungs and is the commonest management error · Rheumatic fever is defined by its interval, 2 to 4 weeks after pharyngitis; a murmur appearing during a viral illness is myocarditis · Kawasaki's fever requirement is five days, and it is mandatory
Pairs with Part II Shock in Children covers the perfusion categories and the cardiogenic-versus-distributive fork. Part I Acute Rheumatic Fever covers Jones and the post-streptococcal interval. Kawasaki Disease covers the five-day fever requirement. Ask: is there a gallop or a new murmur, and how long has the fever run?
Transferable rule When respiratory findings are prominent and cardiac findings are subtle, read the cardiac findings first. A gallop, a new murmur or weak pulses point to the heart as the failing organ. The lung signs are then a consequence rather than a cause.
Unchecked attributeAcute rheumatic fever: fever with a new murmur after an infection is its exact shape, but the antecedent is coryza not pharyngitis, the interval is concurrent not 2 to 4 weeks, and no Jones criteria are met.
Unchecked attributeKawasaki disease: genuinely causes myocarditis, but fever is 4 days and no criteria are met; the nodes are subcentimeter against a 1.5 cm requirement.
True-fact-wrong-slotGlomerulonephritis: oliguria after a URI (upper respiratory infection) fits, but it presents with hematuria and hypertension, and this child is hypotensive with unexplained cardiac findings.
Salient decoyBronchiolitis: the whole respiratory picture and the age fit, but it explains nothing cardiac and the classic wheeze is absent while rales are present.

22q11.2 Deletion Syndrome

the syndrome is given; find the missing piece · CATCH · which syndrome has which finding · read the last sentence firstWhich component did the vignette leave out, and which bedside sign in the exam shows it?

Source vignette Pt – 3 h old F, 38 wk by cesarean for nonreassuring tones, Apgars 8 and 8, moved to the nursery for a dusky appearance; cyanotic and tremulous, with low-set ears, micrognathia and a cleft palate · Labs – pulse oximetry 72% in the right hand and the leg, unchanged after 10 minutes of 100% oxygen by hood · Imaging – chest radiograph shows an absent thymus; echocardiography shows truncus arteriosus · Q – which condition this patient most likely has; options spanned anemia, duodenal atresia, horseshoe kidney, hypocalcemia, hypoglycemia, myelomeningocele and neutropenia
The decision point

The vignette already gives the diagnosis. Conotruncal defect plus absent thymus plus cleft palate plus low-set ears and micrognathia is 22q11.2 deletion. Every answer option is a condition, not a syndrome. CATCH lists the components: Cardiac outflow anomaly, Anomalous face, Thymic hypoplasia, Cleft palate, Hypocalcemia from parathyroid hypoplasia. Four of the five are printed in the vignette; the missing one is hypocalcemia. The clue is in the physical examination: tremulous is neonatal hypocalcemia. This matters because these infants are at real risk of tetany, seizures and arrhythmia.

Defining criteria CATCH-22 – Cardiac outflow tract anomaly such as truncus arteriosus, tetralogy of Fallot or interrupted aortic arch; Anomalous face with prominent nasal bridge, low-set ears and micrognathia; Thymic hypoplasia or aplasia reducing T-cell immunity; Cleft palate; and Hypoparathyroidism producing hypocalcemia · DiGeorge versus velocardiofacial syndrome – both are 22q11.2 phenotypes; DiGeorge requires thymic involvement, with a CD3+ T-cell count under 500/mm3, while velocardiofacial requires facial abnormalities · Pathogenesis – loss of genes controlling third and fourth pharyngeal pouch derivation and neural crest migration, which is why the thymus, parathyroids, palate, face and cardiac outflow tract fail together
Pertinent positives & negatives Absent thymus on chest radiograph – third and fourth pouch failure; the most specific finding in the stem and the reason this is DiGeorge rather than isolated truncus · Truncus arteriosus – a conotruncal defect, the cardiac C · Cleft palate, low-set ears, micrognathia – the C and the A; with the thymus, four of five CATCH letters are printed · Tremulous – neonatal hypocalcemia before it becomes tetany · Saturation 72% in right hand and leg – no differential cyanosis, which excludes severe coarctation and interrupted arch physiology, and with them Turner syndrome · Refractory to 100% oxygen for 10 minutes – a fixed right-to-left shunt, confirming cyanotic structural heart disease rather than lung disease · Apgars 8 and 8, uncomplicated pregnancy, primigravida – no asphyxia and no maternal diabetes, closing the usual setups for hypoglycemia · No abdominal or spinal findings – nothing pointing at duodenal atresia or a neural tube defect
The dysmorphic neonate with a heart defect – which syndrome has which finding
SyndromeIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge)Pouch 3 and 4 failure; conotruncal defect, hypoplastic thymus and parathyroidsAbsent thymus plus conotruncal defect plus cleft palate; hypocalcemia is the fourth member – (the answer)
Down syndrome (trisomy 21)Commonest aneuploidy; AV septal defect, hypotoniaDuodenal atresia with a double bubble, single palmar crease, upslanting fissuresThymus present; no gastrointestinal malformation described
Turner syndrome (45,X)Female, short stature, gonadal dysgenesisHorseshoe kidney, coarctation, webbed neck, wide-spaced nipplesEqual pre- and postductal saturations; no renal or neck findings
CHARGE associationColoboma, choanal atresia, ear anomaliesColoboma and choanal atresia alongside the heart defectNo eye or nasal findings; thymic loss is not its signature
Infant of a diabetic motherMacrosomia, transposition, septal hypertrophyHypoglycemia in the first hours with a high birth weightPregnancy uncomplicated in a primigravida, no macrosomia
Management, in one line Once 22q11.2 is suspected, send an ionized calcium and get an echocardiogram. Confirm the deletion with chromosomal microarray or FISH (fluorescence in situ hybridization). Treat symptomatic hypocalcemia with intravenous calcium. Until normal T-cell immunity is confirmed, these infants get irradiated blood products and no live vaccines.
Decision spine Read the last sentence first. – It asks for a condition, not a diagnosis · Name the syndrome from the cluster. – Conotruncal defect plus absent thymus plus cleft palate is 22q11.2 · Recite CATCH and cross off what is printed. – Cardiac, face, thymus and cleft are all given, so H is missing · Look for its bedside tell. – Tremulous means hypocalcemia · Assign each remaining option to its own syndrome. – Horseshoe kidney to Turner, duodenal atresia to Down, hypoglycemia to the infant of a diabetic mother, myelomeningocele to folate · Check the cell line. – DiGeorge takes lymphocytes, not neutrophils or red cells
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Pulse oximetry on 100% oxygenFirstSaturation unchanged, equal in hand and legFixed intracardiac shunt: cyanotic heart disease
EchocardiographyNextConotruncal defect: truncus, tetralogy or interrupted archRaises suspicion for 22q11.2 deletion
Chest radiographSupportsAbsent thymic shadowThymic hypoplasia or aplasia
Ionized calciumNextLowParathyroid hypoplasia; IV calcium if tremulous or seizing
Chromosomal microarray or FISH for 22q11.2ConfirmsMicrodeletion at 22q11.222q11.2 deletion syndrome
T-cell subsetsStagingCD3 count under 500/mm3DiGeorge immune phenotype: irradiated blood, no live vaccines
Standard karyotypeSkipNormal; the deletion is too small to seeUse microarray or FISH instead
Scenario bank
  1. 3 h old F, cyanosis refractory to 100% oxygen, saturation 72% in right hand and leg, low-set ears, micrognathia, cleft palate, absent thymus on chest film, truncus arteriosus on echocardiography, tremulous on examination → Hypocalcemia → parathyroid hypoplasia in 22q11.2 deletion
  2. Term neonate with truncus arteriosus, cleft palate and an absent thymic shadow on chest radiograph → Chromosomal microarray for the 22q11.2 deletion → a standard karyotype does not resolve a microdeletion
  3. Neonate with known 22q11.2 deletion who develops a generalized seizure; ionized calcium is low → Intravenous calcium gluconate → hypocalcemic seizure from parathyroid hypoplasia
  4. 4 mo old with 22q11.2 deletion and a CD3+ T-cell count of 210/mm3, presenting for routine immunizations → The live attenuated rotavirus vaccine → live vaccines are withheld until CD3 and CD4 exceed 500/mm3 and CD8 exceeds 200/mm3 with a normal mitogen response
  5. Newborn with a double-bubble sign on abdominal radiograph, a single transverse palmar crease and an atrioventricular septal defect → Down syndrome → duodenal atresia
  6. Newborn girl with coarctation of the aorta, a webbed neck, wide-spaced nipples and a horseshoe kidney → Turner syndrome → 45,X
  7. Why the thymus, parathyroids, palate and cardiac outflow tract fail together in this syndrome → Failed third and fourth pharyngeal pouch development with abnormal neural crest migration → one embryologic field, four organs
  8. 6 yo with 22q11.2 deletion, recurrent sinopulmonary infections and poor responses to polysaccharide vaccines → T-cell subsets with quantitative immunoglobulins → humoral failure follows defective T-cell help
Decoy note Tremulous is the bedside sign of both neonatal hypoglycemia and neonatal hypocalcemia. An uncomplicated pregnancy in a primigravida with Apgars of 8 closes off the hypoglycemia route. The equal right-hand and leg saturations read as an incidental vital sign, but they exclude differential cyanosis, and with it coarctation and Turner syndrome.
Pearls Syndrome with a missing component: when a vignette describes most of a syndrome, recite the mnemonic and cross off what is printed. Answer with the remainder; CATCH, JONES and CREST are tested this way · Hypocalcemia and hypoglycemia share a neonatal presentation of jitteriness, tremor and seizure, and the pregnancy history separates them · Differential cyanosis means ductal or arch pathology; equal pre- and postductal saturations mean a fixed intracardiac shunt, which is what truncus produces · DiGeorge takes lymphocytes, so an option of neutropenia or anemia tests which lineage the thymus governs · Until normal T-cell immunity is confirmed, these infants need irradiated blood and no live vaccines · The same deletion has two names: thymic involvement makes it DiGeorge, and facial abnormality makes it velocardiofacial
Pairs with Part I Congenital Heart Disease covers truncus arteriosus within the cyanosis differential, and the oxygen-refractory shunt logic that leads to it. Antibody Deficiencies covers the downstream question of which immunodeficiency the absent thymus produces. Ask: is the thymic shadow present, and does the face carry a syndrome? Part I Genetic Syndromes Recognized at Birth places this syndrome beside CHARGE, VACTERL, trisomy 13 and Fanconi anemia. There, the deciding finding is the one on the fewest lists.
Transferable rule Read the last sentence before the vignette. When a vignette assembles a recognizable syndrome, the diagnosis is given, and the question asks for the component it left out. That component usually has a one-word bedside sign in the physical examination.
True-fact-wrong-slotHorseshoe kidney: a real and memorable syndrome pairing, but it belongs to Turner, and the equal limb saturations already exclude Turner's coarctation.
True-fact-wrong-slotDuodenal atresia: congenital heart disease with low-set ears reads as Down syndrome, but that is where duodenal atresia belongs and Down has no thymic aplasia.
Unchecked attributeNeutropenia: DiGeorge genuinely causes a cytopenia, but the lineage is lymphocytes; red cell and neutrophil counts are unaffected.
Mirror twinHypoglycemia: a tremulous neonate is the classic hypoglycemia cue and also the hypocalcemia cue, but this pregnancy was uncomplicated with normal Apgars.

edits.html:
High Blood Pressure in a Child or Adolescent

device vs auscultation · adult cutoffs from age 13 · staging · recheck interval by stage · ambulatory monitoringHas auscultation confirmed the device reading, and what stage does the averaged value set?

Source vignette Pt – 17 yo M at a pre-participation examination for football; feels well; no illnesses, medications or family history; BMI 29; automated oscillometric reading 138/88 mm Hg, stated as the 95th percentile for age and height, then 140/89 mm Hg on the same device; rest of the examination normal · Q – the most appropriate next step in diagnosis; options spanned auscultatory measurement, echocardiography, 24-hour ambulatory monitoring and repeat device readings daily for 3 days or in 2 weeks
The decision point

Automated oscillometric devices tend to read higher than auscultation for both systolic and diastolic pressure. A high device reading needs confirmation by auscultation, even after the same device has repeated it. Take at least two auscultatory readings at that visit and average them. The averaged auscultatory value sets the category and the recheck interval.

From age 13, the 2017 AAP (American Academy of Pediatrics) guideline uses fixed cutoffs that match the adult categories. By those cutoffs, 138/88 mm Hg falls in stage 1 and 140/89 mm Hg in stage 2. Device readings are not staged until auscultation confirms them. Ambulatory monitoring, echocardiography and drug therapy all come after that confirmation.

Defining criteria, age 13 and older Confirming a high reading – repeat by auscultation at the same visit and average the readings; a device reading alone is not staged · Elevated blood pressure – systolic 120 to 129 mm Hg with diastolic below 80 mm Hg · Stage 1 hypertension – 130/80 to 139/89 mm Hg · Stage 2 hypertension – 140/90 mm Hg or higher · Hypertension diagnosis – auscultatory-confirmed readings of 130/80 mm Hg or higher at 3 separate visits
Management ladder – high blood pressure in an adolescent
TierInterventionEscalate when
1Screening reading at a routine visit; an oscillometric device is acceptable. Yearly from age 3, and at every visit with obesity, kidney disease, diabetes, prior coarctation or a drug that raises blood pressureReading of 120/80 mm Hg or higher
2Repeat by auscultation at the same visit, at least 2 readings, and average themAveraged auscultatory value in the elevated or hypertensive range; that value sets the stage
3Recheck by auscultation on a schedule set by stage: elevated, lifestyle advice and recheck in 6 months; stage 1, lifestyle advice and recheck in 1 to 2 weeks; stage 2, lifestyle advice and specialty referral within 1 weekElevated readings for 1 year, or stage 1 readings at 3 visits
424-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring to confirm hypertensionHypertension confirmed: evaluate for secondary causes and end-organ damage
5Lifestyle change first: the DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) diet and moderate to vigorous activity 3 to 5 days a week. Echocardiography for left ventricular hypertrophy when drug therapy is consideredLifestyle change fails, especially with left ventricular hypertrophy, symptoms or stage 2 without a modifiable cause: start a drug
Scenario bank
  1. 17 yo M at a football pre-participation examination, well, BMI 29, automated oscillometric blood pressure 138/88 mm Hg and 140/89 mm Hg on repeat with the same device, otherwise normal examination → Blood pressure measurement by auscultation → the averaged auscultatory readings set the stage
  2. 15 yo F at a well visit with an automated reading of 136/82 mm Hg; two auscultatory readings at the same visit average 132/78 mm Hg → Stage 1 hypertension → a systolic of 130 to 139 mm Hg sets stage 1 even with a diastolic below 80
  3. 14 yo M at a well visit whose auscultatory readings average 124/76 mm Hg, with a normal examination → Lifestyle advice and recheck in 6 months → elevated blood pressure
  4. 16 yo F with obesity whose auscultatory averages are 134/84, 132/82 and 136/86 mm Hg at three visits over 3 months → 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring → confirms hypertension before workup and treatment
  5. 17 yo M, asymptomatic with a normal examination, whose auscultatory readings at one visit average 146/94 mm Hg → Lifestyle advice and referral within 1 week → stage 2 hypertension
  6. 16 yo M with obesity and hypertension confirmed by ambulatory monitoring whose blood pressure stays high after a trial of diet and exercise, so drug therapy is planned → Echocardiography → measures left ventricular mass before drug therapy
Guideline history The 2004 Fourth Report defined hypertension as a reading at or above the 95th percentile at every age, and older questions still use that definition. The 2017 AAP (American Academy of Pediatrics) guideline set fixed adult cutoffs from age 13 and kept percentiles only for children under 13. Under 13, stage 1 starts at the 95th percentile for sex, age and height, or at 130/80 mm Hg if that is lower. From age 13, stage 1 starts at 130/80 mm Hg regardless of percentile.
Exit ramps A symptomatic adolescent, or a reading above 180/120 mm Hg, goes to the emergency department · Stage 1 or stage 2 readings call for a leg blood pressure; an arm reading higher than the leg suggests coarctation of the aorta · Confirmed hypertension opens a search for secondary causes and end-organ damage
Pearls Electrocardiography is not used to look for left ventricular hypertrophy in a hypertensive child; echocardiography is · Lifestyle change aimed at obesity is the first treatment for most adolescent hypertension · How NBME framed it: with the device reading already repeated, the key is a measurement method, not a diagnosis, heart test or later recheck
Pairs with Part I Hypertension in an Adult covers confirmation, baseline tests and drug choice in adults. Part I Hypertension in an Adult covers the causes to test for once hypertension is confirmed.
Transferable rule A high blood pressure from an automated device is confirmed by averaged auscultatory readings before it is staged, monitored, imaged or treated.
Sequencing trapEchocardiography looks for left ventricular hypertrophy once drug therapy is considered, and this reading is not yet confirmed.
Sequencing trapAmbulatory monitoring is accurate, but it follows auscultatory office readings that stay elevated for 1 year or in stage 1 across 3 visits.
Unchecked attributeDaily device readings for 3 days repeat the same overestimate; the method must change, not the number of readings.
True-fact-wrong-slotA 1 to 2 week recheck follows stage 1 confirmed by auscultation, but a repeat device reading in 2 weeks confirms nothing.

edits.html:
Chronic Cough

chest film first · postnasal drip, asthma or reflux · ACE inhibitor · empiric trials as tests · cancer flagsIs the chest film normal, and which empiric trials have already failed?

The decision point

Chronic cough (>8 weeks) with a normal chest X-ray comes down to three causes: upper airway cough syndrome, asthma, and GERD (gastroesophageal reflux disease). A completed empiric trial is a diagnostic test. Antihistamines and decongestants are the diagnostic trial for upper airway cough syndrome. Failure of that trial ("did not respond to antihistamines and decongestants") effectively excludes it.

Chronic cough – cause → clue → diagnostic move
CauseCluesDiagnostic moveConfirms, then
UACSupper airway cough syndrome / postnasal dripThroat clearing, drainage, cobblestoningEmpiric antihistamine/decongestant – response is the diagnosisResponse to the trial confirms; no response effectively excludes it
Cough-variant asthmaNocturnal + triggers (cold, exercise), ± wheezeSpirometry → methacholine challenge; empiric ICSPositive methacholine challenge when spirometry is normal; cough resolves on ICS
GERDWorse supine/after meals; often silent – no heartburn in 40–75%Empiric PPI × 8 weeks; pH monitoring if refractoryCough resolves on the PPI; if all three trials fail, refer for further testing
ACE inhibitorCheck the med list – onset days to months after startingStop the drug (resolves in 1–4 weeks)Cough resolves off the drug; switch to an ARB if needed
PostinfectiousRecent URI, self-limited<8 weeks by definitionResolves by 8 weeks; if not, work up as chronic cough
Lung cancer / TB Can't missWeight loss, hemoptysis, risk factorsCXR first in all chronic coughAbnormal film or red flags: chest CT, then biopsy; sputum for acid-fast bacilli if TB
Scenario bank
  1. 45 yo F, 3 months of cough, normal chest X-ray, post-nasal drip and throat clearing → Upper airway cough syndrome → first-generation antihistamine trial
  2. 45 yo F on lisinopril with 3 months of dry cough → ACE-inhibitor cough → stop the drug
  3. 45 yo F whose cough is worse at night and with cold air, spirometry normal → Cough-variant asthma → methacholine challenge
  4. 45 yo F with cough and heartburn after failed antihistamine and inhaled steroid trials → Gastroesophageal reflux → proton pump inhibitor trial
  5. 45 yo F, smoker, cough with hemoptysis and 6 kg weight loss → Malignancy → chest CT
  6. 45 yo F with cough for 5 weeks after a viral illness, normal chest X-ray → Postinfectious cough → observation
  7. 55 yo M with 10 weeks of cough and no imaging yet → Chest X-ray → first in all chronic cough, before any empiric trial
  8. 45 yo F on lisinopril with 3 months of dry cough and a normal chest X-ray → Stop lisinopril → ACE-inhibitor cough resolves in 1 to 4 weeks
  9. 30 yo M with chronic cough at night and with exercise and cold air; normal exam and normal spirometry → Methacholine challenge → normal spirometry does not exclude cough-variant asthma
  10. 45 yo F with 3 months of dry cough, normal chest X-ray and no heartburn, after failed antihistamine-decongestant and inhaled corticosteroid trials → Proton pump inhibitor for 8 weeks → GERD cough is often silent; the failed trials have eliminated the other two
Transferable rule When a stem says "did not respond to X," it is not giving history; it eliminates the cause X treats. Read treatment failures as eliminations. Nocturnal dry cough with a normal exam and everything else normal is GERD (gastroesophageal reflux disease) until proven otherwise.

edits.html:
Occupational Lung Disease

matching occupational exposure to lung disease · upper vs lower lobes · pleural plaques · cancer and tuberculosis riskWhat did the patient breathe at work, which lobes are involved, and is the pleura involved?

The decision point

The occupation identifies the dust, and the lobe distribution and pleural involvement confirm it. Asbestosis is the exception: it affects the lower lobes and involves the pleura. Everything else with a mining/quarry history affects the upper lobes.

Occupational lung diseases
DiseaseExposureLobesThe tellAssociation
AsbestosisBrake linings, shipyard, insulation, plumbing, roofingLOWERPleural plaques; ferruginous bodiesBronchogenic CA > mesothelioma; smoking multiplies bronchogenic only
SilicosisSandblasting, mining, foundry, stone countertopsUPPEREggshell calcification of hilar nodes↑ TB risk – annual PPD
Coal workers'Coal miningUPPERCoal macules → progressive massive fibrosisCaplan syndrome (+ RA nodules)
BerylliosisAerospace, nuclearDiffuseNoncaseating granulomas – sarcoid mimicResponds to steroids
ByssinosisCotton / textile mills – "Monday fever" – worse at the start of the work weekObstructive
Hypersensitivity pneumonitisMoldy hay, birds – Episodic fever/cough hours after exposureAvoidance cures
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Chest X-rayFirstUpper versus lower zones; pleural plaques; eggshell hilar nodesUpper: silica or coal; lower with plaques: asbestos
High-resolution CT of the chestSupportsFibrosis pattern with or without pleural plaquesDefines distribution; plaques alone mark exposure and are benign
Pulmonary function testsStagingRestrictive pattern with a low DLCOSeverity of fibrosis; byssinosis is obstructive instead
None: exposure history plus imagingConfirmsNamed dust, typical distribution, latency of decadesBiopsy only when the picture is atypical
Beryllium lymphocyte proliferation testBy branchPositive in a granulomatous pictureBerylliosis rather than sarcoidosis
Tuberculin skin test, yearlyBy branchPositive in a patient with silicosisLatent TB, which silicosis makes more likely
CT and pleural biopsyBy branchPleural mass with an effusionMesothelioma after asbestos exposure
Scenario bank
  1. 62 yo M shipyard insulator with lower-lobe fibrosis and pleural plaques → Asbestosis
  2. 55 yo M sandblaster with upper-lobe nodules and eggshell-calcified hilar nodes → Silicosis
  3. 58 yo M coal miner with upper-lobe nodules and black sputum → Coal workers' pneumoconiosis
  4. 50 yo M aerospace machinist with noncaseating granulomas on biopsy → Berylliosis
  5. 45 yo F cotton mill worker with chest tightness worst on the first day back at work → Byssinosis
  6. 40 yo M pigeon breeder with fever and dyspnea 6 hours after exposure → Hypersensitivity pneumonitis
  7. 62 yo M with asbestos exposure, a pleural mass and an effusion → Mesothelioma
  8. 55 yo M sandblaster and never smoker with silicosis → Annual tuberculin skin test → silicosis raises tuberculosis risk
  9. 66 yo M, retired shipyard worker, asymptomatic, with calcified pleural plaques and normal lung parenchyma on imaging → No treatment → plaques alone mark exposure and are benign
  10. 62 yo M with decades of asbestos exposure who also smokes heavily → Bronchogenic carcinoma → smoking multiplies bronchogenic risk only, not mesothelioma
  11. 50 yo M aerospace machinist with progressive dyspnea and noncaseating granulomas on biopsy, now removed from exposure → Oral corticosteroids → berylliosis responds to steroids
Mnemonic and timing Asbestos comes from the roof but affects the base; silica and coal come from the ground but affect the top. Latency is typically 20–30 years, so exposure that ended decades ago still counts. Pleural plaques alone are a marker of exposure, benign, and need no treatment.
Transferable rule Answering a long stem in under 40 seconds means one cue was pattern-matched and the verification pass was skipped. This costs the most in occupational stems. The lobe distribution usually decides the diagnosis, and it comes at the end of the stem.

edits.html:
Rhinitis

the step-up ladder · nasal steroid after antihistamines fail · start 2 weeks before pollen · immunotherapy is the baitWhich step has the patient already failed, and how far off is the pollen season?

The decision point

For moderate-to-severe seasonal rhinitis that has failed antihistamines, step up to an intranasal corticosteroid. It is the single most effective drug class for allergic rhinitis. A visit in "late winter" points to prophylaxis: start it ~2 weeks before pollen season. The steroid suppresses the mucosal inflammatory response and needs lead time.

Option analysis – why each fails
ChoiceWhy it fails
Minimize outdoor activitiesImpractical for pollen (unlike dust mites or pets); inadequate once disease is complicated
Continue OTC antihistaminesAlready failing – and first-generation agents bring sedation and anticholinergic effects
Desensitization (immunotherapy)The real bait – the only disease-modifying option, but reserved for failure of maximal pharmacotherapy. He has never tried a nasal steroid
MontelukastLess effective than intranasal steroids; carries an FDA boxed warning for neuropsychiatric effects
Oral prednisoneSystemic steroids for a benign chronic condition – never the answer
Scenario bank
  1. 28 yo F with moderate seasonal rhinitis failing OTC antihistamines → Intranasal corticosteroid
  2. 28 yo F seeking durable control after several drug classes have failed → Allergen immunotherapy
  3. 28 yo F advised to minimize outdoor activity for her pollen allergy → Impractical for pollen, unlike dust-mite control
  4. 28 yo F with rhinitis and asthma who wants a single oral agent → Montelukast – with neuropsychiatric counseling
  5. 28 yo F using oxymetazoline for 10 days with worsening congestion → Rhinitis medicamentosa → stop the spray
  6. 28 yo F with clear rhinorrhea, no itch or sneezing, triggered by temperature change → Vasomotor rhinitis
The ladder Start with allergen avoidance (when practical), then an intranasal corticosteroid. Next, add a second-generation oral or intranasal antihistamine. Use immunotherapy only after pharmacotherapy fails. Any first-generation antihistamine in a stem is usually there to be replaced, not continued.
Sequencing trap
