edits.html:
The Distended Abdomen in a Newborn or Infant

enterocolitis vs volvulus vs atresia · bilious emesis, bloody stool · the film tells you which one · excluding malrotationIs there air in the wall, air where bowel should be, or no air at all?

Source vignette Pt – 7-day-old term F with truncus arteriosus in the NICU awaiting repair, poor feeding and abdominal distension; T 35 C, BP 60/30, pulse 180, respirations 65, saturation 82% · Exam – lethargic and cyanotic, moderate distension, absent bowel sounds, bright red blood in stool; nasogastric tube returns bilious fluid · Imaging – abdominal x-ray · Q – the most likely diagnosis; options spanned NEC, malrotation with volvulus, intussusception, milk protein proctocolitis and C difficile colitis
The decision point

The combination of temperature instability, abdominal distension with bloody stools, and pneumatosis intestinalis on the film indicates NEC (necrotizing enterocolitis). NEC is mainly a disease of prematurity, but this infant is term. In a term infant, cyanotic congenital heart disease and hypotension reduce mesenteric oxygen delivery and cause the same ischemic bowel injury.

The bilious return also fits volvulus, so rule it out. Volvulus gives abrupt vomiting in a previously well infant, with proximal gas and a gasless distal abdomen. NEC gives air in the bowel wall with gas still visible in the large bowel. Read the gas pattern first; if malrotation is still possible, only an upper GI (gastrointestinal) series excludes it.

Defining criteria Pneumatosis intestinalis – air within the bowel wall; highly specific for NEC, often with portal venous gas (branching lucencies over the liver) · Pneumoperitoneum – free air under the diaphragm; means perforation and an operation · NEC risk factors – prematurity (the most important), very low birth weight under 1.5 kg, enteral feeding (especially formula), prolonged antibiotics, and in term infants a hypoxic-ischemic insult such as cyanotic heart disease, hypotension or perinatal asphyxia · Volvulus film – proximal gaseous distension with a gasless distal abdomen · Intussusception age – 6 months to 3 years
The distended abdomen in a newborn or infant: the differentialtiming, the stool, and the gas pattern
DiagnosisThe pictureKey discriminatorWhat to do
Necrotizing enterocolitis EmergencyPreterm infant on enteral feeds; lethargy, apnea, hypothermia rather than fever, distension, feeding intolerance, bilious emesis, bloody stools (may be absent early); leukocytosis, metabolic acidosisPneumatosis intestinalis with or without portal venous gas; gas still present distallyNPO, NG decompression, parenteral nutrition, broad-spectrum antibiotics now; surgery for perforation or worsening despite medical care
Malrotation with midgut volvulus EmergencyPreviously well, then abrupt bilious vomiting and pain; any age, most often the first month; older children can have intermittent pain and vomiting insteadProximal gas, gasless distal abdomen; upper GI series shows the ligament of Treitz on the right and a corkscrew or bird's-beak duodenumUpper GI series if stable; emergency laparotomy if not; the operation is the Ladd procedure
Duodenal atresiaBilious vomiting in the first 1 to 2 days, polyhydramnios, trisomy 21; abdomen not distendedDouble bubble with no distal gas, present from birth rather than abruptStop feeds, NG decompression, echocardiogram, then surgical repair
Hirschsprung diseaseNo meconium by 48 hours, poor feeding, distension, bilious vomiting; failed neural crest migration leaves an aganglionic segment, usually rectosigmoid, that cannot relax and stays contracted; usually isolated, but associated with Down syndromeNormal meconium once it passes; tight rectum with an explosive squirt of stool and gas on rectal exam; enema shows a rectosigmoid transition zone with dilated proximal colon; a newborn under 48 hours is not yet lateContrast enema, then rectal suction biopsy (absent ganglion cells confirms); surgical resection of the aganglionic segment
Meconium ileusNo meconium, distension, ± bilious vomiting; thick, sticky meconium obstructs the terminal ileum; cystic fibrosis in about 90%Dilated small bowel with little colonic gas; contrast enema shows a microcolon; empty rectum, no squirt; not a Down syndrome associationHyperosmolar contrast enema, which can also relieve it; surgery if it fails or for free air; sweat chloride test
IntussusceptionColicky pain, currant-jelly stool, right upper quadrant massAge 6 months to 3 years; target sign on ultrasoundAir-contrast enema
Milk protein-induced proctocolitisBlood-streaked stools at 2 to 8 weeksThe infant is well – thriving, undistended, normal vitalsMaternal dairy elimination or hydrolyzed formula
Clostridioides difficile colitisDistension with watery, sometimes bloody stoolNeonates are colonized but lack the toxin receptorsNot a neonatal diagnosis
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Abdominal radiographFirstPneumatosis intestinalis with or without portal venous gas, distal gas presentNEC: NPO, decompression, broad-spectrum antibiotics
Proximal gas, gasless distal abdomenVolvulus: upper GI series if stable, laparotomy if not
Double bubble, no distal gasDuodenal atresia: NG decompression and surgical repair
Diffusely dilated loops, distended abdomen, no air in the rectum, no free airDistal obstruction: Hirschsprung disease or meconium ileus
Free air under the diaphragmPerforation: laparotomy
EchocardiogramBy branchDuodenal atresia with trisomy 21 featuresAbout half of infants with Down syndrome have heart disease (VSD, ASD, AV canal); obtain before surgery, murmur or not
KaryotypeConfirmsTrisomy 21Confirms Down syndrome but is not urgent and does not change the operation
Upper GI series after a diagnostic double bubbleSkipFilm already diagnosticUpper GI is for malrotation, which has distal gas
Contrast enema, then rectal suction biopsyBy branchTransition zone; absent ganglion cellsHirschsprung disease: no meconium by 48 hours with distension
Contrast enema, then sweat chloride testBy branchMicrocolon with inspissated meconium in the terminal ileumMeconium ileus: a hyperosmolar enema can relieve it; about 90% have cystic fibrosis
CBC, blood gas and blood cultureBy branchLeukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, metabolic acidosisNEC: the platelet fall tracks severity; a rising count is often the first sign of improvement
Upper GI contrast seriesConfirmsLigament of Treitz on the right; corkscrew or bird's-beak duodenumMalrotation with midgut volvulus: Ladd procedure; skip it and operate if the infant is unstable
Abdominal ultrasoundBy branchTarget signIntussusception at 6 months to 3 years: air-contrast enema
C difficile toxin testingSkipNeonates lack the toxin receptorsNot a neonatal diagnosis
Scenario bank
  1. 7 day old term F with truncus arteriosus awaiting repair, temperature 35 C, lethargy, distended abdomen with absent bowel sounds, bilious nasogastric return and bright red blood per rectum → Necrotizing enterocolitis → Cyanotic heart disease is a term-infant risk factor – mesenteric hypoperfusion
  2. Preterm neonate on enteral feeds with abdominal distension and bloody stools → Pneumatosis intestinalis → Air within the bowel wall – specific for NEC; portal venous gas may accompany it
  3. Neonate with pneumatosis, distension and bloody stools, hemodynamically stable → Bowel rest, decompression and broad-spectrum antibiotics → Antibiotics immediately – septic shock is the lethal endpoint
  4. Neonate with NEC whose film now shows free air beneath the diaphragm → Laparotomy → Pneumoperitoneum means perforation
  5. 3 day old, well until now, abrupt bilious vomiting, abdominal pain and shock; film shows proximal gas and a gasless distal abdomen → Malrotation with midgut volvulus → Abrupt, previously well, and the mesenteric root twists around the superior mesenteric artery
  6. Stable infant with suspected malrotation → Upper gastrointestinal contrast series → Outlines the duodenojejunal junction and any corkscrew
  7. Newborn with bilious emesis from the first feeds, polyhydramnios in utero, trisomy 21 features, no distal gas on film → Duodenal atresia → Present from birth rather than abrupt – failure of recanalization
  8. 9 month old with intermittent colicky pain, currant-jelly stool and a right upper quadrant mass → Intussusception → Age 6 months to 3 years, target sign on ultrasound
  9. Thriving 5 week old, exclusively breast-fed, blood-streaked stools, no distension and normal vitals → Milk protein-induced proctocolitis → A well infant – the whole point is that nothing else is wrong
  10. Neonate with abdominal distension and bloody stools; which diagnosis should not be entertained → Clostridioides difficile colitis → Neonates are colonized but lack the toxin receptors
  11. 10-hour-old term boy with bilious vomiting, born to a 39-year-old mother without prenatal care; voided once, no meconium yet; hypotonia, flat facies, upslanting palpebral fissures, protruding tongue, single transverse palmar creases and a sandal gap; abdomen soft and not distended; loud holosystolic murmur with a thrill at the left lower sternal border; nasogastric tube in place; film shows a double bubble with no distal gas → Surgical repair → Duodenal atresia in Down syndrome; the echocardiogram comes first because of the likely VSD
  12. 1-day-old girl with trisomy 21 features and bilious vomiting since the first feed; film shows a double bubble with no distal gas; nasogastric decompression and IV fluids started; vital signs stable, no murmur heard → Echocardiography → About half of infants with Down syndrome have heart disease, often silent at birth
  13. 3-day-old term boy with trisomy 21 features, no meconium since birth, bilious vomiting and progressive abdominal distension; film shows diffusely dilated loops of bowel → Hirschsprung disease → Contrast enema, then rectal suction biopsy
  14. 12-hour-old term girl who has not yet passed meconium; breastfeeding well, voided twice, no vomiting, soft nondistended abdomen, patent normally placed anus → Observation → Most term newborns pass meconium within 24 hours and none by 48 hours is delayed; a well, undistended 12-hour-old is not yet late
  15. 52 hour old term girl delivered by cesarean for arrest of labor, voiding but has not passed stool, with a tense distended abdomen and no stool or gas on rectal exam; upright film shows many dilated small-bowel loops with little gas in the colon and rectum, and a decubitus film shows free air; at emergency laparotomy thick, sticky stool is evacuated from the ileum and the colon is diffusely narrow → Chronic rhinosinusitis → Meconium ileus from cystic fibrosis; nasal polyps and sinus opacification follow
  16. 2 day old boy with no meconium since birth, progressive abdominal distension and bilious vomiting; rectal exam finds an empty rectum with no release of stool or gas; film shows dilated small-bowel loops; contrast enema shows a narrow microcolon with pellets of inspissated stool in the terminal ileum → Meconium ileus → Sweat chloride test for cystic fibrosis
  17. 2 day old boy without dysmorphic features, no meconium yet, abdominal distension and bilious vomiting; rectal exam finds a tight anal canal and is followed by an explosive release of normal-appearing stool and gas → Hirschsprung disease → Contrast enema, then rectal suction biopsy
  18. 2 day old girl with distension and no meconium; contrast enema shows a microcolon with inspissated meconium in the terminal ileum; vital signs stable, no free air on film, no signs of peritonitis → Hyperosmolar contrast enema → Uncomplicated meconium ileus; sweat chloride test for cystic fibrosis
  19. 2-day-old term girl born to a 38-year-old mother after a fentanyl epidural; feeding poorly, spit up her last feed, has not passed meconium; firm distended abdomen; shallow 2-mm sacral dimple with intact skin and no hair; rectal exam finds increased tone followed by a release of stool; normal strength and reflexes; abdominal film shows dilated bowel loops with no air in the rectum → Failure of neural crest cell migration → Hirschsprung disease; contrast enema, then rectal suction biopsy
  20. 4-day-old girl without dysmorphic features, no meconium since birth, poor feeding and a distended abdomen; rectal exam is followed by an explosive release of gas and normal-appearing stool; contrast enema shows a narrow rectosigmoid with dilated colon above it → Rectal suction biopsy → Absent ganglion cells confirm Hirschsprung disease; treatment is resection of the aganglionic segment
  21. 3-week-old boy in the NICU born at 28 weeks weighing 900 g, extubated to nasal cannula last week, on continuous nasogastric formula feeds and gaining weight, with small yellow seedy stools until none in the past 24 hours, now has 6 hours of nonbloody bilious vomiting; temperature 35.6 C, BP 75/45, pulse 165, respirations 70; lethargic, with a tense distended abdomen and hypoactive bowel sounds; leukocytosis and metabolic acidosis → Abdominal x-ray with air in the bowel wall and portal veins → Necrotizing enterocolitis; stop feeds, NG decompression and broad-spectrum antibiotics
  22. Girl born at 27 weeks weighing 950 g, now 4 days old, stable on room air in the NICU and about to start enteral feeds; her mother is expressing milk → Exclusive feeding with breast milk → The most effective measure against necrotizing enterocolitis
  23. 7-month-old boy with 6 hours of persistent bilious vomiting, no fever, diarrhea or recent illness, last bowel movement 24 hours ago and no prior surgery; temperature 37 C, BP 70/50, pulse 180, respirations 65; moans with light palpation of a distended, hypertympanic abdomen with absent bowel sounds → Intestinal malrotation with midgut volvulus → Emergency laparotomy, Ladd procedure
  24. 5-week-old term girl with 4 hours of bilious vomiting and inconsolable crying; after a 20 mL/kg saline bolus, pulse is 190, BP 55/30 and capillary refill 4 seconds; abdomen distended and diffusely tender; film shows a dilated stomach and duodenum with little distal gas → Emergency laparotomy → Unstable malrotation with midgut volvulus; Ladd procedure without waiting for contrast
Exit ramps Free air – stop investigating and operate · Unstable with bilious vomiting – laparotomy without waiting for contrast · In a term infant with NEC (necrotizing enterocolitis), look for the perfusion insult: cyanotic heart disease, hypotension, sepsis · NEC worsening despite bowel rest and antibiotics: surgery · Late NEC sequelae – strictures and short-bowel syndrome · Bilious emesis in any infant, at any age, is malrotation until an upper GI (gastrointestinal) series excludes it
Decoy note: delayed meconium Maternal fentanyl epidural – maternal opioids can slow the newborn bowel and delay meconium, but they do not raise rectal tone or cause an explosive release of stool on rectal exam · Mother aged 38 – advanced maternal age raises the risk of Down syndrome, which goes with Hirschsprung disease; most Hirschsprung disease is isolated, so a nondysmorphic infant still fits · Shallow sacral dimple with intact skin and no hair – a normal finding; spina bifida occulta severe enough to cause a neurogenic bowel brings a hair tuft or neurologic deficits, and this exam has normal strength and reflexes · Tight rectum, then a release of normal stool – the squirt sign; meconium ileus gives normal tone, no release, and inspissated meconium in the ileum
Duodenal atresia in Down syndrome The order – stop feeds, NG (nasogastric) decompression and IV (intravenous) fluids, echocardiogram, then surgical repair · Echocardiogram – about half of infants with Down syndrome have heart disease. A loud holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border is a VSD (ventricular septal defect) · No distension – the block is proximal, so the rest of the abdomen stays flat; distension points to a distal obstruction · Meconium timing – about 99% of healthy term newborns pass meconium within 24 hours, so a distended infant with none by then needs evaluation; none by 48 hours is delayed and raises Hirschsprung disease or meconium ileus; a well, undistended newborn a few hours old is not yet late · Pyloric stenosis – nonbilious projectile vomiting at 3 to 6 weeks, not bilious emesis on day 1
Pearls Pneumatosis – gas made by bacteria that have invaded the wall, which is why it is specific · Bilious vomiting means the obstruction is distal to the ampulla; it is urgent until an upper GI (gastrointestinal) series excludes malrotation · NEC (necrotizing enterocolitis) and volvulus both give a distended, bilious, unwell neonate; the gas pattern separates them · A well infant with blood in the stool is almost never surgical; distension and instability suggest a surgical cause · Prematurity is the commonest NEC risk factor, not a required one · Meconium ileus means cystic fibrosis – nearly all patients with cystic fibrosis develop sinopulmonary disease, including chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (sinus opacification by age 1); hypothyroidism and early-onset Alzheimer disease belong to Down syndrome, which goes with Hirschsprung disease
NEC severity and prevention Mild: lethargy, temperature instability, apnea, feeding intolerance, bilious residuals, heme-positive stool; labs and film normal or mild dilation · Moderate: adds absent bowel sounds, tenderness, abdominal wall erythema, thrombocytopenia, metabolic acidosis and pneumatosis · Severe: adds hypotension, peritonitis, DIC (disseminated intravascular coagulation) and pneumoperitoneum · Platelets: the fall tracks severity, and a rising count is often the first sign of improvement · Prevention: exclusive breast milk is the most effective measure; antenatal corticosteroids for a mother likely to deliver preterm within 7 days also lower the risk, along with respiratory distress syndrome and intraventricular hemorrhage
Malrotation beyond the newborn period Age: most present in the first month, but volvulus can happen at any age. In a 7-month-old with bilious vomiting, tachycardia and a silent distended abdomen, malrotation is still the first diagnosis · Older children: intermittent abdominal pain and vomiting, sometimes failure to thrive · Late signs: hematochezia, peritonitis and shock mean the bowel is already ischemic · Not NEC (necrotizing enterocolitis): a disease of preterm infants in the first weeks on feeds · Not pyloric stenosis: that vomiting is nonbilious and projectile at 3 to 6 weeks, in a well infant with an olive-shaped mass
Pairs with Part I Stool Changes in a Well Infant covers the well infant with blood in the stool; this brief covers the sick one. Part II Tracheoesophageal Fistula and Esophageal Atresia covers obstruction above the pylorus. Ask: is the infant well, and what is the gas pattern?
Transferable rule In a distended neonate, the stool and vital signs show severity and the gas pattern identifies the disease: air in the wall, air where bowel should be, or no air at all.
Unchecked attributeIf NEC (necrotizing enterocolitis) is filed under prematurity, a term infant is ruled out without checking perfusion.
Salient decoyBilious nasogastric return pulls toward volvulus before the film is read.
Class-vs-memberRight category of neonatal bowel emergency, wrong member of it.
Sequencing trapKaryotype confirms trisomy 21, but it is not urgent and does not change the need for repair.
Redundant workupAn upper GI (gastrointestinal) series adds nothing once the film shows a double bubble with no distal gas; it is for malrotation.
Unchecked attributeNo meconium sounds like Hirschsprung disease, but a 10-hour-old is not yet late and the abdomen is not distended.
True-fact-wrong-slotEarly-onset Alzheimer disease and hypothyroidism are real Down syndrome associations, but Down syndrome goes with Hirschsprung disease; thick meconium in the ileum with a microcolon is meconium ileus, which means cystic fibrosis and later sinus disease.
Class-vs-memberInspissated meconium is the other cause of no meconium with distension, but it obstructs the ileum with a microcolon, normal rectal tone and no squirt; it is cystic fibrosis, not Hirschsprung disease.
Salient decoyA shallow sacral dimple without a hair tuft is normal; spinal cord dysfunction would bring neurologic deficits, and strength and reflexes are normal.
Salient decoyA maternal fentanyl epidural can cause neonatal ileus, but not increased rectal tone with an explosive release of stool.
Salient decoyBilious vomiting pulls toward a proximal block, but air in the stomach and duodenum with no distal gas is duodenal atresia, which presents with the first feeds; an infant who has been passing yellow seedy stools on full feeds is not obstructed there.
Salient decoyNo stool for a day suggests Hirschsprung disease, but that shows no meconium by 48 hours or chronic constipation, not sudden hypothermia, acidosis and a tense abdomen in a 3-week-old preterm infant.
Unchecked attributeNEC is the right category of sick distended bowel, but it belongs to preterm infants in their first weeks on feeds; a term 7-month-old with bilious vomiting has volvulus.
Unchecked attributePyloric stenosis causes vomiting in infancy, but it is nonbilious and projectile at 3 to 6 weeks; bilious vomiting in any infant is malrotation until proven otherwise.

edits.html:
GI Bleeding in a Child

both scopes first · pertechnetate scan in a child · capsule endoscopy in an adult · visible Meckel bleedingHave both scopes come back negative, and is the patient a child or an adult?

Source vignette Pt – 10-year-old boy, 2 months of exertional fatigue and exercise intolerance; no melena, hematochezia or abdominal pain; no medications · Exam – mucosal pallor, no lymphadenopathy, soft nontender abdomen, stool positive for occult blood · Labs – hemoglobin 9.4, MCV 74, platelets 380,000, leukocytes 7,500; ESR and coagulation normal; upper endoscopy and colonoscopy with biopsies unremarkable · Q – which study most likely reveals the diagnosis; options spanned CT angiography, fecal calprotectin, fecal DNA, technetium 99m pertechnetate scan and tissue transglutaminase antibodies
Source vignette Pt – 2 yo M, dark red formed stool in the diaper; eating and drinking well but more tired than usual; lives on a ranch with cattle and goats; afebrile, pale; abdomen soft, nondistended, nontender, no masses; no anal fissures or hemorrhoids; stool occult blood positive · Labs – WBC 8,000, Hct 27%, platelets 320,000 · Q – the study most likely to confirm the diagnosis; options spanned technetium-99m pertechnetate scan, abdominal CT, abdominal ultrasound, air contrast enema, bacterial stool culture, cow's milk elimination diet and upper endoscopy
The decision point

Iron deficiency anemia with a positive occult blood test and no visible bleeding is occult gastrointestinal bleeding. Upper endoscopy and colonoscopy are both unremarkable, so the source is in the small bowel, which neither scope reaches. In a child, the most common small-bowel bleeding lesion is a Meckel diverticulum. It is found by a technetium 99m pertechnetate scan, which images ectopic gastric mucosa rather than the bleeding.

An adult with the same negative workup gets capsule endoscopy, because adult small-bowel causes are angiodysplasia, neoplasia and ulcers.

A Meckel diverticulum can also bleed visibly. A toddler with painless dark red or maroon stool, pallor and a soft, nontender abdomen, without diarrhea, vomiting or fever, goes straight to the pertechnetate scan. Endoscopy is not done first. Pain suggests a complication or a different disease and changes the first test.

Defining criteria Occult GI bleeding – positive fecal occult blood and/or iron deficiency anemia without visible bleeding · First step regardless of age – upper endoscopy and colonoscopy · Child, source not found – technetium 99m pertechnetate scan for Meckel · Adult, source not found – capsule endoscopy, then CT or MR enterography · Meckel – failed closure of the vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct, the most common congenital GI anomaly, with ectopic gastric mucosa that ulcerates adjacent small bowel
Occult GI bleeding in a child: what each study answers
StudyWhat it detectsWho it is forWhy not here
Tc 99m pertechnetate scanEctopic gastric mucosaChild with small-bowel bleeding – (the answer)
Capsule endoscopyAngiodysplasia, neoplasia, ulcersAdult with small-bowel bleedingRight idea, wrong age branch
CT angiographyBrisk active bleedingHemodynamic instability with visible bleedingOccult bleeding is too slow to see
Fecal calprotectinIntestinal inflammationSuspected inflammatory bowel diseaseNo pain, diarrhea or weight loss; scopes and biopsies clean
Tissue transglutaminaseCeliac diseaseMalabsorptive iron deficiencyCeliac does not cause occult blood
Fecal DNA testingColorectal neoplasiaAverage-risk adults over 45Not a pediatric test
Upper endoscopyUpper GI sourceHematemesis or black, sticky melenaDark red or maroon stool without either is a lower source
Cow's milk eliminationMilk protein proctocolitisInfant, well, with blood-streaked stoolResolves by age 1; a toddler is past the window
Abdominal ultrasound, then air enemaIntussusceptionChild with intermittent severe pain, with or without bloody stoolThe Meckel bleed is painless
Bacterial stool cultureBacterial colitisBloody diarrhea with crampy pain and feverFormed stool, afebrile, no pain
Anal examAnal fissureBright red streaks on a hard stool, painful passageVisible on exam; none here
Abdominal CTBowel and mass lesionsAbdominal trauma, abscess or tumorCannot reliably tell the diverticulum from other bowel loops
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
CBC and stool occult bloodFirstMicrocytic anemia, occult blood positiveOccult GI bleeding
Upper endoscopy and colonoscopyNextUnremarkable, biopsies cleanSource is in the small bowel
Technetium 99m pertechnetate scanConfirmsEctopic gastric mucosaMeckel diverticulum, the child's small-bowel branch
Capsule endoscopyBy branchAngiodysplasia, neoplasia or ulcerAdult branch; then CT or MR enterography
Tissue transglutaminase IgABy branchPositive, with occult blood negativeCeliac disease: iron deficiency from malabsorption, not bleeding
CT angiographySkipNeeds brisk active bleedingOccult bleeding is too slow to show
Abdominal ultrasoundBy branchTarget signIntussusception, when there is intermittent severe pain; air enema confirms and reduces it
Abdominal CTSkipCannot separate the diverticulum from bowel loopsThe pertechnetate scan answers the Meckel question
Scenario bank
  1. 10 year old with 2 months of exertional fatigue, pallor, hemoglobin 9.4 with MCV 74, stool positive for occult blood; upper endoscopy and colonoscopy with biopsies are unremarkable → Technetium 99m pertechnetate scan → Meckel scan – it images ectopic gastric mucosa
  2. How a Meckel diverticulum causes occult bleeding → Ectopic gastric mucosa secreting acid → Ulcerating adjacent small bowel
  3. Child with iron deficiency anemia and a positive fecal occult blood test; the first step → Upper endoscopy and colonoscopy → Localize before reaching for small-bowel studies
  4. Adult with occult gastrointestinal bleeding and a negative upper endoscopy and colonoscopy → Capsule endoscopy → Angiodysplasia, neoplasia and ulcers – the adult small-bowel causes
  5. Child with painless hematochezia and no abdominal pain, age under 2 → Meckel diverticulum → Failed closure of the vitelline duct
  6. Child with slow occult blood loss and stable vital signs; which study is least likely to help → CT angiography → It needs brisk active bleeding to see anything
  7. Child with microcytic anemia, chronic diarrhea and a negative fecal occult blood test → Celiac disease → Malabsorption, not blood loss – the occult blood is negative
  8. 2-year-old boy with dark red, formed stool in his diaper; eating and drinking well but more tired than usual; lives on a ranch with cattle and goats; afebrile and pale; abdomen soft, nondistended and nontender without masses; no anal fissures or hemorrhoids; stool positive for occult blood; hematocrit 27%, leukocytes 8,000/mm3, platelets 320,000/mm3 → Technetium 99m pertechnetate scan → Meckel diverticulum: ectopic gastric mucosa takes up the tracer; painless small-bowel bleeding in a toddler, and dark red stool without hematemesis or melena is not an upper GI bleed
  9. 10-week-old boy fed cow's milk-based formula with several days of mucus and streaks of blood in otherwise soft stools; feeding well, gaining weight, afebrile and playful; mild eczema on the cheeks; abdomen soft and nontender; no anal fissure on exam → Switch to an extensively hydrolyzed formula → milk protein proctocolitis: a non-IgE reaction in infants; bleeding clears once cow's milk protein is removed, and it resolves by age 1
  10. 2-year-old boy with 12 hours of sudden episodes of severe crying with his legs drawn up, quiet and sleepy between episodes; vomited twice; one stool of dark red blood and mucus (currant jelly); afebrile; a sausage-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant → Abdominal ultrasound → intussusception: pain is the tell; target sign on ultrasound, then air enema to confirm and reduce; a Meckel diverticulum can be the lead point
  11. 3-year-old girl with two episodes of painless maroon stool over the past month; pale, hematocrit 28%, vital signs normal; abdomen soft and nontender; technetium-99m pertechnetate scan shows a focus of uptake in the right lower quadrant → Surgical resection → a symptomatic Meckel diverticulum is removed to stop the bleeding and prevent intussusception, diverticulitis and obstruction; iron treats the anemia, not the source
Stool color and bleeding source Stool color follows transit time, not only where the blood started. Dark red or maroon stool in a toddler is a lower source, usually the small bowel, because the blood passes quickly. The upper GI (gastrointestinal) picture is hematemesis with black, sticky melena, and it is more common in adults. This child had neither, so upper endoscopy is not the first test.
Gates Visible bleeding with instability – hematemesis, melena or hematochezia goes to CT (computed tomography) angiography, not a Meckel scan · Scope first for occult bleeding – small-bowel studies are for after a clean upper endoscopy and colonoscopy; a toddler with visible, painless dark red stool goes straight to the pertechnetate scan · Meckel is classically under 2 but presents into adolescence, so age does not exclude it · Balloon-assisted enteroscopy is the fallback when the source stays hidden
Pearls The Meckel scan detects gastric mucosa, not blood, so it works when the lesion is not actively bleeding · Occult bleeding is too slow for angiography · Celiac gives iron deficiency without occult blood; the FOBT (fecal occult blood test) separates them · Here, small bowel means the segment the two scopes cannot reach · Painless hematochezia in a toddler is Meckel until proven otherwise · Rule of 2s: often presents by age 2, usually under 2 inches long, within 2 feet of the ileocecal valve · The bleed is painless; pain comes from complications: intussusception with the diverticulum as lead point, diverticulitis that mimics appendicitis, obstruction or perforation · A symptomatic Meckel diverticulum is surgically resected to stop the bleeding and prevent those complications
Pairs with Part I The Distended Abdomen in a Newborn or Infant covers the obstructed and acutely bleeding infant gut. Part I Microcytic Anemia covers the iron-versus-thalassemia fork that precedes this workup. Ask: is the bleeding visible, and have both ends been scoped?
Transferable rule When an algorithm branches on age, the same negative workup can send a child and an adult to different tests.
Class-vs-memberCapsule endoscopy is the adult small-bowel study; a child gets the pertechnetate scan.
Sequencing trapOrdering a small-bowel study before upper endoscopy and colonoscopy are done.
Salient decoyMicrocytic anemia in a child pulls toward celiac serology, which the positive FOBT (fecal occult blood test) excludes.
Unchecked attributeMilk elimination fits painless blood in an infant, but milk protein proctocolitis resolves by age 1; a 2-year-old is past it.
Salient decoyRanch animals pull toward bacterial colitis, which needs bloody diarrhea, crampy pain and fever.
True-fact-wrong-slotEndoscopy is right for hematemesis and black melena; dark red stool without either points below.

edits.html:
Constipation and Fecal Impaction in an Adult

firm stool in the vault · overflow diarrhea · anticholinergic cause · enema, then manual disimpaction · treat the causeWhat does the rectal exam find, and which drug is slowing the colon?

Source vignette Pt – 77 yo F taking oxybutynin; last bowel movement 5 days ago, and it was loose stool; colonoscopy 3 years ago showed no abnormalities; no hematochezia · Exam – afebrile, warm dry skin, soft abdomen without distension, diffuse tenderness, firm stool in the rectal vault · Q – the most likely diagnosis; options spanned fecal impaction, adhesions, colon cancer, diverticulitis, ischemic bowel and volvulus
The decision point

Rectal examination shows firm stool in the rectal vault. This confirms fecal impaction and is incompatible with adhesive small bowel obstruction, which gives an empty rectum, a distended abdomen, and high-pitched or absent bowel sounds.

The last bowel movement, 5 days ago, was loose stool. Loose stool in a constipated patient is overflow diarrhea: liquid stool passing around a hard impaction. It is near-pathognomonic.

Stem findings → options ruled out
OptionThe sentence that kills it
AdhesionsFirm stool in the rectal vault (SBO empties the rectum); soft, undistended abdomen
Colon cancer"Colonoscopy 3 years ago showed no abnormalities"
DiverticulitisNo fever; diffuse, not focal LLQ, tenderness
Ischemic bowelNo hematochezia; no AF or atherosclerotic risk factors
VolvulusSoft abdomen without distension; no coffee-bean film
Details that change management Oxybutynin is an anticholinergic that slows colonic transit and is the cause here, so treatment includes addressing it. The patient's warm, dry skin is an anticholinergic sign. Constipating drugs: anticholinergics (oxybutynin, TCAs [tricyclic antidepressants], antihistamines, antipsychotics), opioids, verapamil, iron, calcium, aluminum antacids, ondansetron.
Management ladder – fecal impaction
TierInterventionEscalate when
1Enema (in-context: first-line)Fails to clear
2Manual disimpactionEnema unsuccessful
3Treat the cause – stop or reduce the oxybutynin; then maintenance PEG, fluids, mobilityAlways, after clearing
Scenario bank
  1. 77 yo F, 5 days without a BM, empty rectal vault, distended abdomen, high-pitched bowel sounds, prior laparotomy → Adhesive small bowel obstruction → NG decompression + imaging
  2. 77 yo F, sudden severe pain, distended tympanitic abdomen, coffee-bean sign → Sigmoid volvulus → endoscopic decompression
  3. 68 yo M, LLQ pain with fever 38.5 and focal tenderness → Diverticulitis → CT
  4. 72 yo F with atrial fibrillation, crampy pain and hematochezia → Ischemic colitis
  5. 60 yo M, progressive constipation with iron deficiency anemia and weight loss, no recent colonoscopy → Colon cancer → colonoscopy
  6. 77 yo F, impaction cleared by enema, still constipated → Stop the oxybutynin, start PEG
  7. 80 yo M on chronic opioids, 6 days without a BM, hard stool in the vault → Disimpaction + methylnaltrexone or naloxegol
Exceptions Impaction can sit distal to a second lesion, such as a slow-growing tumor or partial obstruction. Here, a normal colonoscopy 3 years ago and no weight loss or anemia mean no further workup is needed. If any one of these is missing, relieve the impaction and also investigate.
Pairs with Part I Constipation in a Child covers the paediatric case, where the rectal vault is empty and an anal fissure rules out the rectal route that is first-line here.
Transferable rule Change an answer only when a new detail makes the current choice impossible, not when another option merely becomes plausible. Check whether the stem contains a finding that excludes the new option. Here, firm stool in the rectal vault excludes small bowel obstruction.
Salient decoy

edits.html:
Tracheoesophageal Fistula and Esophageal Atresia

choking on the first feed · pass a tube before you order a picture · fistula type by abdominal gas · age at presentationDid it start with the first feed, and will a nasogastric tube pass?

Source vignette Pt – 3 h old term boy born at home, coughs and vomits on his first breastfeed, formula mixed with saliva in his mouth, coarse breath sounds with retractions, soft systolic murmur at the upper left sternal border · Q – the most appropriate next step; options spanned nasogastric tube placement, lateral neck radiography and echocardiography
The decision point

Formula mixed with saliva means the milk filled a blind proximal pouch and overflowed without reaching the stomach. With choking on the very first feed and coarse lungs from aspiration, this is esophageal atresia with a distal tracheoesophageal fistula.

The first step is to pass a nasogastric tube at the bedside. It meets resistance at the pouch, and the film shows it coiled. The murmur, maternal drug history and absent prenatal care do not call for imaging or drug treatment first.

Defining criteria Type C – proximal pouch with a distal fistula, about 85% of cases · Gas in the abdomen – a distal fistula is present · Gasless abdomen – pure atresia with no distal fistula · H-type – no atresia, presenting months later with recurrent pneumonia
Neonatal choking and vomiting – the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tell
EA with distal TEFChoking on the first feed, copious frothy secretions, polyhydramnios in uteroFormula mixed with saliva; tube will not pass
Congenital diaphragmatic herniaSevere distress at deliveryScaphoid abdomen, bowel gas in the chest, shifted heart sounds
Congenital heart diseaseFeeding difficulty with cyanosisCyanosis and diaphoresis with feeds, no excess secretions
EpiglottitisFebrile stridor with droolingSchool-aged child, never a newborn
Hypertrophic pyloric stenosisNonbilious projectile vomitingAge 3 to 6 weeks, hungry after vomiting, olive mass
Respiratory distress syndromePreterm surfactant deficiencyGround-glass with air bronchograms, low lung volumes
Neonatal abstinence syndromeMaternal opioid useOnset at or beyond 24 hours, hypertonia and irritability
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Nasogastric tube passageFirstMeets resistance at the pouchEsophageal atresia likely: film with the tube in place
Chest and abdominal x-ray with the tubeConfirmsTube coiled in the upper chestEsophageal atresia
Gas below the diaphragmDistal fistula present (type C)
Gasless abdomenPure atresia, no distal fistula
Echocardiogram and renal ultrasoundNextVACTERL anomaliesScreen after the diagnosis, before repair
Bronchoscopy or prone contrast esophagramBy branchH-type fistulaTube passes; months of cough with feeds and recurrent pneumonia
Barium esophagram or endoscopySkipContrast can aspirate from the blind pouchThe coiled tube on film already confirms atresia
Scenario bank
  1. 3 h old term boy born at home, coughs and vomits on his first breastfeed, formula mixed with saliva in his mouth, coarse breath sounds with retractions, soft systolic murmur at the upper left sternal border → Nasogastric tube placement → Esophageal atresia with distal tracheoesophageal fistula
  2. 2 h old term girl drooling frothy secretions who choked on her first feed; a nasogastric tube meets firm resistance and will not advance → Chest x-ray with the tube in place → A coiled tube confirms atresia; gas below the diaphragm means a distal fistula
  3. Term newborn girl, maternal polyhydramnios, drooling; the feeding tube coils in the upper chest on x-ray and the abdomen is completely gasless → Esophageal atresia without a fistula → No tracheal connection, so no air reaches the stomach
  4. 8 mo old boy with three right upper lobe pneumonias and coughing and choking with liquid feeds since birth; a feeding tube passes easily into the stomach → H-type tracheoesophageal fistula → Bronchoscopy or prone contrast esophagram
  5. Term newborn boy with esophageal atresia and a distal fistula confirmed on x-ray, before surgical repair → Echocardiogram and renal ultrasound → VACTERL association
  6. 4 wk old boy with a week of nonbilious projectile vomiting, hungry after each episode, ultrasound showing a thickened elongated pylorus, low chloride and high bicarbonate → IV fluids and electrolyte repletion → Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis; pyloromyotomy once the alkalosis corrects
  7. Newborn girl with upslanting palpebral fissures and a single palmar crease, maternal polyhydramnios, bilious vomiting on day 1, abdominal x-ray with a double bubble and no distal gas → Nasogastric decompression and IV fluids → Duodenal atresia; repair after stabilization and an echocardiogram
  8. 30 wk preterm boy grunting and retracting at 1 h of life, x-ray with diffuse ground-glass opacities, air bronchograms and low lung volumes → Respiratory distress syndrome → CPAP, then surfactant if the oxygen requirement rises
  9. 36 h old girl, irritable and tremulous with a high-pitched cry, sneezing and feeding poorly; mother maintained on methadone → Swaddling, low stimulation and rooming-in → Neonatal abstinence syndrome; morphine only if nonpharmacologic care fails
  10. Term newborn boy with esophageal atresia and a distal fistula confirmed on x-ray, saturating 96% in room air, awaiting surgical repair → NPO, head elevated, continuous pouch suction → Keeps pooled saliva out of the lungs and gastric acid out of the fistula
Age at presentation Age at presentation narrows the differential. Minutes to hours: TEF (tracheoesophageal fistula) with EA (esophageal atresia), choanal atresia, diaphragmatic hernia, respiratory distress syndrome, Potter sequence. Beyond 24 hours: neonatal abstinence, sepsis, ductal-dependent lesions as the PDA (patent ductus arteriosus) closes, bilious vomiting and malrotation. 3 to 6 weeks: hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. Months: H-type fistula, laryngomalacia.
Pearls Polyhydramnios in utero, because the fetus cannot swallow amniotic fluid · Diagnosis is made by passing the tube: resistance at roughly 9 to 11 cm, confirmed on film · The abdominal gas pattern shows the anatomic type without endoscopy · VACTERL (vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal and limb anomalies) screening after diagnosis: echocardiogram and renal ultrasound at minimum · A soft systolic murmur on day one is usually a closing ductus, not structural disease
Pairs with Part II Posterior Urethral Valves shares the mechanism in reverse: a fetus that cannot make urine has oligohydramnios and Potter sequence, and a fetus that cannot swallow has polyhydramnios and foregut or duodenal atresia. Part I Cyanosis in the Newborn covers cyanosis that worsens with feeding and improves with crying, which is choanal atresia, not a fistula. Part I Genetic Syndromes Recognized at Birth covers VACTERL (vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal and limb anomalies) alongside the syndromes it is mistaken for and what excludes each.
Transferable rule When a newborn chokes or vomits with the first feed, first check whether a nasogastric tube reaches the stomach, before any imaging or drug. Imaging only confirms what the tube found.
True-fact-wrong-slotEpiglottitis is a febrile school-age disease; a 3-hour-old cannot have it.
Sequencing trapEchocardiography is indicated for VACTERL (vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal and limb anomalies) screening after the diagnosis, not before it.
True-fact-wrong-slotPyloric stenosis needs 3 to 6 weeks for the muscle to hypertrophy, and it gives projectile vomiting, not coughing with saliva-mixed formula at 3 hours.
True-fact-wrong-slotSurfactant treats respiratory distress syndrome in the preterm lung; this is a term newborn whose retractions come from aspirated secretions, which surfactant does not fix.
Salient decoyThe maternal drug history points at neonatal abstinence syndrome, but withdrawal typically begins at 24 hours or later, never pools saliva or causes coughing with feeds, and is treated first without drugs.

edits.html:
Umbilical Findings in a Newborn

hernia vs omphalocele vs gastroschisis · skin-covered and reducible: observe · 1.5 cm and age 5 cutoffs · incarcerationIs there skin over it, and how big and how old is it?

Source vignette Pt – 4-hour-old boy, 38 wk, 3.6 kg, mother 18 with no prenatal care, normal vitals; soft, nontender, skin-covered 1.4 cm bulge just below the umbilical stump that enlarges with crying and reduces with gentle pressure · Q – the most appropriate next step for the mass; options spanned observation, abdominal ultrasound, karyotype, immediate surgery and topical silver nitrate
The decision point

A skin-covered, soft, reducible bulge that grows with crying is a congenital umbilical hernia: the fascial ring around the umbilicus has not closed yet. It is common in healthy newborns, and incarceration is very rare. Small hernias usually close on their own, so a well infant needs observation only. The diagnosis is clinical; no imaging or genetic test is needed.

A defect over 1.5 cm is less likely to close. Persistence to about age 5 calls for elective repair, and incarceration calls for repair at any age. Bowel with no skin over it, either in a membranous sac (omphalocele) or bare beside the cord (gastroschisis), goes to surgery right after birth.

Decision cutoffs Skin-covered, soft, reducible: observe · Defect over 1.5 cm: spontaneous closure less likely; keep following · Still present at about age 5: elective surgical repair · Incarcerated (firm, tender, irreducible or discolored, with vomiting): urgent repair at any age · No skin over the bowel: gastroschisis or omphalocele, surgery at birth
Umbilical findings in a newborn: the differential
FindingIllness scriptThe NBME tellNext step
Umbilical herniaUnclosed fascial ring; more frequent with Down syndrome, hypothyroidism, Beckwith-Wiedemann and Ehlers-DanlosSkin-covered, soft, reducible, grows with cryingObserve; repair about age 5 if persistent, sooner if incarcerated
Umbilical granulomaExcess granulation tissue at the base after the cord separatesMoist, red, friable nub that appears after the cord falls offTopical silver nitrate
Patent urachus or omphalomesenteric ductPersistent tract to the bladder (urachus) or the ileum (omphalomesenteric duct)Drainage: urine-like fluid from a urachus, stool or mucus from the ductUltrasound, then surgical excision
OmphaloceleMidline defect at the umbilical ring; bowel, often liver, herniates into the base of the cordMembranous sac with the cord inserting on itSurgery at birth; karyotype and echocardiogram for associated anomalies
GastroschisisFull-thickness wall defect, usually right of the umbilicus; usually isolatedBare bowel, no sac, beside a normally inserted cordCover the bowel, decompress, immediate surgery
Scenario bank
  1. 4-hour-old boy born at 38 weeks to a mother without prenatal care, well-appearing, with a soft, nontender, skin-covered 1.4 cm bulge just below the umbilical stump that enlarges with crying and reduces with gentle pressure → Observation only → Congenital umbilical hernia
  2. 5-year-old girl, well, with a soft, reducible, skin-covered umbilical bulge present since birth that has not decreased in size; defect about 2 cm; no pain or vomiting → Elective surgical repair → Persistent umbilical hernia
  3. 8-month-old boy with a known umbilical hernia that is now firm, tender, discolored and cannot be reduced; he has vomited three times → Urgent surgical repair → Incarcerated umbilical hernia
  4. 12-day-old girl whose cord fell off 4 days ago, now with a 4 mm moist, red, friable, pedunculated nub at the umbilical base with slight serous drainage; afebrile, no surrounding erythema → Topical silver nitrate → Umbilical granuloma
  5. 3-week-old boy with clear, urine-like fluid leaking from the umbilicus that increases when he cries or strains; the skin around the umbilicus is normal → Patent urachus → Ultrasound, then surgical excision
  6. Term newborn with loops of bare, edematous bowel protruding through a defect to the right of a normally inserted umbilical cord, with no covering membrane; vital signs stable → Cover the bowel and arrange immediate surgery → Gastroschisis
  7. Term newborn with a 5 cm midline membrane-covered sac containing bowel and liver at the base of the umbilical cord, with the cord inserting on the sac → Karyotype and echocardiogram → Omphalocele
  8. 7-week-old girl born at home without newborn screening, with a reducible skin-covered umbilical hernia, persistent jaundice, a large tongue, poor tone, constipation and a wide posterior fontanelle → Serum TSH and free T4 → Congenital hypothyroidism
Abdominal wall defect at delivery Exposed bowel loses heat and fluid. Cover it with a sterile moist dressing or bowel bag, place a nasogastric tube, give IV (intravenous) fluids and keep the infant warm. Then proceed to immediate surgery. An omphalocele also needs a karyotype and echocardiogram because it is associated with trisomy 13 and 18, Beckwith-Wiedemann and heart defects. Gastroschisis is usually isolated.
Pearls An umbilical hernia with prolonged jaundice, macroglossia, hypotonia, constipation or a large fontanelle is a reason to check TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone), because congenital hypothyroidism is the treatable association · Karyotype is for Down features or an omphalocele, never for an isolated hernia in a normal infant · Silver nitrate is the treatment for a granuloma; an umbilical lesion that keeps draining urine or stool is a remnant tract and needs imaging and excision
Pairs with Congenital Hypothyroidism: an umbilical hernia is one of its soft signs; ask: is there jaundice, macroglossia or a large fontanelle beside the hernia? Tracheoesophageal Fistula and Esophageal Atresia: after any structural defect, screen for the anomalies that occur with it. For esophageal atresia that means VACTERL (vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal and limb) anomalies; for an omphalocele, a karyotype and echocardiogram.
How NBME framed it A sleepy 2-month-old at his first visit, with an umbilical hernia, persistent jaundice and cool extremities, needed thyroid function tests, not karyotype, sweat chloride or head or liver computed tomography.
Transferable rule For a newborn umbilical finding, ask first whether skin covers it. Observe a skin-covered, reducible bulge, and repair it if still present at about age 5 or incarcerated at any age. Bowel without skin goes to surgery at birth.
Redundant workupAbdominal ultrasound adds nothing to a clinical diagnosis; it is for an acquired hernia in an older child or adult.
True-fact-wrong-slotImmediate surgery belongs to gastroschisis and omphalocele, where no skin covers the bowel.
Salient decoyA young mother without prenatal care invites a genetic workup, but karyotype is for Down features or an omphalocele, and this infant has neither.
Mirror twinSilver nitrate treats an umbilical granuloma, the moist red nub that appears after the cord falls off, not a skin-covered bulge at 4 hours.

edits.html:
Wilson Disease

copper and ATP7B · liver plus brain, eye or red cells · ceruloplasmin, slit lamp, urine copper · chelation or transplantDoes unexplained liver disease come with brain, eye or red-cell findings, and is the ceruloplasmin low?

Source vignette Pt – adolescent with liver disease (hepatitis, possibly progressing to cirrhosis) plus neuropsychiatric change: tremor, slurred speech and altered behavior · Exam – Kayser-Fleischer rings at the corneal margin · Labs – elevated transaminases · Q – the most likely underlying mechanism of the disease
The decision point

Think of Wilson disease in any patient with unexplained liver disease. Think of it especially when liver disease comes with neuropsychiatric signs (tremor, dysarthria, dystonia, depression, personality change, psychosis), Kayser-Fleischer rings, or a Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia. Screen with serum ceruloplasmin (low) and a slit-lamp exam. A high 24-hour urine copper confirms the diagnosis, and liver biopsy copper settles cases where the tests disagree.

Wilson disease is autosomal recessive loss of ATP7B, the hepatocyte transporter that loads copper onto ceruloplasmin and excretes the excess into bile. Copper builds up in the liver (hepatitis, cirrhosis, sometimes acute liver failure). It then spills into the blood and deposits in the basal ganglia, the cornea and red cells. Ceruloplasmin is low because it is unstable without its copper. In patients with liver disease alone, Kayser-Fleischer rings are often absent. Ceruloplasmin can also read normal in these patients because it rises with inflammation. The urine copper or the liver biopsy then makes the diagnosis.

Unexplained liver disease: the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellWhy less likely here
Wilson diseaseAutosomal recessive; child, teen or young adult; hepatitis, cirrhosis or acute liver failure, with movement or psychiatric changeKayser-Fleischer rings, low ceruloplasmin, Coombs-negative hemolysisThe key: the only one that adds brain, eye and red-cell findings to the liver
Autoimmune hepatitisYoung woman, often with another autoimmune disease; acute or chronic hepatitisAntinuclear antibody (ANA) and anti-smooth muscle antibody (anti-LKM1 in children), high IgGNo neurologic signs or corneal rings; Wilson can mimic it, so check ceruloplasmin
Hereditary hemochromatosisAutosomal recessive HFE; iron builds for decades, so middle-aged men and women after menopauseHigh transferrin saturation and ferritin; diabetes, bronze skin, arthropathy, cardiomyopathy, hypogonadismToo young; iron does not cause tremor or corneal rings
Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiencyMisfolded protein retained in hepatocytes; neonatal cholestasis in infants, cirrhosis in adults, early basal emphysemaLow serum alpha-1 antitrypsin; lung disease in a young smokerIts second organ is the lung, not the brain or eye
Viral hepatitisMost common cause; risk factors for hepatitis B or C, or an acute illness with hepatitis APositive serologiesNo neuropsychiatric signs or corneal rings; hemolysis is not a feature
MASLD (metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease)Obesity, diabetes, dyslipidemia; mild alanine aminotransferase (ALT)-predominant riseMetabolic syndrome with a hyperechoic liver; a diagnosis of exclusionNothing outside the liver
Antipsychotic-induced parkinsonismTremor, rigidity or dystonia after starting a dopamine blockerMovement signs follow the drug; liver tests normalDoes not explain the liver disease
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Liver tests: aspartate aminotransferase (AST), ALT, bilirubin, international normalized ratio (INR)FirstHepatocellular rise, from mild to acute liver failureLiver injury; the pattern alone does not name the cause
Hepatitis serologies, iron studies, ANA and anti-smooth muscle antibody, alpha-1 antitrypsin levelFirstNormalExcludes the common mimics
Serum ceruloplasminScreenLow, below the lower limit of normal (usually about 20 mg/dL)Wilson disease; a normal value does not exclude it in active hepatitis, because ceruloplasmin is an acute-phase reactant
Slit-lamp examinationNextKayser-Fleischer ringsCorneal copper; almost always present with neurologic disease, often absent with liver disease alone
24-hour urine copperConfirmsHigh, typically over 100 mcg per day when symptomatic; over 40 mcg/day may indicate it in children or asymptomatic patientsCopper overflow from an overloaded liver; also used to monitor chelation
Liver biopsy with copper measurementBy branchHigh hepatic copperWhen ceruloplasmin, urine copper and the slit-lamp exam disagree
Complete blood count (CBC), reticulocytes, direct Coombs testSupportsAnemia, high reticulocytes, Coombs negativeCopper damages red cells; with acute liver failure, fulminant Wilson disease
Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)SupportsBasal ganglia signal changeNeurologic involvement; not needed for the diagnosis
Scenario bank
  1. 16 yo M with several months of fatigue and mild jaundice, a new hand tremor, slurred speech and irritability with falling grades; elevated AST and ALT; golden-brown rings at the corneal margins on slit-lamp exam → Defective copper transport in hepatocytes → Wilson disease: ATP7B failure blocks biliary copper excretion and copper loading onto ceruloplasmin, so copper deposits in the liver, basal ganglia and cornea
  2. 19 yo F with 3 months of fatigue and a fine hand tremor; ALT 240, AST 190, bilirubin normal; hepatitis B and C serologies negative; ferritin and transferrin saturation normal; ANA and anti-smooth muscle antibody negative; normal body mass index and no alcohol use → Serum ceruloplasmin → screen for Wilson disease in a young patient with unexplained hepatitis and a tremor; slit-lamp exam and 24-hour urine copper follow
  3. 17 yo F with Hashimoto thyroiditis and 6 weeks of fatigue, joint aches and jaundice; ALT 850, AST 700; serum IgG high; ANA and anti-smooth muscle antibody positive; ceruloplasmin normal; no Kayser-Fleischer rings; normal neurologic exam → Autoimmune hepatitis → corticosteroids, with azathioprine to spare steroids
  4. 21 yo M with 1 year of hand tremor and dysarthria; compensated cirrhosis on imaging, INR 1.3, no ascites or encephalopathy; ceruloplasmin low, 24-hour urine copper high, Kayser-Fleischer rings on slit-lamp exam → Oral penicillamine → symptomatic Wilson disease: lifelong chelation (penicillamine or trientine), zinc later for maintenance
  5. 18 yo F with 1 week of jaundice, now confused; INR 3.2; hemoglobin 7.8 with high reticulocytes and a negative direct Coombs test; Kayser-Fleischer rings on slit-lamp exam; no acetaminophen ingestion → Urgent liver transplantation → fulminant Wilson disease: acute liver failure with Coombs-negative hemolysis does not recover with chelation alone
  6. 14 yo M, asymptomatic, whose 17-year-old sister was just diagnosed with Wilson disease; normal growth and development; normal physical and neurologic exam → Serum ceruloplasmin and liver tests → siblings carry a 1 in 4 risk; add a slit-lamp exam and 24-hour urine copper, and treat presymptomatic disease with zinc
  7. 24 yo M with Wilson disease treated with penicillamine for 3 years; tremor resolved, liver tests now normal, urine copper at target; asks about coming off medication → Stopping copper-lowering therapy → treatment is lifelong; stopping can precipitate acute liver failure
Management Symptomatic disease – copper chelation with penicillamine or trientine, lifelong, with a low-copper diet (avoid shellfish, organ meats, nuts, chocolate and mushrooms) · Maintenance or presymptomatic disease – zinc, which blocks intestinal copper absorption · Fulminant liver failure – urgent liver transplantation, which corrects the liver defect · Family – screen first-degree relatives, siblings above all (a 1 in 4 chance of disease, since it is autosomal recessive), with ceruloplasmin, liver tests and a slit-lamp exam · Never stop – stopping therapy can precipitate acute liver failure
Pearls Psychiatric change or falling school performance can precede the liver findings. A young patient with new psychiatric illness and abnormal liver tests needs a ceruloplasmin · Acute liver failure with a Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia in a teen or young adult is fulminant Wilson disease. It needs a transplant center, not chelation alone · A presumed autoimmune hepatitis in a young patient should have ceruloplasmin checked before steroids · Serum total copper is usually low; urine copper is high
Pairs with Part I Fatty Liver Disease lists Wilson disease among the exclusions: is there tremor or Kayser-Fleischer rings, and is the ceruloplasmin low? Part I Abnormal Liver Tests places Wilson in the hepatocellular pattern: are the transaminases, not the alkaline phosphatase, leading? Part II Hemolytic Anemia covers the other Coombs-negative hemolysis of the young: are there spherocytes and an affected parent, or liver disease with corneal rings? Part I Tick-Borne Illness holds the acute mimic: did confusion with transaminitis arrive over hours with fever and a rash, or over months with a tremor?
Transferable rule When unexplained liver disease comes with a finding outside the liver, identify the organ. Brain, cornea or red cells point to copper, and the lung points to alpha-1 antitrypsin. The pancreas, skin, joints and heart in an older patient point to iron.
Class-vs-memberIncreased intestinal iron absorption: the right class, an inherited metal overload of the liver, but the wrong metal; HFE hemochromatosis presents in middle age with diabetes, skin and joint findings, never tremor or corneal rings.
Unchecked attributeHepatocyte retention of a misfolded protease inhibitor: alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is an inherited liver disease of the young, but its second organ is the lung; it does not explain neuropsychiatric signs or Kayser-Fleischer rings.

edits.html:
Scrotal Pain and Masses

painful scrotum and painless mass: separate workups · torsion vs epididymitis · the two hard pairs · tumor markersWas the onset sudden or gradual, and does the mass transilluminate or change with Valsalva?

The decision point

Separate torsion from epididymitis by timeline, location and infection signs. Torsion is sudden and maximal within minutes to hours. A 3-day escalating course with fever, dysuria and posterior tenderness is epididymitis, a clinical diagnosis. Ultrasound and urology are torsion steps; a clinical picture of epididymitis like this one does not need them.

The acute scrotum – the differential
ConditionOnsetThe tellCremastericNext step
Testicular torsion EmergencySudden, minutesHigh-riding transverse testis, N/V, no feverAbsentEmergent urology – salvage window ~6 h
EpididymitisGradual, daysPosterior tenderness, dysuria, fever; Prehn sign +IntactAntibiotics (clinical dx) + NAAT + UA
OrchitisDaysMumps history, unvaccinatedIntactSupportive
Torsion of appendix testisGradual, prepubertalBlue dot sign, superior poleIntactSupportive
Fournier gangrene EmergencyHoursToxic, crepitus, necrosis; diabetic – Emergent debridement
Scrotal mass (painless tree)
FindingDiagnosis
Bag of worms, ↑ standing/Valsalva, ↓ supineVaricocele – ~90% left-sided (left spermatic vein enters the left renal vein at a right angle)
Right-sided, sudden onset, or fails to decompress supineRetroperitoneal mass or RCC invading the renal vein → abdominal imaging
Transilluminates, uniform, testis palpable withinHydrocele
Enlarges with Valsalva, reducible, doesn't transilluminateInguinal hernia
Firm, fixed, painless, on the testis, no transilluminationTumor → ultrasound + AFP/β-hCG/LDH → inguinal orchiectomy, never transscrotal biopsy
Testicular mass with gynecomastia, ↓ libido, or precocious puberty in a boy; markers normalLeydig cell tumor – a sex cord–stromal tumor secreting testosterone or estrogen. Reinke crystals on histology. Mostly benign; the hormonal syndrome is the tell, and AFP/β-hCG are negative
Testicular mass, heterogeneous with calcification and cystic areas on ultrasound; AFP and/or β-hCG elevatedTeratoma (nonseminomatous). In adults, malignant regardless of maturity; in prepubertal boys, benign – the one tumor whose behavior flips with age. Chemoresistant → resect residual masses after chemotherapy
Tumor marker logic AFP elevated → never a seminoma (AFP, alpha-fetoprotein; it indicates a yolk sac or embryonal/teratoma component) · β-hCG (beta human chorionic gonadotropin) can rise in seminoma and nonseminoma; only AFP is exclusionary · both markers normal with a solid mass → pure seminoma or a sex cord–stromal tumor (Leydig, Sertoli); a hormonal syndrome separates them · LDH (lactate dehydrogenase) tracks tumor burden, not histology · Sertoli cell tumor is, like Leydig, stromal and usually benign, but is typically hormonally silent.
Pearls Epididymitis treatment splits by age · <35 / sexually active → ceftriaxone + doxycycline · >35 / low STI risk (STI, sexually transmitted infection) → levofloxacin or TMP-SMX (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) · varicocele is the most common correctable cause of male infertility; testicular size discrepancy in an adolescent is the surgical indication · seminoma never makes AFP (alpha-fetoprotein).
The two hard pairs
  • Varicocele vs. indirect inguinal hernia – both non-transilluminating, both enlarge with Valsalva. Separators: a hernia is reducible, feels like soft tissue or bowel, and you cannot palpate above it (it descends through the canal). A varicocele feels like worms, isn't reducible, and is confined to the scrotum.
  • Varicocele vs. spermatocele – both sit above and separate from the testis. Separators: the spermatocele transilluminates and does not change with position or Valsalva.
  • Femoral hernia presents below the inguinal ligament in the upper thigh, in older women, and anatomically cannot reach the scrotum – high incarceration risk.
Varicocele mechanism ~90% left-sided: the left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein at a right angle · possible "nutcracker" compression between the aorta and the SMA (superior mesenteric artery) · the right gonadal vein drains obliquely into the IVC (inferior vena cava) · subfertility comes from increased scrotal temperature impairing spermatogenesis; a varicocele may also cause ipsilateral atrophy · treatment: observation if asymptomatic · gonadal vein ligation or embolization for pain, >20% testicular volume discrepancy in adolescents, or abnormal semen analysis · scrotal support and NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) for older men not seeking fertility · a varicocele in a prepubertal child, right-sided, or persistent when supine is secondary until proven otherwise · in children think Wilms (with hypertension from renin secretion); in adults think RCC (renal cell carcinoma) invading the renal vein
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Exam with cremasteric reflexFirstAbsent reflex, high-riding transverse testis, sudden painTorsion: emergent urology; do not wait for imaging
Scrotal Doppler ultrasoundBy branchAbsent blood flow to the testisTorsion, used only when the exam is equivocal
Urinalysis and NAAT for chlamydia and gonorrheaSupportsPyuria or a positive NAATEpididymitis, a clinical diagnosis: treat without waiting on results
Transillumination of a painless massFirstMass glows, testis palpable within or separateHydrocele or spermatocele; a solid, dark mass needs ultrasound
Scrotal ultrasound with AFP, beta-hCG and LDHBy branchSolid intratesticular massTesticular tumor; an elevated AFP excludes pure seminoma
Radical inguinal orchiectomyConfirmsHistology names the tumorDiagnostic and therapeutic; never transscrotal biopsy
Ultrasound in gradual, febrile, posterior painSkipWould add delay, not a decisionEpididymitis is clinical; imaging is a torsion answer
Scenario bank
  1. Right-sided varicocele, sudden onset, or one that fails to decompress supine → Retroperitoneal mass or RCC invading the renal vein → abdominal CT
  2. Mass transilluminates with the testis palpable within → Hydrocele → observe (infantile hydroceles usually close by age 1)
  3. Reducible mass extending from the inguinal canal, can't get above it → Indirect inguinal hernia → repair
  4. Firm, fixed, on the testis, no positional change → Ultrasound + AFP, β-hCG, LDH → radical inguinal orchiectomy (never transscrotal – it seeds lymphatics). Cryptorchidism is the biggest risk factor, for both testes
  5. Small transilluminating cyst at the superior pole, unchanging → Spermatocele → reassurance
  6. Adolescent with a varicocele and >20% testicular volume discrepancy → Refer for ligation
  7. Groin bulge below the inguinal ligament in an older woman → Femoral hernia → prompt repair
  8. Sudden severe pain, high-riding transverse testis, absent cremasteric reflex → Testicular torsion → emergent surgery
  9. 4 yo M, painless soft scrotal mass superior to the right testicle that does not decompress supine, blood pressure 160/96 → Secondary varicocele from an abdominal mass → abdominal ultrasonography
Transferable rules A 3-day timeline of scrotal pain excludes torsion. When the clinical findings confirm infection well enough, treat rather than image. Also, read the grammatical form of the answer choices before the stem. If every choice is an anatomic process, the question asks for mechanism; if every choice is a test, the next diagnostic step; if every choice is a drug, treatment.

edits.html:
Polyuria

urine osmolality first · solute vs water diuresis · when water deprivation is indicated · desmopressin responseIs the urine dilute, and has the serum sodium already answered what the deprivation test would?

Source vignette Pt – 8 yo M, 2 months of excessive urination, drinking large volumes, irritable and restless; normal growth and milestones; no medications · Vitals – normal · Exam – physical and neurologic examination normal · Labs – Na 142, K 4.2, Cl 100, HCO₃ 24, BUN 30, creatinine 1.0, Ca 9.2, glucose 100 · Urine – specific gravity 1.001, no protein, blood, glucose or ketones; osmolality 120 mOsm/kg; 24-hour output 3.7 L · Q – the most appropriate next step in management; options spanned chest radiography, fractional excretion of sodium, brain MRI, an oral glucose tolerance test, renal ultrasonography and the water deprivation test
The decision point

Urine osmolality 120 is a water diuresis. The kidney is failing to concentrate, so solute diuresis and every test for it are excluded before any hormone is named. Then serum sodium 142, a normal value, makes the deprivation test necessary rather than redundant. A patient who drinks enough to hold his sodium normal has not yet shown the cause of the dilute urine. It may be a failure to make or to respond to vasopressin, or simply a normal kidney excreting a large water intake. Water deprivation is the manoeuvre that forces that distinction. It drives serum osmolality to the point where vasopressin secretion must be maximal, then shows whether the urine concentrates.

The two imaging studies are right tests in the wrong order. MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) localises an established deficiency, and renal ultrasonography localises an established resistance. Both wait on a diagnosis that has not yet been made.

Defining criteria Polyuria – urine output above 3 L/day in an adult, above 2 L/day/m² in a child · Dilute urine – urine osmolality under 300 mOsm/kg, specific gravity under 1.006 · Concentrated urine – 600 mOsm/kg or above, meaning the kidney can concentrate and the diuresis is driven by solute · Deprivation endpoint – water withheld until serum sodium exceeds 145 and serum osmolality exceeds 295, the point at which vasopressin secretion should be maximal · Deprivation result – urine above 600 is primary polydipsia, urine still under 300 is an AVP disorder · Desmopressin result – urine osmolality rises in deficiency and stays low in resistance
FigureWhen water deprivation testing is indicatedshow

Redrawn from the published indications flowchart. Two deliberate changes: the concentrated-urine branch is labelled with what it means – solute diuresis – rather than only with what not to do, and the indicated branch carries its own interpretation, because the exam asks what the deprivation test showed about as often as it asks whether to order it.

Polyuria with dilute urine – the differentialand the two mimics that never need the test
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Primary polydipsiaDrinking drives the urine; psychiatric illness, or a drug that creates thirstSerum sodium low or low-normal; urine concentrates above 600 after deprivationNot excluded – this is one of the two the test is between
AVP deficiency (central DI)Impaired production or release: trauma, neurosurgery, craniopharyngioma or germinoma, hypophysitis, sarcoid or histiocytosis, a familial AVP mutation, pregnancyUrine stays dilute after deprivation, then rises with desmopressinNot excluded – the desmopressin step is what names it
AVP resistance (nephrogenic DI)The kidney ignores the hormone: AVPR2 or AQP2 mutation, hypercalcaemia, severe hypokalaemia, lithium, chronic tubulointerstitial diseaseUrine stays dilute after desmopressin too; in a child, usually hereditaryNot excluded – complete resistance leaves the osmolality unchanged, partial raises it slightly
Solute (osmotic) diuresisGlucosuria in uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, or an osmotic diuretic such as mannitolPolyuria with a urine osmolality above 600; no deprivation test neededUrine osmolality 120, serum glucose 100, urine glucose negative
SIADHThe mirror image – water retained rather than lost; malignancy, CNS and pulmonary disease, drugsConcentrated urine with hyponatraemia, and no polyuriaDilute urine and a normal sodium – the opposite of the finding
Treatment, and the one child who must not be tested AVP deficiency – desmopressin in nearly all patients, oral, intranasal or parenteral; other agents are rarely needed · AVP resistance – remove the cause first (stop the lithium, correct the calcium and the potassium), then a thiazide with a low-sodium diet as first line; a low-protein diet cuts the solute load further; indomethacin is adjunct; amiloride is the one for lithium, because it blocks lithium entry into the collecting duct · Supervision – the deprivation test is performed in hospital in older children and adults, and is not performed in very young children, because the hypernatraemia it deliberately produces is dangerous in a child who cannot ask for water
Decision spine

1. Is the urine dilute or concentrated? Urine osmolality of 600 or above means the kidney concentrates, so look for solute, not for a hormone. 2. Is there glucose in the urine? Glucosuria explains the whole picture without a hormone. 3. Is the sodium above 145 with osmolality above 295? Then the AVP (arginine vasopressin) disorder is already proven; go straight to desmopressin. 4. Is the sodium frankly low? Polyuria with hyponatraemia is primary polydipsia and needs no deprivation test. 5. Is the sodium normal? That is the only value that calls for the test. 6. After deprivation, did desmopressin raise the urine osmolality? If yes, it is deficiency, so image the brain. If no, it is resistance, so look at the kidney and the drug list.

Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Urine osmolalityFirstDilute, under 300 mOsm/kgWater diuresis; 600 or above means solute, such as glucose
Serum sodium and osmolalityNextSodium normalDiagnosis open: deprivation test; high sodium or low sodium has already answered it
Water deprivation test, inpatientBy branchUrine concentrates over 600Primary polydipsia; still under 300 means an AVP disorder
Desmopressin challengeConfirmsUrine osmolality risesAVP deficiency; unchanged means AVP resistance
MRI of the brainCauseSellar or hypothalamic lesionCause of AVP deficiency
Calcium, potassium and drug listCauseHigh calcium, low potassium or lithiumReversible AVP resistance
Serum vasopressin levelSkipToo unstable to measure routinelyThe desmopressin response is the assay
Scenario bank
  1. 8 yo M, 2 months of polyuria and polydipsia, normal growth and neurologic examination, Na 142, glucose 100, urine specific gravity 1.001 and osmolality 120, output 3.7 L/day → Water deprivation test → a normal sodium is what leaves the diagnosis open
  2. 10 yo M with polyuria, serum Na 149 and serum osmolality 302, urine osmolality 110 → Desmopressin challenge → the deprivation endpoint has already been reached spontaneously
  3. 12 yo F whose urine osmolality stayed at 150 through deprivation and then rose to 620 after desmopressin → MRI of the brain → AVP deficiency needs its cause localized
  4. 9 yo M whose urine osmolality is 140 after deprivation and unchanged after desmopressin, with normal calcium, potassium and no medications → A thiazide with a low-sodium diet → first line once resistance is established and reversible causes are excluded
  5. 8 yo M for whom water deprivation testing has been chosen → Admit for supervised inpatient testing → the test works by producing hypernatremia deliberately
  6. 20-month-old with polyuria and a serum sodium of 148 → Water deprivation testing → severe hypernatremia in a child who cannot obtain water
  7. 14 yo M with polyuria and weight loss, urine osmolality 650, serum glucose 420, urine glucose 4+ → Osmotic diuresis → a concentrating kidney moves the problem to solute
  8. 30 yo F on an antipsychotic with polyuria, urine osmolality 90 and serum sodium 128 → Primary polydipsia → polyuria with hyponatremia needs no deprivation test
  9. Child with polyuria whose urine remains dilute when fluids are withheld → Desmopressin after water deprivation → the hormone itself is too unstable in a sample to measure routinely; serial urine osmolality is what is read
  10. 17 yo F with polyuria, constipation and a serum calcium of 12.8 → Hypercalcemia blunts the response to vasopressin → an acquired, reversible AVP resistance; at the collecting duct
Pearls A sodium above 145 makes the test redundant. A sodium below normal already means primary polydipsia. Only a normal sodium calls for the test. · Serum vasopressin is not measured: its half-life is short and it is unstable in the sample, so the desmopressin response is the assay · AVP deficiency – the current name for central diabetes insipidus · AVP resistance – the current name for nephrogenic diabetes insipidus · Hypothalamic injury kills the magnocellular cell bodies and the deficiency is permanent; injury below the infundibulum is usually transient, because those cell bodies survive · Pregnancy can produce a transient deficiency through placental vasopressinase; it resolves with delivery and returns in the next pregnancy · Lithium causes resistance by inhibiting aquaporin-2, and amiloride is the agent that blocks lithium's entry into the cell
Pairs with Part I Enuresis already links a very low specific gravity to diabetes insipidus and to this test. This brief covers what happens after the test is ordered. Brain Tumors in a Child covers the causes of AVP (arginine vasopressin) deficiency and the post-operative case where the diagnosis is not in doubt. Hypercalcemia covers the commonest acquired resistance. Ask: is the serum sodium high, low, or normal?
Transferable rule When the kidney is making dilute urine, the serum sodium shows whether a water deprivation test is still needed. A high sodium already confirms an AVP (arginine vasopressin) disorder; a low sodium already means primary polydipsia. Only a normal sodium calls for the test.
Sequencing trapMRI (magnetic resonance imaging) of the brain: the right study once a deficiency is proven, and nothing has been proven yet.
Sequencing trapRenal ultrasonography: it images the kidney, which is implicated only if desmopressin fails.
Salient decoyA BUN (blood urea nitrogen) of 30 pulls toward renal disease, but the creatinine is 1.0 and the defect is concentration, not filtration.
True-fact-wrong-slotFractional excretion of sodium: it measures perfusion, and perfusion is not in question here.
Salient decoyChest radiography: it looks for SIADH (syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion), which produces concentrated urine and hyponatraemia, both opposite to the findings here.
