edits.html:
Acute Kidney Injury in a Child

the labs assign the compartment · prerenal pattern · ibuprofen with volume loss · sediment · fluids, stop the drugIs the kidney still concentrating, and what does the sediment show?

Source vignette Pt – 4 yo M, 3 days of vomiting and diarrhea, taking ibuprofen · Labs – BUN/creatinine ratio 32:1, specific gravity 1.028, bland urinalysis · Q – the most appropriate next step; options spanned isotonic fluids with stopping the ibuprofen, furosemide and renal ultrasonography
The decision point

In any AKI (acute kidney injury), use the laboratory data to assign the injury compartment before using the drug to assign the mechanism. BUN/Cr >20:1 + specific gravity >1.020 + bland sediment = prerenal (BUN/Cr, blood urea nitrogen to creatinine ratio). In prerenal injury the kidneys are hypoperfused but intact and still concentrating. Ibuprofen acts hemodynamically. Hypovolemia makes GFR (glomerular filtration rate) prostaglandin-dependent, and COX (cyclooxygenase) inhibition constricts the afferent arteriole. The sediment and the 3-day timeline exclude drug-induced interstitial nephritis.

Defining criteria Prerenal pattern – BUN/Cr >20:1, specific gravity >1.020, bland urine sediment · ATN pattern – muddy brown casts, specific gravity ≈1.010, BUN/Cr <20:1 · Mechanism here – volume depletion makes GFR prostaglandin-dependent; NSAIDs constrict the afferent arteriole
Pediatric oliguria – cause by compartment
CauseIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Prerenal (NSAID + hypovolemia)vomiting/diarrhea; NSAID constricts the afferent arterioleBUN/Cr >20:1 + SG >1.020 + bland sediment
AINacute interstitial nephritisdrug hypersensitivity – NSAIDs after weeks, β-lactams, PPIsfever, rash, eosinophilia; WBCs/WBC casts
ATNacute tubular necrosisischemia or direct toxins (aminoglycosides, contrast)muddy brown casts; SG ≈1.010
HUS Can't missShiga toxin E coli, 5–10 days after bloody diarrheaschistocytes + thrombocytopenia + hematuria/proteinuria
Immune-complex GNPSGN, IgA nephropathypost-streptococcal (2–4 wk) or gross hematuria with URIhematuria + proteinuria ± low C3
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
BUN and creatinineFirstBUN/Cr ratio over 20:1Prerenal pattern
Urinalysis with specific gravityNextSpecific gravity over 1.020, bland sedimentIntact tubules still concentrating: prerenal
Urine microscopyBy branchMuddy brown casts, specific gravity about 1.010Acute tubular necrosis
Urine sediment and CBC with differentialBy branchWBC casts, with eosinophilia or rashAcute interstitial nephritis: stop the drug
CBC and peripheral smearBy branchSchistocytes with low plateletsHemolytic uremic syndrome after bloody diarrhea
Isotonic fluids and stopping the NSAIDConfirmsCreatinine falls with volumePrerenal AKI, confirmed by the response
Renal ultrasonographySkipUsually normal in prerenal AKIAdds nothing once the labs assign the compartment
Scenario bank
  1. 4 yo M, 3 days of vomiting and diarrhea on ibuprofen, BUN/Cr 32:1, SG 1.028, bland urinalysis → Isotonic fluids and stop the ibuprofen
  2. 5 yo F, bloody diarrhea 6 days ago, now pallor, petechiae, oliguria, schistocytes on smear → Hemolytic uremic syndrome → supportive care; avoid antibiotics and antimotility agents
  3. 68 yo F on naproxen for 3 weeks, fever, rash, eosinophilia, WBC casts → Acute interstitial nephritis → stop the NSAID
  4. 60 yo M after septic hypotension, SG 1.010, muddy brown granular casts, BUN/Cr 14:1 → Ischemic acute tubular necrosis
  5. 74 yo M on lisinopril and furosemide who starts ibuprofen, creatinine rising from 1.1 to 2.0 → Discontinue the ibuprofen and give fluids → the "triple whammy" of ACE inhibitor, diuretic and NSAID
  6. 16 yo M, gross hematuria 2 days into a URI, normal C3 → IgA nephropathy → timing with the URI and normal complement decide
  7. 7 yo M, cola-colored urine and periorbital edema 2 weeks after pharyngitis, low C3 → Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis → supportive care
Pearls Prostaglandins dilate the afferent arteriole, and angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole. An NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug) and an ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor drop GFR (glomerular filtration rate) from opposite ends. An NSAID plus an ACE inhibitor or ARB (angiotensin II receptor blocker) plus a diuretic is the "triple whammy" · FENa (fractional excretion of sodium) <1% supports prerenal but is unreliable after diuretics · the AIN (acute interstitial nephritis) triad is present in a minority; WBC (white blood cell) casts carry the diagnosis · PSGN (poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis) vs IgA nephropathy is timing plus complement. PSGN comes 2–4 weeks after the infection with low C3; IgA nephropathy comes during the URI (upper respiratory infection) with normal C3.
Pairs with Part I Anemia with Thrombocytopenia covers sorting by smear and coagulation studies when renal failure comes with a falling platelet count.
Transferable rule Read the ratio, then the specific gravity, then the sediment, and only then the drug. When a full chemistry panel is given, read it before answering.
Salient decoyDrug-induced interstitial nephritis: the named drug draws attention to it, but the timeline and the sediment are wrong.
True-fact-wrong-slotHUS (hemolytic uremic syndrome): gastroenteritis cues it, but it needs bloody diarrhea, schistocytes and an active sediment.

edits.html:
Posterior Urethral Valves

one upstream lesion behind Potter sequence · a palpable bladder names the cause · mimics orphan a finding · drain, then imageWhich single lesion explains every finding, and is there a bladder to feel?

Source vignette Pt – term newborn boy, respiratory distress, flat facies, clubfeet, distended abdomen with a suprapubic midline mass · Q – the most likely diagnosis; options spanned posterior urethral valves, bilateral renal agenesis and congenital diaphragmatic hernia
The decision point

Two independent sets of findings trace to a single lesion upstream of both. Flat facies, clubfeet and pulmonary hypoplasia mean fetal constraint and failed alveolar development, so oligohydramnios occurred. That establishes the sequence but not its cause. Distended abdomen with a soft suprapubic midline mass in a male is a distended bladder, which establishes the cause.

In a newborn boy, bladder outlet obstruction is posterior urethral valves until proven otherwise. Two mimics each explain one finding and leave the rest unexplained. A diaphragmatic hernia explains the respiratory distress, and a Wilms tumour explains the mass.

Defining criteria Oligohydramnios – amniotic fluid index at or below 5 cm, or a single deepest pocket under 2 cm · Potter sequence – the cascade downstream of oligohydramnios: pulmonary hypoplasia, flattened facies, positional limb deformities · Sequence versus syndrome – one initiating defect producing a cascade, versus one cause producing independent anomalies · Why the lungs fail – fetal urine is the major source of amniotic fluid after about 16 weeks, so anything that stops urine output stops lung growth
The newborn with Potter sequence - the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Posterior urethral valvesObstructing membrane in the posterior urethra, males onlyPotter sequence with a palpable suprapubic bladder; weak urinary stream
Bilateral renal agenesisNo kidneys, no urine, anhydramniosPotter sequence with no bladder to palpate and anuria
Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney diseaseEnlarged echogenic kidneys, hepatic fibrosisBilateral flank masses with hepatomegaly
Preterm premature rupture of membranesFluid leaks out despite normal kidneysMaternal fluid leakage with a normal renal ultrasound
Prune belly syndromeDeficient abdominal wall musculatureWrinkled lax abdomen and bilateral undescended testes
Congenital diaphragmatic herniaViscera herniate and crush the lungScaphoid abdomen, bowel gas in the chest
Duodenal atresiaBlocks fetal swallowing of fluidPolyhydramnios, the opposite direction; double bubble
Prenatal hydronephrosis: the differential by level
DiagnosisDilated segmentsBladderThe tell
Posterior urethral valvesRenal pelvis and both uretersThick-walled, trabeculatedBoy with a weak, dribbling stream
Neurogenic bladderRenal pelvis and both uretersThick-walled, trabeculatedSpinal dysraphism or an abnormal lower-limb neurologic exam
Vesicoureteral refluxRenal pelvis and ureter, one or both sidesNormal wallNormal stream; the voiding cystourethrogram shows reflux into the ureters
Duplicated renal collecting systemUsually one side, in one of the two moietiesNormal wallTwo ureters draining one kidney
Ureteropelvic junction obstructionRenal pelvis onlyNormalNo hydroureter; the most common obstructive cause of prenatal hydronephrosis
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Prenatal ultrasoundScreenOligohydramnios with a distended bladder and hydronephrosisOutlet obstruction in a male fetus
Renal and bladder ultrasoundFirstThick-walled distended bladder, bilateral hydroureteronephrosisOutlet obstruction; ultrasound cannot confirm valves
BUN, creatinine and electrolytesStagingCreatinine risingRenal function; correct electrolytes while the bladder drains
Chest radiographSupportsLow lung volumesPulmonary hypoplasia, the usual cause of death
Voiding cystourethrogramConfirmsDilated, elongated posterior urethra, trabeculated bladderPosterior urethral valves, often with secondary reflux
CystoscopyConfirmsValve leaflets seen and ablatedConfirms and treats in one step
Scenario bank
  1. Term newborn boy, respiratory distress, flat facies, clubfeet, distended abdomen with a suprapubic midline mass → Posterior urethral valves → bladder catheterization
  2. Newborn boy with Potter sequence and a distended bladder, most appropriate next step → Bladder catheterization to decompress, then VCUG → renal ultrasound cannot confirm the diagnosis
  3. Newborn, flat facies, clubfeet, severe respiratory distress, anuric at 48 h, no palpable bladder or kidneys → Bilateral renal agenesis
  4. Newborn, Potter facies, respiratory distress, bilateral flank masses, hepatomegaly → Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease → renal ultrasound
  5. Newborn at 32 wk, mother reports clear fluid leaking for 6 weeks, flat facies, clubfeet, respiratory distress, normal renal ultrasound → Preterm premature rupture of membranes
  6. Newborn girl with a distended bladder and bilateral hydronephrosis → Ureterocele → voiding cystourethrogram
  7. Newborn with a wrinkled, lax abdominal wall, bilateral undescended testes, and a dilated urinary tract → Prune belly syndrome
  8. Term newborn with severe distress at delivery, a scaphoid abdomen, heart sounds displaced to the right, bowel gas in the left hemithorax → Congenital diaphragmatic hernia → intubate and place a nasogastric tube
  9. Newborn with bilious vomiting, a double bubble on x-ray, and maternal polyhydramnios → Duodenal atresia
  10. 3 yo with a painless unilateral flank mass that does not cross the midline, hematuria and hypertension → Wilms tumor → abdominal ultrasound
  11. 2 do M, no prenatal care, one wet diaper since birth, weight up 60 g from birth, abdomen distended, saturation 88% with diminished breath sounds and low lung volumes on chest film, urethral meatus intact → Renal and bladder ultrasound → ultrasound precedes the voiding cystourethrogram
  12. Newborn boy whose renal and bladder ultrasound shows a thick-walled distended bladder with bilateral hydroureteronephrosis → Voiding cystourethrogram → posterior urethral dilation confirms the diagnosis
  13. Newborn boy with posterior urethral valves and Potter sequence → Pulmonary hypoplasia → fetal urine makes the amniotic fluid that grows the lungs
  14. Fetus with duodenal atresia → Polyhydramnios → the fetus cannot swallow amniotic fluid; the mirror of the renal lesions
  15. 2 do M, hydronephrosis first seen on prenatal ultrasound at 28 weeks, feeding well, normal vital signs, normal urine output but a weak stream that dribbles; ultrasound shows bilateral hydronephrosis and hydroureter with a thick-walled bladder → Posterior urethral valves → voiding cystourethrogram confirms; endoscopic valve ablation treats
  16. 8 mo M with a repaired lumbosacral myelomeningocele, constant dribbling of urine and recurrent urinary tract infections; ultrasound shows a thick-walled, trabeculated bladder with bilateral hydroureteronephrosis → Neurogenic bladder → clean intermittent catheterization
  17. 3 wk old M with left hydronephrosis first seen on prenatal ultrasound; ultrasound now shows a dilated left renal pelvis and calyces, a single normal-caliber left ureter, a normal bladder and a strong stream → Ureteropelvic junction obstruction → the ureter and bladder are spared
The order of operations Decompress the bladder before imaging, and image before surgery. Place a urethral catheter first, then obtain a voiding cystourethrogram. The cystourethrogram is the confirmatory study; it shows a dilated posterior urethra and a thick-walled trabeculated bladder. Renal ultrasound shows hydronephrosis but cannot confirm the diagnosis. Then complete VACTERL-style screening (vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal and limb anomalies) with echocardiography and renal ultrasound, and perform surgical valve ablation.
Pearls Fetal urine is needed for lung growth, so pulmonary hypoplasia rather than renal failure is the cause of death in Potter sequence · Posterior urethral valves is a male-only diagnosis; a newborn girl with the same picture has a ureterocele or urethral atresia · A sequence is one defect cascading; a syndrome is independent anomalies from a shared cause · The neonatal renal mass differential is hydronephrosis first, then multicystic dysplastic kidney; the neonatal renal tumour is congenital mesoblastic nephroma, not Wilms · Neuroblastoma crosses the midline and Wilms does not
How NBME framed it The stem split the level of obstruction across three findings (prenatal image, voiding exam, postnatal image), and normal urine output drew attention away from obstruction. Every option was a congenital urinary tract cause of hydronephrosis, separated only by the level of the lesion.
Pairs with Part II Tracheoesophageal Fistula and Esophageal Atresia is the mechanistic counterpart. A fetus that cannot make urine develops oligohydramnios, and one that cannot swallow develops polyhydramnios. Part II Lung Disease in the Newborn and Preterm Infant also pairs with this brief; there the fork is whether the lungs are structurally normal. Part I Urinary Tract Infection in a Child sits at the other end of the same imaging pathway. There the voiding cystourethrogram grades reflux; here it finds the obstructing valve. Part II Abdominal Mass in a Young Child covers the solid flank mass after infancy. Part II Spinal Dysraphism covers the neurogenic bladder that mimics valves: is the spine or lower-limb neurologic exam abnormal?
The imaging sequence, and the weight clue Order – renal and bladder ultrasound first, then a voiding cystourethrogram if the ultrasound is abnormal, then cystoscopy to confirm and ablate; bladder drainage and electrolyte correction run alongside · Weight gain in the first 48 hours is abnormal – newborns lose weight, so a gaining newborn is retaining, and in a boy with a distended abdomen what he is retaining is urine
Transferable rule When findings span three unrelated organ systems, look for the one lesion upstream of all of them. For each candidate, name the findings it leaves unexplained, and reject it if any remain.
Class-vs-memberDiaphragmatic hernia and Wilms: each explains the most prominent finding and leaves the rest unexplained.
Trump-card inversionDuodenal atresia: it causes polyhydramnios, the opposite of the oligohydramnios the clubfeet prove.
True-fact-wrong-slotTransient tachypnea: it is mild and self-limited, and cannot explain a mass or clubfeet.
Unchecked attributeDuplicated renal collecting system: it can cause prenatal hydronephrosis with a dilated ureter; it usually involves one kidney and does not thicken the bladder wall or weaken the stream.
Mirror twinNeurogenic bladder: it shares the thick-walled bladder, bilateral hydroureteronephrosis and dribbling; a normal spine and normal neurologic exam leave the urethral outlet as the lesion.
Salient decoyUreteropelvic junction obstruction: it is the most common obstructive cause of prenatal hydronephrosis; it dilates the renal pelvis only, so dilated ureters and a thick bladder wall exclude it.
True-fact-wrong-slotVesicoureteral reflux: it also causes bilateral hydroureteronephrosis; primary reflux leaves the bladder wall and stream normal, and reflux in a boy with valves is secondary to them.

edits.html:
Urinary Incontinence

stress, urge, overflow, fistula · the postvoid residual splits the differential · cough stress test · drug pairingsWhat is the postvoid residual, and which diagnosis does that number make impossible?

Source vignette Pt – woman with urinary leakage; no pelvic surgery, obstetric injury, malignancy or radiation · Labs – postvoid residual 800 mL · Q – the most likely diagnosis; options spanned overflow, stress and urge incontinence and vesicovaginal fistula
The decision point

Postvoid residual 800 mL. Retention of 800 mL points to overflow incontinence. The PVR (postvoid residual) splits the entire differential before any symptom is weighed.

Fistula is not merely unsupported but mechanically impossible. A bladder draining continuously through a fistula cannot hold 800 mL. Two further findings exclude it. Fistula requires pelvic surgery, obstetric injury, malignancy, or radiation, and all are absent. Fistula shows urine pooling in the vagina, but the examination shows no abnormalities.

A positive cough stress test A positive cough stress test normally means stress incontinence. However, a chronically overdistended bladder leaks with any rise in intra-abdominal pressure, so the test loses specificity once the PVR (postvoid residual) is high. A positive test can fail to mean what it usually means, just as a negative test can fail to exclude. In each case, context sets a test's operating characteristics.
Urinary incontinence types
TypeMechanismPresentationPVRTreatment
StressUrethral hypermobility / sphincter deficiencyLeaks with cough, sneeze, liftingLowPelvic floor → pessary → midurethral sling
Urge (OAB)Detrusor overactivitySudden urge then leakage, frequency, nocturiaLowBladder training → antimuscarinic or mirabegron → Botox
OverflowDetrusor underactivity or outlet obstructionHesitancy, weak stream, dribbling, recurrent UTIHIGHIntermittent catheterization; bethanechol; α-blocker if obstructive; stop anticholinergics
FunctionalCognitive or mobility barrierCan't reach the toilet; tract normalNormalScheduled toileting
FistulaAbnormal communicationContinuous leakage, vaginal urine poolingNormal/lowDye test, cystoscopy → repair
The causal chain & a drug pairing T1DM (type 1 diabetes mellitus) since age 6 causes diabetic autonomic neuropathy. The neuropathy causes detrusor underactivity and retention. Retention causes overflow leakage and the recurrent UTIs (urinary tract infections) from stasis. Oxybutynin treats urge incontinence and would worsen overflow. The same drug causes fecal impaction. Gut motility down, bladder emptying down: when oxybutynin appears on an elderly or diabetic patient's medication list, check both.
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
UrinalysisFirstPyuria and nitritesUTI: treat; not chronic incontinence
Postvoid residualSupportsHigh residual volumeOverflow: detrusor underactivity or outlet obstruction
Cough stress testBy branchLeakage with cough, low residualStress incontinence
UrodynamicsBy branchMixed retention and urgencyNeurogenic bladder, such as multiple sclerosis
Dye test and cystoscopyBy branchDye in the vaginaVesicovaginal fistula after surgery, delivery or radiation
Autonomic neuropathy screenCauseOrthostatic hypotension, gastroparesis, resting tachycardiaDiabetic autonomic neuropathy behind detrusor underactivity
Cough stress test with a high residualSkipPositive from overdistension aloneDoes not establish stress incontinence
Scenario bank
  1. 58 yo F, leaks only when coughing, PVR 30, four vaginal deliveries → Stress incontinence → pelvic floor exercises first
  2. 68 yo F, sudden urge then leakage with nocturia, PVR 40 → Urge incontinence from detrusor overactivity
  3. 72 yo M, hesitancy and weak stream, PVR 350, enlarged prostate → Overflow incontinence from outlet obstruction → α-blocker ± 5-α-reductase inhibitor
  4. 28 yo F, continuous leakage two weeks after a difficult delivery, vaginal urine pooling → Vesicovaginal fistula
  5. 84 yo F with dementia, wets before reaching the bathroom, tract normal → Functional incontinence
  6. 68 yo F on oxybutynin with rising PVR and retention → Anticholinergic-induced retention → stop the drug
  7. 45 yo F, urgency and frequency with dysuria, pyuria and nitrites → Urinary tract infection → not chronic incontinence
  8. 40 yo F with multiple sclerosis, mixed retention and urgency → Neurogenic bladder → urodynamics
  9. 32 yo F, T1DM, PVR 800 → Screen for autonomic neuropathy → gastroparesis, orthostatic hypotension and resting tachycardia
Boundary conditions A high PVR (postvoid residual) suggests that overflow is present, not that it is the only mechanism; mixed incontinence is common. A positive cough test may reflect a real coexisting stress component. A PVR is only interpretable when measured after a normal void. PVR thresholds in adults: under 50 mL argues against overflow; over 200 mL suggests overflow as a main contributor.
Transferable rule When a quantitative measure of organ function is given, check whether each candidate diagnosis is compatible with that number before weighing symptoms. Exclude a diagnosis the physiology forbids without arguing from symptoms.

edits.html:
Abdominal Mass in a Young Child

organ of origin · age · Wilms tumor vs neuroblastoma · cystic newborn masses · ultrasound, then CT or MRIWhere does the mass arise, and how old is the child?

Source vignette Pt – 3 yo F at a well-child visit, normal development and immunizations; BP 156/96; mild right upper and lower quadrant tenderness with a palpable right-sided abdominal mass · Imaging – ultrasound shows a 12-cm heterogeneous solitary mass arising within the upper pole of the right kidney · Q – the most likely diagnosis; options spanned Wilms tumor, neuroblastoma, pheochromocytoma, polycystic kidney disease and renal cell carcinoma
The decision point

Ask two questions of any solid abdominal mass in a child: which organ does it arise from, and how old is the child. A mass within the kidney in a 2- to 5-year-old is Wilms tumor. The hypertension fits Wilms tumor and comes from renin secretion or compression of the renal vessels.

Neuroblastoma is the nearest mimic and also causes hypertension, through catecholamines. It arises from neural crest in the adrenal or sympathetic chain and displaces the kidney rather than growing inside it. It usually presents before age 2 and may cross the midline. Pheochromocytoma is also adrenal and presents with episodes of headache, sweating and palpitations.

Abdominal mass in a young child: the differential
DiagnosisAge and originThe NBME tellWhy less likely here
Wilms tumorPeak age 2 to 5; arises within the kidney; child usually looks wellSmooth unilateral flank mass that does not cross the midline; hypertension, hematuria; WAGR, Beckwith-Wiedemann, Denys-Drash; AFP not raised – (the answer)
NeuroblastomaUsually under 2; neural crest of the adrenal medulla or sympathetic chainIrregular mass that may cross the midline, calcifications, raised urine VMA and HVA; periorbital ecchymoses (raccoon eyes), opsoclonus-myoclonus; often an ill childMass lies within the kidney; age 3
PheochromocytomaOlder child or adult; adrenal medulla, often syndromicEpisodic headache, sweating, palpitations with hypertension; raised metanephrinesAdrenal sits on the kidney, not within it; no paroxysms
Hydronephrosis or multicystic dysplastic kidneyNewborn or infant; the commonest neonatal abdominal massesFluid-filled on ultrasound: a dilated collecting system, or noncommunicating cysts with no functioning kidneySolid heterogeneous mass at 3 years
Polycystic kidney diseaseRecessive form in newborns; dominant form in adultsBilateral enlarged cystic kidneys; the newborn form shows large echogenic kidneys and hepatic fibrosisSolitary, unilateral, solid
Renal vein thrombosisNewborn under stress: infant of a diabetic mother, asphyxia, dehydration, polycythemia; clot in the renal veinEnlarged kidney with hematuria and thrombocytopeniaAge 3; well child with a solid mass
HepatoblastomaInfant or toddler; arises in the liver; Beckwith-Wiedemann associationRight upper quadrant hepatic mass with a raised AFPMass arises from the kidney
Renal cell carcinomaAdults; hereditary forms such as VHL present earlierFlank pain, hematuria and a mass in an adultAge 3
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Abdominal ultrasoundFirstSolid mass within the kidneyWilms tumor; a suprarenal calcified mass suggests neuroblastoma; a cystic mass suggests hydronephrosis or MCDK
CT or MRI of the abdomenNextExtent of the tumor, nodes, the other kidneyLocal staging and surgical planning
Urine VMA and HVABy branchRaised catecholamine metabolitesNeuroblastoma; normal in Wilms tumor
Serum AFPBy branchRaised with a liver massHepatoblastoma; not raised in Wilms tumor
Chest CTStagingLung nodulesMetastatic Wilms tumor; the lung is its usual distant site
Excision with pathologyConfirmsNephroblastoma on histologyWilms tumor, staged for chemotherapy with or without radiation
Scenario bank
  1. 3 yo F at a well-child visit, BP 156/96, palpable right abdominal mass; ultrasound shows a 12-cm heterogeneous solid mass arising within the upper pole of the right kidney → Wilms tumor → excision with chemotherapy, with or without radiation
  2. 14 mo M, irritable for weeks, with rapid chaotic eye movements, jerking of the limbs, and a firm irregular abdominal mass crossing the midline; ultrasound shows calcifications → Neuroblastoma → urine VMA and HVA
  3. 18 mo M with weight loss, bruising around both eyes and a firm left upper quadrant mass lying above the kidney on ultrasound → Urine VMA and HVA → neuroblastoma
  4. 2 yo F, well, whose mother felt a firm painless mass in her left flank while bathing her; BP 118/76, mass smooth and does not cross the midline → Abdominal ultrasound → suspected Wilms tumor
  5. 3-day-old boy with a smooth left flank mass; ultrasound shows multiple noncommunicating cysts of varying size replacing the left kidney with no normal parenchyma, right kidney normal → Multicystic dysplastic kidney → nonfunctioning kidney; the other kidney must be checked
  6. 15 yo F with episodes of pounding headache, sweating and palpitations, BP 172/104 during an episode, and a 4-cm mass above the left kidney → Pheochromocytoma → plasma free metanephrines
  7. 6 mo F with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, 1 week of intermittent vomiting and fussiness, macroglossia, right-sided hemihypertrophy and a firm right upper quadrant mass; serum alpha-fetoprotein 15,678 ng/mL, urine homovanillic and vanillylmandelic acid normal → Hepatoblastoma → liver mass with a very high alpha-fetoprotein
  8. 3 yo M with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome; a screening ultrasound shows a 7-cm solid mass arising within the left kidney; serum alpha-fetoprotein and urine catecholamine metabolites are normal → Wilms tumor → kidney origin with a normal alpha-fetoprotein
  9. 9 mo F, fussy, with a firm right upper quadrant mass that ultrasound places within the right lobe of the liver; the kidneys and adrenals are normal → Serum alpha-fetoprotein → hepatoblastoma
  10. Male newborn at 38 weeks after an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery, Apgar scores 8 and 9, normal examination except bilateral flank masses; hematocrit 50%, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, urine with moderate blood and trace protein; ultrasound shows both kidneys enlarged with mixed echogenicity → Polycystic kidney disease → the recessive form; look for hepatic fibrosis
  11. 2-day-old boy whose mother has poorly controlled diabetes, with a new right flank mass, gross hematuria and a platelet count of 70,000/mm3; ultrasound shows one enlarged kidney and a normal left kidney → Renal vein thrombosis → confirm with Doppler ultrasound of the renal vein
Management, in one line Wilms tumor is treated with excision plus chemotherapy, with or without radiation; about 90% of children survive. Tissue at excision or biopsy makes the diagnosis. Ultrasound, not CT (computed tomography), is the first study.
Pearls Establish the origin before weighing age: a mass within the kidney is Wilms tumor; an adrenal or paraspinal mass is neuroblastoma or pheochromocytoma · Hypertension does not separate the two tumors: Wilms raises renin, neuroblastoma releases catecholamines · A well child with a smooth flank mass favors Wilms; an irritable child with weight loss, bone pain or raccoon eyes favors neuroblastoma · Rapid chaotic eye movements with myoclonic jerks in a toddler is opsoclonus-myoclonus, a paraneoplastic sign of neuroblastoma · Two enlarged kidneys in a well newborn suggest ARPKD (autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease); ultrasound shows large echogenic kidneys · ARPKD comes from PKHD1 mutations and brings congenital hepatic fibrosis and Caroli syndrome · Severe ARPKD in utero causes oligohydramnios and Potter sequence · ADPKD (autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease) is the adult form, with kidney and liver cysts and cerebral aneurysms · A creatinine of 0.9 mg/dL on day 1 mirrors the mother's creatinine and does not prove neonatal kidney failure · Neonatal renal vein thrombosis also gives a flank mass and hematuria, usually with thrombocytopenia, in a stressed infant · Avoid repeated deep palpation of a suspected Wilms tumor, because rupture of the capsule spreads tumor · Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome raises the risk of both Wilms tumor and hepatoblastoma, so the syndrome alone cannot pick between them · A firm right upper quadrant mass with a very high AFP (alpha-fetoprotein) in an infant is hepatoblastoma · How NBME framed it: the stem names the syndrome and hides the answer in a lab panel, a very high AFP with normal urine HVA (homovanillic acid) and VMA (vanillylmandelic acid) · A syndrome that carries Wilms risk earns surveillance ultrasounds, covered in Part I Inherited Tumor Syndromes
How NBME framed it For the newborn with two flank masses, the key reads only polycystic kidney disease, and the ultrasound says mixed echogenicity rather than cysts · The options are a mass family sorted by age, three tumors plus one vascular mimic, and the labs plant hematuria and a raised creatinine to fit the decoys
Pairs with Part I Inherited Tumor Syndromes covers WAGR, Beckwith-Wiedemann and the surveillance that follows. Part II Posterior Urethral Valves covers the neonatal flank mass, where hydronephrosis and multicystic dysplastic kidney come first. Part II Acute Leukemia in a Child shares neuroblastoma through marrow infiltration and periorbital ecchymoses. Part I Maternal Effects in the Newborn covers the day-1 creatinine that reflects the mother's kidneys: is the value the mother's or the baby's? Ask: does the mass arise within the kidney, and is the child older than 2?
Transferable rule For a solid mass in a child, name the organ it arises from before naming the tumor, then use age to decide among the rest. A finding two tumors share, such as hypertension, cannot distinguish them.
Unchecked attributeNeuroblastoma is the famous childhood abdominal tumor, but it arises from the adrenal or sympathetic chain and usually before age 2.
Salient decoyPheochromocytoma matches the hypertension and the upper-pole location, but it is adrenal and episodic.
Unchecked attributePolycystic kidney disease gives bilateral cystic kidneys, not one solid mass.
Unchecked attributeRenal cell carcinoma arises within the kidney too, but in adults.
Salient decoyWilms tumor (nephroblastoma): the best-known Beckwith-Wiedemann tumor, but it is a flank mass within the kidney and does not raise AFP (alpha-fetoprotein).
Test-overrides-findingsNeuroblastoma: age 6 months fits it better than Wilms tumor, but urine HVA (homovanillic acid) and VMA (vanillylmandelic acid) are normal.
Unchecked attributeGerm cell tumor: a yolk sac tumor also raises AFP, but in a young child it presents as a pelvic mass, not a firm upper abdominal one.
True-fact-wrong-slotSpina bifida occulta: a raised AFP goes with open neural tube defects in pregnancy, not the closed form, and it makes no abdominal mass.
Unchecked attributeNephroblastoma (Wilms tumor): it shares the flank mass and hematuria; it is usually unilateral and peaks at ages 2 to 5, and this newborn has two masses.
Salient decoyNeuroblastoma: it is the most common solid tumor of infancy; it arises in the adrenal, displaces the kidney rather than enlarging it, and is rarely bilateral.
Unchecked attributeRenal cell carcinoma: it shares a mass within the kidney and hematuria; it is a tumor of adults and adolescents, not newborns.
Unchecked attributeRenal vein thrombosis: it shares a newborn flank mass, hematuria and an enlarged kidney; this baby has no risk factor, with an uncomplicated delivery, good Apgar scores and a normal hematocrit.

edits.html:
Hypokalemia and Acid-Base Disorders in a Child

potassium, acid-base, then blood pressure · anion gap · urine pH during acidosis · distal vs proximal vs type 4Is the gap normal, and is the urine pH above 5.5 during the acidosis?

Source vignette Pt – 18 mo M with poor linear growth; no vomiting or diarrhea; BP 90/60 · Labs – Na 138, Cl 112, K 3.1, bicarbonate 16 mEq/L; urine pH 7.6; arterial pH 7.28 and Pco2 26 mm Hg, with normal oxygenation on room air · Q – the most likely cause of the hypokalemia; options spanned Addison disease, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, hyperparathyroidism, juxtaglomerular cell hyperplasia, pheochromocytoma, primary hyperaldosteronism, pseudohypoaldosteronism, renal artery stenosis and renal tubular acidosis
The decision point

Low potassium with a metabolic acidosis narrows the cause to diarrhea or RTA (renal tubular acidosis). The anion gap is 138 minus (112 plus 16), or 10, so the acidosis is normal gap (hyperchloremic). With no diarrhea, the loss is renal. A urine pH above 5.5 during systemic acidosis means the distal tubule cannot secrete acid. That is distal (type 1) RTA, which wastes potassium and slows growth in young children.

Low potassium with alkalosis is a different group, sorted by blood pressure. High blood pressure points to aldosterone or renin excess. Normal blood pressure points to vomiting, diuretics, or Bartter or Gitelman syndrome. High potassium with a normal-gap acidosis points to low aldosterone effect instead.

Defining criteria Normal anion gap – sodium minus (chloride plus bicarbonate) of about 8 to 12 mEq/L; here it is 10 · Distal renal tubular acidosis – normal-gap acidosis with urine pH above 5.5, usually with low potassium · Proximal renal tubular acidosis – normal-gap acidosis with urine pH below 5.5 once bicarbonate has fallen, often with glucose, phosphate and amino acids in the urine · Type 4 renal tubular acidosis – normal-gap acidosis with high potassium from low aldosterone effect
Low potassium: sorted by potassium, acid-base and blood pressureeach of the nine NBME options sits in one row
PatternCausesWhat separates themWhy less likely here
Low potassium, normal-gap acidosis, normal blood pressureDistal (type 1) renal tubular acidosis; proximal (type 2) renal tubular acidosis; diarrheaUrine pH above 5.5 during acidosis is distal; proximal acidifies the urine once bicarbonate is low and often wastes glucose and phosphate; diarrhea shows in the history and gives a negative urine anion gapThe answer: no diarrhea, and urine pH 7.6 during acidosis
Low potassium, alkalosis, normal blood pressureBartter syndrome (juxtaglomerular cell hyperplasia); Gitelman syndrome; vomiting; diureticsHigh bicarbonate; Bartter raises urine calcium, Gitelman lowers it; vomiting and diuretics come from the historyBicarbonate 16: this child is acidotic
Low potassium, alkalosis, high blood pressurePrimary hyperaldosteronism (renin low); renal artery stenosis (renin high); 11-beta-hydroxylase congenital adrenal hyperplasiaHypertension with alkalosis; renin separates primary aldosterone excess from renin-driven excessBlood pressure 90/60 and an acidosis
High potassium, acidosis, low or normal blood pressureAddison disease; salt-wasting (21-hydroxylase) congenital adrenal hyperplasia; type 1 pseudohypoaldosteronism; type 4 renal tubular acidosisHigh potassium, often with low sodium; aldosterone is low in Addison disease and 21-hydroxylase deficiency, high in type 1 pseudohypoaldosteronismPotassium 3.1 and sodium 138
Episodic high blood pressurePheochromocytomaParoxysms of headache, sweating and palpitations with hypertension; raised metanephrinesNormal blood pressure and no episodes
High calcium, sometimes a mild normal-gap acidosisHyperparathyroidismHigh calcium with a high parathyroid hormone levelNo calcium given, and it does not explain low potassium
Scenario bank
  1. 18 mo M with poor linear growth and no vomiting or diarrhea; BP 90/60; Na 138, Cl 112, K 3.1, HCO3 16 mEq/L; urine pH 7.6; arterial pH 7.28, Pco2 26 mm Hg → Renal tubular acidosis → normal-gap acidosis with urine pH above 5.5 is distal (type 1) renal tubular acidosis
  2. 2 yo F with poor weight gain and polyuria; no vomiting and no diuretic use; BP 88/54; Na 135, Cl 92, K 2.8, HCO3 32 mEq/L; high urine calcium → Bartter syndrome → low potassium with alkalosis, normal blood pressure and high urine calcium
  3. 3 yo M with poor growth and bowed legs; no diarrhea; BP 92/58; Na 138, Cl 113, K 3.2, HCO3 15 mEq/L; normal serum glucose with glucose and phosphate in the urine; urine pH 5.0 → Proximal (type 2) renal tubular acidosis → Fanconi syndrome: the urine acidifies once bicarbonate is low, and glucose and phosphate are wasted
  4. 20 mo F with length below the 3rd percentile; no vomiting or diarrhea; BP 88/56; Na 139, Cl 113, K 3.0, HCO3 15 mEq/L → Urine pH during the acidosis → above 5.5 with a normal-gap acidosis indicates distal renal tubular acidosis
  5. 2 yo M with distal renal tubular acidosis; urine pH 7.0 with HCO3 15 mEq/L and K 3.0 mEq/L; weight and length below the 3rd percentile; nephrocalcinosis on renal ultrasound → Oral alkali therapy with citrate or bicarbonate → correcting the acidosis lets growth recover and lowers urine calcium
  6. 4 yo F with poor growth and nephrocalcinosis on ultrasound; no diarrhea; normal-gap metabolic acidosis with K 3.0 mEq/L; urine pH 6.8 → Impaired hydrogen ion secretion in the distal nephron → distal (type 1) renal tubular acidosis
Management, in one line Treat distal renal tubular acidosis with oral alkali, citrate or bicarbonate, and add potassium when it stays low. Untreated acidosis slows growth in children.
Pearls Distal renal tubular acidosis raises urine calcium and lowers urine citrate, so nephrocalcinosis and kidney stones can follow; serum calcium stays normal · The urine anion gap (urine sodium plus potassium minus chloride) is positive in distal renal tubular acidosis and negative in diarrhea · Winter's formula predicts a Pco2 of 1.5 times 16 plus 8, or 32, plus or minus 2 · The measured 26 is below that range, which suggests an added respiratory alkalosis · Juxtaglomerular cell hyperplasia is the kidney lesion of Bartter syndrome, which gives low potassium with alkalosis and a normal blood pressure
How NBME framed it The lead-in asked for the cause of the hypokalemia, a secondary finding, although the acid-base values decided the answer. The nine options formed a grid of potassium, acid-base status and blood pressure, and only one option fit this child.
Pairs with Part II Abnormal Growth in a Child covers the first step, electrolytes with a venous blood gas when length is also low; this brief covers reading that panel. Part I Hypertension in an Adult covers low potassium with alkalosis and hypertension, where renin separates primary hyperaldosteronism from renal artery stenosis. Part I Polyuria covers the dilute urine that severe hypokalemia can cause. Part I Hypercalcemia covers hyperparathyroidism; distal renal tubular acidosis raises urine calcium, not serum calcium. Ask: is the child acidotic or alkalotic, and is the blood pressure high?
Transferable rule Sort low potassium by acid-base status first, then by blood pressure. Low potassium with a normal-gap acidosis and no diarrhea is renal tubular acidosis, and a urine pH above 5.5 makes it distal.
Unchecked attributeAddison disease: it causes acidosis with a low-normal blood pressure; potassium would be high and sodium low.
Salient decoyCongenital adrenal hyperplasia: an adrenal disorder that affects growth; the salt-wasting form raises potassium, and the hypertensive forms cause alkalosis with high blood pressure.
True-fact-wrong-slotHyperparathyroidism: excess parathyroid hormone can cause a mild normal-gap acidosis; its hallmark is high calcium, and it does not explain low potassium.
Unchecked attributeJuxtaglomerular cell hyperplasia: this is Bartter syndrome, the closest mimic, with low potassium, normal blood pressure and poor growth in a young child; Bartter syndrome causes alkalosis, and this child is acidotic.
Class-vs-memberPheochromocytoma: an adrenal tumor on a list of hormonal causes; it causes episodic hypertension with headache and sweating, and this child is normotensive.
Unchecked attributePrimary hyperaldosteronism: the textbook cause of low potassium; it brings hypertension and alkalosis, and both are absent.
Unchecked attributePseudohypoaldosteronism: it causes a normal-gap acidosis and poor growth in infants; potassium is high in every form.
True-fact-wrong-slotRenal artery stenosis: renin excess does cause low potassium; it brings hypertension and alkalosis, and both are absent.

edits.html:
Child with Puffy Eyes

local to the eye, or the first sign of edema everywhere · red flags · the dipstick splits the branches · minimal change diseaseDoes the swelling belong to the eye or to the whole child, and what does the urine dipstick show?

Source case Pt – 5 yo with puffy eyes, Aquifer Pediatrics 31; the case works from periorbital swelling through generalized edema, fatigue and a growing belly to nephrotic syndrome from minimal change disease · Q – build the differential for periorbital swelling, decide whether the edema is generalized, then diagnose, treat and follow nephrotic syndrome and its complications
The approach

Ask first whether the swelling belongs to the eye or to the whole child. Local swelling comes from allergy (allergic conjunctivitis, an acute allergic reaction) or infection (periorbital cellulitis, conjunctivitis, sinusitis). Generalized edema means protein is lost (nephrotic syndrome, protein-losing enteropathy), not made (liver failure, malnutrition), or salt and water are retained (acute glomerulonephritis, heart failure). Check the airway and the orbit first. In the generalized branch, the urine dipstick eliminates most of the differential at once; the confirmatory test comes last.

Red flags: act before the full history
FindingWhat it points to
Stridor, wheeze, low blood pressure, poor perfusionUnstable: circulation, airway, breathing first
Swollen lips or tongue, or a hoarse voiceAnaphylaxis: intramuscular epinephrine
Proptosis, pain with eye movement, blurred visionOrbital cellulitis: CT and IV antibiotics
Edema with fever, belly pain and reboundSpontaneous peritonitis: cultures, then antibiotics
High blood pressure with headache, vomiting or confusionHypertensive encephalopathy from nephritis

Puffy eyes in a child: the differential

Allergic conjunctivitisLocal: allergyBoth eyes, itchy, watery, ropey mucusSneezing, clear runny nose; seasonal
Acute allergic reactionLocal: allergy, suddenAbrupt swelling of lids, lips or tongueHives, minutes after a food, drug or sting
Periorbital (preseptal) cellulitisLocal: infected lidOne eye; red, warm, tender lidBite, scratch or sinusitis; eye moves freely

Finalists
On arrivalUrinalysisNextConfirmsTreatment and follow-up
Allergic conjunctivitisBoth eyes itchy and watery; sneezingNormalNothing furtherClinicalAvoid the allergen; antihistamine eye drops or oral antihistamine
Periorbital (preseptal) cellulitisOne red, tender lid; fever; eye moves freelyNot neededCheck movement, vision, proptosisClinical; CT only with orbital signsOral antibiotics; recheck in 1 to 2 days
Nephrotic syndrome (minimal change disease)Puffy eyes, then legs, belly, scrotum; BP normal4+ protein, no bloodAlbumin, lipids, creatinineProtein/creatinine ratio; remission on prednisonePrednisone; salt restriction; home dipstick for relapse
Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritisPuffy eyes, dark urine, high BPBlood, casts, some proteinCreatinine, C3Low C3; ASO or anti-DNase BSalt and fluid restriction, furosemide; C3 normal by 8 weeks
Nephrotic syndrome from minimal change disease What it is – heavy proteinuria, albumin below 2.5 g/dL, edema and high lipids; minimal change disease causes 70 to 90% of cases under age 10 · Who – preschool and school-age children; boys about twice as often, a gap that closes by adolescence · Mechanism – the filter loses its negative charge, so albumin and IgG leak; low oncotic pressure moves fluid into the tissues, leaving the plasma volume low, which is why the blood pressure stays normal; the liver makes more lipoprotein and urinary loss of lipoprotein lipase slows clearance · Features – periorbital edema worst on waking, then dependent edema of the legs, scrotum or labia and ascites; tiredness and poor appetite; no blood in the urine, normal blood pressure and creatinine · Diagnosis – dipstick 3+ to 4+ protein, protein/creatinine ratio in the nephrotic range, low albumin, high cholesterol; biopsy only for steroid resistance after 8 weeks, hematuria, hypertension, a high creatinine, or age over 10 to 12 · Treatment – daily prednisone for 4 to 6 weeks, then a taper; salt restriction; albumin with furosemide only for severe edema, since diuretics alone can drop an already low plasma volume · Complications – infection during relapse (spontaneous peritonitis, usually pneumococcal; pneumonia, cellulitis, urinary infection) from urinary loss of IgG and factor B; venous thrombosis, including renal vein thrombosis, from urinary loss of antithrombin III and hemoconcentration; steroid effects: weight gain, hypertension, mood change, high glucose, slowed growth · Follow-up – home urine dipstick; relapse is common and treated with prednisone again; more than 95% respond to steroids, and relapses stop by the end of the second decade without kidney damage; frequent relapsers get a steroid-sparing drug; pneumococcal and yearly influenza vaccines in remission, and no live vaccines on high-dose steroids · Return for – fever or belly pain, swelling that returns, protein on the dipstick, little urine or dizziness, flank or leg pain
What sets it apart

Scenario bank
  1. 5 yo boy with a week of puffy eyelids on both sides, worst when he wakes and better by afternoon, now with swollen ankles, a bigger belly, tiredness and a poor appetite; no itching, redness or discharge; blood pressure normal; urine dipstick 4+ protein and negative for blood → Minimal change disease → Nephrotic syndrome: protein without blood at a normal blood pressure
  2. 5 yo girl with 4 days of puffiness around both eyes, worst on waking; no itching, redness, discharge or fever; her shoes have felt tight since yesterday → Urinalysis → The dipstick shows whether the kidney is leaking protein
  3. 6 yo with hay fever and 5 days of puffy eyelids on both sides each morning, now with ankle swelling; a serum IgE level is high; no urine has been tested → It does not exclude a kidney cause → Atopy is common; the urine dipstick is still the next test
  4. 7 yo with puffy, itchy eyes on both sides every spring, clear watery discharge, sneezing and a runny nose; dark circles and an extra crease below both lower lids; afebrile; urine dipstick negative → Allergic conjunctivitis → Itch and a clean urine separate it from edema; antihistamine eye drops
  5. 3 yo whose eyelids and lips swell within 20 minutes of eating a cashew for the first time, with raised, itchy wheals on the chest; no hoarseness, wheeze or vomiting; blood pressure and oxygen saturation normal → IgE-mediated food allergy → Abrupt swelling with hives; hereditary angioedema brings no hives
  6. 4 yo with 2 days of swelling and redness of the right upper eyelid, which is warm and tender, around a scratch from the family cat; T 38.3 C; full, painless eye movements, normal vision, no proptosis → Periorbital cellulitis → One eye, warm and tender, orbit spared: oral antibiotics
  7. 4 yo with 2 days of a red left eye, thick yellow discharge and lids stuck together each morning, with mild lid puffiness; the eyelid skin is not red, warm or tender; afebrile; vision normal → Bacterial conjunctivitis → Pus and crusting; under 6, bacterial is more likely than viral
  8. 5 yo with puffy eyes and swelling of the ankles and scrotum; BP 96/58; urine dipstick 4+ protein, no blood; serum albumin 1.8 g/dL → Spot urine protein/creatinine ratio → Above 2 mg/mg with low albumin is nephrotic syndrome
  9. 3 yo with 2 weeks of puffy eyelids who tires after a few minutes of play and sweats and breathes fast with meals; RR 44, HR 150; liver edge 4 cm below the costal margin; gallop rhythm; urine dipstick negative for protein → Heart failure → Big liver and a gallop with a clean urine: echocardiogram next
  10. 2 yo with 3 weeks of swollen eyelids and legs and 2 months of loose stools; weight has fallen from the 50th to the 10th percentile; albumin 1.7 g/dL; urine dipstick negative for protein; bilirubin and INR normal → Protein-losing enteropathy → Albumin lost in the gut; stool alpha-1 antitrypsin is high
  11. 4 yo with periorbital and leg edema; BP 132/88; urinalysis 4+ protein with 30 red cells per high-power field; creatinine 1.1 mg/dL; C3 normal → Renal biopsy → Hematuria, hypertension and a high creatinine are atypical for minimal change disease
  12. 6 yo with minimal change disease that went into remission on prednisone, off steroids for 5 months; his home urine dipstick has shown 3+ to 4+ protein for 3 days and his eyes are puffy again; blood pressure normal, no blood in the urine → Restart daily prednisone → A relapse in a steroid-responsive child; relapses are common and do not harm the kidney
  13. 5 yo in a relapse of nephrotic syndrome, before steroids have been restarted, who develops pneumococcal peritonitis → Urinary loss of immunoglobulin and factor B → Opsonins for encapsulated organisms leak into the urine
  14. 5 yo with nephrotic syndrome in relapse and ascites, now with T 39.2 C, severe abdominal pain, guarding and rebound tenderness; HR 140, BP 90/54 → Cultures and IV antibiotics → Spontaneous peritonitis, usually pneumococcal; blood and peritoneal fluid cultures, then broad Gram-positive and Gram-negative cover
  15. 6 yo with severe nephrotic syndrome, albumin 1.4 g/dL, who develops sudden left flank pain, gross hematuria and an enlarged, palpable left kidney; creatinine has risen from 0.4 to 0.9 mg/dL; afebrile → Renal vein thrombosis → Urinary loss of antithrombin III and hemoconcentration; Doppler ultrasound
  16. 5 yo in week 3 of daily prednisone, 2 mg/kg, for a first episode of nephrotic syndrome; his kindergarten vaccines are due → Varicella vaccine → Live vaccines wait until the child is off high-dose steroids
  17. 5 yo discharged in remission from a first episode of minimal change disease; the parents ask how a relapse will be caught early → Home urine dipstick testing → Protein on the morning dipstick comes before the swelling
Pairs with Part I Proteinuria and Nephrotic Syndrome in a Child covers the lesion: minimal change disease versus membranous and FSGS (focal segmental glomerulosclerosis). It also covers starting steroids without a biopsy. Part II Hematuria and Nephritic Syndrome covers PSGN (poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis) and its C3 clock. Part II Anaphylaxis covers the acute allergic reaction and angioedema without hives. Part I Sinusitis and Its Complications covers preseptal versus orbital cellulitis and the orbital CT (computed tomography). Part I The Red Eye covers the conjunctivitis types.
Transferable rule For puffy eyes in a child, decide first whether the swelling belongs to the eye or to the whole child. If it is generalized, the urinalysis sorts it: protein alone means nephrotic syndrome, and blood with high blood pressure means nephritis.
Salient decoyPuffiness worst in the morning in an allergic child, treated as allergy without a urine dipstick.
Mirror twinPSGN also starts with puffy eyes; blood in the urine and a high blood pressure separate it.
Unchecked attributeA swollen lid called cellulitis without checking whether one eye or both, or whether the legs are swollen too.
Treat-the-numberFurosemide alone for nephrotic edema, when the plasma volume is already low.

Male Breast Enlargement

gynecomastia vs male breast cancer · image first · Klinefelter is the risk factor, not the explanationDoes the mass behave like the known condition, or like something it only made more likely?

The decision point

A unilateral, firm, progressive, nontender subareolar mass has only features of cancer. Klinefelter syndrome is the risk factor, not the explanation. It increases male breast cancer risk 20–50× through a chronically elevated estrogen/androgen ratio. Always image first.

Gynecomastia vs male breast cancer
GynecomastiaCancer
LateralityUsually bilateralUnilateral
PositionConcentric to the nippleEccentric, off-center
TextureRubbery, mobileFirm, fixed
TendernessOften tender earlyNontender
MarginsBlends into fatWell-defined or spiculated, ± calcifications
Skin / nippleNormalDimpling, retraction, ulceration, discharge
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Diagnostic mammography, with or without ultrasoundFirstEccentric mass, spiculated or with calcificationsSuspicious for cancer: core biopsy; concentric subareolar tissue is gynecomastia
Core needle biopsyConfirmsInvasive ductal carcinoma, usually ER-positiveMale breast cancer, even with known Klinefelter syndrome
Genetic testingCauseBRCA2 variantOffered to every man with breast cancer
Testicular exam and scrotal ultrasoundBy branchTesticular mass in a man with gynecomastiaGerm cell or Leydig cell tumor
Serum hCG and AFPBy branchHigh hCGhCG-secreting germ cell tumor
Hormone levels before imaging a unilateral hard massSkipKlinefelter labs do not explain the massImage and biopsy first; Klinefelter is the risk factor
Scenario bank
  1. 62 yo M with a unilateral firm nontender subareolar mass and nipple retraction → Male breast cancer → mammography and biopsy
  2. 16 yo M with bilateral tender subareolar discs → Pubertal gynecomastia → reassurance
  3. 62 yo M with a breast mass and known Klinefelter syndrome → Klinefelter is the risk factor, not the explanation → biopsy anyway
  4. 55 yo M on spironolactone with bilateral tender gynecomastia → Drug-induced gynecomastia → change the agent
  5. 30 yo M with gynecomastia and a testicular mass → HCG-secreting germ cell tumor → ultrasound and tumor markers
  6. 62 yo M with soft symmetric fatty enlargement and no discrete mass → Pseudogynecomastia
Male breast cancer Risk factors: Klinefelter, BRCA2 (>BRCA1), family history, cirrhosis, obesity, chest radiation, exogenous estrogen · workup: mammography ± ultrasound → core biopsy · usually invasive ductal, >90% ER-positive → mastectomy + tamoxifen · every man with breast cancer gets genetic testing.
When it really is gynecomastia
  • Physiologic – three windows only: newborn, puberty (13–14, resolves in 1–2 yrs), elderly. Prepubertal gynecomastia is always pathologic.
  • Drugs (largest category): spironolactone, cimetidine, ketoconazole, finasteride, antipsychotics, digoxin, protease inhibitors, anabolic steroids, marijuana, alcohol
  • Cirrhosis · hyperthyroidism (↑SHBG → ↓free testosterone) · CKD · refeeding · hypogonadism
  • Tumors: hCG-secreting germ cell, Leydig/Sertoli, adrenal – gynecomastia + testicular mass → testicular ultrasound, hCG, AFP
Klinefelter 47,XXY; most common cause of primary hypogonadism and male infertility; tall with long limbs, small firm testes, sparse body hair; ↑FSH, ↑LH, ↓testosterone, ↑estradiol; seminiferous tubule hyalinization; also associated with mediastinal germ cell tumors, SLE, osteoporosis. Testosterone replacement does not restore fertility.
Transferable rule A known condition in the past medical history raises the prior probability but does not make the diagnosis. If the lesion behaves differently from the known disease, the known disease is the risk factor and something else is the diagnosis.

edits.html:
Hyperprolactinemia

inferring the unnamed drug · antipsychotic ranking · causes by category · cheap tests before MRI · cabergoline firstIs the prolactin in the drug range or the prolactinoma range, and which drug is behind it?

The decision point

When a patient with a known illness remains on an unnamed medication, identify the drug by two-step inference. First identify the drug class the illness requires. Then choose the member whose side-effect profile matches the complaint. In psychosis, the class is an antipsychotic, and the member is the one with the highest prolactin liability.

The prolactin level separates drug-induced hyperprolactinemia from prolactinoma. Drug-induced hyperprolactinemia runs 25–100 and rarely exceeds 200; a prolactinoma typically produces >200. In this patient, a level of 70 is in the drug-induced range and excludes prolactinoma without any imaging.

Mechanism & the antipsychotic ranking Dopamine is prolactin-inhibiting factor. D2 blockade in the tuberoinfundibular pathway removes that inhibition. Highest prolactin effect: risperidone and paliperidone, plus high-potency typicals such as haloperidol. Lowest: aripiprazole (a D2 partial agonist that can lower prolactin), quetiapine and clozapine. Aripiprazole is therefore the antipsychotic least likely to cause hyperprolactinemia and the one to switch to.
Hyperprolactinemia – causes by category
CategoryExamplesDiscriminator
PhysiologicPregnancy, nipple stimulation, stress, exercise, sleepPregnancy test first
DrugsAntipsychotics, metoclopramide, methyldopa, verapamil, SSRIs, opioids, estrogens, H2 blockersLevel 25–100
ProlactinomaMicro- or macroadenomaLevel >200; macroadenoma adds headache and bitemporal hemianopsia
Stalk effectAny sellar mass compressing the stalkModest elevation (<100) with a large mass on MRI
Hypothyroidism↑TRH stimulates lactotrophsTSH elevated
CKD, cirrhosisReduced clearance –
Workup order & two pituitary pearls For elevated prolactin, first get a pregnancy test, TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone), medication review and renal function. Order an MRI pituitary only if all are negative. Do not image before excluding the cheap causes. Hook effect: a very large prolactinoma can saturate the assay and give a falsely low value; repeat with dilution. Prolactinoma is the pituitary tumor you treat medically. First-line treatment is dopamine agonists (cabergoline > bromocriptine), even for macroadenomas, because they shrink the tumor. Surgery is for medical failure, intolerance, or apoplexy.
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Serum prolactinFirstOver 200, or 25 to 100Over 200 suggests prolactinoma; 25 to 100 fits drugs or other causes
Pregnancy testNextPositivePhysiologic hyperprolactinemia
TSHNextHigh TSHPrimary hypothyroidism: TRH drives prolactin; treat with levothyroxine
Medication review and renal functionNextAntipsychotic, metoclopramide or other culprit; or CKDDrug-induced or reduced clearance; no imaging needed
Pituitary MRIConfirmsAdenoma once the cheap causes are excludedProlactinoma if level over 200; large mass with level under 100 is stalk effect
Prolactin repeated on a diluted sampleBy branchLevel much higher after dilutionHook effect in a giant prolactinoma
Serum FSH and LHSkipLow from suppression, does not name the causeProlactin, pregnancy test and TSH come first
Scenario bank
  1. Prolactin >200 with bitemporal hemianopsia → Macroprolactinoma → MRI → cabergoline
  2. Patient needs continued antipsychotic coverage → Switch to aripiprazole or quetiapine
  3. Prolactin 60 + TSH 25 + fatigue and cold intolerance → Hypothyroidism → levothyroxine
  4. Prolactin 45 on metoclopramide for gastroparesis → Drug-induced hyperprolactinemia
  5. Large sellar mass with prolactin only 45 → Stalk effect → a non-functioning mass, not a prolactinoma
  6. Huge pituitary mass with a normal-looking prolactin → Hook effect → dilute and repeat
  7. Amenorrhea + galactorrhea + negative pregnancy test → Prolactin and TSH before imaging
  8. Years of untreated hyperprolactinemia → Hypogonadism → infertility and osteoporosis
  9. Woman on an SSRI with new galactorrhea → Modest drug-induced elevation
Pairs with Part I Brain Tumors in a Child covers the localization once the trophic-hormone pattern points to the region.
Transferable rule When a lab value has a well-known range that separates two candidate causes, use the value rather than the history to decide between them.

edits.html:
Congenital Hypothyroidism

newborn screen · thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) direction locates the defect · goiter or none · dysgenesis as the default · treat before imagingIs TSH high or low, and is there a goiter?

Source vignette Pt – 1 mo old, home birth with no newborn screen, sleepy and feeding poorly, jaundiced since the first week, large tongue; no goiter described, maternal diet balanced with prenatal vitamins · Labs – TSH 110, thyroxine (T4) 0.6 · Q – the most likely cause; options spanned thyroid dysgenesis, dyshormonogenesis, iodine deficiency, panhypopituitarism and neonatal Graves disease
The decision point

TSH 110 with T4 0.6 (TSH, thyroid-stimulating hormone; T4, thyroxine) puts the lesion below the pituitary. The feedback loop is intact, so panhypopituitarism is excluded outright. Neonatal Graves gives a suppressed TSH with high T4, so it is excluded in the opposite direction. Among the primary causes, the exam is silent on goiter and the maternal history is clean (balanced diet, prenatal vitamins). This removes the tell of the two goitrous causes, dyshormonogenesis and iodine deficiency. The default remains: dysgenesis (agenesis, hypoplasia, or an ectopic gland arrested along the thyroglossal tract). The home birth is not a cause. It explains only why a screen-detected, asymptomatic diagnosis instead presented at one month, as maternal T4 washed out.

Defining criteria Primary congenital hypothyroidism – elevated TSH with low T4 (in-context: "increased TSH and decreased T4"); the diagnosis is made by newborn screening, not by symptoms · Prolonged (pathologic) neonatal jaundice – unconjugated jaundice persisting beyond age 2 weeks; it is the finding that converts a sleepy feeder into a thyroid workup
Pertinent positives & negatives TSH 110 with T4 0.6 – primary (glandular) failure; excludes panhypopituitarism and any central cause · Macroglossia + hoarse cry – mucopolysaccharide deposition in tongue and larynx; the specific soft-tissue signature of thyroid hormone deficiency, not of sepsis or a storage disease at this age · Direct bilirubin 0.7 of 8 – unconjugated; excludes biliary atresia and the cholestatic causes of the sick jaundiced neonate, and points at slowed gut motility plus reduced hepatic conjugating enzyme activity · No goiter described – argues against dyshormonogenesis and iodine deficiency, both of which enlarge the gland under TSH drive · Mother ate well and took prenatal vitamins; infant is formula-fed – iodine deficiency is excluded (formula is iodine-supplemented) · Normal tone with decreased activity – hypometabolism, not a neuromuscular disease; hypotonia may appear later and its absence does not exclude the diagnosis · Symptomatic at 1 month, not at birth – maternal T4 crossed the placenta and masked the deficit; this timing is characteristic of the disease
Congenital hypothyroidism: locating the defect
DiagnosisIllness script + buzzwordsThe National Board of Medical Examiners (NBME) tellExcluded here by
Thyroid dysgenesis (agenesis/hypoplasia/ectopy)Failed formation or descent of the thyroid diverticulum from the pharyngeal floor along the thyroglossal duct; sporadic, no family historyHigh TSH, low T4, NO goiter, unremarkable maternal history; ectopic lingual tissue on scintigraphy(the answer)
Dyshormonogenesis (e.g., thyroid peroxidase defect)Autosomal recessive enzyme block in organification; gland present but cannot make hormone, so TSH drive enlarges itGoiter in a hypothyroid newborn; consanguinity or affected sibling; deafness if PendredNo goiter, no family history; a minority of cases
Iodine deficiencyMaternal dietary lack in an endemic region; substrate, not machinery, is missing; goitrousMaternal diet/geography stated; goiter in mother and infantBalanced diet + prenatal vitamins; all formula contains iodine
Central (panhypopituitarism)Pituitary/hypothalamic failure; TSH is the deficient hormoneLOW or inappropriately normal TSH with low T4; midline defects (cleft lip/palate), micropenis, hypoglycemiaTSH 110: the axis is intact and driving
Transplacental TSH-receptor stimulating antibodyMaternal Graves immunoglobulin G (IgG) crosses to the fetus → neonatal Graves, usually transient as antibody clears, generally within 6 monthsLow TSH, high T4, tachycardia, irritability, hyperphagia with poor weight gainDirection is inverted: TSH 110, T4 0.6, poor feeding and lethargy
Management, in one line A maternal blocking antibody against the TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) receptor is the rare counterpart of the stimulating antibody. It causes transient primary hypothyroidism with high TSH; scintigraphy can show no uptake, so ultrasound is needed to show the gland is present.
Decision spine Is TSH high or low? – High → primary; the pituitary causes are excluded · Is T4 low? – Yes → hypothyroid, not a compensated or antibody-stimulated state · Is there a goiter? – No → not dyshormonogenesis, not iodine deficiency · Is there a maternal story? – Diet fine, no Graves → no acquired/transplacental cause · What's left is the default – dysgenesis, the most common cause; the home birth explains the delay in detection, not the disease
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Newborn screen (heel prick at 24 to 48 hours)ScreenHigh TSH (some programs measure T4 first)Recall the infant for serum tests the same day
Serum TSH and free T4ConfirmsHigh TSH, low free T4; or low or normal TSH with low free T4Primary: start levothyroxine now. Central: check adrenal function and replace cortisol before levothyroxine unless adrenal function is intact, then pituitary magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
Thyroid ultrasound or radionuclide scanCause, optionalEctopic gland, or no gland on ultrasound; or an enlarged gland in placeDysgenesis; or dyshormonogenesis. Never delays treatment
Maternal TSH-receptor antibodiesBy branchPositive in a mother with autoimmune thyroid diseaseTransient hypothyroidism from blocking antibody
Serum thyroglobulin aloneSkipCannot stand in for imagingDoes not name the cause by itself
Scenario bank
  1. 3 wk M, home birth with no newborn screen, sleepy and feeding poorly, jaundiced since week 1, large tongue; TSH 140, T4 0.5 → Start levothyroxine now → Congenital hypothyroidism from thyroid dysgenesis
  2. 2 wk F with lethargy and poor feeding, firm anterior neck mass, older brother on levothyroxine, consanguineous parents; TSH 120, T4 0.4 → Dyshormonogenesis from a thyroid peroxidase defect → Levothyroxine; ultrasound shows an enlarged gland in place
  3. 5 d M with cleft palate, micropenis and fasting hypoglycemia; T4 low with TSH 0.8 → Central hypothyroidism from panhypopituitarism → Cortisol replacement before levothyroxine, then pituitary MRI
  4. 6 d F whose mother had Graves disease treated by thyroidectomy; infant tachycardic, irritable, poor weight gain despite hyperphagia; TSH undetectable, T4 elevated → Start a beta blocker and methimazole → Neonatal Graves disease from transplacental TSH receptor stimulating antibody
  5. Newborn screen at 48 hours returns TSH 60 with low T4; the infant is asymptomatic and feeding well on examination → Start levothyroxine without waiting for imaging → Congenital hypothyroidism
  6. 3 wk M with poor feeding and prolonged jaundice, TSH 90 and T4 0.6, no palpable goiter → Thyroid ultrasound or radionuclide uptake scan → An ectopic gland, or no gland on ultrasound, confirms dysgenesis
  7. 4 wk F starting levothyroxine for congenital hypothyroidism; the parent asks how to administer the crushed tablet → Mixing the dose into soy formula or an iron containing supplement → Crush and give in a small volume of water or breast milk
  8. 5 wk M with congenital hypothyroidism, total bilirubin 9 with direct 0.6, stools normally pigmented → Slowed gastrointestinal motility with reduced hepatic bilirubin conjugating enzyme activity → Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia that resolves with levothyroxine
  9. 2 mo M diagnosed at 6 weeks and on levothyroxine for 4 weeks; TSH 45 with low normal free T4, parents confirm daily dosing → Increase the levothyroxine dose and recheck in 4 weeks → Under replacement
  10. 3 mo F born where newborn screening is unavailable, never treated, now with developmental delay, poor linear growth and constipation; TSH 180, T4 0.3 → Start levothyroxine immediately → Untreated congenital hypothyroidism
Decoy note The home birth is not a cause. It explains the missed newborn screen and therefore the unusual symptomatic presentation. The balanced maternal diet with prenatal vitamins excludes iodine deficiency. Primigravida, age 24, unremarkable family history: none of these points to a cause, although the absent family history modestly argues against a recessive enzyme defect.
Pearls High TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone), low T4 (thyroxine) and no goiter mean dysgenesis; a goiter means a synthesis defect, and a low TSH means the pituitary. · Symptom onset at weeks to months, not at birth, is characteristic of congenital hypothyroidism. Placental maternal T4 covers the first weeks, so a normal newborn exam never reassures. · Unconjugated jaundice past 2 weeks of age calls for considering thyroid disease and galactosemia; conjugated jaundice at any age calls for considering a biliary cause. · Macroglossia plus hoarse cry is mucopolysaccharide deposition in hypothyroid soft tissue. It is distinct from Beckwith-Wiedemann (macroglossia with hemihyperplasia and hypoglycemia). · Treat on the screening result. Imaging to name the cause never delays levothyroxine, because the neurodevelopmental window is measured in weeks. Most children treated early and adequately have normal neurodevelopmental outcomes. · A goiter in a hypothyroid newborn points to a synthesis problem or an iodine problem; dysgenesis has no gland to enlarge. · In central hypothyroidism, give cortisol before levothyroxine unless adrenal function is shown to be intact: thyroid hormone is thought to accelerate cortisol clearance and can precipitate adrenal crisis.
Pairs with Jaundice in a Newborn shares the complaint of a jaundiced newborn with an abnormal screen. Ask: is the hyperbilirubinemia conjugated, and is the infant ill or merely slow? Thyroid Disease in an Adult covers the adult version of the same TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) direction logic. It also covers the dosing loop that this brief only points at. Part I Hypotonia in an Infant covers the other causes of low tone in infancy and the yearly TSH in Down syndrome.
Transferable rule In any hormone deficiency, the trophic hormone's direction locates the lesion. High TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) puts it in the gland; low TSH puts it in the pituitary. Within the gland, the presence or absence of an organ (goiter or none) separates a machinery defect from a formation defect.
Class-vs-memberDefective thyroid peroxidase activity: A minority of cases, and it almost always produces a goiter, which this exam does not describe; no family history in a recessive condition
True-fact-wrong-slotTransplacental TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) receptor–stimulating antibody: It causes neonatal Graves, with suppressed TSH, high T4 (thyroxine), tachycardia and hyperphagia. Every value and symptom here is inverted
Salient decoyIodine deficiency, endemic goiter: The balanced diet plus prenatal vitamins excludes it, and all formula contains iodine
Test-overrides-findingsPanhypopituitarism: TSH 110 proves the pituitary is working; central disease gives a low or inappropriately normal TSH plus midline defects and micropenis
