edits.html:
Inherited Tumor Syndromes

the visible lesion and organ pattern name the syndrome · von Hippel-Lindau · neurofibromatosis type 1 · tuberous sclerosisWhat exactly is the retinal lesion, what color is the skin patch, and how many patches are there?

Source vignette Pt – 16 yo M, bilateral retinal hemangioblastomas, mother had an adrenal tumor resected, one light brown facial patch without freckling · Q – the most likely diagnosis; options spanned von Hippel-Lindau disease, neurofibromatosis type 1 and Sturge-Weber syndrome
The decision point

Bilateral retinal hemangioblastoma points to von Hippel-Lindau, because no other listed syndrome produces one. NF1 (neurofibromatosis type 1) gives optic gliomas and Lisch nodules. MEN2B (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B) gives conjunctival and corneal neuromas. Sturge-Weber gives a leptomeningeal and choroidal vascular malformation. Li-Fraumeni gives sarcomas with no characteristic eye finding. The mother's resected adrenal tumor reads as a pheochromocytoma transmitted in autosomal dominant fashion. Hemangioblastoma plus adrenal medullary tumor is the von Hippel-Lindau organ pattern, with clear cell renal carcinoma the third member. A single light brown facial macule is a normal café-au-lait spot. It is not the multiple macules of NF1 and not a red-purple port-wine stain.

Consider a teenager found confused after an unwitnessed fall. A fibroma growing from under a toenail and calcified nodules lining the lateral ventricles on CT (computed tomography) indicate tuberous sclerosis complex. The fall was a seizure, and the nodules are subependymal hamartomas. The nail lesion is a periungual fibroma, which appears in adolescence. NF1 puts neurofibromas on the trunk and a glioma on the optic nerve. Ataxia-telangiectasia starts with ataxia in early childhood. The nail-bed sign of endocarditis is a splinter hemorrhage, not a fibroma.

Defining criteria The VHL (von Hippel-Lindau) testing gate – any patient with a retinal or cerebellar hemangioblastoma undergoes VHL gene testing, family history or not · The café-au-lait gate – an isolated macule is normal; six or more with regular borders plus axillary freckling is NF1 (each macule over 5 mm before puberty or over 15 mm after puberty); macules with jagged, irregular borders that usually respect the midline and follow the lines of Blaschko suggest McCune-Albright. Count, border, distribution and freckling are four separate criteria, and the exam varies whichever one is not being checked · Patch color as a criterion – Sturge-Weber's lesion is a red-purple vascular port-wine stain; a light brown patch is pigmented and belongs to a different family
Pertinent positives & negatives Bilateral retinal hemangioblastomas – essentially syndrome-defining; retinal hemangioblastoma may be the first neoplasm of VHL (von Hippel-Lindau) and by itself triggers gene testing · Mother's adrenal tumor removed – pheochromocytoma in a first-degree relative; autosomal dominant transmission, and the second organ of the VHL pattern · A single light brown 4-cm patch – one café-au-lait macule, a normal finding, lacking the multiplicity of NF1 (neurofibromatosis type 1) and the color of Sturge-Weber · Age 16 with painless progressive blurring – VHL can present at any age but usually presents in early adulthood. Vision falls from retinal edema and distortion · Blood pressure 110/72 mm Hg and an otherwise normal examination – no clinically active pheochromocytoma today, which does not exclude one and is why surveillance is needed
Inherited tumor syndromes: the differential
SyndromeIllness scriptThe NBME (National Board of Medical Examiners) tellExcluded here by
Von Hippel-LindauAutosomal dominant loss of the VHL tumor suppressor on chromosome 3; tumors of retina, central nervous system, adrenal medulla and kidneyRetinal or cerebellar hemangioblastoma, pheochromocytoma, clear cell renal carcinoma(the answer)
Neurofibromatosis type 1Autosomal dominant neurocutaneous disorder of skin, nerve and eyeMultiple café-au-lait macules with axillary freckling; cutaneous neurofibromas on the trunk; optic glioma and Lisch nodules; seizures in someOne macule only, which is normal; the retinal lesion is a hemangioblastoma
Sturge-Weber syndromeLeptomeningeal and ocular capillary-venous malformationRed-purple port-wine stain, seizures, glaucomaThe patch is light brown and pigmented, not vascular
Multiple endocrine neoplasia 2BRET proto-oncogene; medullary thyroid carcinoma and pheochromocytomaConjunctival or corneal neuromas, mucosal neuromas, marfanoid habitusEye lesion is a hemangioblastoma; no thyroid disease
Li-Fraumeni syndromeAutosomal dominant TP53 loss; many tumor types across a young familySoft tissue sarcoma, early breast cancer, adrenocortical carcinoma; no characteristic eye or skin lesionNo hemangioblastoma belongs to it
Tuberous sclerosis complexAutosomal dominant TSC1 or TSC2 mutation, inherited or new; benign hamartomas of brain, eye, skin, heart and kidney; epilepsy in most, intellectual disability and autismAsh-leaf macules, facial angiofibromas, shagreen patch, periungual fibromas; calcified subependymal nodules on CT; cardiac rhabdomyoma, renal angiomyolipomaNo skin hamartoma here, and its brain lesions are nodules and tubers, not hemangioblastomas
Neurofibromatosis type 2Autosomal dominant tumors of nerve sheath and meningesBilateral vestibular schwannomasThe eighth nerve, not the retina
Management, in one line Confirm with VHL gene testing (VHL: von Hippel-Lindau). Then begin lifelong surveillance: retinal examination, plasma or urine metanephrines, MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) of brain and spine, and MRI of abdomen. Resect tumors as they appear. For the retinal lesions, laser therapy is the preferred treatment.
Tuberous sclerosis complex Skin – hypopigmented ash-leaf macules, facial angiofibromas over the cheeks and nose, a shagreen patch (orange-peel plaque on the lower back), and periungual fibromas, which appear in adolescence or adulthood · Brain – subependymal nodules, calcified on CT along the ventricles; cortical tubers, best seen on MRI; a nodule can grow into a subependymal giant cell astrocytoma that obstructs CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) flow and causes hydrocephalus, which needs resection · Seizures – epilepsy in most, often infantile spasms, but the first seizure can come at any age, adolescence included; intellectual disability, autism and behavior disorders · Heart and kidney – cardiac rhabdomyoma; renal angiomyolipoma · Surveillance – skin and eye exams, serial MRI of brain and kidneys, baseline echocardiogram and serial ECGs (electrocardiograms), baseline EEG (electroencephalogram), and neuropsychiatric screening · Not tuberous sclerosis – NF1 (neurofibromatosis type 1): café-au-lait macules, trunk neurofibromas, optic glioma; VHL (von Hippel-Lindau): cerebellar and retinal hemangioblastomas; ataxia-telangiectasia: ataxia from early childhood, poorly coordinated eye movements, conjunctival telangiectasias; endocarditis: fever, murmur and splinter hemorrhages
Neurofibromatosis type 1: tumor risk Optic nerve glioma – the most common brain tumor in neurofibromatosis type 1; usually a low-grade pilocytic astrocytoma of one or both optic nerves or the chiasm · Presentation – insidious vision loss, proptosis and optic atrophy · Eye surveillance – children with neurofibromatosis type 1 need an eye examination yearly until age 8, then every 2 years until 18 · Pheochromocytoma – risk also raised · No established link – medulloblastoma, craniopharyngioma, and arteriovenous malformation, which belongs to Wyburn-Mason syndrome
Decision spine Name the retinal lesion exactly. – Hemangioblastoma → VHL (von Hippel-Lindau) · If it is a different eye lesion: – optic glioma or Lisch nodules point to NF1 (neurofibromatosis type 1). Conjunctival neuromas point to MEN2B (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B). Glaucoma with a choroidal malformation points to Sturge-Weber · Read the skin patch's color. – Light brown pigmented = café-au-lait; red-purple vascular = port-wine · Count the skin lesions. – One café-au-lait macule is normal; multiple plus axillary freckling is NF1 · Read the family's tumor for its organ. – Adrenal medulla with kidney and CNS (central nervous system) points to VHL. Adrenal medulla with thyroid points to MEN2 (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2)
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Dilated retinal examinationFirstRetinal hemangioblastomaVon Hippel-Lindau suspected, with or without a family history
VHL gene testingConfirmsPathogenic VHL variantVHL disease; offer testing to first-degree relatives now
Plasma or urine metanephrinesStagingElevated metanephrinesPheochromocytoma: alpha blockade before beta blockade, then resection
MRI of brain and spineStagingCerebellar or spinal hemangioblastomaCNS tumors of VHL
MRI of abdomenStagingEnhancing renal massClear cell carcinoma: nephron-sparing partial nephrectomy
Noncontrast head CT after a first seizureBy branchCalcified subependymal nodules along the ventriclesTuberous sclerosis complex; brain MRI shows cortical tubers
Whole-body PET (positron emission tomography) imagingSkipAdds nothing to gene testing and targeted MRIVHL testing follows the lesion; surveillance covers the four organs
Scenario bank
  1. 16 yo M with bilateral retinal hemangioblastomas, a mother who had an adrenal tumor resected, and one light brown facial patch → Von Hippel-Lindau disease → The eye lesion names the syndrome
  2. 34 yo M with a solitary cerebellar hemangioblastoma and no family history of tumors → VHL gene testing → Testing follows the lesion, not the pedigree
  3. Patient with newly confirmed von Hippel-Lindau disease → Retinal, adrenal, neuraxis and abdominal surveillance→ retinal examination, plasma metanephrines, MRI of brain and spine, and MRI of abdomen; The four organs the syndrome occupies
  4. 22 yo F newly diagnosed with von Hippel-Lindau disease who has an asymptomatic 15-year-old brother → Offer him VHL gene testing now → each first-degree relative carries a 50% risk, and surveillance starts in childhood
  5. 40 yo M with von Hippel-Lindau disease and a 3 cm enhancing renal mass → Nephron-sparing partial nephrectomy → Clear cell carcinoma, with more lesions expected
  6. 28 yo F with von Hippel-Lindau disease, an adrenal mass and elevated metanephrines, scheduled for resection → Alpha blockade started before any beta blockade → Unopposed alpha stimulation otherwise
  7. 4-month-old with a red-purple patch over the V1 distribution and a focal seizure → Brain MRI and ophthalmology referral→ for a leptomeningeal angioma and for glaucoma screening; Sturge-Weber syndrome
  8. 7-year-old with 8 cafe-au-lait macules, axillary freckling, Lisch nodules and an optic glioma → Neurofibromatosis type 1 → Multiplicity is the criterion, not presence
  9. 24-year-old with medullary thyroid carcinoma, a pheochromocytoma, mucosal neuromas of the lips and a marfanoid habitus → Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B → Neuromas rather than hemangioblastomas
  10. The molecular defect underlying von Hippel-Lindau disease → Loss of a tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 3 → Autosomal dominant inheritance
  11. 9 year old with painless firm rubbery tongue nodules, marfanoid habitus and long fingers → Medullary thyroid carcinoma → MEN2B: aggressive and early; prophylactic thyroidectomy before age 1 year
  12. Child with newly diagnosed MEN2B; what else must be evaluated → Plasma fractionated metanephrines → About half have pheochromocytoma
  13. Adult with primary hyperparathyroidism, a prolactinoma and a gastrinoma → Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 → No marfanoid habitus and no mucosal neuromas
  14. Patient with medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma and parathyroid hyperplasia, with a normal habitus → Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A → Parathyroid rather than neuromas separates 2A from 2B
  15. Child with perioral pigmented macules and recurrent intussusception → Peutz-Jeghers syndrome → Pigmented macules, not neuromas; the risk is polyps and cancer
  16. Adult with recurrent epistaxis and ruby mucosal papules that blanch with pressure → Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia → Telangiectasias blanch; neuromas do not
  17. Newborn with bilateral absence of the iris, hypospadias and an undescended left testis → Wilms tumor → WAGR (Wilms tumor, aniridia, genitourinary anomalies, range of developmental delay): abdominal ultrasonography every 3 months until about age 5 to 8 years
  18. Newborn with aniridia and genitourinary anomalies; the underlying lesion → An 11p13 deletion → WAGR: Wilms, Aniridia, Genitourinary, Range of developmental delay
  19. Why Wilms tumor in WAGR differs from isolated Wilms tumor → It is often bilateral and presents earlier → Isolated disease is usually unilateral at age 2 to 5
  20. Macrosomic newborn with macroglossia and hemihyperplasia at risk for embryonal tumors → Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome → Overgrowth rather than aniridia
  21. 17 yo M found confused at the bottom of the stairs after an unwitnessed fall, most likely a seizure; 2-cm forehead contusion; a firm flesh-colored fibroma growing from beneath a toenail; head CT shows calcified nodules along the walls of the lateral ventricles → Tuberous sclerosis complex → Periungual fibroma plus calcified subependymal nodules; surveillance of brain, kidney, heart, eyes and skin
  22. 8 yo F newly diagnosed with tuberous sclerosis complex after a first seizure, with ash-leaf macules and facial angiofibromas; normal blood pressure and development so far → Brain and kidney MRI, echocardiogram and ECG, EEG, and skin and eye exams → Surveillance follows the organs the hamartomas occupy, plus neuropsychiatric screening
  23. Asymptomatic 17 yo M at a sports physical with about 10 light brown macules 0.6 to 2 cm across the trunk and limbs and freckling in both axillae → Optic nerve glioma → Neurofibromatosis type 1; eye examination yearly until age 8, then every 2 years until 18
  24. 6-year-old with 7 café-au-lait macules over 5 mm, inguinal freckling, normal vision and a normal examination otherwise → Yearly eye examination → Neurofibromatosis type 1; screens for optic nerve glioma
  25. 9-year-old with neurofibromatosis type 1 and months of painless vision loss in one eye, mild proptosis and a pale optic disc → Optic nerve glioma → Usually a low-grade pilocytic astrocytoma
Decoy note The skin patch drew nearly two in five readers: 20% chose NF1 (neurofibromatosis type 1) and 18% chose Sturge-Weber. A solitary café-au-lait macule is normal, so this most conspicuous physical finding does not discriminate. The mother's adrenal tumor supplies both the inheritance pattern and the second organ. The normal blood pressure does not help the diagnosis, but it indicates that no pheochromocytoma is active yet.
Pearls Retinal hemangioblastoma is von Hippel-Lindau until gene testing says otherwise; the pheochromocytoma and clear cell renal carcinoma follow. · A retinal or cerebellar hemangioblastoma by itself warrants referral to genetics. VHL (von Hippel-Lindau) testing follows the lesion, with or without a family history. · Eye lesions by syndrome: hemangioblastoma → VHL · optic glioma with Lisch nodules → NF1 (neurofibromatosis type 1) · conjunctival and corneal neuromas → MEN2B (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B) · choroidal malformation with glaucoma → Sturge-Weber. · Read a patch's color, not merely its presence. Light brown pigmented is café-au-lait, red-purple vascular is port-wine, and they belong to different syndromes. · VHL surveillance covers its organs: retina, brain and spine, adrenal medulla and kidney. The follow-up is therefore an eye exam, metanephrines, and two MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) scans. · Up to 35% of pheochromocytomas may be germline, so genetic testing should be considered for every patient; a younger age at presentation or bilateral tumors make a hereditary syndrome more likely. The syndromes include VHL, MEN2 (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2), NF1, and succinate dehydrogenase gene variants. · Before resecting a pheochromocytoma, alpha blockade precedes beta blockade; reversing the order leaves alpha stimulation unopposed. · How NBME framed it: a well 17-year-old at a sports physical has about 10 light brown macules and axillary freckling, and the syndrome is never named. After puberty only macules over 15 mm count, so the axillary freckling supplies the second criterion. The lead-in asks which lesion carries a raised risk compared with the general population.
Pairs with Part I Hypertension in an Adult covers pheochromocytoma from the blood-pressure side, reaching the same tumor from a different complaint. Ask: is the pheochromocytoma isolated, or is it one organ of a syndrome? Related conditions without their own brief: the neurocutaneous syndromes as a set, namely NF1 (neurofibromatosis type 1), NF2 (neurofibromatosis type 2), tuberous sclerosis and Sturge-Weber. Part I Puberty covers the border and distribution attributes of café-au-lait macules. Part II Abdominal Mass in a Young Child covers the mass itself. Ask: is it within the kidney, and is the child older than 2? Part I Antibody Deficiencies covers ataxia-telangiectasia and its infections. Ask: is the skin lesion vascular, or a fibrous tumor? Part I Brain Tumors in a Child covers optic pathway glioma and craniopharyngioma as masses. Ask: does the visual field loss come from the optic nerve or from the sella?
Transferable rule When a visible lesion identifies a syndrome, the lesion's category is shared across syndromes, but its identity is not. Name the tissue and the color before matching. The most conspicuous physical finding may be the one that does not discriminate.
Unchecked attributeNeurofibromatosis type 1, for two café-au-lait macules: Two macules sit between the isolated-is-normal rule and the six of NF1. A count rule alone therefore lands on NF1. The border, the distribution that respects the midline and the absent freckling all argue against it.
Salient decoyNeurofibromatosis type 1: One macule is normal; NF1 requires multiple with axillary freckling, and its eye lesions are optic glioma and Lisch nodules, never a hemangioblastoma
Unchecked attributeSturge-Weber syndrome: The patch is the wrong kind; port-wine stains are red-purple vascular malformations, and this one is light brown and pigmented
True-fact-wrong-slotLi-Fraumeni syndrome: TP53 disease is sarcomas, early breast and adrenocortical carcinoma, with no characteristic eye or skin lesion and no hemangioblastoma
Class-vs-memberMultiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B: Its eye findings are conjunctival and corneal neuromas, and it brings medullary thyroid carcinoma, which nobody in this stem has
Class-vs-memberNeurofibromatosis type 1, for the teenager with the toenail fibroma: Also autosomal dominant with seizures, but its skin tumors are neurofibromas on the trunk and its brain tumor is an optic glioma; calcified subependymal nodules belong to tuberous sclerosis
Unchecked attributeAtaxia-telangiectasia: Autosomal recessive, with ataxia from early childhood and vascular telangiectasias rather than a fibrous nail tumor, and no ventricular nodules
Salient decoyBacterial endocarditis: The nail finding pulls toward it, but endocarditis gives splinter hemorrhages with fever and a murmur, not a firm periungual fibroma
Salient decoyMedulloblastoma, for the teenager with 10 café-au-lait macules: The most common malignant brain tumor of childhood, with raised intracranial pressure and ataxia, but neurofibromatosis type 1 does not raise its risk
True-fact-wrong-slotCraniopharyngioma: A Rathke pouch remnant that causes bitemporal field loss; neurofibromatosis type 1 does not raise its risk
True-fact-wrong-slotArteriovenous malformation: Retinal and midbrain arteriovenous malformations belong to Wyburn-Mason syndrome, not neurofibromatosis type 1
True-fact-wrong-slotCerebral aneurysm: An adult cause of intracranial hemorrhage; the tumor this skin pattern predicts is an optic nerve glioma

edits.html:
Anemia with Thrombocytopenia

hemolytic uremic syndrome triad · smear · Coombs test · coagulation studies · its four mimicsAre two cell lines down, is the smear sheared, and are the coagulation studies normal?

Source vignette Pt – 7 yo, bloody diarrhea a week ago, now anuric and icteric · Q – the expected laboratory value; options spanned a decreased platelet count, an increased serum haptoglobin and a positive direct Coombs test
The decision point

Scleral icterus with fatigue is hemolytic anemia, and anuria for 24 hours with pedal edema is acute kidney injury. The third feature of hemolytic uremic syndrome is thrombocytopenia. Shiga toxin damages endothelium, platelets are consumed into microthrombi, and red cells are sheared as they pass. The platelet count falls because of the same process that produces the schistocytes and the bilirubin. The exposure is bloody diarrhea a week ago, in a cluster of people who ate together and recovered.

Defining criteria HUS (hemolytic uremic syndrome) triad – microangiopathic hemolytic anemia + thrombocytopenia + acute kidney injury (rising blood urea nitrogen [BUN] and creatinine) · Microangiopathic hemolysis – red cells sheared by platelet microthrombi, giving schistocytes, increased indirect bilirubin, and decreased haptoglobin · The preceding illness – Shiga toxin–producing E. coli O157:H7 or Shigella dysenteriae; bloody diarrhea first, with HUS appearing about a week later · Coombs in HUS – negative, because the red cells are destroyed mechanically rather than coated by antibody
Pertinent positives & negatives Bloody diarrhea one week ago – Shiga toxin colitis; the one-week latency between the diarrhea and the syndrome is characteristic · Shared meal with relatives who recovered – a point-source exposure that confirms the organism but does not explain the labs; most infected people never develop HUS (hemolytic uremic syndrome) · Anuria for 24 hours with normal intake, plus 2+ pedal edema – acute kidney injury with volume overload, the renal feature of the triad · Scleral icterus – indirect hyperbilirubinemia from hemolysis, the hemolytic feature of the triad · Fatigue and refusing to get out of bed – symptomatic anemia rather than ongoing volume loss; the diarrhea has resolved · No bruising or petechiae described – consumptive thrombocytopenia in HUS is often not severe enough to bleed; its absence never argues against the diagnosis · No fever or neurologic change – the absent neurologic change argues against TTP (thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura)
Anemia with thrombocytopenia: the differential
ProcessIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Hemolytic uremic syndromeChild, Shiga toxin colitis, then endothelial injury with platelet microthrombi ~1 week laterBloody diarrhea → anemia + low platelets + acute kidney injury (AKI), normal coags, negative Coombs(the answer)
Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpuraUsually adult; ADAMTS13 deficiency leaves ultralarge von Willebrand multimersNeurologic changes, more common than in HUS; plasma exchange, not supportive careAge 7, no neurologic findings
Disseminated intravascular coagulationA severely ill patient (sepsis, trauma, malignancy); consumption of factors as well as plateletsProlonged prothrombin time (PT) and activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) with low fibrinogen alongside the schistocytesPT is normal in HUS; no critical illness described
Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemiaIgG coats red cells; lupus, lymphoproliferative disease, or a drugDirect Coombs positive; spherocytes, not schistocytes; platelets and kidneys sparedRenal failure and edema, which antibody-mediated hemolysis does not cause
Isolated thrombocytopenia (immune)Low platelets alone after a viral illness; bruising and petechiae in a well childNormal hemoglobin and a normal smear: one cytopenia, not twoAnemia, jaundice and anuria are all present
Management, in one line HUS (hemolytic uremic syndrome) is treated supportively with fluid and electrolyte management, transfusion, and dialysis when needed. Withhold antibiotics and antimotility agents in suspected Shiga toxin infection.
Decision spine How many cell lines are down? – Anemia plus a consumed platelet count → the microangiopathy family, not a single-lineage problem · Is the hemolysis mechanical or immune? – Schistocytes with a negative Coombs → mechanical shearing · Are the coagulation studies normal? – Yes → HUS (hemolytic uremic syndrome) or TTP (thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura), not DIC (disseminated intravascular coagulation) · Which organ, and what came first? – Kidney, after bloody diarrhea in a child → HUS · Marker directions from the mechanism – haptoglobin consumed and falling, reticulocytes rising, indirect bilirubin rising, Coombs negative
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Complete blood count (CBC) with platelets and reticulocytesFirstAnemia with low platelets, reticulocytes highTwo cell lines down with hemolysis: consumption, not marrow failure
Peripheral smearNextSchistocytesMechanical shearing; spherocytes would point to an antibody
Direct Coombs testNextNegativeMechanical destruction; positive means autoimmune hemolysis
PT, aPTT and fibrinogenNextNormalHUS or TTP; prolonged times with low fibrinogen mean DIC
Bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and haptoglobinSupportsIndirect bilirubin and LDH up, haptoglobin lowHemolysis; haptoglobin is consumed binding free hemoglobin
BUN, creatinine and urinalysisConfirmsRising creatinine, little or no urineCompletes the HUS triad after bloody diarrhea; stool Shiga toxin testing names the cause
Bone marrow biopsySkipNot needed once the smear shows schistocytesThe platelets are consumed, not underproduced
Mnemonic TTP pentad (thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura): microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, fever, neurologic signs, renal injury. Most patients do not have all five; anemia with schistocytes plus low platelets is enough to act.
Scenario bank
  1. 7 yo with bloody diarrhea a week ago, now anuric and icteric; which laboratory value is expected → A decreased platelet count → The third leg of the HUS triad
  2. 5 yo on day 3 of bloody diarrhea, stool culture pending, well hydrated and making urine → Supportive care with fluids, withholding antibiotics → Antibiotics may increase the risk of HUS
  3. 7 yo with hemolytic uremic syndrome, hemoglobin 6.2, urine output 10 mL/h, potassium 6.8 → Hemodialysis → Supportive care includes dialysis
  4. 42 yo F with fever, confusion, schistocytes, platelets 15,000, normal PT and normal creatinine → Plasma exchange → Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
  5. 42 yo F with thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, platelets 12,000, no active bleeding → Platelet transfusion → It can worsen TTP; reserve for overt bleeding or an invasive procedure
  6. 60 yo M with gram-negative sepsis, schistocytes, platelets 40,000, prolonged PT and aPTT, low fibrinogen → Treat the underlying sepsis → Disseminated intravascular coagulation is secondary
  7. 9 yo F with 2 weeks of jaundice and fatigue, spherocytes on smear, direct Coombs positive, normal platelets and creatinine → Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia → Antibody-coated cells rather than sheared ones
  8. Child with brisk hemolysis; why the serum haptoglobin falls rather than rises → It binds free hemoglobin and the complex is cleared → Consumed, unlike the acute-phase reactants
  9. 6 yo with bloody diarrhea 6 days ago, now pale with hemoglobin 8 and platelets 60,000; confirming the mechanism → Peripheral blood smear for schistocytes → Mechanical hemolysis
  10. 5 yo, well appearing, petechiae 2 weeks after a viral illness, platelets 20,000, hemoglobin 12.8, otherwise normal smear → Immune thrombocytopenia → One cytopenia with no hemolysis
Decoy note The cookout and the recovered relatives are epidemiology: they confirm a point-source Shiga toxin exposure but settle no laboratory value. The stool blood "has since resolved"; it stopped days ago and was never chronic, so it does not support iron deficiency. The absence of bruising or petechiae does not argue against a low platelet count. Consumptive thrombocytopenia in HUS (hemolytic uremic syndrome) frequently produces no bleeding at all.
Pearls Bloody diarrhea a week ago plus anuria and jaundice is HUS (hemolytic uremic syndrome): schistocytes, low platelets, rising creatinine and a negative Coombs test. · Two cytopenias with schistocytes mean mechanical destruction. In mechanical destruction the Coombs test is by definition negative, because no cell is antibody-coated. · Haptoglobin is consumed in hemolysis, while ferritin and other acute-phase reactants rise. A marker falls if the process uses it up and rises if the liver makes more of it. · Reticulocytes rise in hemolysis and fall in marrow failure. A reticulocyte count that fails to rise in a known hemolytic patient is a hematologic emergency. · Normal coagulation studies separate HUS and TTP (thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura) from DIC (disseminated intravascular coagulation). Kidney injury after bloody diarrhea in a child points to HUS; brain involvement in an adult points to TTP. · Withhold platelet transfusion in TTP unless there is overt bleeding or an invasive procedure, because it can worsen TTP. Withhold antibiotics in suspected Shiga toxin colitis, because they may increase the risk of HUS.
Pairs with Part II Acute Kidney Injury in a Child covers the acute-kidney-injury compartments and carries the hemolytic uremic syndrome row from the renal side. Part II Hemolytic Anemia covers Coombs-negative hemolysis when the platelets and kidneys are normal. This brief covers the case where both cell lines fall together. Ask: is a second cell line down, and is the smear sheared or spherocytic? Part I Hemolytic Anemia covers hemolysis with a normal platelet count and an antibody rather than a clot. Aquifer Bruising and Purpura in a Child starts one step earlier, from the bruise, and sorts it by the platelet count.
Transferable rule For a laboratory abnormality "associated" with a stated mechanism, what matters is the direction each marker moves, not the marker's name. Derive the direction from the mechanism: consumed or produced, mechanical or immune. When the findings form a named syndrome, list its triad rather than re-deriving each component.
Unchecked attributeIncreased serum haptoglobin: Haptoglobin binds free hemoglobin and is consumed, so it falls in hemolysis
True-fact-wrong-slotPositive direct Coombs test: Coombs detects antibody-coated cells; HUS (hemolytic uremic syndrome) destroys red cells mechanically, so the test is negative. Antibody hemolysis would not cause anuria and edema
Salient decoyDecreased ferritin level: The bleeding was acute and has resolved; ferritin is an acute-phase reactant and rises with inflammation
Class-vs-memberIncreased PT: DIC (disseminated intravascular coagulation) also consumes clotting factors and needs a critically ill patient; in HUS the PT is normal
Unchecked attributeDecreased reticulocyte count: Hemolysis is expected to produce reticulocytosis, a rise, as the marrow responds to the anemia

edits.html:
Dark Urine: Hemoglobin, Myoglobin or Blood

heme-positive dipstick, no red cells · hemoglobin vs myoglobin · creatine kinase and hemolysis labs · valve hemolysisDoes microscopy show red cells, and is the pigment hemoglobin or myoglobin?

Source vignette Pt – 62 yo M with a mechanical mitral valve, dark urine · Labs – dipstick heme-positive with 1 RBC per high-power field, LDH 380, haptoglobin undetectable · Smear – schistocytes · Q – the most likely cause; options spanned intravascular hemolysis from the prosthetic valve, warfarin-related hematuria and infective endocarditis
The decision point

The urine dipstick detects the heme moiety; it cannot distinguish hemoglobin, myoglobin and intact red blood cells. When the dipstick is positive but microscopy shows 0–2 RBC/hpf (red blood cells per high-power field), the urine contains free hemoglobin or myoglobin, not blood. This patient has a mechanical valve, schistocytes, elevated LDH (lactate dehydrogenase) and low haptoglobin, the classic picture of intravascular hemolysis. The free pigment is hemoglobin released from red cells sheared as they pass through the prosthetic valve.

Do not read the dark urine as gross hematuria when the dipstick is positive and microscopy is not.

Defining criteria Dipstick-microscopy mismatch – heme-positive dipstick with ≤2 RBC/hpf on microscopy means free pigment, not bleeding · Hemoglobinuria clues – low haptoglobin, elevated LDH, schistocytes, indirect hyperbilirubinemia · Myoglobinuria clues – CK >10,000, muscle pain, recent crush/exertion/seizure
Heme-positive urine – the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded by
Mechanical valve hemolysisProsthetic valve, chronic mild hemolysis, dark urineDipstick+, no RBCs, schistocytes, low haptoglobin –
Anticoagulant hematuriaOn warfarin; dark/red urineRBCs present on microscopy0–2 RBC/hpf
RhabdomyolysisCrush injury, exertion, seizure; dark urineCK >10,000; also dipstick+/RBC−No muscle symptoms, no CK elevation
GlomerulonephritisProteinuria, dysmorphic RBCs, RBC castsRBCs and casts on microscopyNo RBCs, no casts
EndocarditisProsthetic valve + fever, new murmurFever, positive blood cultures, vegetationsAfebrile, no systemic infection
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Urine dipstickScreenHeme-positiveBlood, hemoglobin or myoglobin; the strip cannot tell them apart
Urine microscopyFirst0 to 2 RBCs per high-power fieldFree pigment, not bleeding; many RBCs or casts mean true hematuria
Serum creatine kinaseNextMarkedly high, often over 10,000Myoglobin from rhabdomyolysis; normal CK points to hemoglobin
LDH, haptoglobin and indirect bilirubinBy branchLDH up, haptoglobin lowIntravascular hemolysis releasing hemoglobin into the urine
Peripheral smearConfirmsSchistocytesMechanical fragmentation, here from the prosthetic valve
Echocardiogram, if hemolysis worsensBy branchParavalvular leakValve repair or replacement
Renal ultrasound or urine cultureSkipNo RBCs means no bleeding source to findPigment in the urine is not a urinary tract problem
Scenario bank
  1. 62 yo M with a mechanical mitral valve, dark urine, heme-positive dipstick with 1 RBC per high-power field, LDH 380, haptoglobin undetectable, schistocytes on smear → Intravascular hemolysis from the prosthetic valve → monitor hemoglobin, supplement iron and folate
  2. 28 yo M found unconscious after a building collapse, dark brown urine, heme-positive dipstick with 0 RBCs, CK 45,000 → Rhabdomyolysis → aggressive IV normal saline
  3. 45 yo F with dark urine and a heme-positive dipstick showing 0 RBCs on microscopy → Serum creatine kinase
  4. 58 yo M with a mechanical aortic valve and worsening hemolytic anemia despite optimized anticoagulation, hemoglobin 7.2, reticulocytes 18% → Refer for valve replacement or repair → severe paravalvular hemolysis
  5. Why the dipstick is positive for blood when no red blood cells are seen on microscopy → The dipstick detects the heme moiety in free hemoglobin or myoglobin, not intact red blood cells
  6. 35 yo F with SLE, dark urine, heme-positive dipstick with dysmorphic RBCs and red cell casts → Lupus nephritis → renal biopsy
  7. 24 yo M after a marathon, dark urine, heme-positive dipstick with 0 RBCs, CK 32,000, creatinine 2.4 → IV normal saline at 200 to 300 mL per hour → rhabdomyolysis with AKI
Pearls The dipstick detects heme, not cells; a positive dipstick with no RBCs (red blood cells) means free pigment · Hemoglobin vs myoglobin: CK (creatine kinase) separates them: CK >10,000 with muscle symptoms means myoglobin, and normal CK with hemolysis markers means hemoglobin · Mild chronic hemolysis from a well-functioning mechanical valve is expected; worsening anemia or rising LDH (lactate dehydrogenase) suggests paravalvular leak → echocardiography, then possible reoperation · Schistocytes confirm mechanical fragmentation and tie the hemolysis to the valve rather than to an autoimmune or drug cause · Haptoglobin: consumed by binding free hemoglobin; most sensitive marker of intravascular hemolysis but also an acute-phase reactant (can be falsely normal during infection)
Pairs with Hemolytic Anemia also brings hemolysis labs and dark urine, but the cause is immune: spherocytes and a positive direct antiglobulin test, not schistocytes. Ask: is there a mechanical source?
Transferable rule When the dipstick is positive for blood but microscopy shows no red cells, look for the source of free pigment, not a bleeding site. CK (creatine kinase) separates muscle from red cell, and the clinical context identifies the mechanism.
Unchecked attributeAnticoagulant hematuria: the patient is on warfarin, but urine microscopy shows almost no RBCs (red blood cells).
Salient decoyEndocarditis: there is a prosthetic valve, but no fever or systemic infection.
Mirror twinRhabdomyolysis: it also causes a positive dipstick with no RBCs, but there are no muscle symptoms and no CK (creatine kinase) elevation.

edits.html:
Microcytic Anemia

iron studies before electrophoresis · iron deficiency masks thalassemia trait · lead and chronic disease · the CBC aloneIs the patient iron replete yet, and do the RDW and red cell count fit deficiency or trait?

The decision point

Both iron deficiency anemia and beta-thalassemia trait produce a low MCV (mean corpuscular volume). Hemoglobin electrophoresis is not the first test, because iron deficiency lowers HbA2 (hemoglobin A2), the marker electrophoresis uses to diagnose beta-thalassemia trait. In an iron-deficient patient, a falsely normal HbA2 on electrophoresis will mask coexisting thalassemia. Order iron studies first, correct the iron, then electrophoresis.

Defining criteria Iron studies first – ferritin, serum iron, TIBC, transferrin saturation; iron deficiency must be corrected before electrophoresis is interpretable · HbA2 masking – iron deficiency suppresses delta-globin chain production, lowering HbA2 into the normal range · Beta-thalassemia trait HbA2 – elevated (>3.5%) only when iron stores are replete
Microcytic anemia – the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellFirst testConfirms, then
Iron deficiency anemiaMenstrual loss, vegan/poor diet, GI bleed; low MCVLow ferritin, high TIBC, low transferrin satIron studiesLow ferritin; oral iron, then electrophoresis if the MCV stays low
Beta-thalassemia minorMediterranean/Asian, lifelong mild anemia, target cellsElevated HbA2 >3.5% on electrophoresis (only when iron-replete)Iron studies firstHbA2 over 3.5% once iron-replete; genetic counseling
Alpha-thalassemia minorSoutheast Asian/African, mild microcytic anemiaNormal electrophoresis; diagnosis by exclusion or gene testingIron studies → electrophoresis → gene analysisAlpha-globin gene deletion analysis
Lead poisoningChild in old housing, developmental delay, abdominal painBasophilic stippling; elevated lead levelLead levelElevated venous lead level; chelation if high
Anemia of chronic diseaseChronic infection, autoimmunity, malignancyLow iron, low TIBC (iron sequestered, not absent); ferritin normal/highIron studiesLow iron and TIBC with normal or high ferritin; treat the underlying disease
Scenario bank
  1. 15 yo F vegan with heavy menses, MCV 68, hemoglobin 9.2 → Iron studies → iron deficiency must be assessed before electrophoresis is interpretable
  2. 15 yo F with confirmed iron deficiency anemia from heavy menses, hemoglobin 9.2, hemodynamically stable → Oral iron supplementation and reassess in 4 to 6 weeks
  3. 22 yo M of Mediterranean descent, MCV 64, hemoglobin 11.5, iron studies normal, HbA2 5.8% → Beta-thalassemia minor → genetic counseling
  4. Why hemoglobin electrophoresis can miss beta-thalassemia trait in an iron-deficient patient → Iron deficiency suppresses HbA2 production, normalizing a value that would otherwise be elevated
  5. 3 yo M in old housing with developmental delay, microcytic anemia, and basophilic stippling on smear → Lead poisoning → serum lead level and chelation if elevated
  6. 28 yo F of Southeast Asian descent, MCV 72, hemoglobin 11.0, normal iron studies, normal electrophoresis → Alpha-globin gene deletion analysis → alpha-thalassemia minor
  7. 18 yo F treated for iron deficiency with 3 months of oral iron, ferritin now 45, but MCV remains 66 and hemoglobin 10.8 → Hemoglobin electrophoresis → possible coexisting thalassemia trait
  8. 2 yo M, well-child visit, five 8-oz cups of whole cow milk daily, pale with tachycardia and a flow murmur, Hb 8, MCV 70, erythrocytes 3.1 million/uL, platelets and leukocytes normal → Elevated red cell distribution width → iron deficiency anemia
  9. 2 yo of Greek descent, MCV 65, Hb 10.2, erythrocytes 5.4 million/uL, RDW normal, ferritin and iron studies normal → Beta-thalassemia trait → a normal red cell count with a low MCV
  10. 2 yo M with Hb 8 and MCV 70 whose diet is cheese, yogurt and roughly 40 oz of whole cow milk daily → Limit cow milk below 24 oz per day and begin an empiric oral iron trial → iron deficiency from excessive milk intake
  11. Why the red cell distribution width rises in iron deficiency but stays normal in thalassemia trait → Iron available for erythropoiesis fluctuates, so cells are made at varying sizes → thalassemia produces uniformly small cells
  12. 16 yo F with heavy menses, a low MCV, a low erythrocyte count, an elevated RDW and a low ferritin → Iron deficiency anemia → oral iron
  13. 58 yo M with rheumatoid arthritis and a microcytic anemia; serum iron low, TIBC low, ferritin normal → Anemia of chronic disease → iron is sequestered, not absent
Pearls Iron studies → then electrophoresis: a required order, not a preference, because iron deficiency suppresses delta-globin chain production, lowering HbA2 (hemoglobin A2) into the normal range · Ferritin is the most specific single test for iron deficiency; TIBC (total iron-binding capacity) and transferrin saturation add sensitivity when ferritin is borderline (ferritin is an acute-phase reactant) · Alpha-thalassemia minor has a normal electrophoresis. It is diagnosed by exclusion or gene testing and is the one microcytic anemia that electrophoresis cannot diagnose · The Mentzer index is MCV (mean corpuscular volume) divided by RBC (red blood cell count). It is a screening heuristic: under 13 suggests thalassemia and over 13 suggests IDA (iron deficiency anemia). It is not diagnostic and is never the most appropriate test · If the anemia does not correct with iron, look for a second cause; that is when to order electrophoresis
Pairs with Sickle Cell Disease and Trait also uses hemoglobin electrophoresis. Ask: is the electrophoresis interpretable, or must iron be corrected first?
Telling them apart on the CBC alone RDW – elevated in iron deficiency because the iron available for erythropoiesis varies through the day, so cells are made at varying sizes; normal or low in thalassemia trait, where every cell is uniformly small · Erythrocyte count – low in iron deficiency because the marrow lacks substrate, but normal or elevated in thalassemia trait, which makes plenty of small cells · Mentzer index – MCV divided by RBC; over 13 favours iron deficiency and under 13 favours thalassemia trait · TIBC direction – elevated in iron deficiency as transferrin is upregulated, and low in anemia of chronic disease · MCHC – low in both iron deficiency and thalassemia, and elevated in hereditary spherocytosis from loss of membrane surface area · Cow milk threshold – over 24 oz per day after age 1 is the named risk factor, because milk is iron-poor, its calcium and caseinophosphopeptide block absorption, and volume displaces iron-rich food
Transferable rule When two diseases share a lab value and one suppresses the marker used to diagnose the other, testing order is a dependency, not a preference. Correct the confounder first, then run the definitive test.
Sequencing trapHemoglobin electrophoresis: it checks for thalassemia, but iron deficiency makes it uninterpretable.
Class-vs-memberBone marrow biopsy: it can look like the definitive hematology test, but it is invasive and unnecessary when a dietary cause is obvious.

edits.html:
Hemophilia

refractory bleeding on replacement: alloantibodies · the mixing study proves it · bleeding to lab pattern · arthropathyIs the partial thromboplastin time still long on adequate factor, with normal platelets and prothrombin time?

The decision point

A patient with known severe hemophilia A on factor VIII replacement has bleeding that does not respond to increased dosing. The aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time) is 112 seconds, massively prolonged despite daily infusions that should be correcting it. The infused factor VIII is being neutralized by alloantibodies. This is inhibitor development, which occurs in ~25% of patients with severe hemophilia A.

An aPTT of 112 on replacement therapy means the intrinsic pathway remains uncorrected even though the missing factor is being given. Platelets of 150K and a normal PT (prothrombin time) exclude every platelet and common-pathway cause.

Defining criteria Inhibitor development – alloantibodies (IgG) against infused factor VIII; ~25% of severe hemophilia A patients · Clinical clue – bleeding refractory to adequate factor replacement therapy · Lab clue – prolonged aPTT that does not correct on a mixing study · Bethesda assay – quantifies inhibitor titer; guides treatment (low <5 BU vs high ≥5 BU)
Refractory bleeding in a hemophiliac – the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded by
Inhibitor developmentKnown hemophilia on replacement; increasing bleedsRefractory bleeding + prolonged aPTT on replacement + mixing study does not correct –
Acquired von Willebrand diseaseAutoimmune, lymphoproliferative; mucocutaneous bleedingMucosal bleeding; low vWF antigen and ristocetin cofactorHemarthrosis, not mucocutaneous
Fibrinogen dysfunctionDIC, liver failure; diffuse bleedingBoth PT and aPTT prolonged; low fibrinogenPT is normal
Heparin-induced thrombocytopeniaHeparin exposure; thrombosis + falling plateletsThrombocytopenia + thrombosis; 4T score, PF4 antibodyPlatelets 150K (normal)
Platelet dysfunctionUremia, ASA; mucocutaneous bleedingNormal coagulation studies + prolonged PFA-100aPTT 112; hemarthrosis, not petechiae
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
PT, aPTT and platelet countFirstaPTT prolonged; PT and platelets normalIntrinsic pathway defect, not platelets or the common pathway
Mixing study, incubated at 37 CNextaPTT does not correctAn inhibitor; correction means a simple factor deficiency
Factor VIII and IX activityConfirmsLow factor VIII or IX, when the mix correctsNew diagnosis: hemophilia A or B
Bethesda assayConfirmsInhibitor titer, 5 BU or more is highHigh titer: bypassing agents; low titer: high-dose factor VIII
MRI of the kneeBy branchSynovial thickening and cartilage damageEarly hemophilic arthropathy when radiographs are still normal
Platelet function assay (PFA-100)SkipNormal in hemophiliaJoint bleeding with a long aPTT is a factor problem, not a platelet problem
Bleeding pattern first Factor (clotting) defect – deep bleeding: hemarthroses, muscle hematomas, large ecchymoses, excess bleeding after surgery; the PT or aPTT is prolonged · Platelet defect – mucocutaneous bleeding: nosebleeds, gum bleeding, heavy periods, petechiae, small bruises; the count is low or aggregation is abnormal · PT – factors VII, X, V, II and fibrinogen; factor VII is the only one the PT measures alone · aPTT – factors XII, XI, IX, VIII, X, V, II and fibrinogen · Hemophilia by age – easy bruising in infancy; hemarthroses and deep hematomas once the toddler walks · Factor XI deficiency – the hemophilia lab pattern, but bleeding mainly with surgery or major trauma
Bleeding pattern to lab pattern
DisorderWho bleeds, and howLab pattern (platelets, PT, aPTT)Separating clue
Hemophilia A or B (factor VIII or IX)X-linked, boys; joints, deep muscle, large ecchymosesPlatelets normal, PT normal, aPTT prolonged; aggregation normalA joint or deep bleed in a boy; factor VIII and IX levels confirm
Factor VII deficiencyRare; factor-type bleedingPlatelets normal, PT prolonged, aPTT normalAn isolated long PT
Vitamin K deficiencyNewborn without vitamin K at birth, malabsorption, broad-spectrum antibioticsPlatelets normal, PT prolonged first, then aPTT tooFactor VII has the shortest half-life, so the PT lengthens first; corrects with vitamin K
DICAn ill patient (sepsis, trauma); oozing from lines, petechiae and deep bleedingPlatelets low, PT and aPTT prolonged; fibrinogen low, D-dimer highSick patient; platelets and factors consumed together
Immune thrombocytopeniaWell child; petechiae, small bruises, nose or gum bleedingPlatelets low, PT and aPTT normalIsolated thrombocytopenia
Glanzmann thrombastheniaMucocutaneous bleeding from infancyPlatelets normal, PT and aPTT normal, aggregation abnormalA qualitative platelet defect at a normal count
Von Willebrand diseaseEither sex; nosebleeds, gum bleeding, heavy periods; severe forms bleed like hemophiliaPlatelets normal, PT normal, aPTT normal or mildly prolongedvWF carries factor VIII, so low vWF lowers VIII; the vWF panel confirms
Factor XII deficiencyNo bleedingPlatelets normal, PT normal, aPTT markedly prolongedA long aPTT on preoperative screening in a child who has never bled
Factor XIII deficiencyUmbilical stump bleeding, intracranial hemorrhage soon after birthAll normalXIII cross-links fibrin after the clot forms, so the PT and aPTT miss it
Scenario bank
  1. 15 yo M with hemophilia A on prophylactic factor VIII, 5 days of right elbow swelling despite daily infusions, aPTT 112, PT normal, platelets normal → Inhibitor development → bypassing agent for acute bleed
  2. 12 yo M with hemophilia A and a known high-titer inhibitor (35 Bethesda units), acute hemarthrosis of the knee → Recombinant activated factor VII → bypasses factor VIII in the coagulation cascade
  3. 8 yo M with hemophilia A and a newly detected low-titer inhibitor (2 Bethesda units), long-term management → Immune tolerance induction with regular high-dose factor VIII → inhibitor eradication
  4. 10 yo M with hemophilia A on replacement therapy, recent increase in bleeding episodes, aPTT prolonged → Mixing study followed by Bethesda assay → confirm and quantify inhibitor
  5. Why a mixing study fails to correct the aPTT in a patient with a factor VIII inhibitor → The inhibitor is a time- and temperature-dependent antibody that neutralizes the normal factor VIII added in the mix
  6. 60 yo F with no bleeding history, new-onset large ecchymoses, aPTT 85, PT normal, mixing study does not correct after 2-hour incubation → Acquired hemophilia A → anti-factor VIII antibody titer
  7. 15 yo M with hemophilia A and inhibitor, life-threatening intracranial hemorrhage not responding to recombinant factor VIIa → Activated prothrombin complex concentrate → second-line bypassing agent
  8. 3 yo M with immediate right knee swelling after a fall, a large hip ecchymosis last week and scattered shin bruises; hemoglobin 13, platelets 187,000, leukocytes 8,500; radiograph shows a large effusion without fracture → Coagulation studies → hemarthrosis after minor trauma suggests a factor deficiency
  9. 4 yo M with recurrent hemarthroses; prothrombin time and platelet count are normal and the activated partial thromboplastin time is prolonged → Factor VIII and factor IX activity levels → separates hemophilia A from B
  10. 3 yo M with suspected severe hemophilia presenting with hemarthrosis and easy bruising → Bone marrow biopsy → contraindicated in severe hemophilia because of bleeding risk
  11. 16 yo M with past episodes of sudden knee swelling without injury and prolonged bleeding after a tooth extraction, now 6 months of worsening knee pain with a boggy swelling and a knee he cannot fully extend → Hemosiderin deposition and fibrosis → hemophilic arthropathy after recurrent hemarthroses
  12. 3 yo M with severe hemophilia A and a second spontaneous knee hemarthrosis this year → Regular factor VIII prophylaxis → prevents the bleeds that build arthropathy
  13. 14 yo M with hemophilia A, repeated bleeds into the same knee and persistent swelling, with normal radiographs → MRI of the knee → shows synovial and cartilage damage before radiographs
  14. Adult with mild hemophilia A due for a dental extraction → Desmopressin → releases stored factor VIII and von Willebrand factor
  15. 15 mo M, walking since 12 months and bruising after minor bumps since then; now a swollen, tender left ankle with reduced motion after play and no fever; large ecchymoses on both thighs at recent vaccination sites; nares and oropharynx clear, no organomegaly; ankle radiograph shows no fracture → Normal platelet count, normal PT, prolonged PTT, normal platelet aggregation → Hemophilia A or B: deficiency of intrinsic factor VIII or IX
  16. 3-week-old M born at home whose parents declined newborn injections, exclusively breastfed, well-appearing and afebrile, now oozing from the circumcision site with a large scalp bruise → Normal platelet count, prolonged PT, prolonged PTT → Vitamin K deficiency bleeding: factors II, VII, IX and X are low
  17. 6-day-old M who received vitamin K at birth, bleeding from the umbilical stump; platelet count, PT and aPTT all normal → Factor XIII deficiency → XIII cross-links fibrin after the clot forms, so the PT and aPTT stay normal
  18. 5 yo M whose preoperative labs before tonsillectomy show a markedly prolonged aPTT with a normal PT and platelet count; a circumcision and a dental extraction caused no abnormal bleeding, and no relative bleeds → Factor XII deficiency → a long aPTT with no bleeding tendency
Hemophilic arthropathy Hemophilia – X-linked recessive deficiency of factor VIII (A) or factor IX (B); prolonged aPTT with normal PT and platelets; severity tracks factor activity · Hemarthrosis – spontaneous or trivial-trauma bleeding into a large joint, often a knee, with sudden severe swelling · The link – iron from the extravasated red cells is stored as hemosiderin in the synovium, which inflames it · Then – the synovium thickens and turns boggy, fibroses, and the cartilage and subchondral bone are destroyed · Result – chronic pain, swelling and loss of motion, including a joint that will not fully extend actively or passively · Imaging – radiographs show only late disease; MRI detects damage earlier · Prevention – early prophylaxis with factor concentrate lowers the risk · Treatment – factor replacement; desmopressin for mild hemophilia A · Versus JIA or RA – autoimmune cartilage destruction, no bleeding history · Versus disseminated gonococcal infection – acute onset, not 6 months · Versus avascular necrosis – sickle cell disease, or Legg-Calvé-Perthes at the hip between 4 and 12 · Versus Lyme arthritis – knee effusion, but no bleeding history
Pearls Mixing study – mix patient plasma 1:1 with normal plasma. Correction of the aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time) means factor deficiency; no correction means an inhibitor. A factor VIII inhibitor is time- and temperature-dependent (incubate at 37°C for 1–2 hours before reading) · Bethesda assay – low-titer (<5 BU) may respond to high-dose factor VIII; high-titer (≥5 BU) requires bypassing agents: rFVIIa (recombinant activated factor VII) or activated PCC (prothrombin complex concentrate) · Immune tolerance induction – repeated high-dose factor VIII to desensitize the immune system; the long-term eradication strategy · Acquired hemophilia A – the adult analogue: autoantibodies in a patient with no prior bleeding history, often autoimmune, malignancy, or postpartum · Hemarthrosis versus petechiae – hemarthrosis indicates a factor problem and petechiae a platelet problem; this division sorts most bleeding disorders before any lab is read
Pairs with Anemia with Thrombocytopenia also uses the coagulation workup. Ask: does the aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time) correct on mixing? Part II Vitamins and Nutritional Deficiencies covers vitamin K deficiency. Ask: is the PT (prothrombin time) long first, and is factor V normal (vitamin K) or low (liver)?
Transferable rule Bleeding on factor replacement therapy that does not respond to dose escalation, with an aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time) still prolonged despite adequate dosing, means the infused factor is being neutralized. The mixing study proves it.
Unchecked attributePlatelet dysfunction: platelets are normal, and the abnormal value is the aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time), which is not a platelet test.
True-fact-wrong-slotAcquired vWD (von Willebrand disease): it can lower factor VIII but presents with mucocutaneous bleeding, not hemarthrosis. The patient already has a known factor deficiency.
Unchecked attributeFibrinogen dysfunction: the PT (prothrombin time) is normal, and a fibrinogen (common pathway) defect would prolong both the PT and the aPTT.

edits.html:
Transfusion Reactions

onset and company · urticarial vs anaphylactic · hemolytic and bacterial emergencies · when to resume · most need nothingWhat are the vitals, and what else is on the skin besides hives?

Source vignette Pt – 12 yo F with idiopathic aplastic anemia, new petechiae and bruising over a week; during a platelet transfusion a chest rash spreads over the body · Labs – absolute neutrophil count 420, platelets 7,000 · Exam – T 37.2 °C, blood pressure (BP) 110/82 mm Hg, heart rate (HR) 90/min, respiratory rate (RR) 18/min, saturation 98%; oropharynx normal, lungs clear; diffuse urticarial rash on trunk and limbs plus pinpoint nonblanching macules and bruises at the extremities · Q – the best next step in evaluation of the reaction; options spanned culture of the product, direct Coombs test, no additional evaluation, peripheral smear and coagulation studies
The decision point

Blood pressure is normal, there is no wheeze, the lungs are clear and the oropharynx is normal. This is isolated urticaria in a hemodynamically stable patient. The rash improved after an antihistamine, with an hour of stable observation. It is an urticarial transfusion reaction, caused by preformed IgE reacting against a soluble allergen in the donated plasma, or the reverse. Management is what has already been done: stop the transfusion, give an antihistamine and observe. Improvement with the antihistamine confirms the diagnosis, and the transfusion may be resumed without additional evaluation.

Defining criteria Urticarial reaction – hives and itching only, onset hours into the transfusion, from preformed IgE against a soluble plasma allergen; stop, antihistamine, resume if otherwise asymptomatic, no workup · Anaphylactic reaction – onset seconds to minutes, from anti-IgA antibodies in an IgA-deficient recipient reacting to donor IgA; respiratory distress or wheeze, angioedema, hypotension; epinephrine, and washed products thereafter · Acute hemolytic reaction – ABO incompatibility from clerical error; fever, flank pain, hypotension, hemoglobinuria, direct Coombs positive · Transfusion-transmitted bacterial infection – fever, chills, hypotension, most common with platelets; culture both the recipient and the product
Transfusion reactions: timing, company and the movethe vitals sort them faster than the rash does
ReactionOnsetThe company it keepsWhat to do
UrticarialHoursHives and itching, nothing else; vitals normalStop, antihistamine, resume; no workup
Anaphylactic EmergencySeconds to minutesWheeze, angioedema, hypotension; IgA-deficient recipientEpinephrine; future transfusions washed
Acute hemolytic EmergencyMinutes to hoursFever, flank pain, hypotension, dark urineStop; direct Coombs, smear, prothrombin time (PT) and partial thromboplastin time (PTT); supportive
Bacterial contamination EmergencyMinutes to hoursFever, rigors, hypotension; platelets most oftenCulture recipient and product; empiric antibiotics
Febrile nonhemolyticDuring or within 4 hFever and chills without hemolysisStop, antipyretic; leukoreduction reduces its incidence
TACO (transfusion-associated circulatory overload) / TRALI (transfusion-related acute lung injury)TRALI within 6 h; TACO within 12 hRespiratory distress: volume overload vs noncardiogenic edemaStop; diuretic for TACO, supportive care for TRALI
Pertinent positives & negatives BP 110/82 mm Hg, HR 90/min, saturation 98% – hemodynamically stable, which excludes anaphylaxis, hemolysis and sepsis · Lungs clear, oropharynx normal – no bronchospasm, no angioedema; the two findings that would make this anaphylaxis · Afebrile at 37.2 °C – excludes both a febrile reaction and bacterial contamination · Rash improved with diphenhydramine and stayed stable for an hour – confirms the diagnosis · Petechiae and bruises were present before the transfusion – they reflect a platelet count of 7,000 from aplastic anemia, not a new consumptive process · No flank pain, no dark urine – the findings of a hemolytic reaction are absent · It was a platelet transfusion – platelets are the product most associated with bacterial contamination; without fever, culture is not indicated
Decision spine What is the blood pressure and the saturation? – Normal → the dangerous reactions are out · Is there a fever? – No → not hemolytic, not bacterial, not febrile · Wheeze, angioedema or hypotension? – None → urticaria is isolated, so not anaphylaxis · How fast did it start? – Late, not in the first minutes → urticarial · Did it respond to the antihistamine? – Yes → that is the confirmation · So what is needed? – Nothing further; the transfusion may be resumed
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Vital signs, lung and airway examFirstNormal vitals, clear lungs, hives onlyThe dangerous reactions are excluded
None: clinical diagnosisConfirmsHives improve with an antihistamine, vitals stay stableUrticarial reaction; resume the transfusion, no tests
Direct Coombs test, smear, PT and PTTBy branchFever, flank pain, dark urine: Coombs positiveAcute hemolytic reaction from ABO incompatibility
Blood cultures of the recipient and the productBy branchFever, rigors, hypotension: growth in bothBacterial contamination, most often a platelet unit
Serum IgA levelBy branchAfter anaphylaxis: IgA absentAnti-IgA anaphylaxis; wash future products
Coombs test or product culture for hives aloneSkipAfebrile and stable: no indicationNothing to find; pre-existing petechiae come from the low platelets
Scenario bank
  1. 12 yo F with aplastic anemia developing a diffuse urticarial rash late in a platelet transfusion; BP 110/82 mm Hg, saturation 98%, afebrile, lungs clear; rash improves after diphenhydramine and vitals stay stable for an hour → No additional evaluation is indicated → urticarial reaction; the transfusion may be resumed
  2. 30 yo F who develops wheezing, facial angioedema and a blood pressure of 70/40 mm Hg two minutes into a red cell transfusion → Intramuscular epinephrine → anaphylactic transfusion reaction
  3. Patient with selective IgA deficiency and a history of transfusion anaphylaxis who now requires red blood cells → Transfuse washed red blood cells → washing removes donor plasma IgA
  4. 45 yo who develops fever, flank pain, hypotension and dark urine 20 minutes into a red cell transfusion → Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction → ABO incompatibility from a clerical error
  5. 60 yo M who develops fever to 39 °C with rigors and hypotension 30 minutes into a platelet transfusion → Culture the recipient and the transfused product and start empiric antibiotics → bacterial contamination, most common with platelets
  6. The mechanism of an isolated urticarial transfusion reaction → Preformed IgE reacting against a soluble allergen in donor plasma → or donor IgE against a recipient allergen
  7. 12 yo with aplastic anemia and platelets of 7,000 who develops hives during transfusion; pinpoint nonblanching macules were documented on her limbs before the transfusion began → Pre-existing thrombocytopenia → the petechiae are not part of the reaction
  8. IgA-deficient patient with prior transfusion anaphylaxis who urgently requires red blood cells → Standard unwashed packed red blood cells → residual donor plasma IgA triggers anaphylaxis
Decoy note The petechiae and ecchymoses look like a new hemorrhagic complication, and they appear in the skin examination beside the urticaria as though they arrived together. They were present before the transfusion: she had bruising a week ago, and her platelet count is 7,000. A finding documented before the intervention cannot be a reaction to it.
Pearls Vital signs: normal blood pressure, no fever and no hypoxia eliminate anaphylaxis, hemolysis, bacterial contamination and TRALI · Isolated urticaria is the only reaction in which the transfusion may continue: stop, give an antihistamine, observe, then resume the same unit · Timing separates the two allergic reactions: seconds to minutes with wheeze and hypotension is anaphylaxis; hours with hives alone is urticarial · Anaphylaxis to blood suggests IgA deficiency; the long-term fix is washed products · Platelets carry the bacterial risk because they are stored at room temperature; fever and rigors during a platelet transfusion call for cultures
Pairs with Part I Antibody Deficiencies covers selective IgA deficiency and already keys washed red cells; this brief covers the same topic from the transfusion side. Ask: what are the vitals, and what else is on the skin besides hives?
Transferable rule When a treatment has already been given and the response is reported, the response serves as the diagnostic test, and usually nothing further is needed. Check the reported response before ordering anything.
Redundant workupDirect Coombs test: answers "is this hemolysis?", already excluded by normal vitals, no fever, no flank pain and no dark urine.
Salient decoyPT and PTT: indicated only for hemolysis complicated by disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC); her bruising is thrombocytopenic and predates the transfusion.
Redundant workupPeripheral smear: would show schistocytes if microangiopathy were present; there is no hemolysis to look for.
Unchecked attributeCulture of the product: platelets do carry the bacterial risk, but culture requires fever, chills or hypotension; she is afebrile and stable.

edits.html:
Acute Leukemia in a Child

pancytopenia with bone pain · counts down vs up · screen versus confirm · marrow before steroidsAre two or more cell lines down, and has the marrow been sampled before any steroid?

Source vignette Pt – 5 yo M, 2 weeks of fatigue, 1 week of leg pain, 1 day of fever with petechiae; pale, liver 4 cm below the costal margin, cervical and axillary adenopathy · Q – the most useful test; options spanned complete blood count with differential and smear, C-reactive protein and partial thromboplastin time
The decision point

Together, tri-lineage cytopenia, diaphyseal bone pain and diffuse nontender adenopathy with splenomegaly fit only one disease. They indicate marrow replacement, which is confirmed in the marrow.

The complete blood count is the initial and most useful first test: cheap, fast, and enough to convert a vague illness into an oncologic emergency. It raises the suspicion of leukemia; the bone marrow aspirate is the diagnostic test that confirms it.

Defining criteria Pancytopenia – reduction in all three lineages, the word that eliminates every single-lineage disease · ALL diagnostic gate – at least 20% lymphoblasts of marrow nucleated cells · M1, M2, M3 marrow – under 5%, 5 to 25%, over 25% blasts, a burden and response category rather than the diagnostic gate · Leukemic bone pain – diaphyseal or metaphyseal tenderness from marrow expansion, distinct from joint-line pain · Petechiae – a platelet problem, so PT and PTT are normal
The pale child with bone pain – the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Acute lymphoblastic leukemiaPeak 2 to 5 yr; marrow replaced by lymphoblastsPancytopenia with diaphyseal pain and nontender adenopathy; counts go down
Sickle cell aplastic crisisParvovirus B19 arrests erythropoiesisIsolated anemia with reticulocytopenia; platelets and WBC normal
Infectious mononucleosisAdolescent, prolonged fever and fatigueTender posterior cervical nodes, atypical lymphocytosis, transaminitis
Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritisQuotidian fever, evanescent rashCounts go up – leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, ferritin high
Aplastic anemiaMarrow failure without infiltrationPancytopenia with an empty exam: no adenopathy, no organomegaly, no bone pain
Neuroblastoma Can't missUnder 5 yr; marrow metastases give identical cytopenia and bone painPeriorbital ecchymoses, proptosis, midline-crossing abdominal mass
Immune thrombocytopeniaPost-viral, well-appearing childIsolated thrombocytopenia with normal PT and PTT
Nonaccidental traumaVague or shifting history, bruises in areas that are not injury-prone (trunk, ears, neck)Normal blood counts; trauma never lowers them
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
CBC with differential and peripheral smearFirstTwo or more cell lines low, with or without blastsMarrow replacement; a normal white count does not exclude ALL
Uric acid, potassium, phosphate, calcium, creatinineNextHigh uric acid, potassium and phosphateTumor lysis risk; hydrate before and during induction
Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy with flow cytometryConfirms20% or more lymphoblastsALL and its lineage; obtain before any corticosteroid
Chest radiographStagingAnterior mediastinal massT-cell ALL
Lumbar punctureStagingBlasts in the CSFCNS disease
C-reactive protein or PTTSkipCRP nonspecific; PTT normal with petechiaeNeither selects or excludes leukemia
Scenario bank
  1. 5 yo M with 2 wk of fatigue, 1 wk of leg pain and 1 day of fever with petechiae, pale, liver 4 cm below the costal margin, cervical and axillary adenopathy → Complete blood count with differential and peripheral smear → bone marrow confirms afterwards
  2. 5 yo M whose complete blood count shows hemoglobin 7, platelets 22,000 and WBC 3,100 → Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy → greater than 20% lymphoblasts
  3. 4 yo M, 3 wk fever, pallor, petechiae, nontender diffuse adenopathy, splenomegaly, midshaft femoral tenderness, WBC 2,800 and platelets 18,000 → Acute lymphoblastic leukemia → bone marrow aspirate and biopsy
  4. 4 yo M with fever, limp and pancytopenia in whom a colleague proposes empiric prednisone for presumed systemic JIA → Obtain bone marrow before any corticosteroid → steroids partially treat ALL and destroy the specimen
  5. 5 yo M with 4 wk of fatigue and pallor, pancytopenia, no adenopathy, no organomegaly and no bone pain → Aplastic anemia → bone marrow biopsy showing a hypocellular marrow
  6. 6 yo F, 5 wk of daily spiking fever, evanescent salmon rash, WBC 24,000 and platelets 700,000 → Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis
  7. 4 yo M with petechiae and bruising 2 wk after a viral illness, well-appearing and afebrile, platelets 12,000 with normal hemoglobin and WBC → Immune thrombocytopenia → observation
  8. 8 yo M with sickle cell disease, hemoglobin 4.2, reticulocytes 0.2%, normal platelets and WBC → Parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis → transfuse and supportive care
  9. 3 yo M with fever, refusal to walk, pancytopenia, periorbital ecchymoses and proptosis, and an abdominal mass crossing the midline → Neuroblastoma → urine HVA and VMA
  10. 16 yo M, 3 wk fever, sore throat, tender posterior cervical nodes, splenomegaly and atypical lymphocytes → Infectious mononucleosis → avoid contact sports for 3 to 4 weeks
  11. 6 yo F with petechiae and gum bleeding, platelets 9,000, PT and PTT normal, otherwise well → No further coagulation testing is needed → petechiae are a platelet problem
  12. 5 yo M with pancytopenia and adenopathy in whom a normal white count on an earlier CBC is offered as reassurance → Accepting a normal white count as excluding leukemia → some ALL presents with under 1% circulating blasts
  13. 7 yo M, day 3 of ALL induction, potassium 6.8, phosphate 8.1, uric acid 14, calcium 6.8 and creatinine 2.1 → Tumor lysis syndrome → intravenous hydration and urate-lowering therapy
  14. 7 yo M on day 3 of ALL induction with rising potassium, phosphate and uric acid, a low calcium and a rising creatinine → IV hydration and urate-lowering therapy → tumor lysis syndrome
  15. 14 yo M with pancytopenia, marrow lymphoblasts and an anterior mediastinal mass on chest film → T-cell lineage → a mediastinal mass points to T-cell ALL
  16. 5 yo F brought by her mother and the mother's boyfriend a week after a fall from the couch, now leg pain worse at night and refusing to walk; a month of dry cough, temperature 38.3 C, pale, liver 3 cm below the costal margin, bilateral proximal tibial tenderness, scattered bruises on the chest and back; hemoglobin 8, platelets 30,000, WBC 3,000 → Acute lymphoblastic leukemia → bone pain plus pancytopenia
  17. 2 yo with bruises of different ages on the ears, neck and trunk, a history that changes between caregivers, and a normal CBC and coagulation profile → Nonaccidental trauma → normal counts; bruises away from injury-prone areas
  18. 5 yo with ALL and scattered truncal bruises whose family links them to a recent fall → Marrow replacement by blasts → thrombocytopenia, not trauma
  19. 4 yo M with 1 month of bruises on the chest, back and legs, more fatigue and longer naps, poor appetite, and 1 week of gum bleeding with brushing; tonsillectomy last year without complications; a paternal uncle has hemophilia; normal vital signs; pale; buccal mucosal hematomas; bruises and petechiae on the shins, chest and back; nontender bilateral anterior cervical nodes; hepatosplenomegaly; no joint swelling → Platelet production → Acute lymphoblastic leukemia replacing the marrow
  20. 3 yo M with a warm, swollen, painful knee after a minor fall; prolonged bleeding after circumcision as a newborn; a maternal uncle has hemophilia; no pallor, adenopathy or organomegaly; hemoglobin, platelets and WBC normal; PT normal, PTT prolonged → Hemophilia A → Factor VIII activity level
Never steroids before the marrow Corticosteroids partially treat ALL (acute lymphoblastic leukemia). They transiently improve the child while destroying the diagnostic specimen and degrading risk stratification. Separate systemic JIA (juvenile idiopathic arthritis) from ALL before treatment, not after. A normal white count does not exclude ALL; the cytopenias are the clue, not the blasts.
Leukemic bone pain blamed on a fall The story – families often date leukemic bone pain to a fall; the pain is dull, in the long-bone shafts, worse at night, and the child limps or refuses to walk · What makes it systemic – fever, hepatomegaly, bilateral tibial tenderness and two or more cytopenias · The bruises – thrombocytopenia explains truncal bruising; trauma cannot depress three cell lines · When to think abuse – a vague history with bruising away from injury-prone areas, and normal counts · The white count – often low early, since normal production falls; later high as blasts spill into the blood · Versus aplastic anemia – pancytopenia from a hypocellular marrow, so no bone pain and rarely hepatomegaly · Versus immune thrombocytopenia – hemoglobin and white count normal, no bone pain or organomegaly · Workup – marrow biopsy with flow cytometry (20% or more blasts), then lumbar puncture for CNS (central nervous system) disease · Prognosis – 5-year survival above 85% in children with multidrug chemotherapy
A paternal family history of hemophilia Paternal uncle with hemophilia – hemophilia A is X-linked recessive, so a boy inherits it through his mother; his father's brother cannot pass it to him · Uneventful tonsillectomy last year – a surgical challenge passed without bleeding argues against any inherited bleeding disorder · New bleeding plus pallor, nodes and hepatosplenomegaly – an acquired marrow problem: blasts crowd out megakaryocytes, so platelet production fails · Hemophilia – joint and muscle bleeds after trauma, prolonged PTT (partial thromboplastin time), normal counts and no organomegaly · Von Willebrand disease – lifelong mucosal bleeding with a normal platelet count and a normal exam
Pearls Leukemia lowers blood counts; systemic JIA (juvenile idiopathic arthritis) raises them, with ferritin, platelets and WBC (white blood cell count) all rising · Neuroblastoma and ALL (acute lymphoblastic leukemia) are confirmed by the same test; periorbital ecchymoses and a midline-crossing mass separate them · A mediastinal mass points to T-cell ALL and can compress the airway or cause superior vena cava syndrome; a normal chest film does not exclude B-cell ALL · About half of children with ALL present with bleeding (petechiae, bruising, gum oozing) from thrombocytopenia · Extramedullary spread also shows as testicular enlargement and as leptomeningeal disease with cranial nerve deficits or meningismus, which is why a lumbar puncture is part of the workup · Inflammatory markers monitor disease; they do not distinguish between diagnoses that all raise them · Tumor lysis: potassium up, phosphate up, uric acid up, calcium down, with acute kidney injury
Pairs with Part I Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis is the mirror twin, and Part I The Limping Child shares the presenting complaint. Ask: are the counts up or down? Part I Leg Pain in a Child covers the benign nocturnal limb pain whose normal examination excludes this diagnosis. Aquifer Bruising and Purpura in a Child places leukemia among the other causes of bruising in a child. Part I Hemophilia covers the bleeding-pattern-to-lab table: is the PT (prothrombin time) or the PTT (partial thromboplastin time) long, and are the platelets normal?
How NBME framed it A systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis diagnosis made 2 months earlier, partly improved on ibuprofen, was the anchor; new pancytopenia with hepatosplenomegaly still meant bone marrow aspiration, not imaging or liver biopsy.
Transferable rule Choose laboratory tests by what a result could change, not by their sophistication. A test that is abnormal in every diagnosis on the differential discriminates nothing. A test of an uninvolved compartment does not address the clinical question.
Salient decoyEthnicity and travel are epidemiologic priors, not findings, and cannot outrank the blood count.
True-fact-wrong-slotSplenomegaly and generalised adenopathy are not features of Kawasaki or of leukemia's mimics in the way offered.
Class-vs-memberPTT is the right class of haematologic test on the wrong compartment.
Salient decoyThe fall and the mother's boyfriend pull toward abuse, but trauma cannot explain fever, hepatomegaly or three low cell lines.
