edits.html:
Oral Lesions in a Child

vesicles vs exudate · front of the mouth or back · herpangina vs herpetic gingivostomatitis · the palm and sole rashAre the lesions vesicles or exudate, and do they sit at the front of the mouth or the back?

Source vignette Pt – 5 yo M, 3 days of fever with 2 days of throat pain and poor intake; T 38.3, HR 108 · Exam – scattered 1 mm vesicles on the anterior palatine pillars with gray shallow ulcers on the soft palate and uvula; tongue, lips and buccal mucosa spared; no rash · Q – the most likely associated pathogen; options spanned adenovirus, coxsackievirus, Epstein-Barr virus, herpes simplex virus and Streptococcus pyogenes
The decision point

The lesions are vesicles and ulcers, not exudate. This removes every bacterial and mononucleosis-type pharyngitis. Adenovirus, EBV (Epstein-Barr virus) and S. pyogenes all produce tonsillar exudate, and none produces oral vesicles. The lesions are posterior (soft palate, uvula, anterior palatine pillars), with the tongue, lips and buccal mucosa explicitly spared. Herpangina, from coxsackievirus A, affects the back of the mouth. In herpetic gingivostomatitis, lesions affect the front, with red swollen gums. The spared structures are exactly those HSV (herpes simplex virus) would involve.

Defining criteria Herpangina – coxsackievirus A; ages 3 to 10; late summer and early fall; fever and pharyngitis with gray vesicles progressing to fibrin-coated ulcers on the posterior oropharynx, and no rash; treatment is supportive · Herpetic gingivostomatitis – HSV-1; 6 months to 5 years; no seasonality; clusters of vesicles on the anterior oral mucosa and lips with erythematous, edematous gingiva; treated with oral acyclovir · Hand-foot-and-mouth disease – also coxsackievirus, but anterior oral lesions plus vesicles on palms and soles; herpangina's defining negative is the absent rash
Pertinent positives & negatives Vesicles and ulcers, not exudate – excludes adenovirus, EBV and group A streptococcus in one move · Soft palate, uvula and palatine pillars involved – the posterior distribution, herpangina territory · Tongue, lips and buccal mucosa spared – a stated negative that excludes HSV gingivostomatitis, whose distribution is precisely those structures · No rash – separates herpangina from hand-foot-and-mouth disease · No gingival erythema or edema described – a second strike against HSV, whose gingivitis is near-universal · Age 5, starting the fall term in 2 weeks – age 3 to 10 and late summer, both epidemiological features; the school detail is dating the season, not flagging exposure · No adenopathy or splenomegaly – nothing to support mononucleosis
Oral lesions in a child – the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Herpangina (coxsackievirus A)3 to 10 yrs, late summer and early fall, abrupt high feverPosterior gray vesicles becoming ulcers: soft palate, uvula, pillars; no rash – (the answer)
Herpetic gingivostomatitis (HSV-1)6 months to 5 years, any season; drooling, refuses to drinkAnterior clusters on buccal mucosa, tongue and lips; swollen red gingivaThose exact sites are stated as spared
Hand-foot-and-mouth diseaseSame virus family, same seasonAnterior oral lesions plus palms and solesThe skin has no rash
Streptococcal pharyngitisFever, sore throat, no coughTonsillar exudate, tender anterior nodes, palatal petechiaeVesicles and ulcers rather than exudate
Infectious mononucleosisAdolescent with prolonged fatigueExudate plus posterior cervical nodes plus splenomegalyNo exudate, no adenopathy, no splenomegaly
Adenoviral tonsillitisFever, cough, sore throat, sometimes conjunctivitisExudate without vesiclesVesicular lesions are not its picture
Decision spine Vesicles and ulcers, or exudate? – Vesicles means a viral enanthem, and the bacterial and EBV options fall · Front of the mouth or back? – Back means herpangina · Are the gums red and swollen? – Not described, which argues against HSV · Is there a rash on palms and soles? – No, so not hand-foot-and-mouth · Age and season? – Five years in late summer corroborates · So what is the management? – Supportive; it self-resolves within a week
Scenario bank
  1. 5 yo M, 3 days of fever with throat pain, 1 mm vesicles on the anterior palatine pillars and gray shallow ulcers on the soft palate and uvula, tongue and lips and buccal mucosa spared, no rash → Coxsackievirus A → herpangina
  2. 2 yo with fever, drooling and refusal to drink; clusters of vesicles on the gingiva, tongue and lips with erythematous edematous gums → Herpetic gingivostomatitis → oral acyclovir
  3. 3 yo with fever, oral ulcers and vesicles on the palms and soles → Hand-foot-and-mouth disease → supportive care
  4. 5 yo with posterior oral vesicles and ulcers, drinking less but with moist mucous membranes and normal vital signs → Cold non-acidic fluids with analgesia → herpangina resolves within a week
  5. 8 yo with fever, tonsillar exudate and tender anterior cervical nodes, without cough or oral vesicles → Group A streptococcal pharyngitis → rapid antigen testing before treating
  6. 16 yo with 2 weeks of fatigue, exudative pharyngitis, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly → Epstein-Barr virus infection → avoid contact sports
  7. 5 yo with gray vesicles and ulcers confined to the soft palate and uvula, no rash, well hydrated → Oral acyclovir → herpangina is an enteroviral illness, not a herpesvirus one
  8. 4 yo with herpangina now refusing all fluids, with dry mucous membranes and no urine output for 10 hours → Intravenous rehydration → dehydration is the principal complication
  9. 5 yo in late summer with abrupt fever and sore throat; gray vesicles and shallow ulcers on the soft palate, uvula and anterior pillars; gums, lips and tongue normal; no rash → Herpangina → coxsackievirus A; supportive care
Pearls Anterior is herpes, posterior is coxsackie – both diseases otherwise present with fever, sore throat and a miserable child · Vesicles and ulcers exclude exudate-producing pathogens wholesale: strep, EBV and adenovirus make exudate, not blisters · Herpangina has no rash; hand-foot-and-mouth does – same virus family, separated by the skin · Red swollen gingiva is the HSV signature, and its absence is as informative as any positive finding · Starting the fall term in two weeks is dating the season, not describing an exposure · The virus can stay in stool for weeks after infection, so hand hygiene is the public-health answer
Pairs with Part I Respiratory Infection in a Child covers the exudative pharyngitis fork and the Centor rule; this brief covers vesicular lesions. Ask: are the lesions exudate or vesicles, and are they front or back? Part II Fever and Rash in a Child sorts hand-foot-and-mouth disease among the other rashes with fever.
Transferable rule When two diseases share a lesion type, the discriminating attribute is usually anatomical, not clinical. Ask where the lesions are before asking what they are. Treat a stated spared structure as an active exclusion, not as background.
Unchecked attributeHerpes simplex virus: oral vesicles in a child retrieves HSV automatically, but HSV is anterior and those sites are explicitly spared, with no gingival swelling.
Class-vs-memberAdenovirus: a common cause of pediatric fever with sore throat, but it produces exudative tonsillitis, not vesicles or ulcers.
Class-vs-memberStreptococcus pyogenes: exudate with tender anterior nodes; vesicles and ulcers argue against it.
True-fact-wrong-slotEpstein-Barr virus: exudate, posterior cervical nodes, splenomegaly and adolescent age; none present.

edits.html:
Neutrophil Disorders: Number and Function

number vs function · catalase-positive organisms · granulomas and abscesses · oxidative burst test · low countsIs the neutrophil count low, or are there granulomas with infection outside the chest?

Source vignette Pt – 2 yo M, 3 days of fever, cough and irritability; perirectal abscess drained at 9 months; T 38.9, bilateral lower-lobe crackles · Imaging – bilateral pneumonia on chest film; after 3 days of antibiotics still febrile, CT shows a small left effusion with paratracheal and hilar lymphadenopathy · Labs – lymph node and lung biopsy shows granuloma formation; culture grows Burkholderia (Pseudomonas) cepacia · Q – the mechanism responsible; options spanned decreased immunoglobulin production, decreased superoxide production, defective opsonization, impaired clearing of airway secretions and impaired neutrophil chemotaxis
Source vignette · NBME Pediatrics CMS Pt – 2 yo M, 2 days of fever and mouth sores, fussy and refusing food, now improving; a year of similar episodes about every 3 weeks, each lasting 3 to 5 days; normal growth and development · Exam – T 38.4 C, HR 120; scattered aphthous ulcers; skin clear; no lymphadenopathy · Labs – Hb 11.5; WBC 4,000 with 4% segmented neutrophils, 84% lymphocytes, 12% monocytes; platelets 250,000 · Q – the most likely diagnosis; options spanned Chédiak-Higashi syndrome, cyclic neutropenia, dyskeratosis congenita, Fanconi syndrome, hypersplenism, leukemia, severe congenital neutropenia, viral illness and vitamin B12 deficiency
The decision point

The pneumonia does not name the defect. Granulomas on biopsy and a Burkholderia cepacia culture together point at one disease: chronic granulomatous disease. It is a disorder of NADPH oxidase, commonly X-linked with autosomal recessive forms. The enzyme drives the neutrophil respiratory burst, so its loss means decreased superoxide production. Phagocytes migrate normally and ingest normally, but have impaired intracellular killing. Neutrophils can borrow hydrogen peroxide made by the pathogen itself. Susceptibility therefore particularly involves characteristic catalase-positive organisms that destroy their own peroxide; this is not an exclusive organism list. The granulomas are the same defect seen histologically: phagocytes arrive but clear pathogens poorly, contributing to granuloma formation.

Defining criteria Chronic granulomatous disease – NADPH oxidase disorder, commonly X-linked with autosomal recessive forms; impaired respiratory burst and reduced reactive oxygen species, so intracellular killing is impaired · The organism pattern – particular susceptibility to characteristic catalase-positive bacteria and fungi, because catalase degrades the pathogen's own hydrogen peroxide and denies the neutrophil a borrowed oxidant: S aureus, B cepacia, Serratia marcescens, Nocardia, Aspergillus · Sites – lungs, skin, liver and lymph nodes; perirectal abscess is characteristic, with diffuse granulomas in the gastrointestinal and genitourinary tracts · Diagnosis – measure neutrophil superoxide production: dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry preferred, nitroblue tetrazolium the older equivalent · Treatment – prophylaxis with TMP-SMX, itraconazole and interferon gamma; haematopoietic cell transplant is curative
Recurrent infection – reading the mechanismwhich defect, by organism and by histology
MechanismDiseaseThe NBME tellExcluded here by
↓ superoxide productionChronic granulomatous diseaseCatalase-positive organisms + granulomas + abscesses (perirectal, liver) – (the answer)
Impaired airway clearanceCystic fibrosisNasal polyps, clubbing, steatorrhoea; also gets B cepaciaNo granulomas; infections confined to the sinopulmonary tract
↓ immunoglobulin productionX-linked agammaglobulinaemiaEncapsulated organisms; all isotypes low, absent B cellsNo granulomas, no abscesses, wrong organism
Defective opsonisationComplement (C3) deficiencyEncapsulated organisms, recurrent pyogenic infectionSame – and B cepacia is not the pattern
Impaired neutrophil chemotaxisLeukocyte adhesion deficiencyDelayed umbilical cord separation (over 3 weeks), skin and mucosal infections without pus (cellulitis, periodontitis), poor wound healing, marked leukocytosis with neutrophilia; CD18 integrin defectPus was present (abscess drained); no granulomas
Impaired Th17 signalling (JAK-STAT)Hyper-IgE (Job) syndromeCold staphylococcal and Candida abscesses, severe eczema, eosinophilia with a normal white countNo eczema or eosinophilia; granulomas and Burkholderia point to the oxidative burst
Pertinent positives & negatives Granulomas on biopsy – the most specific finding; excludes CF, XLA, complement deficiency and leukocyte adhesion deficiency, none of which form them · Burkholderia cepacia – catalase-positive, and shared with cystic fibrosis, which is exactly why it is not sufficient alone · Perirectal abscess at 9 months – extrapulmonary abscess; CF does not do this, and it is the finding that separates the two · Persistent fever after 3 days of appropriate antibiotics – killing is defective, not coverage · Hilar and paratracheal lymphadenopathy – node involvement, part of the CGD site pattern · Male, age 2 – consistent with the common X-linked form presenting in early childhood; autosomal recessive forms also occur · Normal ear, nose and throat examination – no chronic rhinosinusitis, arguing further against CF
Decision spine Are there granulomas? – Yes → CGD, essentially alone among the immunodeficiencies · What grew? – A catalase-positive organism → confirms · Where are the infections? – Lung and perirectal → extrapulmonary, so not CF · Was there pus? – Yes → chemotaxis and adhesion intact, so not leukocyte adhesion deficiency · What is the mechanism of that defect? – NADPH oxidase → decreased superoxide · How is it confirmed? – Dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
CBC with differentialFirstNeutrophils present, count normal or highThe defect is killing, not number; marked leukocytosis without pus suggests LAD; an absolute neutrophil count under 500 is a number problem instead
Biopsy and culture of abscess or nodeNextGranulomas with a catalase-positive organismCGD pattern; B. cepacia alone also fits cystic fibrosis
Dihydrorhodamine 123 flow cytometryConfirmsAbsent or reduced oxidative burstChronic granulomatous disease
Nitroblue tetrazolium testConfirmsNeutrophils fail to turn the dye blueCGD; the older equivalent of the DHR test
Neutrophil counts 2 to 3 times a week for 6 weeks, if the count is lowBy branchNadirs about every 21 days, normal between; or persistently lowCyclic neutropenia if periodic; severe congenital neutropenia if persistent
Sweat chloride, if no granulomasBy branch60 mmol/L or moreCystic fibrosis, which also grows B. cepacia
Genetic testing of NADPH oxidase genesCauseX-linked or autosomal recessive variantInheritance and family counseling
Quantitative serum immunoglobulinsSkipNormal or high in CGDAntibody production is intact
First fork: neutrophil number or function Number – the neutrophil count is low; infections are bacterial, with fever, mouth ulcers, gingivitis and skin, lung or gut infection when the count is lowest · Function – the count is normal or high and the cells fail at a step: adhesion (leukocyte adhesion deficiency), killing (chronic granulomatous disease), granule traffic (Chédiak-Higashi syndrome, which also lowers the count) · Absolute neutrophil count – WBC × (segmented neutrophils + bands); 4,000 × 4% is about 160; under 1,500 is neutropenia and under 500 is severe · Name trap – Fanconi syndrome is proximal renal tubule wasting of glucose, phosphate, bicarbonate and amino acids; Fanconi anemia is inherited marrow failure
Low neutrophil count in a child: the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe tellExcluded in the periodic-fever child by
Cyclic neutropeniaInherited, neutrophil elastase (ELANE) mutation; well between episodesEvery 21 days, lasting 3 to 6 days: fever, oral ulcers, pharyngitis; periodontal disease and early tooth loss; ANC often under 200 at the nadir – (the answer)
Severe congenital neutropeniaInherited, often ELANE; presents in the first months of lifePersistent severe neutropenia with omphalitis, pneumonia, abscesses; high risk of AMLPeriodic episodes with health between; first symptoms after infancy
Viral marrow suppressionParvovirus B19, EBV, CMV, HIV, other virusesTransient dip with the illness and its other symptomsA year of regular 3-week episodes; a virus does not keep a calendar
Acute leukemiaMalaise, weight loss, bone painAnemia and thrombocytopenia, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, blastsNormal platelets, no nodes or spleen, well between episodes
HypersplenismSplenic sequestrationSplenomegaly with all three cell lines lowNo splenomegaly; hemoglobin and platelets preserved
Fanconi anemiaInherited marrow failurePancytopenia with short stature, thumb or radial anomalies, microcephaly, café au lait spots, developmental delayNormal growth, only one line low
Dyskeratosis congenitaInherited marrow failureReticular hyperpigmentation, dystrophic nails, oral leukoplakia; pancytopeniaSkin and nails normal; only one line low
Chédiak-Higashi syndromeLysosomal trafficking defect (LYST)Oculocutaneous albinism, giant granules, neuropathy; frequent bacterial infectionsNormal pigment and neurologic examination
Vitamin B12 deficiencyDiet, malabsorptionMacrocytic anemia, hypersegmented neutrophilsNo macrocytic anemia; not periodic
Cyclic neutropenia: confirm and treat Confirm – one normal count between episodes proves nothing; check neutrophil counts 2 to 3 times a week for at least 6 weeks to catch the nadirs; genetic testing for the elastase mutation supports it · During an episode – treat any infection, keep up oral and dental hygiene · Long term – G-CSF (granulocyte colony-stimulating factor) keeps the count up and prevents episodes; the same drug treats severe congenital neutropenia
Scenario bank
  1. 2 yo M with a perirectal abscess drained at 9 months, now with bilateral pneumonia still febrile after 3 days of antibiotics; biopsy shows granulomas and culture grows Burkholderia cepacia → Decreased superoxide production → NADPH oxidase defect in chronic granulomatous disease
  2. 3 yo M with recurrent Serratia marcescens skin abscesses and hepatic granulomas on imaging → Dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry → measures the neutrophil respiratory burst
  3. Why are characteristic catalase-positive organisms associated with chronic granulomatous disease? → Catalase degrades the organism's own hydrogen peroxide → the neutrophil cannot borrow the pathogen's oxidant
  4. 2 yo newly diagnosed with chronic granulomatous disease, currently well between infections → TMP-SMX, itraconazole and interferon gamma prophylaxis → bacterial, fungal and immunomodulatory cover
  5. 5 yo with chronic granulomatous disease and repeated life-threatening infections despite full prophylaxis → Hematopoietic cell transplantation → the only curative therapy
  6. Newborn with delayed umbilical cord separation and a soft tissue infection producing no pus, with a leukocyte count of 38,000 → Leukocyte adhesion deficiency → impaired chemotaxis and adhesion
  7. 4 yo with nasal polyps, digital clubbing, steatorrhea and Burkholderia cepacia pneumonia; biopsy shows no granulomas → Cystic fibrosis → sweat chloride testing
  8. 9 mo M with recurrent Streptococcus pneumoniae infections, all immunoglobulin isotypes low and absent CD19+ B cells → X-linked agammaglobulinemia → immunoglobulin replacement therapy
  9. 3 yo M with a Staphylococcus aureus liver abscess, a perirectal abscess drained in infancy and granulomas on biopsy → Chronic granulomatous disease → confirm with dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry
  10. 3 yo M with eczema since infancy and recurrent Staphylococcus aureus and Candida abscesses, now a nontender fluctuant buttock abscess, afebrile; leukocytes 9,000 with 30% neutrophils and 40% eosinophils → Hyper-IgE syndrome → impaired Th17 signaling blunts neutrophil recruitment
  11. 2 yo with recurrent staphylococcal skin infections, silvery hair, pale skin and neutropenia → Chédiak-Higashi syndrome → lysosomal trafficking defect
  12. Why the abscesses of hyper-IgE syndrome are cold, without erythema or tenderness → Th17 defect blunts neutrophil recruitment → few neutrophils arrive, so little inflammation
  13. 2 yo M with a Staphylococcus aureus perianal abscess drained at 2 months after failed oral antibiotics, left inguinal lymphadenitis at 7 months, and now a fluctuant right arm abscess that grows Serratia marcescens; leukocyte and platelet counts normal, B and T cells normal; dihydrorhodamine test abnormal → Itraconazole → antifungal prophylaxis in chronic granulomatous disease
  14. 3 yo M with chronic granulomatous disease on TMP-SMX and itraconazole prophylaxis, due for vaccines before his family moves to a country where tuberculosis is common → BCG vaccine → live bacterial vaccine; live viral and inactivated vaccines are safe
  15. 2 yo M with 2 days of fever and painful mouth sores, now improving; a year of similar episodes about every 3 weeks, each lasting 3 to 5 days, well and growing normally between them; T 38.4 C, scattered aphthous ulcers, no lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly; Hb 11.5, WBC 4,000 with 4% segmented neutrophils, platelets 250,000 → Cyclic neutropenia → neutrophil elastase (ELANE) mutation; confirm with serial counts, treat with G-CSF
  16. 4 yo F with fever, mouth ulcers and sore throat that recur about every 3 weeks and last 4 to 5 days, for 10 months; well between episodes with normal growth; today, on a well day, the examination is normal and a CBC shows WBC 7,200 with 45% neutrophils, normal hemoglobin and platelets → Neutrophil counts twice weekly for 6 weeks → cyclic neutropenia; a single count between episodes can be normal
  17. 5 yo M with cyclic neutropenia confirmed by serial counts and an ELANE mutation; despite good dental care he has painful mouth ulcers every 3 weeks, early periodontal disease and two pneumonias this year, each during a nadir → Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor → keeps the count up and prevents episodes
  18. 2-month-old boy with omphalitis at 3 weeks and now a perianal abscess; the umbilical cord separated at 10 days and the wound drains pus; absolute neutrophil count under 200 on every CBC over 4 weeks, with normal hemoglobin and platelets → Severe congenital neutropenia → G-CSF; lifelong risk of myelodysplasia and AML
Separating chronic granulomatous disease from cystic fibrosis Burkholderia cepacia belongs to two diseases: cystic fibrosis and chronic granulomatous disease. It therefore identifies neither alone. Granulomas and extrapulmonary abscesses are what split them. In the vignette, a perirectal abscess in an infant is the single most specific clue to chronic granulomatous disease. It sits in the past medical history, where it is easy to skim.
Reading the CBC in recurrent abscesses Eosinophilia, normal white count – hyper-IgE syndrome · Marked leukocytosis with neutrophilia – leukocyte adhesion deficiency · Neutropenia with oculocutaneous albinism – Chédiak-Higashi syndrome: giant cytoplasmic granules in neutrophils on the smear, recurrent bacterial infection, progressive neurodegeneration with peripheral neuropathy; autosomal recessive lysosomal trafficking defect · Small platelets with bruising – Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome · Lymphopenia – DiGeorge syndrome, whose infections are invasive viral, fungal and bacterial rather than cold abscesses · Unremarkable CBC with Candida infections – myeloperoxidase deficiency · Job syndrome, the rest – autosomal dominant; eczema from the first weeks of life, recurrent sinopulmonary infection, broad nose and prominent forehead, retained primary teeth; genetic testing confirms; skin care and antibiotic prophylaxis
Pearls Granulomas plus abscesses plus a catalase-positive organism is CGD, and no other immunodeficiency assembles that trio · Catalase-positive is a mechanism, not a list – the neutrophil can use the organism's own peroxide, helping explain susceptibility to characteristic catalase-positive organisms; other organisms are not excluded · Dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry has replaced nitroblue tetrazolium as the preferred test; both measure the same respiratory burst · Prophylaxis – TMP-SMX for bacteria plus itraconazole for fungi such as Aspergillus, with interferon gamma added for severe disease; transplant is the only cure · Not CGD prophylaxis – G-CSF, because the neutrophil count is normal; IVIG, because immunoglobulins are normal (it treats antibody deficiency such as XLA); valacyclovir, which belongs to T-cell defects · Vaccines – avoid BCG and other live bacterial vaccines; live viral and inactivated vaccines are safe · Phagocytes in CGD migrate and ingest normally; the failure is intracellular killing, which is why pus forms and chemotaxis-defect diseases look different
Pairs with Part I Antibody Deficiencies covers the antibody deficiencies, and this brief covers the phagocyte defects. Together the two cover the common primary immunodeficiencies. Ask: are there granulomas, and is the infection outside the chest?
How NBME framed it No organism or granuloma was named; the clue was a maternal uncle who died of fungal pneumonia, which points to X-linked disease. Four of the five options were steps in leukocyte function, and the key named the killing defect as impaired microbicidal activity.
Transferable rule When an organism belongs to two diseases, it cannot separate them; find the finding that belongs to only one. Here the shared organism is B cepacia, and the findings that belong to only one disease are the granuloma and the perirectal abscess.
Unchecked attributeImpaired clearing of airway secretions: cystic fibrosis makes no granulomas, and its infections stay sinopulmonary; a perirectal abscess is outside its territory.
Class-vs-memberDefective opsonization: complement deficiency gives encapsulated-organism infection without granulomas.
Class-vs-memberImpaired neutrophil chemotaxis: leukocyte adhesion deficiency gives pus-free infections with delayed cord separation; pus was drained here.
True-fact-wrong-slotDecreased immunoglobulin production: XLA gives encapsulated sinopulmonary infection; no granulomas, wrong organism.
Unchecked attributeSevere congenital neutropenia: the right category and often the same gene, but it is persistent from the first months with severe infections; this child is well between regular 3-week episodes.
Salient decoyViral illness: fever and mouth sores look viral, and viruses do lower the count, but once, not every 3 weeks for a year.
True-fact-wrong-slotFanconi syndrome: a proximal tubule disorder, not a marrow one; the marrow disease is Fanconi anemia, which lowers all three lines and brings short stature and thumb anomalies.

edits.html:
Deep Neck Infections

trismus with a deviated uvula needs no imaging · deep neck spaces by age · epiglottitis and Ludwig angina: airway firstHow old is the child, and is it trismus, pain on neck extension, or tripoding with stridor?

Source vignette Pt – 14 yo M, a week of worsening unilateral sore throat, trismus, muffled voice, uvula deviated left · Q – the most likely diagnosis; options spanned peritonsillar abscess, retropharyngeal abscess and infectious mononucleosis
The decision point

A week of worsening unilateral sore throat with trismus, a muffled voice and a uvula deviated away from the swelling is a peritonsillar abscess. It is a clinical diagnosis, so imaging adds nothing. The next step is needle aspiration or incision and drainage plus antibiotics.

The deep neck spaces sort by age and by what the child cannot do. Trismus and uvular deviation are peritonsillar; pain on neck extension with a bulging posterior wall is retropharyngeal; tripoding with stridor and a normal-looking pharynx is epiglottitis.

Defining criteria Peritonsillar abscess – trismus, muffled hot-potato voice, uvula deviated to the contralateral side, unilateral tonsillar bulge · Retropharyngeal abscess – pain on neck extension, bulging posterior pharyngeal wall, typically under 5 years · Epiglottitis – toxic, tripoding, drooling, stridor, with a deceptively normal oropharynx
The child or adolescent with a severe sore throat - the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Peritonsillar abscessAdolescent or young adult, days of worsening unilateral painTrismus with uvular deviation; no imaging required
Retropharyngeal abscessUnder 5 years, often after a pharyngeal infectionPain on neck extension, bulging posterior wall; CT neck with contrast
EpiglottitisUnvaccinated child, hours not daysTripoding with stridor and a normal pharynx; secure the airway in theatre
Infectious mononucleosisBilateral exudates, posterior cervical nodesSplenomegaly; avoid amoxicillin and contact sports
Ludwig anginaDental source, floor of mouthTongue elevation and submental induration; airway first
Lemierre syndrome Can't missAfter oropharyngeal infectionPersistent fever with nodular lung opacities; internal jugular thrombophlebitis
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Oropharyngeal examFirstTrismus, muffled voice, uvula deviated away from the swellingPeritonsillar abscess; a clinical diagnosis, no imaging needed
Needle aspirationConfirmsPus aspiratedAbscess, drained in the same step; send for culture
Intraoral ultrasoundBy branchPhlegmon versus abscess unclear: fluid collectionAbscess to drain
Heterophile antibody testBy branchBilateral exudates and splenomegaly: positiveMononucleosis; avoid amoxicillin and contact sports
CT neck with contrastBy branchNew neck swelling or torticollis: deeper collectionParapharyngeal or retropharyngeal spread
Lateral neck radiographSkipDoes not show a peritonsillar collectionDelays drainage; it is a retropharyngeal or epiglottitis study
Scenario bank
  1. 14 yo M, week of worsening unilateral sore throat, trismus, muffled voice, uvula deviated left → Peritonsillar abscess → no imaging - needle aspiration or incision and drainage plus antibiotics
  2. 14 yo M with a peritonsillar abscess, what must the antibiotics cover → Group A Streptococcus and respiratory anaerobes
  3. 4 yo M, fever and drooling with pain on neck extension and a bulging posterior pharyngeal wall → Retropharyngeal abscess → CT neck with contrast
  4. 5 yo M, unvaccinated, toxic and tripoding with stridor and a normal-looking pharynx → Epiglottitis → secure the airway in the operating room
  5. 17 yo F back from camp, bilateral exudative tonsils, posterior cervical nodes, splenomegaly → Infectious mononucleosis → heterophile antibody, avoid amoxicillin and contact sports
  6. 14 yo M whose drained abscess is followed by persistent fever, pleuritic chest pain and nodular lung opacities → Lemierre syndrome → contrast CT and anaerobic coverage
  7. 50 yo M with a dental infection, floor-of-mouth induration and tongue elevation → Ludwig angina → airway first
  8. 14 yo M with tonsillar swelling where phlegmon versus abscess is uncertain → Intraoral ultrasound
  9. 14 yo M with tonsillar swelling who develops new neck swelling and torticollis → Parapharyngeal extension → CT neck with contrast
  10. 14 yo M with a third peritonsillar abscess this year → Tonsillectomy
  11. 6 yo F with bilateral exudates, no trismus, no uvular deviation, positive rapid strep → Group A streptococcal pharyngitis → penicillin or amoxicillin
Airway before anything In Ludwig angina and epiglottitis, the airway is the emergency. Examination can precipitate obstruction, so do not depress the tongue or instrument the pharynx of a tripoding child outside the operating theatre. Recurrent peritonsillar abscess, three or more in a year, is an indication for tonsillectomy.
Pearls Peritonsillar abscess is diagnosed clinically; intraoral ultrasound only helps when phlegmon versus abscess is genuinely uncertain · Retropharyngeal abscess hurts on extension; meningitis hurts on flexion · Amoxicillin in undiagnosed mononucleosis produces a florid morbilliform rash · Lemierre syndrome is Fusobacterium necrophorum with septic pulmonary emboli after an oropharyngeal infection
Pairs with Part I Respiratory Infection in a Child covers the uncomplicated end of this spectrum. Ask: is anything unilateral?
Transferable rule When a diagnosis is clinical and the complication is airway compromise, imaging is almost always the wrong next step. It cannot change what is already known, and it costs time the airway may not have.
Sequencing trapImaging before drainage in a clinically obvious abscess.
Mirror twinRetropharyngeal abscess is the younger child's version, separated by extension versus trismus.

edits.html:
Congenital Infections (TORCH)

organism first, then its signature sequela · where calcifications sit · rubella triad · parvovirus · herpes without vesiclesWhere are the calcifications, and what is that organism's signature sequela?

Source vignette Pt – 2 mo F, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, microcephaly · Imaging – periventricular calcifications · Q – the most likely diagnosis; options spanned congenital cytomegalovirus, congenital toxoplasmosis and congenital rubella
The decision point

Identify the organism, then its signature sequela.

Calcifications along the ventricular margin (periventricular) indicate CMV (cytomegalovirus). Calcifications scattered through the parenchyma indicate toxoplasmosis. An indoor cat suggests toxoplasmosis but is compatible with congenital CMV.

Defining criteria Periventricular calcifications – CMV · Diffuse parenchymal calcifications – toxoplasmosis, with chorioretinitis · Subcortical calcifications with arthrogryposis – Zika · Diagnostic window – urine or saliva PCR within the first 3 weeks of life, after which congenital and perinatal acquisition cannot be separated
Congenital infection – the differential
InfectionIllness scriptThe NBME tell
CMVMost common congenital infection; hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, thrombocytopenia, microcephalyPeriventricular calcifications with microcephaly; sequela is sensorineural hearing loss
ToxoplasmosisCat litter, undercooked meatDiffuse parenchymal calcifications and chorioretinitis; sequela is obstructive hydrocephalus
RubellaUnvaccinated motherCataracts and a continuous machine-like PDA murmur
SyphilisUntreated maternal infectionSnuffles, palm-and-sole rash, periostitis; no CNS calcifications
HSV Can't missIntrapartum acquisitionDays 5 to 21, vesicles, seizures, temporal lobe; without vesicles, cerebrospinal fluid with lymphocytes and red cells and normal glucose
ZikaMaternal travelSevere microcephaly with subcortical calcifications and arthrogryposis
Parvovirus B19Maternal febrile illness with arthralgia; risk highest before 20 weeksHydrops fetalis or fetal loss; congenital anomalies are rare in survivors
Listeria monocytogenes Can't missNonspecific maternal febrile illness, often foodborneSevere neonatal sepsis with disseminated abscesses in liver, spleen, lung, kidney and brain
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Head ultrasound or CTFirstPeriventricular calcificationsCMV; diffuse parenchymal: toxoplasmosis; subcortical with arthrogryposis: Zika
Saliva CMV PCR, first 3 weeksScreenPositiveNeeds urine PCR to confirm; saliva gives false positives
Urine CMV PCR, first 3 weeksConfirmsPositiveCongenital CMV; after 3 weeks, perinatal acquisition cannot be excluded
Dilated eye examBy branchChorioretinitis, or cataractsChorioretinitis with diffuse calcifications: toxoplasmosis; cataracts: rubella
Infant rubella IgMBy branchPositiveCongenital rubella syndrome; serology, not PCR
Cerebrospinal fluid herpes simplex virus PCRBy branchPositiveNeonatal herpes encephalitis; start intravenous acyclovir before the result
Serial audiology through childhoodStagingSensorineural hearing loss, often late-onsetCMV's main sequela; a passed newborn screen does not end follow-up
Infant CMV IgGSkipMaternal IgG crosses the placentaCannot separate infant from maternal antibody
Mnemonic TORCH: Toxoplasmosis, Other (syphilis, varicella, parvovirus B19, HIV), Rubella, Cytomegalovirus, Herpes simplex virus
Scenario bank
  1. 2 mo F, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, microcephaly, periventricular calcifications → Congenital CMV → valganciclovir
  2. 2 mo F with symptomatic congenital CMV, greatest long-term risk → Sensorineural hearing loss
  3. Newborn with diffuse parenchymal calcifications, chorioretinitis and ventriculomegaly → Congenital toxoplasmosis
  4. Newborn with cataracts and a continuous machine-like murmur → Congenital rubella
  5. Newborn with snuffles, a palm-and-sole rash and long-bone periostitis → Congenital syphilis → penicillin
  6. 7 yo with notched incisors, saddle nose and interstitial keratitis → Late congenital syphilis
  7. Neonate on day 10 with vesicles, seizures and temporal-lobe changes → Neonatal HSV → intravenous acyclovir
  8. Newborn with severe microcephaly, subcortical calcifications and arthrogryposis after maternal travel → Congenital Zika
  9. Newborn with suspected congenital CMV → Urine or saliva PCR in the first 3 weeks of life
  10. Newborn with a positive saliva CMV PCR → Confirm with urine PCR → saliva gives false positives
  11. Newborn with symptomatic congenital CMV, treatment duration → 6 Months of valganciclovir
  12. Newborn with congenital CMV who passes the newborn hearing screen → Serial audiology through childhood → the loss is often late-onset
  13. Infant with congenital CMV and enlarged ventricles → Hydrocephalus ex vacuo → parenchymal volume loss
  14. 2-day-old, failed hearing screen bilaterally, absent red reflex, continuous murmur at the left second interspace, hepatosplenomegaly, growth below the 5th percentile, mother with a first-trimester febrile illness and arthralgia → Congenital rubella syndrome → hearing loss, cataracts and patent ductus arteriosus
  15. Why the first trimester is rubella's dangerous window → Transplacental infection during organogenesis → spontaneous abortion or congenital rubella syndrome
  16. Newborn with suspected congenital rubella syndrome; establishing the diagnosis → Infant rubella IgM serology → serology rather than PCR, because the PCR window belongs to cytomegalovirus
  17. Pregnant woman with fever and arthralgia at 16 weeks whose fetus develops ascites, effusions and skin edema → Parvovirus B19 with hydrops fetalis → anomalies are rare in survivors
  18. 29 yo woman at 18 weeks' gestation, an elementary school teacher, exposed during a school outbreak of slapped-cheek rash; she has mild arthralgia; parvovirus B19 IgM positive, IgG negative; ultrasound today shows a normally grown fetus without hydrops → Serial ultrasound with MCA Doppler → Acute maternal parvovirus B19 infection; watch for fetal anemia and hydrops
  19. 26 yo woman at 14 weeks' gestation whose 5-year-old has a slapped-cheek facial rash and lacy rash on the arms; she has had fatigue and aching wrists and knees for 3 days → Parvovirus B19 IgM → Acute maternal infection; then serial fetal ultrasonography
  20. 31 yo woman at 23 weeks' gestation with confirmed acute parvovirus B19 infection 4 weeks ago, followed with serial ultrasonography; middle cerebral artery Doppler now indicates severe fetal anemia, and there is new fetal ascites and skin edema → Intrauterine transfusion → Hydrops fetalis from parvovirus B19 fetal anemia
  21. 8-day-old girl with apnea during a feed, then a focal seizure with bicycling leg movements and eye deviation; lethargic and hypotonic with brisk reflexes and bilateral Babinski signs; cerebrospinal fluid glucose 55 mg/dL, protein 65 mg/dL, 350 erythrocytes/mm3, 70 leukocytes/mm3 with 80% lymphocytes; empiric antibiotics started → Herpes simplex virus → confirm with cerebrospinal fluid PCR and add intravenous acyclovir
  22. 10-day-old boy with lethargy and a focal seizure and no skin lesions; cerebrospinal fluid shows normal glucose, mildly raised protein, 90 leukocytes/mm3 that are mostly lymphocytes, and many erythrocytes; empiric antibiotics are running → Add intravenous acyclovir now → empiric antiviral therapy before the PCR result
  23. 12-day-old with poor feeding, lethargy and focal seizures; cerebrospinal fluid shows a lymphocytic pleocytosis with many erythrocytes and normal glucose → CSF HSV PCR → neonatal herpes simplex encephalitis
Shared sequela Rubella also causes sensorineural hearing loss. Hearing loss therefore does not separate rubella from CMV (cytomegalovirus); the calcification pattern does.
The rubella triad Sensorineural hearing loss – a failed newborn hearing screen · Cataracts – an absent red reflex, or leukocoria · Patent ductus arteriosus – a continuous machine-like murmur at the left second interspace · Plus – growth restriction, hepatosplenomegaly and a purpuric blueberry-muffin rash · Maternal arthralgia after a febrile illness in pregnancy – rubella causes organ malformation from first-trimester organogenesis; parvovirus B19 causes hydrops and no malformation
Parvovirus B19 in pregnancy Exposure – a child with slapped cheeks at home, school or day care; a child with the rash is no longer contagious, so exposure happened earlier; most maternal infections are asymptomatic, others flu-like with rash or symmetric arthralgia · Maternal serology – B19 IgM positive means acute infection; IgG positive with IgM negative means past infection and immunity; B19 DNA testing if immunocompromised · Fetal risk – the virus infects erythroid progenitors, so the danger is fetal anemia, then hydrops or fetal death, not malformation · Acute infection – serial ultrasonography with middle cerebral artery Doppler to detect fetal anemia and hydrops · Severe fetal anemia – intrauterine transfusion
Neonatal herpes without vesicles Timing – seizures, lethargy or apnea in the second or third week of life; vesicles are often absent · Cerebrospinal fluid – normal or mildly low glucose, mildly raised protein, a modest pleocytosis that is mostly lymphocytes, and many red cells · Bacterial meningitis – low glucose and a neutrophil-predominant leukocyte count, often over 1,000/mm3 · Confirm – herpes simplex virus PCR (polymerase chain reaction) of the cerebrospinal fluid · Treat – add intravenous acyclovir to empiric antibiotics without waiting for the PCR · How NBME framed it: no vesicles are given and antibiotics are already begun, so the day of life and the lymphocytic, bloody cerebrospinal fluid identify the virus.
Pearls CMV (cytomegalovirus) is the most common congenital infection and the leading non-genetic cause of childhood sensorineural hearing loss · Only about 10% are symptomatic at birth, and that group carries up to 50% hearing-loss risk untreated · Six months of valganciclovir is better than six weeks: 8% versus 13% hearing worsening at one year · Hearing loss is progressive and can be late-onset, so passing the newborn screen does not discharge the child from audiology · CMV – ventricles enlarge ex vacuo from volume loss · Toxoplasmosis – ventricles enlarge from obstruction
Pairs with Part I Hearing Loss and Chronic Ear Disease covers the childhood sensorineural causes. Part I Cerebral Palsy covers the same imaging; the calcification pattern and the white-matter injury each point to a different cause. Part II Fever and Sepsis in the Newborn: does the cerebrospinal fluid show low glucose with over 1,000 neutrophil-predominant leukocytes, or lymphocytes and red cells with normal glucose?
Transferable rule Identifying the complication of a syndrome takes two independent steps: name the syndrome, then its complication. When anatomic distribution and exposure history are both given, always rely on anatomic distribution.
Unchecked attributeCytomegalovirus and toxoplasmosis both follow a mild maternal flu-like illness, but neither produces cataracts or a cardiac defect. The maternal history is shared; the fetal organ pattern separates them.
Salient decoyToxoplasmosis: the indoor cat suggests it, but a cat is also compatible with cytomegalovirus.
True-fact-wrong-slotRubella: it causes cataracts, but not periventricular calcifications.
Salient decoyGroup B streptococcus: the antibiotics already begun point toward it, but neonatal bacterial meningitis gives low glucose and a neutrophil-predominant count, often over 1,000/mm3.
Unchecked attributeEscherichia coli: a common cause of neonatal meningitis, but a count of 70 that is mostly lymphocytes, with normal glucose, does not fit a bacterial cause.
True-fact-wrong-slotCytomegalovirus: symptomatic congenital infection shows at birth with periventricular calcifications and hearing loss, not as an acute encephalitis in the second week.
True-fact-wrong-slotToxoplasma gondii: congenital infection shows chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus and diffuse calcifications, not a new encephalitis on day 8.

edits.html:
Anaphylaxis

organ-system criteria · hypotension not required · mast cell mechanism · bradykinin angioedema · delayed drug reactionsHow many organ systems are involved, and how soon after the exposure?

Source vignette Pt – 12 yo M, 30 minutes of burning, swollen eyes, a scratchy, tight throat and crampy abdominal pain; seen earlier the same day for several days of sore throat and started on amoxicillin; no known drug allergies · Exam – T 37.2, BP 116/68, HR 92; bilateral periorbital swelling, mild conjunctival redness, scattered wheals on the trunk · Q – the pathogenesis of his symptoms; options spanned Epstein-Barr virus infection, immune complex formation, impaired bradykinin degradation, mast cell activation and systemic vasculitis
The decision point

Anaphylaxis is a clinical diagnosis based on the number of organ systems involved and the time since exposure; hypotension is not required. Within minutes to hours of a likely allergen, skin or mucosal findings plus one more system (respiratory, gastrointestinal or cardiovascular) meet criteria. This boy has wheals and periorbital swelling (skin), throat tightness (respiratory) and cramps (gut) 30 minutes after amoxicillin. He therefore has anaphylaxis despite a normal blood pressure. The mechanism is IgE-mediated mast cell and basophil degranulation releasing histamine, prostaglandins and leukotrienes. A history of no known drug allergies does not argue against it. An earlier exposure sensitized him without a reaction, and re-exposure triggers the release.

The exception is angioedema without hives. Swelling of the lips, tongue, face or bowel wall with no wheals and no itch from an ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor or hereditary angioedema is bradykinin-mediated. It builds over hours and responds poorly to epinephrine and antihistamines. Rashes that arrive days into a drug or an infection are delayed reactions, not anaphylaxis.

Defining criteria Anaphylaxis is likely with acute onset (minutes to hours) and any 1 of: · 1 – skin or mucosal involvement (hives, flushing, swollen lips, tongue or eyes) plus respiratory compromise or hypotension · 2 – 2 or more systems after a likely allergen: skin or mucosa, respiratory, cardiovascular, persistent gastrointestinal symptoms · 3 – hypotension alone after a known allergen for that patient
Anaphylaxis and its mimics – the differential
DiagnosisTiming after exposureMechanismThe NBME tell
AnaphylaxisMinutes to a few hoursIgE-mediated mast cell activation (type I)Skin plus a second system: wheeze, stridor, throat tightness, vomiting or cramps, hypotension
Acute urticaria aloneMinutes to hoursMast cell activation, often IgEHives and itch with no second system; normal airway, gut and blood pressure
Bradykinin angioedema (ACE inhibitor, hereditary angioedema)Hours; ACE inhibitor reactions can start months or years into therapyImpaired bradykinin degradation (ACE inhibitor); C1 inhibitor deficiency (hereditary, low C4)Lip, tongue or bowel-wall swelling with no hives or itch; little response to epinephrine or antihistamines
Serum sickness-like reaction5 to 14 days into a drugDelayed drug hypersensitivity; true serum sickness is immune complexUrticarial rash with fever, arthralgia and nodes
Epstein-Barr virus with an aminopenicillinDays into amoxicillinVirus-driven drug rash, not IgEMaculopapular rash with fever, exudative pharyngitis, posterior nodes, left upper quadrant pain
Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritisDays to weeks after pharyngitisImmune complex (type III)Edema building over days with hypertension and cola-colored urine
Systemic vasculitis (IgA vasculitis)DaysImmune complex vessel inflammationPalpable purpura, fever, arthralgia, colicky abdominal pain
Vasovagal syncopeSeconds, with pain or fear (needles)Vagal surgeBradycardia, pallor and sweating; no hives, no wheeze
Scenario bank
  1. 12 yo M, 30 minutes of burning, swollen eyes, a scratchy, tight throat and crampy abdominal pain; earlier today diagnosed with pharyngitis after several days of sore throat and started on amoxicillin; no known drug allergies; T 37.2, BP 116/68, HR 92; bilateral periorbital swelling, mild conjunctival redness, scattered wheals on the trunk → Mast cell activation → anaphylaxis: skin, respiratory and gastrointestinal involvement within 30 minutes of amoxicillin, after sensitization by an earlier course; intramuscular (IM) epinephrine
  2. 7 yo F at a birthday party, 10 minutes after eating a cookie made with peanut butter, develops hives on the face and trunk, wheezing and 2 episodes of vomiting; no previous reactions to food; T 37.0, BP 98/60, HR 128, RR 30, SpO2 94% on room air; diffuse expiratory wheezes → Intramuscular epinephrine → anaphylaxis by skin plus respiratory and gastrointestinal involvement; blood pressure need not fall
  3. 9 yo M, itchy raised wheals on the trunk and arms 1 hour after eating strawberries for the first time this season; no lip or tongue swelling, throat symptoms, cough, vomiting or abdominal pain; BP 104/66, HR 90, SpO2 99%; lungs clear; blanching urticarial plaques → Oral cetirizine → acute urticaria alone: one system, so criteria for anaphylaxis are not met
  4. 15 yo M treated in the emergency department for hives, throat tightness and wheezing 20 minutes after eating cashews, his first reaction to food; one dose of intramuscular epinephrine was given, and after 6 hours of observation he is asymptomatic with normal vital signs and clear lungs → Epinephrine autoinjector prescription → anaphylaxis, observed for a biphasic reaction; discharge with self-injectable epinephrine, an action plan, avoidance and allergy referral
  5. 58 yo M with hypertension and diabetes, 6 hours of progressive swelling of the lips and tongue; no itching, hives, wheezing or abdominal pain; takes lisinopril, which he started 2 years ago, and metformin; no new foods or medications; swelling did not improve after intramuscular epinephrine and diphenhydramine → Impaired bradykinin degradation → ACE inhibitor angioedema: no urticaria and little response to epinephrine; stop the ACE inhibitor permanently
  6. 16 yo F with recurrent episodes over 3 years of painless, nonpruritic swelling of the hands, face and once the throat, each lasting 2 to 3 days, and separate episodes of colicky abdominal pain with vomiting; no hives; takes no medications; her mother has similar episodes; antihistamines and epinephrine have not helped; examination between episodes is normal → Serum C4 level → hereditary angioedema from C1 inhibitor deficiency; low C4, bradykinin-mediated, so epinephrine disappoints
  7. 17 yo F, 5 days of fever, sore throat and fatigue, treated with amoxicillin for presumed strep pharyngitis; 4 days later, a diffuse, mildly itchy maculopapular rash on the trunk and limbs; T 38.4, BP 112/70; tonsillar exudates, tender posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, left upper quadrant tenderness; no wheals, no lip swelling, lungs clear → Infectious mononucleosis → an aminopenicillin rash during Epstein-Barr virus infection; not an IgE-mediated penicillin allergy
  8. 34 yo F with a known severe shellfish allergy becomes lightheaded 15 minutes after eating a dish she later learns contained shrimp; no rash, flushing, lip swelling, wheeze or vomiting; BP 76/44, HR 132, warm extremities; lungs clear → Anaphylaxis → hypotension alone after a known allergen meets criteria; give IM epinephrine
  9. 22 yo F with recurrent episodes since adolescence of painless, nonpruritic swelling of the lips and one hand lasting 2 to 3 days, the latest starting the day after a dental extraction; separate bouts of colicky abdominal pain with vomiting; no hives; takes a combined oral contraceptive and no other medications; her father has similar episodes; epinephrine and diphenhydramine in the emergency department did not help; serum C4 low → C1 inhibitor deficiency → hereditary angioedema: bradykinin-mediated swelling without urticaria; confirm with C1 inhibitor level and function
  10. 19 yo M with known hereditary angioedema, 4 hours of progressive swelling of the face and tongue with a hoarse voice after a facial injury in a basketball game; no stridor; SpO2 98% on room air; no hives; no improvement after intramuscular epinephrine and intravenous diphenhydramine → Intravenous C1 inhibitor concentrate → acute hereditary angioedema attack with laryngeal involvement: give specific therapy and be ready to secure the airway
  11. 45 yo F with hereditary angioedema, low C4 and a family history, now with blood pressure 152/96 on three separate visits; no diabetes or kidney disease → Lisinopril → ACE inhibitors block bradykinin breakdown and provoke attacks
Management First – IM epinephrine in the anterolateral thigh, 0.01 mg/kg of the 1 mg/mL solution (max 0.5 mg adult, 0.3 mg child); lie the patient flat with legs raised · Repeat – every 5 to 15 minutes if symptoms persist; persistent hypotension gets isotonic fluid boluses and then an epinephrine infusion; glucagon if the patient takes a beta-blocker · Adjuncts only – H1 and H2 antihistamines for itch and hives, albuterol for residual wheeze, glucocorticoids; none of them treats airway obstruction or shock, and none replaces or delays epinephrine · Observe – for a biphasic reaction, symptoms returning hours later without re-exposure; 1 symptom-free hour may be reasonable without severe risk features; extended observation up to 6 hours or longer, including admission, may be appropriate at higher risk · Discharge – epinephrine autoinjector with training and an action plan, avoidance of the trigger, and allergy referral
Hereditary angioedema Mechanism – autosomal dominant C1 inhibitor deficiency; unchecked kallikrein makes excess bradykinin · The tell – recurrent nonpitting swelling of the face, lips, limbs or bowel wall (colicky abdominal attacks) with no urticaria and no itch, often with a family history · Triggers – dental work, trauma, stress, estrogen (oral contraceptives, pregnancy) · Avoid – ACE inhibitors, which block bradykinin breakdown and worsen attacks · Tests – screen with C4 (low), confirm with C1 inhibitor level and function · Acute attack – secure the airway if the larynx is involved; give C1 inhibitor concentrate, icatibant (bradykinin B2 receptor blocker) or ecallantide (kallikrein inhibitor); epinephrine, antihistamines and steroids do not work
Pearls Waiting for hypotension is a deadly delay; in children hypotension is a late sign. Throat tightness or wheeze with hives is enough to give epinephrine · Diagnosis is clinical; a serum tryptase drawn early can support mast cell activation afterward but never delays treatment · Bradykinin swelling is the one angioedema in which epinephrine works poorly. Stop the ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor for life, and check C4 when swelling recurs without a drug · Most childhood anaphylaxis is from food (peanut, tree nuts, milk, egg); insect stings and drugs such as beta-lactams follow
Pairs with Part II Fever and Rash in a Child covers the serum sickness-like reaction: did the hives start 5 to 14 days into the drug, with joint pain? Part I Transfusion Reactions covers anaphylaxis during transfusion: is the recipient IgA deficient? Aquifer Shock in Children covers anaphylactic shock as a distributive subtype: is perfusion abnormal? Part I Stool Changes in a Well Infant covers FPIES (food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome), the non-IgE mimic: is it hours of vomiting without hives? Part I Childhood Vaccine Schedule and Contraindications covers anaphylaxis after a vaccine dose as a contraindication. Aquifer Child with Puffy Eyes places the acute allergic reaction among the other causes of swollen eyelids: is it one eye or both, and does the urine contain protein?
Transferable rule Skin or mucosal involvement plus any second system within minutes to hours of an exposure is anaphylaxis. Treat it with IM (intramuscular) epinephrine first. Swelling with no hives points to bradykinin. A rash that arrives days later points to a delayed drug or immune complex reaction.
Unchecked attributeImpaired bradykinin degradation: the swollen eyes suggest angioedema, but bradykinin swelling has no wheals or itch; he has wheals on the trunk plus throat and gut symptoms, which is mast cell release.
Unchecked attributeImmune complex formation: the sore throat invites poststreptococcal disease or serum sickness, but immune complexes take days to form; this began 30 minutes after the drug.
True-fact-wrong-slotEpstein-Barr virus infection: mononucleosis really does cause a rash after amoxicillin, but that rash is maculopapular, comes days later and brings fever and nodes; he is afebrile with wheals.
Salient decoySystemic vasculitis: crampy abdominal pain recalls IgA vasculitis, but vasculitis develops over days with fever and palpable purpura, not wheals within minutes.

edits.html:
Isolation Precautions

particle size · droplet, airborne or contact · gear and room · when it ends · neutropenic precautionsHow big is the particle, and who is being protected from whom?

Source vignette Pt – 8 mo M with fever and lethargy; BP 70/40; antibiotics started and admitted to the pediatric ICU (intensive care unit) · Labs – CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) Gram stain: gram-negative diplococci · Q – which isolation precautions to institute; options spanned airborne, contact, droplet, neutropenic and standard
The decision point

Choose the precaution by how the organism travels. Droplets are 5 microns or larger and fall within 3 to 6 feet, so a surgical mask within that range is enough. Droplet organisms include N. meningitidis, H. influenzae type b, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, influenza, adenovirus (plus contact for pneumonia) and pertussis. Airborne particles are under 5 microns and stay suspended, so they need an N95 respirator and a negative-pressure room. Airborne organisms include tuberculosis, measles, varicella and SARS (severe acute respiratory syndrome). Contact organisms spread by hands and surfaces and need a gown and gloves. They include MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus), VRE (vancomycin-resistant enterococci), C. difficile, E. coli O157:H7 (diapered or incontinent), scabies and RSV (respiratory syncytial virus). Gram-negative diplococci in the CSF are meningococcus. This infant therefore needs droplet precautions until 24 hours of effective antibiotics.

Standard precautions apply to every patient, so they are never the added precaution. Neutropenic precautions protect the patient from the environment rather than others from the patient.

Defining criteria Droplet – particles 5 microns or larger, fall within 3 to 6 feet · Airborne – particles under 5 microns, remain suspended and travel on air currents · Contact – spread by direct touch or contaminated surfaces · Neutropenic (protective) – shields an immunocompromised patient, usually severe neutropenia (ANC (absolute neutrophil count) under 500)
Isolation precautions – the differential
PrecautionOrganismsGear and roomEnds when
StandardEvery patientHand hygiene; gloves, gown, mask or eye protection when contact with blood or body fluids is expectedNever; always in effect
DropletN. meningitidis, Hib (Haemophilus influenzae type b), Mycoplasma, influenza, adenovirus (plus contact for pneumonia), pertussis, mumps, rubellaSurgical mask within 3 to 6 feet; private roomMeningococcus and Hib: 24 hours of effective antibiotics; pertussis: 5 days of effective antibiotics
AirborneTuberculosis, measles, SARS (plus droplet and contact)N95 respirator and a negative-pressure single room; nonimmune staff stay out of measles roomsTB (tuberculosis): improving clinically on therapy with 3 consecutive negative sputum AFB (acid-fast bacilli) smears; measles: 4 days after rash onset (duration of illness if immunocompromised)
Airborne plus contactVaricella, disseminated zosterN95 and negative-pressure room, plus gown and glovesAll lesions crusted
ContactMRSA, VRE, C. difficile, E. coli O157:H7 (diapered or incontinent), scabies, RSVGown and gloves; dedicated equipment; soap and water for C. difficile because alcohol does not kill sporesDuration of illness for C. difficile and RSV; scabies: 24 hours after effective therapy starts
NeutropenicProtects a patient with severe neutropenia (chemotherapy, stem cell transplant)Hand hygiene, private room with filtered air; no fresh flowers, plants or animals; no rectal thermometers, enemas or suppositoriesNeutrophil count recovers
Scenario bank
  1. 8 mo M with fever and lethargy; BP 70/40; lumbar puncture shows gram-negative diplococci on CSF Gram stain; intravenous antibiotics have been started, and he is being admitted to the pediatric ICU → Droplet precautions → Neisseria meningitidis: surgical mask within 3 to 6 feet until 24 hours of effective antibiotics
  2. 2 yo M, unvaccinated, 4 days of fever to 40 C, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes, then a maculopapular rash that began at the hairline and spread to the trunk; small gray-white spots on the buccal mucosa; admitted for dehydration → Airborne precautions → measles: N95 respirator and a negative-pressure room
  3. 4 mo F admitted with 3 days of cough, rhinorrhea and increased work of breathing, SpO2 88% on room air; diffuse crackles and wheezes; nasal swab positive for respiratory syncytial virus → Contact precautions → RSV spreads mainly by hands and contaminated surfaces: gown and gloves
  4. 48 yo M with 2 months of cough, night sweats and weight loss, admitted with an upper lobe cavity on chest radiograph; sputum smear positive for acid-fast bacilli; four-drug therapy and airborne isolation were started 3 days ago → Three negative sputum AFB smears → active pulmonary TB: airborne isolation ends when the patient is improving clinically on effective therapy and three consecutive sputum smears are negative
  5. 3 yo F admitted with cellulitis of the thigh complicating chickenpox that began 3 days ago; several vesicles on the trunk and scalp have not yet crusted; T 38.9 → Airborne and contact precautions → varicella: N95, negative-pressure room, gown and gloves until every lesion has crusted
  6. 6 yo F with acute lymphoblastic leukemia admitted during induction chemotherapy; afebrile; absolute neutrophil count 200/mm3; placed in a private room under neutropenic precautions → Rectal temperature measurement → neutropenic precautions protect the patient: no rectal thermometers, enemas or suppositories, no fresh flowers or plants
  7. 8 yo M on clindamycin for an abscess develops 6 watery stools a day and cramping; stool PCR (polymerase chain reaction) positive for Clostridioides difficile toxin; admitted for dehydration → Contact precautions with soap-and-water hand washing → alcohol-based rubs do not kill C. difficile spores
Management Meningococcal disease – droplet precautions for the first 24 hours of effective antibiotics, plus chemoprophylaxis (rifampin, ciprofloxacin or ceftriaxone) for close contacts: household, day care, and anyone exposed to oral secretions; staff need it only after unprotected exposure such as intubation without a mask · Suspected TB or measles – airborne isolation before the workup or treatment; a patient who must leave the room wears a surgical mask
Pearls Adenovirus pneumonia needs droplet plus contact precautions; RSV (respiratory syncytial virus) needs contact precautions · For C. difficile, the hand-hygiene method matters: alcohol rub fails against spores · The 24-hour rule applies to meningococcus and Hib. TB isolation ends with clinical improvement and 3 consecutive negative smears, and varicella isolation ends with crusting · A patient with a rash and fever of unknown cause gets airborne and contact precautions until measles and varicella are excluded
Pairs with Part I Bacterial Meningitis covers the CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) grid, the organism by age and chemoprophylaxis: who counts as a close contact? Part II Fever and Rash in a Child covers measles and varicella, including postexposure prophylaxis: is the contact immune, and how long since exposure? Part I Tuberculosis covers the latent-versus-active distinction: is the radiograph abnormal or are there symptoms? Part II Scabies covers the contact-spread rash whose treatment includes the household.
Transferable rule Pick the precaution by the particle and the route. Large droplets that fall within 6 feet need a surgical mask. Small particles that hang in the air need an N95 and a negative-pressure room. Organisms on skin, stool or surfaces need a gown and gloves. Neutropenic precautions protect the patient rather than the staff.
Unchecked attributeAirborne precautions: the right idea, a respiratory route, with the wrong particle size; meningococcus travels in large droplets that fall within 3 to 6 feet, and airborne isolation is for TB, measles and varicella.
Salient decoyContact precautions: a septic, possibly petechial infant in the ICU feels like a gown-and-gloves patient, but meningococcus spreads by respiratory droplets, not by skin or surfaces.
True-fact-wrong-slotStandard precautions: they apply to every patient, including this one, but they are the baseline, not the transmission-based precaution the organism requires.
Unchecked attributeNeutropenic precautions: the direction is reversed; they protect an immunocompromised patient, and this infant is the source of infection.

edits.html:
Infectious Diarrhea

timing gates · organism by food source · stool culture, blood culture or neither · who gets an antibioticWhat did the patient eat, how soon did it start, and does that organism need a blood culture or an antibiotic?

Source vignette Pt – 14-year-old girl with 2 days of cramping, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea, today with fever and blood in the stool; home from a week-long summer camp, well while there; CVID on immunoglobulin replacement; sinusitis a month ago treated with amoxicillin-clavulanate · Exam – T 38.2 C, HR 102; mild diffuse tenderness, no peritoneal signs · Labs – stool ova and parasites negative; stool culture grows Salmonella · Q – the most likely underlying cause of her illness; options spanned food handling, seafood, contaminated infusions, antibiotic disruption of gut flora and typhoid vaccine failure
The decision point

Identify the organism from the exposure. Nontyphoidal Salmonella comes from undercooked poultry and eggs. Food left unrefrigerated lets it multiply. Symptoms start within 3 days with fever, vomiting, cramps and diarrhea, which can be bloody in children. Camp food fits this source, and her stool culture confirms Salmonella.

The organism then determines the workup and treatment. Invasive diarrhea needs a stool culture. A fever-first illness after travel is typhoid and needs a blood culture. Most bacterial diarrhea needs only rehydration.

Timing gates 1 to 6 hours, vomiting first, no fever – preformed toxin: S aureus or B cereus · Within about 3 days, fever and diarrhea – invasive bacteria: nontyphoidal Salmonella, Campylobacter, Shigella; Shiga toxin E coli with little fever · Fever for days to weeks after travel, diarrhea minor – typhoid · During or after antibiotics, watery – C difficile
Diarrhea by source: the differential
OrganismSource and settingThe NBME tellTest and treatment
Nontyphoidal SalmonellaUndercooked poultry and eggs, poor refrigeration; reptiles and backyard poultryFever, vomiting, cramps; bloody stools possible in childrenStool culture; supportive; antibiotics only for infants under 3 months, immunocompromise, sickle cell disease or bacteremia
Typhoid (S Typhi)Travel to areas with poor sanitation; contaminated food or waterFever and bacteremia first; abdominal pain, rose spots, relative bradycardia; later splenomegaly, intestinal perforationBlood culture; ceftriaxone; the vaccine covers only typhoidal strains
CampylobacterUndercooked poultry, unpasteurized milkFever, bloody diarrhea, pain that can mimic appendicitis; Guillain-Barre weeks laterStool culture; supportive unless severe or prolonged
Shiga toxin E coli (O157:H7)Undercooked ground beef, petting zoosBloody diarrhea with little fever; HUS about a week laterStool culture and Shiga toxin test; no antibiotics, no antimotility drugs
ShigellaDay care; spreads person to person from a very small inoculumHigh fever, bloody diarrhea, seizures in young childrenStool culture; azithromycin shortens illness and spread
Vibrio parahaemolyticusRaw or undercooked seafood, shellfishWatery diarrhea and cramps after raw oystersSupportive
S aureus and B cereus toxinToxin already in the food: S aureus in ham, mayonnaise or custard; B cereus in reheated riceVomiting within 1 to 6 hours, no fever, several diners illClinical; supportive
C difficileRecent antibioticsWatery diarrhea at onset, cramps, leukocytosisStool toxin or PCR; oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Stool culture, with Shiga toxin testing if bloodyFirstNames the organismFor fever with bloody diarrhea, immunocompromise, severe or prolonged illness, or an outbreak
Blood cultureBy branchS Typhi or other bacteremiaFever-first illness after travel, infants under 3 months, immunocompromise
C difficile toxin or PCRBy branchPositiveWatery diarrhea during or after antibiotics
Stool ova and parasites or Giardia antigenBy branchGiardiaProlonged watery, greasy diarrhea after untreated water; common in CVID and IgA deficiency
Stool studies for brief watery diarrhea without fever or bloodSkip Self-limited; rehydrate
Scenario bank
  1. 14-year-old girl with CVID on immunoglobulin replacement has 2 days of cramping, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea, and today fever and bloody stools; she just returned from a week-long summer camp; she took amoxicillin-clavulanate for sinusitis a month ago; T 38.2 C, HR 102, mild diffuse abdominal tenderness without peritoneal signs; stool ova and parasites negative; stool culture grows Salmonella → Inadequate cooking and refrigeration of chicken and eggs → nontyphoidal Salmonella from undercooked poultry or eggs starts within 3 days, and warmth lets it multiply; bloody stools are common in children
  2. 10-year-old boy and his sister begin vomiting repeatedly 2 hours after a lunch of fried rice left out overnight from a takeout meal and reheated; mild cramps, no fever, no diarrhea yet; normal vital signs apart from mild tachycardia → Bacillus cereus food poisoning → vomiting within hours from a toxin already in the food; reheated rice is the classic source; supportive care
  3. 16-year-old boy develops watery diarrhea and abdominal cramps 18 hours after eating raw oysters at a coastal cookout; temperature 37.9 C; no blood in the stool; he ate no poultry or eggs → Vibrio parahaemolyticus infection → raw or undercooked shellfish; self-limited, supportive care
  4. 6-year-old girl has 2 days of crampy abdominal pain and grossly bloody diarrhea 3 days after eating an undercooked hamburger at a barbecue; temperature 37.4 C; mildly dry mucous membranes; stool testing for Shiga toxin is pending → Oral azithromycin → antibiotics and antimotility drugs raise the risk of hemolytic uremic syndrome in Shiga toxin E coli infection; rehydrate and watch hemoglobin, platelets and creatinine
  5. 17-year-old girl returned 12 days ago from visiting family in rural South Asia; for 6 days she has had fever rising to 39.8 C, headache, abdominal pain and constipation; heart rate 82 at that temperature; faint pink macules on the upper abdomen; she is alert and hemodynamically stable → Blood cultures → typhoid presents as fever and bacteremia; the blood culture confirms it before empiric ceftriaxone
  6. 6-week-old boy has 1 day of fever to 38.4 C and loose stools with streaks of blood; both parents had fever and diarrhea after a family picnic with undercooked chicken; stool culture grows nontyphoidal Salmonella; he feeds well and is well hydrated → Blood culture and antibiotic therapy → infants under 3 months with Salmonella are at risk of bacteremia and meningitis, so they are treated
  7. 11-year-old girl has 3 days of fever, cramps and loose stools with some blood after a summer barbecue where chicken was undercooked; she is otherwise healthy; today she is afebrile, drinking well, and her stools are fewer; stool culture grows nontyphoidal Salmonella → Oral rehydration and supportive care → antibiotics do not shorten uncomplicated nontyphoidal Salmonella in a healthy child and prolong carriage
Management Rehydrate first – oral rehydration for nearly everyone · Antibiotics only for – typhoid; Shigella; C difficile; nontyphoidal Salmonella in infants under 3 months, immunocompromise, sickle cell disease or bacteremia, since treating others prolongs carriage · Suspected Shiga toxin E coli – never antibiotics or antimotility drugs, which raise the risk of HUS
Pearls Exposures to know: a pet turtle, reheated rice, raw oysters, a hamburger · Humoral immunodeficiency such as CVID (common variable immunodeficiency) raises the risk of Salmonella, Campylobacter and Giardia infection; it does not change which food carries which organism · A vaccine exists for typhoid, not for nontyphoidal Salmonella · In sickle cell disease, Salmonella is the organism of osteomyelitis, which is why these children are treated
Pairs with Part I Antibody Deficiencies covers CVID (common variable immunodeficiency): are IgG and at least one other isotype low, with poor vaccine responses? Part I Right Lower Quadrant Pain covers Campylobacter and Yersinia pseudoappendicitis and its list of who gets antibiotics: is the pain from the appendix or the ileocecum? Part I Anemia with Thrombocytopenia covers HUS (hemolytic uremic syndrome), which follows Shiga toxin E coli infection: is a second cell line down a week after bloody diarrhea? Part II Sickle Cell Disease and Trait covers Salmonella osteomyelitis: is it trait or disease?
Transferable rule In infectious diarrhea, name the organism from the exposure and the timing. That organism then determines the culture and whether to treat. A risk factor for a different organism is not the exposure.
Salient decoyAntibiotic disruption of gut flora: the recent amoxicillin-clavulanate is real, but it predisposes to C difficile, which starts watery; the culture grew Salmonella.
Class-vs-memberTyphoid vaccine failure: the vaccine covers only typhoidal strains, and there is no vaccine for nontyphoidal Salmonella; CVID blunting the response does not matter here.
True-fact-wrong-slotRaw or unrefrigerated seafood: a real foodborne source, but of Vibrio parahaemolyticus, not Salmonella.
Salient decoyContaminated immunoglobulin infusions: rare, and they cause bacteremia with high fever and chills found on blood culture, not gastroenteritis with a positive stool culture.
