edits.html:
Fever in an Infant

urine, blood, meninges, lungs, or a virus · red flags · workup by age, appearance and vaccines · the culture confirmsDoes the infant look ill, and if well, how old and how vaccinated is the infant?

Source case Pt – 6-month-old with fever, Aquifer Pediatrics 10; the case works a fever without a source through the serious bacterial infection workup to a first febrile urinary tract infection (pyelonephritis) · Q – decide which tests the infant’s age, appearance and vaccines call for, read the urine, CBC and CSF, then choose the setting, the antibiotic, the dose and the imaging
The approach

Fever without a source means a complete history and examination found no focus. Most of these infants have a virus (roseola, other viral syndromes). A small minority have a serious bacterial infection. The urine is the commonest source: a UTI (urinary tract infection). Other sources are the blood (occult bacteremia, sepsis), the meninges (bacterial meningitis), the lungs (pneumonia), or rarely bone, joint or gut. Look at the child first: an ill-appearing infant gets the full workup. In a well infant, age and vaccine status decide how much testing is needed. The catheter urine culture, blood culture or CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) culture confirms the infection.

Red flags: act before the full history
FindingWhat it points to
Slow capillary refill, low blood pressure, altered mental statusSeptic shock: circulation, airway, breathing first
Fast heart or breathing rate in an ill childEarly sepsis: cultures and antibiotics now
Hypothermia in a young infantSepsis; fever may be absent
Bulging fontanelle, lethargy, seizureMeningitis: lumbar puncture
Workup by age, appearance and vaccines
InfantWorkup
21 days or youngerFull workup with lumbar puncture, whatever the appearance
22 to 60 days, ill-appearingFull workup with lumbar puncture
22 to 60 days, well-appearingLumbar puncture only if inflammatory markers are abnormal
Over 2 months, ill-appearingUrine, CBC, blood culture; consider lumbar puncture
3 to 36 months, well, fully immunizedUrine if at risk; nothing else
3 to 36 months, well, underimmunizedUrine, CBC and blood culture
Infant with fever: the differential
DiagnosisSourceWhat it looks likeFirst clue
Urinary tract infectionUrineFever, no focus; fussy, eating lessPositive leukocyte esterase and nitrite
Occult bacteremiaBloodFever in a well-appearing childUnderimmunized; positive blood culture
SepsisBlood, with a systemic responseIll-appearing; fast heart and breathingPoor perfusion; hypothermia in young infants
Bacterial meningitisMeningesIrritable or lethargic, bulging fontanelle, poor feedingCries when picked up; no neck signs
Viral meningitisMeningesMilder; loose stools, rash or cold symptomsEnterovirus; lymphocytes in the CSF
PneumoniaLungsCough, fast breathing, crackles, low saturationRarely silent; lower lobe can cause belly pain
RoseolaVirus (HHV-6)3 to 5 days of high fever, well childRash as the fever breaks; under age 2
Acute otitis mediaEarRed eardrum that bulges and moves poorlyRedness alone predicts nothing
HSV gingivostomatitisMouthFever and fussiness, then oral vesicles and ulcers10 months to 3 years
Viral upper respiratory infectionNose and throatCongestion, cough, runny noseA source, so not fever without one
Kawasaki diseaseVesselsFever 5 days or more, red eyes, lips, rashInfants often have incomplete forms
History: what each answer points to
ClueWhat it points to
Fussy and eating less, nothing elseUTI, meningitis and viral illness all do this, so it separates nothing
Fewer than 2 doses of PCV and HibUnderimmunized: bacteremia risk higher
DTaP or PCV in the last few daysVaccine fever, within a few days
Girl under 2, or uncircumcised boy under 1UTI risk: test the urine
Circumcised boy 6 months or olderLow UTI risk if nothing else
Prior UTI, urinary tract anomaly, fever over 48 hoursUTI risk: test the urine
Cough, congestion, runny noseViral respiratory infection
Examination: what each finding points to
FindingWhat it points to
Ill appearanceFull workup for serious bacterial infection
Bulging fontanelle; cries when picked upMeningitis
No Kernig or Brudzinski sign under 12 monthsUsually absent in infant meningitis; excludes nothing
Fast breathing, crackles, low saturationPneumonia
Red eardrum that moves and does not bulgeNot otitis media
Vesicles and ulcers in the mouthHSV gingivostomatitis
Normal examination, well childFever without a source: age and vaccines set the tests
First tests
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Catheterized urinalysisFirstLeukocyte esterase and nitrite positiveUTI strongly suggested: culture, start antibiotics
Leukocyte esterase alone positivePyuria has other causes; the culture decides
Nitrite negativeDoes not exclude UTI; infants void often
NormalUTI unlikely; look elsewhere or follow closely
CBC with differentialBy branchHigh white count, bandsMore likely bacterial, if ill or underimmunized
Chest x-rayBy branchInfiltrateFor chest findings, or fever over 39 C with WBC 20,000 or more
Lumbar puncture: cells, glucose, protein, Gram stainBy branchNeutrophils, low glucose, high proteinBacterial meningitis; lymphocytes with normal glucose: viral
Urine culture, catheter specimenConfirmsGrowth of one uropathogenUTI; E. coli in 85 to 90%
Blood cultureConfirmsGrowth in a well-appearing childOccult bacteremia; in an ill child, sepsis
CSF cultureConfirmsOrganism grown; Gram stain may be negativeBacterial meningitis
None: clinicalConfirmsRash as the fever breaksRoseola
CBC in a well, immunized childSkipA high count is almost always a false positiveBacteremia is now too rare to predict
Bag urine for cultureSkipHigh contamination rateScreening only; catheterize to culture
Group A strep test under age 3SkipStrep throat and rheumatic fever rareNot recommended at this age
Finalists
On arrivalUrinalysisNextConfirmsTreatment and follow-up
PyelonephritisFever, fussy, eating less; no focusEsterase and nitrite positiveDecide oral or IVCatheter urine cultureOral cephalexin if well; IV ceftriaxone if toxic; ultrasound under age 2
Bacterial meningitisIrritable or lethargic; bulging fontanelleNormalLumbar puncture; blood cultureCSF cultureAdmit; IV antibiotics
Occult bacteremiaWell; underimmunized; high feverNormalCBC and blood cultureBlood culture in a well childRecall and reexamine if the culture grows
RoseolaWell; 3 to 5 days of high feverNormalObserveClinical: rash as fever breaksReassurance; no treatment
Febrile urinary tract infection (pyelonephritis) in an infant What it is – bacterial infection of the kidney; the commonest serious bacterial infection behind fever without a source · Who – girls under 2, uncircumcised boys under 1, circumcised boys under 6 months; prior UTI or a urinary tract anomaly · Mechanism – bowel flora ascend the urethra to the bladder and kidney; E. coli in 85 to 90% of first episodes, the rest Klebsiella, Proteus or enterococcus · Features – fever with no focus, fussiness and poor appetite; an infant cannot report dysuria or flank pain · Diagnosis – catheterized urinalysis: pyuria over 5 WBC/hpf, and esterase and nitrite positive, strongly suggest it; the catheter culture confirms. Collect by catheter in a child not toilet trained; suprapubic aspiration only if catheterization fails; a bag specimen is never cultured · Setting – most are treated orally at home; IV and admission for a toxic child, one who cannot keep oral medicine down, or doubtful adherence · Treatment – oral cephalexin or another cephalosporin by local resistance; TMP-SMX and amoxicillin-clavulanate work but are not first choices; IV ceftriaxone after the first month (it displaces bilirubin in neonates; no calcium in the same line); ampicillin plus gentamicin also works, and ampicillin covers enterococcus, which ceftriaxone misses; nitrofurantoin reaches only the urine, so it treats cystitis, not pyelonephritis · Dosing – mg/kg per day times weight, divided by doses per day; prefer fewer daily doses and a whole-number volume · Follow-up – improvement expected in 48 to 72 hours; renal and bladder ultrasound after a first febrile UTI under age 2, usually after the course; VCUG if the ultrasound is abnormal, fever of 39 C or more with an organism other than E. coli, or a second febrile UTI · Complications – renal scarring; vesicoureteral reflux behind recurrences · Return for – fever or fussiness after 2 to 3 days of antibiotics, vomiting that stops the medicine, lethargy, any new fever later
What sets it apart
VersusWhat separates it
Occult bacteremiaA positive urine names the source
Bacterial meningitisWell child, normal fontanelle: no lumbar puncture needed
RoseolaRoseola has a normal urine and a rash as fever ends
CystitisFever puts the infection in the kidney
Scenario bank
  1. 6-month-old girl with 2 days of fever to 39.4 C, fussier than usual and taking less formula; no cough, runny nose, vomiting or diarrhea; vaccines up to date; well-appearing with a normal examination, including a flat fontanelle, clear lungs and normal eardrums; catheterized urinalysis shows positive leukocyte esterase and nitrite with many white cells → Pyelonephritis → a febrile UTI in an infant is an upper-tract infection; catheter culture next
  2. 7-month-old girl with 2 days of fever to 39.2 C and no other symptoms; vaccines up to date; playful and well hydrated, with a normal fontanelle, clear lungs, normal eardrums and no rash → Urinalysis by catheter → UTI is the commonest serious bacterial infection behind a fever without a source
  3. 10-month-old circumcised boy with 1 day of fever to 38.9 C; vaccines up to date; no prior urinary infection or known urinary tract anomaly; playful and drinking well, with a normal examination → Clinical follow-up alone → low UTI risk and well-appearing: no testing needed
  4. 9-month-old boy whose parents declined all vaccines, with 1 day of fever to 39.6 C and no other symptoms; alert and playful, with a flat fontanelle, supple neck and normal examination → CBC, blood culture, and urine → underimmunized: bacteremia is more likely, so blood tests join the urine
  5. 12-month-old unvaccinated boy with fever to 39.8 C and no source on examination; a blood culture drawn in clinic grows gram-positive diplococci the next day, when he is afebrile, playful and eating well, with a normal fontanelle and no rash → Occult bacteremia → a positive blood culture in a well-appearing child; recall and reexamine
  6. 5-month-old boy with 1 day of fever, irritability and poor feeding; neck supple; Kernig and Brudzinski signs absent → Does not exclude meningitis → these signs are usually absent in infants with meningitis
  7. 7-month-old girl with fever to 39.3 C, no source on examination and a normal fontanelle; vaccines up to date; catheterized urinalysis shows pyuria with positive leukocyte esterase and nitrite → Urine culture → the catheter culture confirms the UTI and names the organism
  8. 8-month-old girl with 2 days of fever, lethargy and vomiting and a bulging fontanelle; cerebrospinal fluid shows a high white cell count, mostly neutrophils, low glucose and high protein; Gram stain shows no organisms → Bacterial meningitis → a negative Gram stain does not exclude it; the culture confirms
  9. 10-month-old boy with 4 days of fever to 40 C who stayed playful and fed well throughout; the fever stopped yesterday and today he has a pink, blanching rash on the trunk; examination otherwise normal → Reassurance → roseola (HHV-6): no tests or treatment needed
  10. 9-month-old fully immunized girl with fever to 39 C for 1 day; well-appearing and playful, with a normal examination; a CBC obtained at urgent care shows a white count of 17,000 with a mild left shift → Probably a false positive → bacteremia is rare in a well, immunized child, so the count predicts little
  11. 6-month-old girl with fever and no source on examination, not toilet trained; a urine specimen is needed to rule out infection → Culture of a bag specimen → high contamination rate; a bag specimen is for screening only
  12. 6-month-old girl with pyelonephritis on catheterized urinalysis, culture pending; well-appearing, taking formula and keeping it down; reliable parents with a phone and transportation → Oral cephalexin at home → most febrile UTIs are treated orally
  13. 6-month-old girl started on oral cephalexin for pyelonephritis 1 day ago now vomits every dose, is sleepier and has cool hands with a capillary refill of 3 seconds → Admit for IV ceftriaxone → toxic, or unable to keep oral medicine down
  14. 7-month-old boy with fever to 39.5 C and a catheter urine culture growing E. coli susceptible to all oral agents tested; well-appearing and ready to go home on oral therapy → Nitrofurantoin → therapeutic levels in the urine only, not the kidney
  15. 5-month-old girl admitted on IV ceftriaxone for pyelonephritis is still febrile after 48 hours; the catheter urine culture grows Enterococcus faecalis susceptible to ampicillin → Switch to ampicillin → ceftriaxone does not cover enterococcus
  16. 8-kg infant is prescribed an oral antibiotic at 50 mg/kg/day divided every 12 hours; the suspension contains 250 mg per 5 mL → 4 mL twice daily → 400 mg a day, 200 mg a dose, at 50 mg per mL
  17. 6-month-old girl with her first febrile UTI, E. coli on catheter culture, afebrile within 48 hours on oral therapy and now finishing the course; normal growth and blood pressure → Renal and bladder ultrasound → first febrile UTI under age 2; VCUG only if abnormal or recurrent
  18. 9-month-old boy with 2 days of fever to 39.6 C, no cough, fussy with feeds and a mildly uncomfortable belly; vaccines up to date; well-appearing, breathing comfortably, lungs clear; catheterized urinalysis normal; white count 22,000 → Chest x-ray → occult pneumonia: high fever and a white count of 20,000 or more with no other source
Pairs with Part II Fever and Sepsis in the Newborn covers the decision to tap once other sources are closed: is there a meningeal sign, or only a fever? Part I Urinary Tract Infection in a Child covers the imaging rules after a febrile UTI (urinary tract infection) and the child not improving by 72 hours. Part I Urinary Tract Infection in a Child covers the child once the VCUG (voiding cystourethrogram) shows reflux. Part I Bacterial Meningitis covers the CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) grid. Part II Fever and Sepsis in the Newborn covers the first month of life. Part II Fever and Rash in a Child covers roseola among the rashes. Part I Kawasaki Disease covers fever of 5 days or more with red eyes and lips.
Transferable rule In an infant with fever and no source, appearance, age and vaccine status decide how much testing is needed. Test the urine of any child at risk, and collect it by catheter. The culture, not the dipstick, confirms the infection.
Salient decoyFussiness and poor feeding come with UTI, meningitis and viral illness alike and cannot separate them.
Unchecked attributeA supple neck and no Kernig or Brudzinski sign under 12 months do not exclude meningitis.
Test-overrides-findingsA high white count in a well, fully immunized infant is almost always a false positive.
Class-vs-memberNitrofurantoin treats bladder infection but never reaches the kidney, so it cannot treat a febrile UTI.

edits.html:
The Red Eye

three triage questions · conjunctivitis types · red eyes that cannot be missed · contact lens wearersIs acuity down, is the pain deep, or is the pupil, cornea or globe abnormal?

The decision point

1. Is visual acuity affected? 2. Is there true deep pain (not gritty or itchy)? 3. Is the pupil, cornea, or globe abnormal? Any "yes" means this is not simple conjunctivitis and points toward urgent ophthalmology.

Conjunctivitis types
TypeDiscriminatorTreatment
Viral (adenovirus)Watery, follicular tarsal conjunctiva, preauricular node, URI prodromeSupportive – cool compresses, artificial tears
BacterialPurulent, lids stuck shut on waking, papillaryErythromycin ointment or polymyxin-trimethoprim
Contact lens wearerAny red eye → think PseudomonasFluoroquinolone; remove lens; urgent ophtho if infiltrate
AllergicITCHING is the hallmark; bilateral, cobblestone papillaeOlopatadine, ketotifen
Gonococcal EmergencyHyperacute (<24 h), copious purulence – can perforate the corneaIM ceftriaxone + irrigation + urgent ophtho
ChlamydialChronic >3 weeks, follicular, sexually active adultOral azithromycin/doxycycline + treat partners
The can't-miss red eyes
DiagnosisThe tellAnswer
Acute angle-closure glaucomaSevere pain, halos, vomiting, mid-dilated fixed pupil, hard globe; triggered by dark rooms or anticholinergicsTimolol + apraclonidine + pilocarpine + IV acetazolamide → laser peripheral iridotomy
HSV keratitisDendritic ulcer on fluorescein, ↓ corneal sensationTopical trifluridine or oral acyclovir – never steroids
Herpes zoster ophthalmicusV1 vesicles + Hutchinson signOral antivirals + ophtho
Anterior uveitisCiliary flush, cell and flare, consensual photophobia; HLA-B27, JIA, sarcoidTopical steroid + cycloplegic – the one place prednisolone is right
ScleritisBoring pain that wakes from sleep, does not blanch with phenylephrine; RA, GPASystemic NSAIDs/steroids
EpiscleritisSectoral, minimal pain, blanches with phenylephrineSupportive
EndophthalmitisPost-op or post-injection, pain + ↓VA + hypopyonIntravitreal antibiotics – emergency
Orbital cellulitisProptosis, pain with EOM, ophthalmoplegiaCT orbits + IV antibiotics (preseptal has none of those)
Scenario bank
  1. 24 yo M with bilateral watery red eyes, a preauricular node, recent URI and normal vision → Viral conjunctivitis → supportive care
  2. 24 yo M contact lens wearer with pain, photophobia and a corneal infiltrate → Bacterial keratitis → urgent ophthalmology, never patch
  3. 62 yo F with severe pain, halos, a mid-dilated fixed pupil and vomiting → Acute angle-closure glaucoma → topical agents plus acetazolamide
  4. 24 yo M with a dendritic corneal ulcer on fluorescein staining → HSV keratitis → topical antiviral, never steroids
  5. 30 yo M with ankylosing spondylitis, photophobia, ciliary flush and anterior chamber cells → Anterior uveitis → topical steroid plus cycloplegic
  6. 55 yo F with rheumatoid arthritis and severe boring eye pain that wakes her at night → Scleritis
  7. Newborn with purulent conjunctivitis on day 3 of life → Gonococcal conjunctivitis → parenteral ceftriaxone
  8. 9 yo M with bilateral eye itching, watery discharge, cobblestone papillae under the upper eyelids, nasal congestion each spring → Allergic conjunctivitis → olopatadine or ketotifen drops
  9. 5 yo F, 3 days of photophobia with lids crusted shut on waking, diffuse bulbar and palpebral erythema, mucopurulent discharge, acuity unchanged → Bacterial conjunctivitis → Mucopurulent discharge with normal acuity
  10. School-age child with mucopurulent conjunctivitis and no contact lens use; the likeliest organism → Haemophilus influenzae → With S pneumoniae and Moraxella catarrhalis
  11. Child with an undifferentiated red eye and mucopurulent discharge; which is contraindicated before slit-lamp examination → Topical corticosteroid drops → Steroid on an unrecognized HSV keratitis worsens it
Neonatal conjunctivitis by day of onset Day 0–1 chemical · day 2–5 gonococcal → IM/IV ceftriaxone + irrigation · day 5–14 chlamydial → oral erythromycin, or oral azithromycin as the alternative (counsel on pyloric stenosis with either) · day 6–14 HSV (herpes simplex virus) → IV acyclovir. Birth prophylaxis (erythromycin ointment) prevents gonococcal but not chlamydial disease.
How NBME framed it A home birth delivered by the father stood in for missing eye prophylaxis, and Kawasaki disease was listed under its formal name, mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome.
Pairs with Part II Eyelid Lumps and Swelling in a Child covers the red eye that comes from a tender lump on the lid margin, and its lid-swelling mimics. Ask: is there a lump on the lid?
The steroid rule Steroids are indicated in anterior uveitis (topical) and scleritis (systemic). Topical steroids are catastrophic in HSV (herpes simplex virus) keratitis, bacterial/fungal keratitis, and undifferentiated red eye. If you cannot name the diagnosis with certainty, do not give steroids.

edits.html:
Primary Headache in an Adult

migraine, cluster, tension · the autonomic tell · attack length · glaucoma and dissection · oxygen, then verapamilHow long do the attacks last, and are there autonomic signs on the same side?

Source vignette Pt – 27 yo M, nightly 90-minute attacks of stabbing left periorbital pain with tearing, ptosis and rhinorrhea · Q – the most likely diagnosis; options spanned cluster headache, trigeminal neuralgia and acute angle-closure glaucoma
The decision point

Acute unilateral periorbital pain with ipsilateral autonomic signs (ptosis, miosis, lacrimation, rhinorrhea, conjunctival injection) is a cluster headache. Attacks wake the patient from sleep, peak fast, last ~90 minutes, and recur several times daily for weeks before remitting. Acute treatment is 100% oxygen; sumatriptan aborts attacks but is second-line (slower onset, side effects). Vision stays intact in cluster headache; vision change or a fixed mid-dilated pupil moves the diagnosis to angle-closure glaucoma.

Defining criteria Cluster attack – excruciating periorbital pain lasting 15–180 minutes with ipsilateral autonomic signs, often nocturnal onset · Pattern – several attacks daily for 6–8 weeks, then remission lasting months to years · Abortive – 100% oxygen first-line; sumatriptan second · Prophylaxis – verapamil
Headache types – the differential
MigraineClusterTension
SexF > MM > FF > M
OnsetVariableDuring sleep, similar timing dailyUnder stress
LocationOften unilateralBehind one eyeBand-like, bilateral
CharacterPulsatile, throbbingExcruciating, sharp, steadyDull, tight, persistent
Duration4–72 h15–180 min30 min to months
AssociatedPhotophobia, phonophobia, nausea, ± auraIpsilateral autonomic signs – tearing, ptosis, miosis, rhinorrhea, flushingPericranial muscle tenderness
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
History and neurologic exam, including pupilsFirstAttacks of 15 to 180 minutes with ipsilateral autonomic signsCluster headache; attacks lasting seconds point to trigeminal neuralgia
Visual acuity and intraocular pressureBy branchRaised pressure, fixed mid-dilated pupil, halosAcute angle-closure glaucoma, an eye emergency
CT or MR angiography of the neckBy branchCarotid dissectionHorner syndrome that persists between attacks, or neck pain
MRI of the brainBy branchA structural lesion, such as a pituitary massExcludes a secondary cause when the exam is abnormal or attacks are atypical
None: clinical diagnosisConfirmsNo test confirms cluster headacheTests only exclude mimics; relief with 100% oxygen supports it
Sinus CTSkipRhinorrhea here is autonomic, not infectiveEpisodic attacks without fever or congestion are not sinusitis
Scenario bank
  1. 27 yo M, nightly 90-minute attacks of stabbing left periorbital pain with tearing, ptosis, and rhinorrhea → Cluster headache → abort with 100% oxygen
  2. 27 yo M with cluster headaches recurring nightly for 3 weeks; best prophylaxis → Verapamil
  3. 24 yo F, 8 hours of unilateral throbbing pain with nausea and photophobia, prior similar episodes → Migraine → NSAID or triptan early
  4. 35 yo F under work stress, band-like bilateral head tightness with neck muscle tenderness, normal exam → Tension headache
  5. 55 yo M, seconds-long electric shocks over the cheek and jaw triggered by chewing and brushing → Trigeminal neuralgia → carbamazepine
  6. 63 yo F, acute eye pain with halos around lights, decreased vision, fixed mid-dilated pupil → Acute angle-closure glaucoma → pressure-lowering drops, then laser iridotomy
Pearls Autonomic signs are nearly universal in cluster headache; their absence should force a second look · agitation during the attack points to cluster (migraineurs lie still) · rhinorrhea plus facial pain suggests sinusitis, but sinusitis pain is not episodic and brings congestion and fever, not ptosis · trigeminal neuralgia lasts seconds; cluster lasts an hour and a half.
Pairs with Part I Headache in a Child: Imaging and Treatment covers the pediatric red-flag check that comes before this headache-type differential.
Transferable rule Classify headache by duration and associated features: seconds = neuralgia; minutes-to-hours with autonomic signs = cluster; hours-to-days with nausea/photophobia = migraine. Establish the duration before the character of the pain.
Salient decoySinusitis: rhinorrhea suggests it, but the episodic pattern and the autonomic signs point away from it.
Class-vs-memberSumatriptan: it aborts cluster attacks, but oxygen is the first-line abortive.

edits.html:
Headache in a Child: Imaging and Treatment

when a child's headache needs imaging · migraine vomiting is not a pressure sign · the treatment ladder · drugs that raise pressureIs anything abnormal outside the headache history: the examination, the fundus, the growth chart or the vitals?

Source vignette Pt – 13 yo F, 2 years of similar headaches: unilateral, pulsatile, hours long, worse with activity, with nausea; now monthly instead of every other month, same characteristics; menarche at 12, periods now regular; this one began after a sleepover, she vomited twice and could not finish her homework; intermittent acetaminophen only · Exam – temperature 37 °C, alert and oriented, pupils equal and reactive, remainder of the neurologic examination normal, no papilledema described · Q – the most appropriate next step; options spanned no additional testing, computed tomography (CT) of the head, a urine toxicology screen, serum electrolytes and lumbar puncture
The decision point

This headache is already diagnosable: unilateral, pulsatile, hours long, worsened by activity, with nausea and vomiting, in an adolescent girl with a two-year history of the same thing. Image only if a feature meets an imaging indication. None of the following three features meets one. Vomiting is a diagnostic criterion of migraine, not a pressure sign. The disability ("could not finish her homework") measures severity, and no guideline images for severity. The increase in frequency is a change in rate, not in character. The headaches "have the same characteristics" and remain monthly. The change tracks the arrival of regular menses since menarche. The examination is normal, including the pupils, and no papilledema is described. No additional testing is needed. Imaging is reserved for an abnormal neurologic examination, signs of raised intracranial pressure, or a dramatic change in headache characteristics.

When papilledema is present, imaging is indicated. Then find why the pressure is high; the medication list often answers it. An adolescent on isotretinoin with a month of morning headache and vomiting, brief blurring of vision, bilateral disc edema and full visual fields has drug-induced intracranial hypertension. A mass at the optic chiasm would cut the fields. Optic neuritis is painful, acute and usually affects one eye.

Defining criteria Indications for neuroimaging in pediatric headache – (1) abnormal neurologic examination findings, such as weakness or ataxia; (2) signs of raised intracranial pressure, such as papilledema; (3) a dramatic change in headache characteristics. None is present here · Not an indication – a modest rise in frequency when the headaches keep the same character, remain relatively infrequent, and have a physiologic explanation for the change · Migraine, diagnostic features – pulsatile, unilateral (may be bilateral in children), hours to days; photophobia and phonophobia; nausea or vomiting; ± aura; normal neurologic examination. Formal criteria add ≥5 prior attacks lasting 2–72 hours in patients under 18 (4–72 in adults); beyond 72 hours is status migrainosus (ICHD-3, International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition)
Pertinent positives & negatives Two years of similar headaches – recurrent and stereotyped; excludes "first and worst," which is the thunderclap gate · Vomited twice – a migraine criterion; it becomes a pressure sign only when it is morning vomiting, projectile, or paired with papilledema · Pupils equal and reactive, remainder of the neurologic examination normal – closes indication (1) and, in the absence of described disc edema, indication (2) · Menarche at 12, now regular cycles – the physiologic explanation for the change in rate, so the change is explained · Afebrile, alert and oriented – excludes meningitis, so lumbar puncture is not indicated · Began after a sleepover – sleep deprivation is a named migraine trigger, not evidence of ingestion
Classify first: headache in a child
AxisThe stem sentence that settles itConsequence for management
Examination and fundus normal?"Pupils equal and reactive... remainder of neurologic examination normal"; no papilledemaCloses both of the first two imaging indications, and the IIH (idiopathic intracranial hypertension) branch with them (in-context: papilledema would be expected)
Character or only rate?"Similar headaches over the past 2 years"; "every other month… now monthly," same featuresRecurrent, not first-and-worst; a rate change only, which does not meet "dramatic change in characteristics"
Explanation for the change?"Menarche at age 12; menstrual periods now regular"A physiologic cause is identified, so the change is accounted for
Systemic signs?"Temperature 37 C," alert, normal vitalsNo infection, no toxidrome
Tier fingerprint done: nothing but intermittent acetaminophen · failed: 2 years of attacks with inadequate abortive dosing and timing, the actual unmet need · bothered: missed schoolwork, which justifies better treatment, not more testing.
Management ladder: headache in a child
TierInterventionEscalate when
1Clinical diagnosis; trigger diary (sleep, meals, menses, screens); sleep-hygiene and hydration counseling; no laboratory or imagingAny red-flag gate is breached, or attacks recur despite trigger control
2Abortive therapy at first symptom, at full weight-based dose: ibuprofen or acetaminophen, rest in a dark quiet room, antiemetic if vomiting blocks oral dosingAn early, adequately dosed NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug) fails
3Triptan for refractory attacks, then consider daily prevention (propranolol, amitriptyline with cognitive behavioral therapy, topiramate) if attacks are frequent or disablingReassess prevention after a trial of at least 2 months
Exit / de-escalationMedication-overuse headache: withdraw the offending analgesicSimple analgesics on ≥15 days/month, or triptans, or any combination of triptans, analgesics or opioids, on ≥10 days/month, for more than 3 months
Numbers that gate & exit ramps Diagnostic: up to 3 days per attack; ≥5 prior attacks of 2–72 hours. Escalation: frequent or disabling attacks (consider prevention), and the overuse thresholds above. The exam answer versus clinical practice: the exam keys the preventive rung, though a pediatric trial found amitriptyline and topiramate no better than placebo. That trial result does not change the keyed rung. · Papilledema → magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with MR (magnetic resonance) venography, then LP (lumbar puncture) with an opening pressure; a normal MRI with a high opening pressure means intracranial hypertension, idiopathic or drug-induced. · Fever with meningismus → lumbar puncture. A thunderclap headache → noncontrast CT, then LP if negative. · Wakes from sleep, worse on waking or with Valsalva → MRI, however migrainous the rest sounds. · Focal deficit or ataxia → Brain Tumors in a Child. A falling height percentile or arrested puberty → MRI with sellar views; see Brain Tumors in a Child. · Household all symptomatic → carboxyhemoglobin. Image any child who is immunocompromised, shunted, or anticoagulated.
Intracranial hypertension: check the drug list Who – women of childbearing age, obesity or recent weight gain, and drugs: retinoids and vitamin A (isotretinoin for acne), tetracyclines (minocycline, doxycycline) and growth hormone · Symptoms – daily headache worse lying flat and in the morning, better standing, with nausea and vomiting; transient visual obscurations; pulsatile tinnitus; diplopia from a cranial nerve VI palsy · Signs – bilateral papilledema with enlarged blind spots and full visual fields, otherwise a normal neurologic exam; a lesion at the chiasm would cut the fields (bitemporal hemianopia) · Workup – MRI with MR venography first, to exclude a mass, hydrocephalus and venous sinus thrombosis; then LP (lumbar puncture): opening pressure over 250 mm H2O with normal CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) · Treatment – stop the offending drug, which usually resolves it; weight loss; acetazolamide
Decision spine Is the neurologic examination normal, including the fundus? – Yes → the strongest two indications are closed · First and worst, or recurrent and familiar? – Recurrent → no urgent pathway · Did the character change, or only the rate? – Rate only → not a dramatic change · Is there a physiologic explanation for the change? – Menarche and regular cycles → yes · Any systemic signal: fever, altered sensorium, abnormal vitals, growth failure? – None → make a diagnosis and a treatment plan, not a test
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Neurologic exam, fundi and growth chartFirstNormal exam, no papilledema, growth on trackPrimary headache, usually migraine: no testing
None: clinical diagnosis of migraineConfirmsNo test confirms migraineDiagnosis rests on the history and a normal exam
MRI of the brain, for a red flagBy branchMass or hydrocephalusRed flags: focal deficit, papilledema, waking from sleep, change in character
Noncontrast head CTBy branchBlood in a thunderclap headacheSubarachnoid hemorrhage; LP if the CT is negative
MRI of the brain with MR venography, for papilledemaBy branchNormal: no mass, hydrocephalus or venous sinus thrombosisRaised pressure without a structural cause; proceed to LP
Lumbar puncture with opening pressureBy branchOpening pressure over 250 mm H2O with normal CSF, after a normal MRI and MR venographyIntracranial hypertension, idiopathic or drug-induced; with fever and meningismus, LP for meningitis
CarboxyhemoglobinBy branchElevated, with the household affectedCarbon monoxide exposure
Head CT for recurrent headache, normal examSkipStable character, normal examNo imaging needed; chronic headache that earns imaging gets MRI
Scenario bank
  1. 10 yo M, 1 year of bilateral throbbing headaches with photophobia and vomiting, relieved by sleep, normal examination → Reassurance, trigger diary, and early-dose ibuprofen → Pediatric migraine
  2. 13 yo F with 2 years of migraines, now with papilledema and vomiting on waking → MRI of the brain → Suspected intracranial mass
  3. 16 yo F, obese, daily headache with pulsatile tinnitus and papilledema, MRI of the brain normal → Lumbar puncture with opening pressure → Idiopathic intracranial hypertension
  4. 15 yo M, sudden headache maximal within seconds while lifting weights, worst of his life, normal examination → Noncontrast CT of the head → Suspected subarachnoid hemorrhage
  5. 4 yo M, 12 h of headache with T 39.2, nuchal rigidity, irritable, no focal deficit or papilledema → Lumbar puncture → Bacterial meningitis
  6. 8 yo F, 6 months of headaches with a normal neurologic examination, height crossed from 50th to 5th percentile with weight held → MRI of the brain with sellar views → Suprasellar mass
  7. 12 yo M with morning headaches and nausea on winter weekdays; mother and brother affected, all better away from home → Carboxyhemoglobin level → Carbon monoxide exposure
  8. 6 yo F, frontal headaches only on school afternoons, squints at the board, normal neurologic examination → Ophthalmologic examination with refraction → Uncorrected refractive error
  9. 13 yo F, 3 years of episodic headaches now monthly and predictable in the 2 days before each period, unchanged in character → Menstrual migraine → Trigger counseling and timed NSAIDs
  10. 15 yo M using ibuprofen or acetaminophen on 20 days per month for a headache that is now daily and dull → Continuing the daily as-needed analgesic → Medication-overuse headache
  11. 16 yo M taking oral isotretinoin for severe acne, with 1 month of daily throbbing frontal headache that is worse in the morning, occasional nausea and vomiting, partial relief from acetaminophen, and brief blurring of the left eye at sports practice; blood pressure 130/80 mm Hg; pupils equal and reactive; bilateral optic disc edema with decreased visual acuity and full visual fields; no meningismus; normal strength, reflexes and sensation → Drug-induced intracranial hypertension → Isotretinoin (a retinoid) impairs CSF resorption; MRI with MR venography, then LP; stop the drug
  12. 15 yo M taking minocycline for acne for 3 months, with daily morning headache and pulsatile tinnitus; bilateral papilledema with full visual fields; MRI of the brain with MR venography is normal; lumbar puncture opening pressure is 340 mm H2O with normal CSF → Discontinue minocycline → Tetracycline-induced intracranial hypertension; it usually resolves off the drug, with acetazolamide added for persistent symptoms
  13. 11 yo M started on growth hormone 4 months ago for growth hormone deficiency, with 3 weeks of headache that is worse lying down and on waking, brief episodes of graying vision, and bilateral papilledema; full visual fields and an otherwise normal neurologic exam → MRI of the brain with MR venography → Exclude a mass, hydrocephalus and venous sinus thrombosis before LP; growth hormone-induced intracranial hypertension
Decoy note Awakening from sleep would indicate imaging, and it is absent here. The homework detail measures disability, which sets the treatment tier and never the imaging threshold. The near-doubling of frequency is real but explained.
Pearls A change in frequency needs an explanation; a change in character, an examination finding or a pressure sign needs a scan. · Reassurance is defensible only when you can name the criteria you cleared. · Change in rate ≠ change in character. Ask what changed. If the only change is "more often," look for the physiologic cause (menarche, a new schedule, a new medication) before you look at the brain. · MRI for chronic and progressive; CT for acute and hemorrhagic. The right decision to image still needs the right modality. · Boundary: nocturnal awakening, morning vomiting, and headache worsened by Valsalva are pressure signs even when the rest is textbook migraine. They take precedence over the migraine features. · Migraine onset and changes in frequency cluster around menarche. Through the same estrogen link, menstrual migraine is the commonest cause of headaches that got worse this year in an adolescent.
Pairs with Brain Tumors in a Child covers the same complaint at the same age and sex, on the opposite side of the imaging gate. There, the headache came with papilledema, a height percentile crossing, and Tanner 1. Here it comes with a normal examination and an explained change in frequency. Ask: is anything abnormal outside the headache history (the fundus, the growth chart, the Tanner stage, the neurologic examination)? Primary Headache in an Adult covers the headache-type differential once imaging has been excluded. Low Back Pain in an Adult uses the same gating logic in a different region. The pain's severity never opens the gate, and a specific finding always does. Part II Vitamins and Nutritional Deficiencies covers vitamin A excess as a cause of pseudotumor cerebri. Ask: is the patient taking a retinoid or a vitamin A supplement? Part I Headache in a School-Age Child covers the whole workup once the gate opens, through the posterior fossa tumor it most often finds. Ask: does the exam show ataxia as well as papilledema?
Transferable rule Findings, not suffering, cross an imaging threshold. The examination, the fundus, the tempo of change in character, and the systemic signs decide imaging. Frequency, duration, and disability decide only the treatment tier. When a pattern changes and you can name why, the change is explained and is not a red flag.
Mirror twinCT scan of the head: Imaging requires examination findings, pressure signs, or a change in character, and none is present; even where imaging is indicated for a chronic pediatric headache, the modality is MRI
Salient decoyUrine toxicology screen: Toxic ingestion presents with altered sensorium, pupillary abnormality, respiratory depression, or seizure; she is alert with reactive pupils, and the sleepover is a sleep-deprivation trigger
Sequencing trapSerum electrolyte measurement: Two episodes in a well-hydrated, alert adolescent change no management decision; the clinical findings already answer the question electrolytes would ask
True-fact-wrong-slotLumbar puncture: She is afebrile with a normal examination, and IIH (idiopathic intracranial hypertension) would show papilledema; lumbar puncture before imaging in a patient with pressure signs is also out of order
Unchecked attributeCluster headache, for the adolescent on isotretinoin: Unilateral periorbital or temporal attacks in men aged 20 to 50, with no papilledema; this headache is daily, frontal, worse in the morning and comes with bilateral disc edema
Salient decoyOptic chiasm glioma: The blurred vision pulls toward the visual pathway, but a chiasm lesion causes bitemporal field loss, and his fields are full
True-fact-wrong-slotOptic neuritis: Disc swelling with blurred vision is real there, but it brings acute vision loss and eye pain, usually in one eye, without morning headache and vomiting
Salient decoyViral encephalitis: Headache and vomiting fit, but encephalitis needs fever and altered mental status; he is afebrile and alert with no meningismus

Seizure with Fever in a Child

benign only inside the age window · intracranial signs · fontanelle and tone, not the neck · when to tapIs the child inside the febrile-seizure age window, and is any sign of intracranial infection present?

Source vignette Pt – 10 wk F, fever and vomiting, a 4-minute generalized seizure, drowsy an hour later, open and full anterior fontanelle, weak suck, decreased tone · Q – the most appropriate next step; options spanned lumbar puncture, neuroimaging and reassurance with discharge
The decision point

At 10 weeks old, febrile seizure is excluded by age. Simple febrile seizures are defined between 6 months and 5 years. A child outside that window with fever and a seizure needs a meningitis workup by definition, before any other finding is weighed. Three other findings independently indicate the same step. A full anterior fontanelle and vomiting are signs of raised intracranial pressure. The drowsiness persisting an hour is a postictal period far beyond the ten minutes a simple febrile seizure allows. A supple neck is not reassuring, because nuchal rigidity is unreliable in infants; read the fontanelle and the tone instead. Perform a lumbar puncture.

Defining criteria Simple febrile seizure – age 6 months to 5 years, generalized, lasting under 15 minutes, with a brief postictal period under 10 minutes and rapid return to baseline, in a child with no signs of intracranial infection; the diagnosis is clinical and needs no laboratory studies or imaging · Findings that mandate urgent lumbar puncture – age outside 6 months to 5 years, signs of intracranial infection such as headache, vomiting, a bulging or full fontanelle or nuchal rigidity, prolonged altered mental status meaning a postictal period beyond 10 minutes, and a petechial rash concerning for meningococcal disease · Additional considerations for tapping – current antibiotic therapy, which masks meningitis, and an incomplete immunization history · The open-fontanelle exemption – signs of raised intracranial pressure usually require imaging before lumbar puncture, but an open fontanelle acts as a pop-off valve, limiting herniation risk and generally negating the need for a head computed tomography (CT) first
Pertinent positives & negatives Age 10 weeks – outside the febrile-seizure window entirely; this alone rules out discharge · Full anterior fontanelle – a sign of intracranial infection and raised pressure, and an indication to tap rather than a reason to image · Fontanelle open – acts as a pop-off valve, so CT is not needed first · Drowsy one hour after a 4-minute seizure – a postictal period beyond 10 minutes. This is prolonged altered mental status and an indication on its own · Weak suck and decreased tone – altered mental status in an infant, whose neurologic examination is feeding and tone rather than orientation · Neck supple – excludes nothing, because meningeal signs can be subtle or absent under 12 months · Seizure generalized, single, 4 minutes, now stopped – no benzodiazepine, since she is not seizing and it was under 5 minutes. No EEG (electroencephalography), since it was not focal, prolonged or recurrent · Skin normal – no petechiae, so meningococcemia is not the presentation; four other findings already indicate the tap · Vaccinations up to date – the incomplete-immunization consideration no longer applies, but the indication for the tap remains
Seizure with fever in a child: the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe National Board of Medical Examiners (NBME) tellExcluded here by
Bacterial meningitis Can't missAny age, and infants localize poorly, so systemic and pressure signs substitute for neck signsSeizure with fever plus a full fontanelle, vomiting, hypotonia or prolonged altered mental status, with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) culture decidingNone (the answer to pursue)
Simple febrile seizureViral fever triggers a generalized seizure in a neurologically normal childAge 6 months to 5 years, under 15 minutes, back to baseline within 10 minutes, otherwise normal examinationAge 10 weeks, postictal drowsiness at 1 hour, full fontanelle
Complex febrile seizureThe same trigger, but focal, prolonged, or recurrent within 24 hoursFocal features, longer than 15 minutes, or recurrence within 24 hours; EEG may be considered, and imaging only with abnormal or focal examination findingsThe seizure was single, generalized and 4 minutes
Herpes simplex encephalitis Can't missNeonatal or later, and parenchymal rather than meningealProlonged altered mental status with focal or temporal findings and CSF lymphocytes; red cells may be presentNot excluded; the same tap tests for it, and acyclovir is given until it is excluded
Meningococcemia Can't missN. meningitidis sepsis with rapid decompensationPetechial or purpuric rash with fever and shock, where antibiotics precede the tapSkin examination normal, normotensive
Abusive head trauma Can't missInfant with subdural collectionsSeizure with a bulging fontanelle and retinal hemorrhages, with increased irritabilityNot excluded by the stated findings
Decision spine How old? – Ten weeks → outside the window, so this is not a febrile seizure and discharge is ruled out · Is she seizing now? – No, it stopped in 4 minutes → no benzodiazepine · Was it focal, prolonged or recurrent? – No → no EEG (electroencephalography) · Any sign of intracranial infection? – Full fontanelle, vomiting, hypotonia, still drowsy → yes · Does she need a CT first? – The fontanelle is open → no, so perform the lumbar puncture
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Age, exam and time to return to baselineFirstAge 6 months to 5 years, back to baseline within 10 minutesSimple febrile seizure: no tests needed
Lumbar punctureBy branchCSF pleocytosis; lymphocytes, and red cells may be present, in herpes simplex encephalitisMeningitis or encephalitis; tap for age under 6 months, full fontanelle or prolonged drowsiness
Serum electrolytes and glucoseBy branchLow sodium or glucoseProvoked seizure; order with vomiting or diarrhea
Head CT or magnetic resonance imagingBy branchSubdural blood, a mass or edemaFocal signs, or papilledema with a closed fontanelle; infant with retinal hemorrhages
EEGBy branchFocal or epileptiform dischargesMay be considered for a complex febrile seizure, meaning one that is focal, over 15 minutes, or recurrent within 24 hours
None: clinical diagnosisConfirmsNo test confirms a simple febrile seizureTests are for red flags, to exclude infection and other causes
Head CT before lumbar puncture, open fontanelleSkipThe open fontanelle decompresses the pressureTap without a CT first
Scenario bank
  1. 10-week-old girl with fever, vomiting, a 4-minute generalized seizure, drowsiness persisting an hour later, an open and full anterior fontanelle, weak suck and decreased tone → Lumbar puncture → Age outside the window plus signs of intracranial infection
  2. 18-month-old boy with temperature 39.1 C and a single 3-minute generalized seizure who is alert with a normal examination 20 minutes later → Reassurance and discharge → Simple febrile seizure
  3. 2-year-old girl with fever who is still convulsing 8 minutes after the seizure began → Intravenous lorazepam → Duration gates the benzodiazepine
  4. 3-year-old boy with fever, a generalized seizure, a spreading petechial rash and hypotension → Give empiric intravenous antibiotics immediately and perform the lumbar puncture afterward → Meningococcemia
  5. 12-month-old girl with fever and a seizure who has papilledema and a new focal neurologic deficit, with a closed anterior fontanelle → Antibiotics, then head CT, then lumbar puncture → The imaging exception
  6. 6-week-old boy, afebrile, with a seizure, a bulging fontanelle and retinal hemorrhages on fundoscopy → Neuroimaging → Abusive head trauma
  7. 4-year-old boy, now postictal after his third seizure of this febrile illness, this one left-sided and lasting 20 minutes → Electroencephalography → Complex febrile seizure (focal, 20 minutes, recurrent); EEG may be considered when a febrile seizure is focal or recurrent; he is no longer seizing, so no lorazepam, and a complex seizure warrants more than reassurance
  8. 2-year-old with fever, seizure and persistently altered mental status whose cerebrospinal fluid shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with red blood cells → Herpes simplex encephalitis → Add acyclovir to empiric therapy
  9. Why an open anterior fontanelle removes the usual requirement for head CT before lumbar puncture → It acts as a pop-off valve that decompresses rising intracranial pressure, limiting herniation risk → The anatomy suspends the rule
  10. Infant with fever, petechiae and hypotension in whom the lumbar puncture will be delayed; which action is inappropriate → Delaying antibiotics until the lumbar puncture is completed → Treat first, tap after
  11. 2 yo M, 2 days of rhinorrhea, fever 39.2 C this morning, a 3-minute generalized seizure, sleepy and confused when paramedics arrived, now alert and playful with a normal examination; uncle has epilepsy; immunizations current → Reassurance and discharge home → simple febrile seizure; the postictal drowsiness has resolved and an uncle's epilepsy changes nothing
  12. Parents of a 2 yo after a first simple febrile seizure ask what to expect → About 30% have another; epilepsy risk stays about 1 to 2% → antipyretics do not prevent the next one
  13. 2 yo back to baseline after a brief generalized febrile seizure, but with 2 days of profuse vomiting and diarrhea and dry mucous membranes → Serum electrolytes and glucose → hypoglycemia or hyponatremia can provoke a seizure
  14. 11-month-old boy is evaluated after a 2-minute generalized seizure at home. Temperature 39.2 °C, heart rate 150/min. He is now alert and playful with a normal examination. He has received no pneumococcal or Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) vaccine doses → Lumbar puncture → incomplete immunization at 6 to 12 months lowers the bar to tap; maintenance antiseizure drugs are usually not indicated; EEG is not recommended after a simple febrile seizure with a normal examination
Decoy note A supple neck excludes nothing, because nuchal rigidity is unreliable in infants. The criteria list substitutes the fontanelle, the tone and the feeding. The rest of the examination is normal: tympanic membranes, oropharynx, lungs, abdomen and skin. With no source found, this strengthens the case for tapping rather than weakening it. When every peripheral source is excluded in a febrile infant with neurologic signs, the meninges are what is left. Up-to-date vaccinations remove one of the modifiers on the list but leave the four indications already present.
Counseling, and what each test is for Recurrence – about 30% have another febrile seizure · Epilepsy – risk slightly raised, about 1 to 2% · Antipyretics – treat discomfort, do not prevent the next seizure · Course – resolves by school age, with no effect on development · Risk factors – fever of 39.5 °C or higher, a viral illness such as roseola or influenza, recent immunization, a family history of febrile seizures or epilepsy · Timing – usually the first day of the illness, sometimes before the viral symptoms appear · Brain imaging – focal neurologic signs · EEG – recurrent unprovoked seizures, not a simple febrile seizure · Admission – not back to neurologic baseline · Electrolytes and glucose – vomiting or diarrhea, since hypoglycemia and hyponatremia can provoke a seizure · Lumbar puncture – also at 6 to 12 months with incomplete pneumococcal or Hib immunization, or when already on antibiotics
Pearls Fever with seizure under 6 months, or with a full fontanelle or prolonged drowsiness, needs a lumbar puncture. An open fontanelle needs no CT. · The febrile-seizure diagnosis has an age gate on both ends, 6 months and 5 years. It is the fastest disqualifier, so check it before anything else. · An open fontanelle is a pop-off valve, so infants tolerate rising intracranial pressure that would herniate an older child. The CT-before-tap rule therefore generally does not apply to them. · The same finding can be both the indication and the apparent contraindication. Then ask what the rule is protecting against, and whether that risk exists in this patient. · Infants may lack neck signs; read the fontanelle, the tone, the suck and the cry instead. A supple neck excludes nothing under 12 months. · A postictal period beyond 10 minutes is altered mental status, not a long febrile seizure, and it indicates a tap on its own. · With petechiae and hypotension, reverse the order: antibiotics first, tap after. A sterilized Gram stain is an acceptable price.
Pairs with Part II Fever and Sepsis in the Newborn covers the workup when there is no seizure, up to the decision to tap. This brief covers what a seizure adds to that decision. Part I Bacterial Meningitis covers the cerebrospinal fluid grid that interprets the fluid once it is obtained. Ask: is this child inside the age window, and is any sign of intracranial infection present?
Transferable rule For a benign diagnosis defined by an age range, check the age before weighing the findings, because age disqualifies it first. When a rule and a finding point in opposite directions, ask what the rule was built to prevent. If the anatomy has already prevented it, the rule does not apply.
True-fact-wrong-slotNeuroimaging: The rule exists to prevent herniation, and an open fontanelle decompresses the pressure, so the risk it guards against is not present and CT is generally unnecessary
Mirror twinReassurance and discharge: Requires age 6 months to 5 years; at 10 weeks this was never a febrile seizure, and the postictal drowsiness and full fontanelle each independently disqualify it
Salient decoyElectroencephalography: EEG may be considered for seizures that are prolonged, recurrent or focal, and this was single, generalized and four minutes
True-fact-wrong-slotIntravenous lorazepam: Given for generalized convulsions lasting over 5 minutes, and she stopped at four and is no longer seizing

Cerebral Palsy

early signs · the magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) pattern names the cause · periventricular leukomalacia · stroke, asphyxia, infection · spinal mimicsWhat does the MRI actually describe, and are the findings unilateral or global?

Source vignette Pt – 7 mo, born at 31 weeks, left-sided spasticity · Imaging – MRI shows white matter injury beside the right lateral ventricle · Q – the most likely cause; options spanned ischemic injury of the periventricular white matter of prematurity, transplacental Toxoplasma infection and inherited thrombophilia with perinatal stroke
The decision point

White matter injury adjacent to the lateral ventricle is periventricular leukomalacia. It is ischemia and necrosis in the poorly perfused zone beside the ventricles, and the signature injury of prematurity. The examination independently confirms a unilateral injury. Increased tone, 3+ reflexes and ankle clonus on the left only, with a right-sided lesion, is spastic hemiplegia. A congenital infection produces global deficits, not one-sided spasticity.

Defining criteria Cerebral palsy – nonprogressive motor dysfunction caused by a neurologic injury; the etiology is often multifactorial and may never be identified · Periventricular leukomalacia – ischemia and necrosis of the poorly perfused white matter adjacent to the lateral ventricles, seen as white matter injury on MRI; premature infants are at greatest risk, and their friable germinal matrix vessels also predispose to intraventricular hemorrhage · Early signs that should raise suspicion – motor delay (not rolling by 4 months corrected), early hand preference before age 1, persistent neonatal reflexes (tonic neck beyond 6 months), abnormal tone · The tone evolution – infants may be hypotonic initially, with spasticity developing over time, accompanied by hyperreflexia and often clonus
Pertinent positives & negatives White matter injury adjacent to the lateral ventricle – periventricular leukomalacia, which points to prematurity; each other cause has a different imaging signature · Born at 31 weeks – prematurity is a significant risk factor for cerebral palsy · Left-sided findings with a right-sided lesion – spastic hemiplegia matching a unilateral injury; intrauterine infection produces global, not one-sided, deficits · Increased tone, 3+ reflexes, sustained clonus – upper motor neuron; excludes spinal dysraphism, where lower-extremity tone and reflexes are decreased · Early hand preference at 7 months – abnormal before age 1, and one of the earliest signs · Not rolling over – motor delay, judged against corrected age in a 31-weeker · Head circumference at the 50th percentile – no microcephaly, which argues further against congenital infection · Babinski present bilaterally – normal up to 24 months only in an otherwise normal examination; the abnormal sign is the asymmetry of tone and reflexes · Veterinary office, inconsistent prenatal care – suggest toxoplasmosis, but the MRI pattern refutes it
Cerebral palsy: the MRI pattern names the cause
EtiologyIllness scriptThe National Board of Medical Examiners (NBME) tell: imagingExcluded here by
Prematurity / low birth weightIschemia in the watershed white matter beside the ventricles; friable germinal matrix vesselsPeriventricular leukomalacia; intraventricular hemorrhage(the answer)
Hypoxic-ischemic injuryPerinatal asphyxia in a term infant; low Apgars, encephalopathy, seizuresWatershed injury; basal ganglia and thalamic lesionsBorn preterm; no depressed Apgars or neonatal encephalopathy described
Perinatal stroke (± inherited thrombophilia)Arterial infarct around the time of birth; hemiplegia emerging in infancyInfarct in a vascular distribution, most often the middle cerebral arteryThe lesion is periventricular white matter, not a territory
Intrauterine infectionCytomegalovirus (CMV), toxoplasmosis; transplacental transmissionIntracranial calcifications; microcephaly; global deficitsPeriventricular white matter injury, normocephaly, unilateral findings
Neural tube defect (folate deficiency)Spinal dysraphismA spinal lesion, and the examination is lower motor neuron: decreased lower-extremity tone and reflexesHypertonia with hyperreflexia and clonus
Magnesium sulfate exposureGiven to the mother for preterm laborTransient neonatal hypotonia onlyFindings at 7 months, and they are hypertonic
Management, in one line Cerebral palsy is managed supportively and lifelong. Care includes early intervention and physical therapy, tone management, and surveillance of hips, feeding and growth, and seizures, with vision and hearing evaluation. No treatment reverses the static injury itself.
Decision spine Upper or lower motor neuron? – Increased tone, 3+ reflexes, clonus → upper · Unilateral or global? – Left side only → a single-sided lesion, so global insults are excluded · What does the MRI actually say? – Periventricular white matter → leukomalacia · What produces that pattern? – Prematurity; she was born at 31 weeks · Does any exposure in the history produce it? – No: infection calcifies, thrombophilia infarcts a territory, magnesium is transient, folate affects the spine
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Developmental exam at corrected ageFirstAsymmetric tone, early hand preference, motor delaySuspected cerebral palsy: brain MRI and early intervention
Brain MRICauseThe lesion pattern names the insultPeriventricular white matter: prematurity; a territory: stroke; calcifications: infection
Thrombophilia and stroke risk evaluationBy branchArterial infarct on MRIPerinatal stroke
Spinal MRIBy branchLow leg tone and absent reflexes, sacral dimpleClosed spinal dysraphism, not cerebral palsy
Metabolic and genetic evaluationBy branchLoss of milestones, or a normal MRIProgressive or genetic disorder; reopen the workup
Serum uric acidBy branchHigh, in a boy with new dystonia and self-injuryLesch-Nyhan syndrome, a hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT) deficiency, not cerebral palsy
None: clinical diagnosisConfirmsNonprogressive motor deficit on serial examsCerebral palsy; MRI supports it and finds the cause
TORCH (toxoplasmosis, other agents, rubella, cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex) titers for an exposure storySkipMRI shows no calcificationsThe imaging pattern, not the exposure, names the cause
Scenario bank
  1. 7 mo born at 31 weeks with left-sided spasticity and MRI showing white matter injury beside the right lateral ventricle → Ischemic injury of the periventricular white matter of prematurity → Periventricular leukomalacia
  2. Term infant with Apgars 2 and 4, neonatal encephalopathy and seizures; MRI shows watershed and basal ganglia lesions → Hypoxic-ischemic injury → The term-infant pattern
  3. 4 mo term infant with new left arm weakness; MRI shows infarct in the right middle cerebral artery territory → Evaluate for perinatal stroke risk factors including thrombophilia → A vascular distribution, not leukomalacia
  4. Newborn with microcephaly, periventricular calcifications, sensorineural hearing loss and petechiae → Congenital cytomegalovirus infection → Calcifications rather than white matter injury
  5. 7 mo infant with early hand preference and asymmetric tone, growing normally → Refer for brain MRI and early intervention therapy → Suspected cerebral palsy
  6. 3 yo with spastic diplegia, toe-walking and tight hamstrings, ambulating with difficulty → Physical therapy with orthoses and focal tone management → The commonest cerebral palsy subtype
  7. 7 mo infant born at 31 weeks who is not yet rolling; parents ask whether she is delayed → Assess milestones against her corrected age of about 5 months → Correct the age before judging delay
  8. 6 mo infant with decreased lower-extremity tone, absent reflexes and a sacral dimple → Spinal imaging → Closed spinal dysraphism
  9. 4 yo with known cerebral palsy who has lost independent ambulation over 6 months → Attributing the regression to the cerebral palsy → Cerebral palsy is nonprogressive
  10. 5 yo with spastic quadriplegic cerebral palsy at a routine health maintenance visit → Hip surveillance imaging with feeding, growth, vision, hearing and seizure review → The comorbidities of a static injury
  11. 2 yo M, term, hypotonic at 4 months and sitting only at 10 months; over the past 3 months has developed spasticity and dystonia with involuntary hand and foot movements, and for the past month bites his fingers and hands, pinches himself and bangs his limbs; family history unremarkable; nonverbal; hypertonia, hyperreflexia and bilateral extensor plantar responses; new and healing abrasions on the fingers and hands → Lesch-Nyhan syndrome → HGPRT deficiency; check serum uric acid
  12. 2 yo F who babbled, reached for toys and said a few words by 12 months, then over 6 months stopped speaking and using her hands purposefully; now makes constant hand-wringing movements; head growth has slowed from the 50th to the 10th percentile → Rett syndrome → MECP2 testing; regression is not consistent with cerebral palsy
Decoy note The veterinary office evokes cat litter, and the inconsistent prenatal care reinforces it, but the MRI refutes it. Of the three maternal drugs named, the antenatal corticosteroids actually lowered this infant's risk rather than raising it. The asymmetry of tone and reflexes is the abnormal sign.
Pearls White matter injury beside the lateral ventricle is periventricular leukomalacia, and prematurity is what causes it. · The imaging pattern maps to the insult: periventricular white matter → prematurity · watershed or basal ganglia → hypoxic-ischemic injury · a vascular territory → perinatal stroke · calcifications → congenital infection. · Distribution defines the subtype: both legs is spastic diplegia, the commonest; one side is spastic hemiplegia, which should match a unilateral lesion. · Hand preference before age 1 is abnormal, and it is often the earliest sign a parent reports. · Cerebral palsy is nonprogressive; losing an acquired milestone is not consistent with cerebral palsy and reopens the workup. · Infants with cerebral palsy may begin hypotonic and become spastic later, so normal early tone never excludes it. · Magnesium sulfate given before anticipated early preterm birth is neuroprotective and reduces cerebral palsy risk in surviving infants.
When it is not cerebral palsy Lesch-Nyhan syndrome – a boy who is hypotonic and delayed in infancy, then by about age 3 develops new dystonia, spasticity and hyperreflexia and self-mutilation (biting fingers and hands, banging limbs); X-linked recessive HGPRT deficiency (hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase) with high uric acid, and gouty arthritis and obstructive nephropathy later if untreated · Rett syndrome – a girl with normal early development who regresses after about 6 months, losing speech and purposeful hand use, with hand wringing · Autism spectrum disorder – social and language deficits, sometimes self-injury, but no spasticity, dystonia or pyramidal signs · Progression – cerebral palsy is nonprogressive, so new movement signs or self-injury after a hypotonic infancy mean a progressive or metabolic disease
Pairs with Part II Follow-Up of the Preterm Infant covers periventricular leukomalacia and intraventricular hemorrhage as prematurity outcomes, and the corrected-age arithmetic this brief uses. Part II Congenital Infections (TORCH) covers the calcification pattern and the global-deficit picture, which is where toxoplasmosis belongs. Part II Spinal Dysraphism covers the upper-versus-lower motor neuron examination that separates a brain lesion from a spinal one. Part I Tics and Tic Disorders covers Tourette syndrome, and Part I Developmental Milestones and Normal Growth covers the regression red flags. Ask: what does the imaging actually describe, and are the deficits one-sided or global? Part I Hypotonia in an Infant covers the floppy infant before any spasticity appears: is the problem in the brain or the motor unit? Part II Imprinting Disorders: Angelman and Prader-Willi separates Rett syndrome from Angelman syndrome. Ask: did the child lose skills, or never gain them?
Transferable rule An exposure in the history suggests a cause; only a described imaging pattern decides it. When a stem gives both, read the imaging first.
Salient decoyTransplacental Toxoplasma gondii: Congenital infection produces intracranial calcifications and global deficits; this MRI describes periventricular white matter and the findings are strictly one-sided, in a normocephalic infant
True-fact-wrong-slotLack of maternal folic acid: Folate deficiency causes neural tube defects, in which lower-extremity tone and reflexes are decreased, the opposite of this examination
Unchecked attributeMaternal magnesium sulfate: It causes transient hypotonia in the immediate newborn period, not lasting spasticity at 7 months
Class-vs-memberInherited thrombophilia: Stroke shows an infarct in a vascular distribution, usually the middle cerebral artery, not periventricular leukomalacia

edits.html:
Sinusitis and Its Complications

double worsening · orbital and intracranial flags · preseptal vs orbital · image before lumbar punctureAre there orbital or intracranial flags, even with a nonfocal neurologic exam?

Source vignette Pt – child with acute bacterial rhinosinusitis in a double-worsening pattern, now with focal headache, early-morning vomiting and drowsiness; neurologic examination nonfocal · Q – the most appropriate next step; options spanned oral antibiotics, lumbar puncture and urgent neuroimaging
The decision point

A double worsening course indicates acute bacterial rhinosinusitis. Focal headache, early-morning vomiting and drowsiness are intracranial extension flags. Vomiting is worst in the early morning because ICP (intracranial pressure) rises in recumbency. These flags call for urgent imaging rather than oral antibiotics.

"Neurologic examination is nonfocal" does not exclude a brain abscess; frontal lobe abscesses are neurologically silent until late. When raised ICP is suspected, image before LP (lumbar puncture).

Sinusitis complications – features → next step
ComplicationFeaturesNext step
Preseptal (periorbital) cellulitisEyelid swelling; normal EOM, normal vision, no proptosis; often from a skin break such as an insect bite, eczema or traumaOral antibiotics
Orbital (postseptal) cellulitisProptosis, pain with EOM, ophthalmoplegia, ↓ acuity; usual source is ethmoid or maxillary sinusitis (cheek tenderness), less often a maxillary dental infection or orbital traumaCT orbits and sinuses + IV antibiotics; surgical drainage for an abscess
Pott puffy tumorFrontal bone osteomyelitis with subperiosteal abscess – doughy forehead swellingCT/MRI + IV antibiotics + surgery
Brain abscess EmergencyFocal headache, early-morning vomiting, drowsiness, ± focal deficitCT/MRI → ring-enhancing lesion; IV antibiotics + drainage
MeningitisDiffuse headache, nuchal rigidity, photophobiaImage first if ICP signs, then LP
Cavernous sinus thrombosisCN III, IV, V1–V2, VI palsies, proptosis, spreads bilaterallyMRI/MRV + IV antibiotics
Where orbital cellulitis comes from Sinusitis – the most common source; ethmoid or maxillary, spreading contiguously into the orbit (streptococci, S aureus); cheek tenderness points to the maxillary sinus · Dental infection – only maxillary (upper) teeth sit near the sinus and orbit; a mandibular abscess, especially on the opposite side, does not explain it · Skin break (eczema, insect bite, trauma) – causes preseptal cellulitis, anterior to the orbital septum, without proptosis, vision change or painful eye movements · Otitis media – spreads to the mastoid or meninges, not the orbit
Signs of raised ICP & abscess essentials Early-morning headache and vomiting (recumbent CO₂ retention → cerebral vasodilation) · papilledema · altered mental status · late, the Cushing triad. Contiguous sinus spread means Streptococcus anginosus/milleri group and anaerobes; CT with contrast shows a ring-enhancing lesion, and MRI with restricted diffusion on DWI separates abscess from tumor. Treat with vancomycin + ceftriaxone + metronidazole plus drainage. Ring-enhancing differential: abscess, glioblastoma, metastasis, toxoplasmosis, tuberculoma, lymphoma.
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Clinical course and neurologic historyFirstDouble worsening with no red flagsUncomplicated sinusitis: oral antibiotics, no imaging
Eye exam: movements, acuity, proptosisBy branchPain with eye movement or proptosisOrbital cellulitis: CT of the orbits and sinuses with contrast, which shows the source sinus and any abscess to drain
CT or MRI of the head with contrastNextRing-enhancing lesionBrain abscess; order for morning vomiting or drowsiness, even with a nonfocal exam
MRI with diffusion-weighted imagingSupportsRestricted diffusion in the lesionAbscess rather than tumor
MRI with MR venographyBy branchCavernous sinus thrombosisCranial nerve palsies with proptosis, becoming bilateral
Drainage with Gram stain and cultureConfirmsStreptococcus anginosus group or anaerobesNames the organism; drainage is also treatment
Lumbar puncture before imagingSkipRisk of herniation with raised pressureImage first; LP without CT only when no pressure signs
Scenario bank
  1. Eyelid swelling but normal EOM and vision → Preseptal cellulitis → oral antibiotics
  2. Proptosis and painful eye movement → Orbital cellulitis → CT orbits + IV antibiotics
  3. Doughy swelling over the forehead → Pott puffy tumor → imaging + IV antibiotics + drainage
  4. CN VI palsy with proptosis becoming bilateral → Cavernous sinus thrombosis → MRV
  5. Fever + nuchal rigidity with no ICP signs → Lumbar puncture without prior CT
  6. A child has rhinosinusitis with a double-worsening course, focal headache, and 12 days of symptoms. The neurologic examination is nonfocal, and there is no vomiting or drowsiness. → Uncomplicated acute bacterial rhinosinusitis → amoxicillin-clavulanate
  7. Ring-enhancing lesions in an HIV patient with CD4 <100 → Toxoplasmosis or CNS lymphoma → multiple basal ganglia lesions favor toxoplasmosis
  8. Child with morning headache and vomiting plus ataxia, no infection → Posterior fossa tumor → same ICP syndrome, non-infectious cause
  9. Adult with a ring-enhancing lesion and recent dental infection → Brain abscess by contiguous spread
  10. 5 yo M, right eye pain since morning with blurred vision for several hours; history of frequent ear infections, recurrent sinusitis, many dental caries, atopic dermatitis and hives after mosquito bites; T 39.4, HR 120; right eye acuity 20/70 with proptosis, conjunctival injection, periorbital swelling and redness, and pain with limited adduction; normal fundus; right cheek tenderness; a large foul-smelling cavity in the left lower second molar → Bacterial sinusitis → Orbital cellulitis from contiguous ethmoid or maxillary spread
  11. 6 yo with a week of purulent rhinorrhea, now fever, proptosis, painful and limited eye movements, and falling visual acuity despite 2 days of IV antibiotics; CT shows ethmoid sinusitis with a large subperiosteal orbital abscess → Surgical drainage with continued IV antibiotics → Orbital abscess
  12. 7 yo with a week of nasal congestion and cough, now fever, a swollen red upper eyelid, proptosis and pain with eye movement; normal mental status and no neck stiffness → CT of the orbits and sinuses with contrast → Orbital cellulitis; start IV antibiotics
Pairs with Part II Eyelid Lumps and Swelling in a Child covers the hordeolum and dacryocystitis that can spread into preseptal cellulitis. Ask: is the swelling a focal lump or the whole lid?
Transferable rule A normal neurologic exam is a low-sensitivity test for intracranial pathology. When the symptom pattern is positional and progressive (morning headache, morning vomiting, declining alertness), symptoms of raised ICP (intracranial pressure) outweigh a reassuring exam.
Test-overrides-findingsSequencing trap
