edits.html:
Scaly Rashes

psoriasis vs other scaly plaques · extensor vs flexural · the nails · exam findings outweigh the exposure historyWhere are the plaques, are the nails involved, and does the exam agree with the history?

The decision point

Nail dystrophy together with extensor-surface scaly plaques indicates psoriasis. An extensor distribution indicates psoriasis; a flexural distribution indicates eczema. An occupational "wet work" history does not override these findings. Psoriasis does show the Koebner phenomenon, so friction can localize it.

Scaly plaques – the differential
DiagnosisDistributionThe tellNails?
PsoriasisExtensor, scalp, trunkSalmon plaques, silvery scale, Auspitz sign, KoebnerYes – pitting, onycholysis
Atopic dermatitisFlexuralPruritus first, rash second; lichenification; atopy triadNo
Nummular eczemaExtremitiesCoin-shaped, intensely pruriticNo
Tinea corporisAnywhereAnnular with central clearing; KOH shows hyphaeSeparate (onychomycosis)
Seborrheic dermatitisScalp, nasolabial, browsGreasy yellow scale; MalasseziaNo
Pityriasis roseaTrunkHerald patch → Christmas-tree patternNo
Lichen planusWrists, ankles, mucosa6 Ps: pruritic purple polygonal planar papules; Wickham striaeCan
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
KOH preparation of the scaleFirstHyphae in an annular plaque with central clearingTinea corporis; a steroid would cause tinea incognito
RPRBy branchReactive with a truncal or palm and sole eruptionSecondary syphilis, the mimic of pityriasis rosea
None: clinical diagnosisConfirmsExtensor silvery plaques with nail pittingPsoriasis; the tests only exclude tinea and syphilis
Skin biopsy, only if atypicalSupportsParakeratosis with Munro microabscessesPsoriasis when the exam is not typical
X-ray of the handsBy branchPencil-in-cup erosions at the DIP jointsPsoriatic arthritis in a patient with dactylitis
Interferon-gamma release assay or PPDNextLatent tuberculosis excludedRequired before the first dose of a TNF-alpha inhibitor
Wood lamp examinationSkipDoes not diagnose tinea corporisKOH answers the question at the bedside
Scenario bank
  1. 34 yo M with extensor-surface silvery plaques and nail pitting → Psoriasis
  2. 34 yo M with flexural lichenified pruritic patches and a history of asthma → Atopic dermatitis
  3. 34 yo M with an annular scaly patch with central clearing and an active border → Tinea corporis → KOH preparation
  4. 34 yo M with a herald patch followed by a Christmas-tree truncal eruption → Pityriasis rosea
  5. 34 yo M with purple polygonal pruritic papules and oral Wickham striae → Lichen planus
  6. 34 yo M whose plaques bleed at pinpoints when the scale is lifted → Auspitz sign
  7. 34 yo M with psoriasis, dactylitis and DIP joint involvement → Psoriatic arthritis
  8. 34 yo M with a few silvery extensor plaques on the elbows and knees and nail pitting → Topical steroid plus calcipotriene → first rung before phototherapy and systemics
  9. 34 yo M with a single annular scaly trunk plaque with central clearing and an active border → KOH preparation → if tinea, a steroid causes tinea incognito
  10. 34 yo M with severe psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis about to start a TNF-alpha inhibitor → Test for latent tuberculosis → TNF blockade can reactivate tuberculosis
  11. 34 yo M with extensive plaque psoriasis who was started on oral prednisone for an asthma flare → Abrupt discontinuation of prednisone → abrupt steroid withdrawal can trigger a pustular flare
Psoriasis facts they attach Pathology: parakeratosis, acanthosis, Munro microabscesses, thinned suprapapillary plates (→ Auspitz) · immunology: Th17 / IL-17 / IL-23 (T helper 17 cell / interleukin 17 / interleukin 23) axis · drugs: secukinumab (IL-17), ustekinumab (IL-12/23), TNF-α (tumor necrosis factor alpha) inhibitors after screening for latent TB (tuberculosis) · associations: psoriatic arthritis with DIP (distal interphalangeal) joints, "pencil-in-cup," dactylitis; metabolic syndrome and CV (cardiovascular) risk · ladder: topical steroids + calcipotriene first, then narrowband UVB (ultraviolet B), then systemics · abrupt steroid withdrawal can trigger a pustular flare · for tinea, order a KOH prep (potassium hydroxide preparation), never a steroid (tinea incognito).
Pairs with Part I Hair Loss in a Child is the scalp version, where follicular invasion changes the therapy from topical to oral.
Transferable rule Exposures can suggest a diagnosis, but examination findings determine it. When the history and the exam conflict, rely on the exam.
Salient decoy

edits.html:
Skin and Soft Tissue Infection

border and depth · erysipelas vs cellulitis · purulent vs nonpurulent · necrotizing fasciitis · bilateral mimicsHow sharp is the border, is there pus, and is the pain out of proportion?

The decision point

A flat border indicates cellulitis; a raised, sharply demarcated border indicates erysipelas. Superficial infection stops at a sharp edge because superficial infection is contained by tissue planes. Deeper infection fades into an indistinct edge because deeper infection diffuses through fat.

Skin & soft-tissue infections by depth
LayerInfectionThe tellOrganism
Epidermis / superficial dermis + lymphaticsErysipelasRaised, sharply demarcated, intense erythema; rapid onset, early feverS. pyogenes
Deep dermis + subcutaneous fatCellulitis (nonpurulent)Flat, poorly demarcated; indolent over days; fever laterBeta-hemolytic strep, MSSA
Same, with drainageCellulitis (purulent) / abscessPurulent drainage; furuncle → carbuncleS. aureus incl. MRSA
FasciaNecrotizing fasciitis EmergencyPain out of proportion, crepitus, hemorrhagic bullae, necrosis, anesthesia over the lesion, hourly progressionPolymicrobial (type I) or GAS ± Clostridium (type II)
The treatment fork is purulent vs. nonpurulent Nonpurulent infection: cover streptococci with cephalexin or dicloxacillin (penicillin for erysipelas). Purulent infection: incision and drainage, plus coverage of MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) with TMP-SMX (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole), doxycycline, or clindamycin. Necrotizing infection: emergent surgical exploration, which is both diagnostic and therapeutic. Never wait for imaging.
Mimics – roughly 30% of "cellulitis" is misdiagnosed
MimicThe tell
Stasis dermatitisBilateral, chronic, hemosiderin staining, afebrile – the single most common misdiagnosis
DVTSwelling without a sharply defined rash; recent surgery or immobility
Contact dermatitisItchy, geometric border, afebrile
Erythema nodosumBilateral tender nodules on anterior shins; sarcoid, IBD, strep
Erythema migransExpanding with central clearing, minimally tender
Ruptured Baker cystPopliteal fossa and posterior calf
The bilateral rule Cellulitis is nearly always unilateral. Bilateral lower-extremity erythema is stasis dermatitis until proven otherwise; treat with compression, not antibiotics.
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
None: clinical diagnosisConfirmsUnilateral warm erythema with a flat, indistinct borderCellulitis; tests exclude abscess, DVT and deeper infection
Bedside ultrasoundBy branchFluid collection under the erythemaAbscess: incision and drainage plus MRSA coverage
Culture of drained pusBy branchS. aureus, with susceptibilitiesGuides antibiotic choice in purulent infection
Duplex ultrasound of the legBy branchNoncompressible veinDVT, the swollen-leg mimic
Blood culturesBy branchUsually negative in uncomplicated cellulitisDraw only with systemic toxicity, immunosuppression, or bite or water exposure
Emergent surgical explorationConfirmsNecrotic fascia, dishwater fluid, little bleedingNecrotizing fasciitis; debride in the same operation
CT or MRI before surgerySkipMay show gas but delays the operationPain out of proportion or crepitus goes straight to the OR
Scenario bank
  1. Raised, sharply demarcated, intensely erythematous, rapid onset with early fever → Erysipelas → penicillin
  2. Purulent drainage or a fluctuant abscess → Incision and drainage plus MRSA coverage
  3. Pain out of proportion, crepitus, hemorrhagic bullae, hourly progression → Necrotizing fasciitis → emergent surgical exploration
  4. Bilateral, chronic, hemosiderin staining, afebrile → Stasis dermatitis → compression
  5. Saltwater exposure + cirrhosis + hemorrhagic bullae → Vibrio vulnificus → doxycycline + ceftriaxone (high mortality)
  6. Cat bite with cellulitis within 24 hours → Pasteurella multocida → amoxicillin-clavulanate
  7. Dog bite in an asplenic or cirrhotic patient → Capnocytophaga canimorsus → fulminant sepsis risk
  8. Clenched-fist human bite → Eikenella corrodens
  9. Rose gardener with nodules ascending the lymphatics → Sporothrix schenckii → itraconazole
  10. Aquarium exposure with nodular lesions → Mycobacterium marinum
  11. Recurrent cellulitis in the same leg → Find and treat the portal of entry → usually tinea pedis with toe-web maceration, or lymphedema
Transferable rule Terms that describe morphology usually reflect an underlying anatomic fact. A "sharply demarcated" border shows how deep the process is.

edits.html:
Hair Loss in a Child

the scalp surface and the nodes identify the cause · tinea capitis needs oral therapy · trichotillomania and alopecia areataIs the patch scaly, and are the draining nodes enlarged?

Source vignette Pt – 8 yo, enlarging scaly bald patch with pruritus, tender occipital and postauricular nodes · Q – the most likely diagnosis; options spanned tinea capitis, trichotillomania and alopecia areata
The decision point

Two examination findings, not the history, identify the cause. The patch has overlying scale, which means an inflammatory or infectious process in the skin rather than hair that is simply being pulled or shed. The occipital and posterior auricular nodes are enlarged and tender, which is regional lymphadenopathy draining an infected scalp. Together these findings indicate tinea capitis. Unlike tinea of the body, this dermatophyte invades the hair follicle and shaft. As a result, the hair breaks and the patch expands centrifugally over weeks. The recent school change and the anxiety suggest trichotillomania, but neither scale nor tender nodes occurs in trichotillomania.

Defining criteria Tinea capitis – scaly erythematous patch with hair loss and localized lymphadenopathy, with or without black dots (broken hairs at the follicle) and with or without a tender boggy kerion · Why systemic therapy is required – the organism invades the follicle and shaft, which topical agents penetrate poorly, so oral griseofulvin or terbinafine is needed · Confirmation – the diagnosis is clinical; Potassium hydroxide (KOH) examination of proximal hair shafts or fungal culture confirms it
Pertinent positives & negatives Scale over an enlarging bald patch – an inflammatory or infectious scalp process; scale is what separates infection from every non-inflammatory alopecia · Tender occipital and posterior auricular lymphadenopathy – the nodes that drain the scalp; expected in tinea capitis and absent in traction alopecia and trichotillomania · Frequent scratching – pruritus, an inflammatory feature that argues against a purely mechanical cause · Recent school change with anxiety – a psychosocial cue for hair-pulling, which the scale and the nodes exclude · Age 8, previously healthy – the peak age; tinea capitis is predominantly a disease of children and the immunocompromised
Patchy hair loss in a child: the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Tinea capitisTrichophyton or Microsporum acquired from a contact or a fomite (shared comb, hat, pillowcase); invades follicle and shaftScaly patch with hair loss plus regional lymphadenopathy; black dots; kerion(the answer)
Alopecia areataAutoimmune, non-scarring; abrupt, sharply circumscribedRound, smooth patch completely devoid of hair, scale-free, no lymphadenopathy; exclamation-point hairs; nail pittingThe patch is scaly and the nodes are enlarged
TrichotillomaniaRecurrent pulling the patient cannot stop; most common in children and adolescent girls; loss hidden under hats or wigs; swallowed hair can form a trichobezoarIrregular patch with hairs of varying lengths, often sparse eyebrows or eyelashes; no scale, no erythema, nonscarringScale and tender lymphadenopathy
Traction alopeciaProlonged pulling from bands or braidsGeometric loss along the traction sites, most often frontal and temporal or along braids; no scale, no nodes; never thins the eyebrowsNo hairstyle history; scale and nodes present
Telogen effluviumSynchronized shedding a few months after a stressor such as illness, surgery or childbirthDiffuse thinning over the whole scalp, not a patchThe loss is a single patch with scale and nodes
Seborrheic dermatitisScalp scaling, i.e. dandruff, with pruritusScale without hair lossIt cannot explain the alopecia or the nodes
Discoid lupus erythematosusCutaneous lupus; scarring, well-demarcated inflammatory plaquesAdult women, with face and neck lesions, and the alopecia scarsAge 8 and no facial or neck involvement
Trichotillomania: the tells Irregular patch, hairs of different lengths – hairs pulled and regrowing at different times; alopecia areata leaves a round patch that is completely bald · Sparse eyebrows or eyelashes – pulling reaches other sites; traction and tinea stay on the scalp · Hats or wigs – used to hide the loss; even when another reason for them is given, traction does not explain the eyebrows or a parietal patch · No scale, no erythema, no scarring – excludes tinea capitis and discoid lupus · Treatment – cognitive behavioral therapy with habit reversal · Complication – swallowing the hair (trichophagia) can form a gastric trichobezoar
Management, in one line Treatment requires oral griseofulvin or terbinafine, because topical antifungals do not reach the organism inside the hair follicle.
Decision spine Is there scale on the patch? – Yes → an inflammatory or infectious cause, not a pulling one · Are the draining nodes enlarged? – Yes → infection, which excludes trichotillomania and traction alopecia · Are the remaining hairs broken? – Black dots are shafts snapped at the follicle; the fungus is inside the hair · Any traction history or geometric pattern? – No · Confirm and treat – KOH of the proximal shafts; oral, never topical alone
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Scalp exam with a check of the draining nodesFirstScale plus tender occipital and postauricular nodesInfection: tinea capitis; a smooth patch without nodes is not
Close look at the remaining hairsBy branchBroken hairs of varying lengths in an irregular patch, no scale; eyebrows or lashes sparseTrichotillomania; exclamation-point hairs point to alopecia areata
KOH of plucked proximal hair shaftsConfirmsSpores within or around the hair shaftTinea capitis: start oral griseofulvin or terbinafine
Fungal culture of hairs or scaleConfirmsTrichophyton or Microsporum growsTinea capitis; results take weeks, so do not wait to treat
Wood lampSupportsGreen fluorescence only with MicrosporumNegative with Trichophyton tonsurans, the common US cause
Serum fungal antibody titersSkipNo role in dermatophyte infectionKOH or culture of the hair confirms it
Scenario bank
  1. 8 yo with an enlarging scaly bald patch, pruritus, and tender occipital and postauricular nodes → Tinea capitis → Regional lymphadenopathy plus scale
  2. Child with clinically confirmed tinea capitis; appropriate treatment → Oral griseofulvin or terbinafine → Topicals cannot reach the follicle
  3. Child with tinea capitis; which therapy will not clear the infection → Topical antifungal shampoo used alone → Adjunctive at best
  4. 8 yo with a smooth, scale-free, sharply demarcated bald patch, no lymphadenopathy, and nail pitting → Topical or intralesional glucocorticoid → Alopecia areata
  5. 10 yo with irregular patches of broken hairs of varying lengths, no scale, no lymphadenopathy, after a recent stressor → Habit-reversal behavioral therapy → Trichotillomania
  6. 12 yo with symmetric temporal thinning along tightly pulled braids, no scale and no lymphadenopathy → Loosen the hairstyle → Traction alopecia is reversible if caught early
  7. Child on oral antifungal therapy for tinea capitis who develops a boggy tender scalp mass with pustules → Continue systemic antifungal therapy → A kerion is the same infection
  8. Child with a scaly patch of alopecia and regional lymphadenopathy → KOH examination of proximal hair shafts or fungal culture → The diagnosis is otherwise clinical
  9. Why tinea capitis requires oral therapy while tinea corporis responds to topical treatment → It invades the hair follicle and shaft → Body lesions remain in the epidermis
  10. Child newly diagnosed with tinea capitis → Examine close contacts and stop sharing combs, hats and pillowcases → Fomite transmission
  11. 15 yo F cast as the lead in a school play a month ago, wearing hats and wigs to stay in character; her mother noticed bald spots a few days ago; doing well in school, no substance use, regular menses, body mass index 22 kg/m²; a 3 x 5 cm irregular right parietal patch of hair loss bordered by hairs of uneven length, sparse eyebrows, no scale or erythema → Trichotillomania → Cognitive behavioral therapy with habit reversal
  12. 9 yo with a round, sharply bordered bald patch that appeared over 2 weeks; the scalp inside is completely smooth with no scale or erythema; a few short hairs at the margin taper toward the scalp; eyebrows normal; no lymphadenopathy → Alopecia areata → Topical or intralesional glucocorticoid
  13. 16 yo F shedding handfuls of hair in the shower for 3 weeks, 3 months after hospitalization for pneumonia; thinning is spread evenly over the whole scalp with no patches, no scale and normal eyebrows → Telogen effluvium → Reassurance; regrowth over months
  14. 15 yo F with long-standing hair pulling who also chews and swallows the hair, now with early satiety, weight loss, halitosis and a firm, mobile epigastric mass → Gastric trichobezoar → Endoscopic or surgical removal
Decoy note A new school and anxiety about teachers and friends make a complete, plausible causal story. The examination refutes it. "Frequently scratches at the area" seems to support it, since scratching sounds like a behavior. However, scratching reflects pruritus, an inflammatory symptom, and it points the other way. The patch is nontender, which is easy to misread as a general absence of tenderness. The nodes are tender, and that tenderness is the key finding.
Pearls A scaly, enlarging bald patch with tender occipital nodes in a child is tinea capitis, and it needs an oral antifungal. · Scale plus regional lymphadenopathy means infection rather than a simple alopecia; the two pulling alopecias, traction and trichotillomania, have neither. · Tinea capitis invades the follicle and shaft, so it needs an oral antifungal, the single most tested management point on the topic. · Black dots are hair shafts broken at the follicular orifice; a boggy tender mass is a kerion, which is the same infection inflamed, not a bacterial abscess to drain. · Alopecia areata causes a smooth, scale-free, sharply circumscribed patch with no lymphadenopathy, sometimes with nail pitting. · Fomites such as combs, hats and pillowcases carry it, so the household is examined rather than treated blindly. · A scaly scalp plaque that scars, in an adult woman with facial lesions, is discoid lupus rather than tinea.
Pairs with Part I Scaly Rashes covers the scaly-plaque differential of the body. It also covers the rule that a scaly annular lesion needs a KOH preparation rather than a steroid. This brief covers the scalp version, where the follicle changes the therapy. Ask: is there scale, and are the draining nodes enlarged?
Transferable rule In hair loss, the surface of the patch identifies the diagnosis. Scale with regional nodes means infection. A smooth patch means an autoimmune or traction cause. Broken hairs of unequal length mean the hair is being pulled. Examine the scalp before you accept a psychosocial explanation.
Class-vs-memberTraction alopecia: Traction produces geometric loss along the sites of pulling (temporal areas, along braids), with no scale and no lymphadenopathy
Salient decoyTrichotillomania: Hair-pulling leaves broken hairs of varying lengths in an irregular pattern, without scale or nodes
Class-vs-memberCutaneous candidiasis: Candida causes intertrigo in warm moist skinfolds; it does not scale the scalp or take hair
True-fact-wrong-slotSeborrheic dermatitis: It explains only the scale and the pruritus, not the hair loss or the nodes
True-fact-wrong-slotDiscoid lupus erythematosus: It occurs mostly in adult women, involves the face and neck, and scars

edits.html:
Scabies

a close contact with the same rash outweighs morphology · permethrin specifics · itch after treatmentDoes anyone close have the same rash, and does the drug kill the cause or only treat the itch?

Source vignette Pt – 63 yo M, itchy web-space papules; roommate has the identical rash · Q – the most appropriate treatment; options spanned permethrin, topical triamcinolone and a single dose of oral ivermectin
The decision point

A roommate with the identical itchy rash means the rash is transmissible by prolonged skin contact. That fact alone excludes contact dermatitis, drug eruption and every non-communicable itch. With the distribution and the timeline added, only scabies fits. Treat with permethrin 5%.

Stem findings & their diagnostic weight
FindingWhy it matters
Severe itchMost pruritic common dermatosis; classically worse at night
Hands/wrists → other hand → waistlineTextbook map: finger web spaces, flexor wrists, axillae, belt line, periumbilical, genitals. Spares head and neck in adults
"Spots turned into scabs"Excoriations, not vesicular crusts
Roommate moved in a few weeks agoMatches the 3–6 week incubation on first infestation – a sensitization delay, not a replication delay
Distractors Oral acyclovir: zoster is dermatomal, unilateral, painful. It does not migrate from one hand to the other hand and then to the waist, and it does not infect a roommate. Oral cephalexin: there is no crusting or spreading erythema, and impetigo causes honey-colored crust. Oral prednisone / topical triamcinolone: both treat the itch, not the mite, and steroids produce scabies incognito, a masked, worsening infestation. The pruritus is a type IV hypersensitivity to mite antigen, and suppressing the response does not affect the organism.
Treatment specifics Permethrin 5%, neck-down (whole body in infants), left on 8–14 hours, repeated in 1 week because the first application does not kill eggs · treat all household and close contacts simultaneously, symptomatic or not · wash bedding and clothing hot, or bag 72 hours · oral ivermectin (200 mcg/kg, repeat day 8) for crusted scabies, outbreaks, or adherence problems; avoid in pregnancy and under 15 kg.
Itch after treatment Post-scabetic pruritus persists 2–4 weeks after successful treatment. It is the leading reason therapy is thought to have failed. Triamcinolone and antihistamines are correct at that stage, once the mite is dead; they do not replace killing it.
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
History of contacts and a map of the lesionsFirstClose contact with the same itchy rashTransmissible: scabies, with web spaces, wrists and belt line involved
Skin scraping of a burrow in mineral oilConfirmsMites, eggs or fecesScabies; a typical story is enough to treat without it
Dermoscopy of a burrowSupportsDelta-wing sign at the end of the burrowThe mite in place
Scraping of thick hyperkeratotic crustsBy branchNumerous mitesCrusted scabies: oral ivermectin plus topical therapy, contact isolation
Culture of crusted, red lesionsBy branchS. aureus or streptococciImpetiginized scabies: permethrin plus cephalexin
Repeat workup for itch after treatmentSkipItch for 2 to 4 weeks with no new burrowsPost-scabetic pruritus: topical steroid, not re-treatment
Scenario bank
  1. 63 yo M, web-space papules, roommate with the same rash → Permethrin ×2 a week apart, treat contacts, launder linens
  2. 63 yo M, still itching 3 weeks after permethrin, no new burrows → Post-scabetic pruritus → topical steroid, not re-treatment
  3. 78 yo M in a nursing home, thick hyperkeratotic plaques, minimal itch, immunosuppressed → Crusted (Norwegian) scabies → oral ivermectin + topical, contact isolation
  4. 6 mo F, itchy vesicles on palms, soles, scalp, face → Infantile scabies → apply including the head
  5. 28 yo M, new apartment, itchy welts on exposed skin in linear clusters, no web-space lesions → Bedbugs
  6. 63 yo M with honey-colored crust and surrounding erythema → Impetiginized scabies → permethrin plus cephalexin
  7. 34 yo pregnant woman with scabies → Permethrin is safe; avoid ivermectin
  8. 63 yo M whose rash returns at 6 weeks → Contacts untreated, or the second application skipped
Transferable rule A close contact with the same condition carries more weight than morphology. It narrows the differential to transmissible causes before you interpret a single lesion. When the dominant symptom is itch, check whether a drug kills the cause or only treats the sensation.

edits.html:
Ectopic Pregnancy

transvaginal ultrasound first · discriminatory zone · serial hCG · methotrexate eligibility · unstable means surgeryWhere is the pregnancy, and is the patient stable enough to image?

The decision point

The urine test has already confirmed pregnancy. The next step is to find where the pregnancy is. Only transvaginal ultrasound can localize it. A single serum β-hCG localizes nothing.

Defining criteria Methotrexate eligibility – unruptured, hCG <5,000, <3.5 cm, no fetal cardiac activity, reliable follow-up · Unstable ectopic – hypotension, rebound, or shoulder pain → emergent laparoscopy/laparotomy
Where β-hCG actually belongs
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Urine or serum hCGFirstPositivePregnant: the question becomes where the pregnancy is
Transvaginal ultrasoundNextIntrauterine gestational sac with a yolk sacIntrauterine pregnancy: stop; heterotopic pregnancy is rare outside IVF
ConfirmsExtrauterine sac, or adnexal mass with free fluidEctopic pregnancy: methotrexate if eligible, otherwise surgery
Quantitative serum β-hCGBy branchAbove 1,500 to 2,000 with an empty uterusIndeterminate scan: presumed ectopic
Serial β-hCG every 48 hoursBy branchRise of less than 35 to 50%Abnormal pregnancy, likely ectopic; a normal one doubles, a miscarriage falls
Emergent laparoscopyConfirmsTubal pregnancy or hemoperitoneumUnstable patient: operate without waiting for imaging
Single serum β-hCG before ultrasoundSkipA number cannot localize the pregnancyTransvaginal ultrasound answers the location question
  1. Symptomatic + positive pregnancy test → Transvaginal ultrasound now
  2. Intrauterine pregnancy seen → Stop the workup → heterotopic pregnancy is rare outside IVF
  3. Adnexal mass or free fluid → Ectopic pregnancy → treat
  4. TVUS indeterminate → Check the β-hCG against the discriminatory zone → above 1,500 to 2,000 with an empty uterus is a presumed ectopic, and below it serial hCG q48h (a normal IUP doubles; ectopic rises <35–50%; miscarriage falls)
Unstable ectopic Hypotension, rebound or shoulder pain (diaphragmatic irritation from hemoperitoneum) → skip the rest of the workup and go to emergent laparoscopy/laparotomy. Image the stable patient and operate on the unstable one, the same logic as in PE (pulmonary embolism).
Pearls The biggest acquired risk factor is prior PID (pelvic inflammatory disease), through tubal scarring. Others are prior ectopic, tubal surgery, IUD (intrauterine device) in place and smoking, which impairs ciliary transport · half of ectopics have no palpable adnexal mass · methotrexate if unruptured, hCG (human chorionic gonadotropin) <5,000, <3.5 cm, no fetal cardiac activity, reliable follow-up · Rh-negative mother with any bleeding in pregnancy → RhoGAM.
Transferable rule When two tests both seem reasonable, choose the one whose result changes management. A single hCG (human chorionic gonadotropin) does not change management tonight; the ultrasound does.

edits.html:
Contraception

pregnancy test first · injection window and fertility · no-estrogen situations · emergency contraception · amenorrheaCould she be pregnant, and does anything rule out estrogen?

The decision point

When two explanations produce identical symptoms, test for the one that changes management and can't be missed. DMPA (depot medroxyprogesterone acetate) causes breast soreness, weight gain, fatigue and amenorrhea, which are indistinguishable from early pregnancy. DMPA is due every 13 weeks; her last injection was 4 months ago, so she has been uncovered.

Inserting an IUD (intrauterine device) into an established intrauterine pregnancy can disrupt it. As a rule, a pregnancy test precedes every contraception decision, every amenorrhea workup, and absolutely every IUD placement.

Defining criteria DMPA dosing window – every 13 weeks with a ~2-week grace period · Return to fertility – delayed up to 10 months · Before any contraceptive decision – a pregnancy test
DMPA facts Suppresses GnRH (gonadotropin-releasing hormone), so there is no LH (luteinizing hormone) surge and no ovulation; thickens cervical mucus · every 13 weeks with a ~2-week grace period · irregular bleeding early, then amenorrhea in ~50% at 1 year · weight gain from appetite stimulation · reversible loss of bone mineral density (boxed warning) · the unique one: delayed return to fertility up to 10 months · no estrogen, so safe in smokers ≥35, migraine with aura, VTE (venous thromboembolism) history, and immediately postpartum.
Contraception rules by situation
SituationRule
Smoker ≥35Avoid estrogen (WHO category 4) → progestin-only, IUD, implant
Migraine with auraAvoid estrogen – stroke risk
VTE history, uncontrolled HTN, SLE with antiphospholipid antibodiesAvoid estrogen
<21 days postpartum (or <42 if breastfeeding / VTE risk)Avoid estrogen; progestin-only and IUD are fine
Heavy menstrual bleedingLNG-IUD – copper makes bleeding worse
Emergency contraceptionCopper IUD most effective (up to 5 days); ulipristal > levonorgestrel, especially if BMI >30
Enzyme-inducing antiepilepticsCOC and implant efficacy drops → DMPA or IUD
Wants pregnancy soonAvoid DMPA
Secondary amenorrhea framework Defined as no menses >3 months with previously regular cycles (or >6 months if previously irregular). Pregnancy test first, then TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone), prolactin, FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone). FSH high → primary ovarian insufficiency · FSH low/normal → hypothalamic or pituitary · prolactin high → prolactinoma, dopamine blockers, or hypothyroidism · no withdrawal bleed even to estrogen + progesterone after a D&C (dilation and curettage) → Asherman syndrome.
Scenario bank
  1. Negative pregnancy test → Offer any method she prefers → copper IUD, combined pill or implant
  2. Positive test → Prenatal care; DMPA exposure is not teratogenic
  3. A patient requesting contraception wants to conceive within a year. → DMPA → fertility return takes up to 10 months
  4. 38-year-old smoker requesting contraception → A progestin-only method or an IUD → not an estrogen-containing method
  5. Migraine with aura → No estrogen-containing method
  6. Needs emergency contraception 4 days after unprotected sex → Copper IUD → or ulipristal
  7. On DMPA 3 years, concerned about bone density → Counsel that loss is reversible, ensure calcium and vitamin D, consider alternatives
  8. Woman with 4 months of amenorrhea and a negative pregnancy test → TSH, prolactin, FSH
  9. Amenorrhea after a D&C → Asherman syndrome
  10. Exclusively breastfeeding, <6 months postpartum, amenorrheic → Lactational amenorrhea method requires all three; formula-feeding voids it
Transferable rule When a drug-effect explanation is plausible for symptoms that overlap a can't-miss diagnosis, the drug effect is a diagnosis of exclusion. This applies especially when the dates show the drug was not actually working.

edits.html:
Teratogenic Exposures

the teratogen from the malformation pattern · critical periods · phenytoin vs alcohol · anticoagulation in pregnancyWhich single malformation belongs to only one agent, and when in pregnancy was the exposure?

Source vignette Pt – newborn male, growth restricted at 2.5 kg at 38 weeks, mother 29 with no prenatal care, forceps delivery for fetal heart rate abnormalities, Apgars 6 and 8 · Exam – microcephaly, a wide anterior fontanelle, cleft palate, and hypoplasia of the distal phalanges · Q – which maternal history would be found; options spanned alcohol use, cocaine use, lisinopril use, phenytoin use and untreated syphilis
The decision point

Cleft palate and distal phalangeal hypoplasia are the two findings that alcohol does not cause. Together they are fetal hydantoin syndrome, from in utero exposure to a folate-antagonising antiepileptic, classically phenytoin. The drug crosses the placenta and produces low fetal folate with high oxidative metabolites. The wide anterior fontanelle and microcephaly complete the pattern. Fetal alcohol syndrome shares the microcephaly and the midface hypoplasia but has no association with clefting. Its signature is a smooth philtrum with a thin vermilion border and short palpebral fissures, none of which is described in this newborn.

Defining criteria Critical periods – 0–2 weeks all-or-none (death or no effect); 3–8 weeks organogenesis, the structural-malformation window; beyond 8 weeks growth restriction, CNS and functional deficits rather than structural defects · Fetal hydantoin syndrome – microcephaly, wide anterior fontanelle, cleft lip and palate, distal digit and nail hypoplasia, cardiac defects, neural tube defects · Fetal alcohol syndrome – smooth philtrum, thin vermilion border, short palpebral fissures, midface hypoplasia, microcephaly, and no clefting · Antiepileptic management – switch to a lower-risk agent such as levetiracetam 6 months before conception, 4 mg folic acid from 3 months before conception, and make no changes after conception; screen with alpha-fetoprotein and anatomy ultrasonography
Teratogenic medications – drug to signaturethe malformation that belongs to only one agent
DrugSignature defect
PhenytoinDistal digit and nail hypoplasia, cleft lip/palate, wide fontanelle, microcephaly, cardiac, neural tube defects
ValproateNeural tube defects – the highest-risk antiepileptic
CarbamazepineNeural tube defects, less than valproate
TopiramateOral clefts, growth restriction, neurodevelopmental effects
PhenobarbitalCardiac, orofacial and urogenital malformations
IsotretinoinMicrotia and small ears, microcephaly, cleft palate, cardiac, thymic hypoplasia, hydrocephalus
MethotrexateLimb and craniofacial defects, cranial ossification defects, neural tube defects, abortion
ACE inhibitors / ARBsRenal dysgenesis → oligohydramnios → Potter sequence, growth restriction
WarfarinNasal hypoplasia and stippled epiphyses, limb hypoplasia; fetal haemorrhage later
LithiumEbstein anomaly
MethimazoleAplasia cutis, oesophageal atresia, facial anomalies
TetracyclinesTooth discolouration, inhibited long-bone growth
FluoroquinolonesCartilage and bone toxicity
DiethylstilbestrolClear cell adenocarcinoma of vagina and cervix, uterine malformation
ThalidomidePhocomelia
Pertinent positives & negatives Cleft palate – present in hydantoin and absent in fetal alcohol syndrome; the single most discriminating finding in this newborn · Hypoplasia of the distal phalanges – near-specific for antiepileptic exposure · Wide anterior fontanelle – part of the hydantoin pattern, and easily overlooked · Symmetric growth restriction with microcephaly – shared by alcohol, phenytoin, isotretinoin and cocaine, so it discriminates nothing · No smooth philtrum, thin vermilion border or short palpebral fissures – the fetal alcohol facial triad is absent · No prenatal care – explains why a maternal medication history was never taken · No snuffles, hepatomegaly or maculopapular rash – congenital syphilis is excluded on its own features
Decision spine Is there a structural malformation? – Yes → exposure fell in the 3–8 week window · List the findings that only one agent causes. – Cleft palate and distal digit hypoplasia · Which agent causes both? – Phenytoin · Check the nearest mimic. – Alcohol shares the microcephaly but never the cleft · Is there an alternative explanation for the growth restriction? – It is nonspecific and belongs to every option · What would have prevented it? – Pre-conception switch plus 4 mg folate
Scenario bank
  1. Newborn male, growth restricted at 38 weeks to a mother with no prenatal care, with microcephaly, a wide anterior fontanelle, cleft palate and hypoplasia of the distal phalanges → Maternal phenytoin use → fetal hydantoin syndrome
  2. Child with a smooth philtrum, thin vermilion border, short palpebral fissures and midface hypoplasia with microcephaly, and no cleft lip or palate → Fetal alcohol syndrome → alcohol is not associated with clefting
  3. Newborn with severe oligohydramnios, pulmonary hypoplasia, flat facies and positional limb deformities; the mother took an antihypertensive throughout pregnancy → Maternal ACE inhibitor use → renal dysgenesis causing Potter sequence
  4. Newborn with Ebstein anomaly on echocardiography whose mother is treated for bipolar disorder → Maternal lithium use → apical displacement of the tricuspid valve
  5. Newborn with nasal hypoplasia and stippled epiphyses on radiograph; the mother has a mechanical mitral valve → Maternal warfarin use in the first trimester → low molecular weight heparin should have been substituted
  6. 26 yo on valproate for epilepsy who hopes to conceive in about a year → Switch to levetiracetam now and begin 4 mg folic acid → change the regimen before conception, not after
  7. 28 yo on carbamazepine who presents newly pregnant at 9 weeks gestation → Switching to a different antiepileptic now → organogenesis is largely complete and overlapping agents doubles exposure
  8. 22 yo about to start isotretinoin for nodulocystic acne → Two negative pregnancy tests 19 or more days apart with two forms of contraception → iPLEDGE risk-management requirements
  9. 2-week-old boy born at 38 weeks to a 27-year-old first-time mother after an uncomplicated pregnancy, with no maternal alcohol or drug history recorded; birth weight about 2.3 kg; length, weight and head circumference at the 5th percentile; short palpebral fissures, flat midface, small jaw and thin upper lip; soft systolic murmur with normal femoral pulses; mild hypotonia → Fetal alcohol syndrome → the face and growth decide without an exposure history; the palpebral fissures are short, not upslanting
Anticoagulation in pregnancy Low molecular weight heparin and unfractionated heparin have no fetal effects; warfarin is teratogenic to bone and cartilage. Heparins do not cross the placenta, and warfarin does. Patients with mechanical valves therefore take LMWH in the first trimester, warfarin in the second and third, and unfractionated heparin near delivery.
Pearls Cleft plus distal digit hypoplasia is phenytoin; alcohol affects the philtrum and the palpebral fissures, not the palate or the fingertips · Timing predicts the kind of damage – before 2 weeks all-or-none, 3–8 weeks structure, after 8 weeks growth and brain · Change antiepileptics before conception, never after; once pregnancy is recognised organogenesis is mostly done, and switching adds seizure risk plus a second teratogen · Valproate is the worst antiepileptic and levetiracetam the usual substitute · Oligohydramnios with Potter sequence should suggest ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors as well as renal agenesis, two different first causes of the same cascade · Lithium → Ebstein anomaly is the one psychiatric-drug-to-cardiac-lesion pairing worth memorising outright
Fetal alcohol syndrome without an exposure history FAS (fetal alcohol syndrome) can be diagnosed from the examination when no exposure history is given. The 2016 revised Institute of Medicine criteria require all four of these. First, 2 of 3 facial features: short palpebral fissures (at or below the 10th percentile), a thin upper lip vermilion and a smooth philtrum. Second, height or weight at or below the 10th percentile. Third, a head circumference at or below the 10th percentile, a structural brain anomaly, or recurrent nonfebrile seizures. Fourth, neurobehavioral impairment, which under age 3 means developmental delay. Confirmed alcohol exposure is not required; a confirmed absence of exposure excludes the diagnosis. Short fissures point to FAS. Upslanting fissures with epicanthal folds, a flat facial profile and a single palmar crease point to Down syndrome.
How NBME framed it No maternal alcohol history was given; the face, with length, weight and head size at the 5th percentile, made the diagnosis in a hypotonic 2-week-old. Short palpebral fissures separated it from Down syndrome, whose fissures slant upward; trisomy 13, fragile X, Klinefelter syndrome and congenital toxoplasmosis were the other decoys.
Pairs with Part II Posterior Urethral Valves covers the oligohydramnios cascade that this brief reaches from the drug side. Part I Congenital Heart Disease covers Ebstein anomaly. Ask: which single malformation does only one drug on the roster cause?
Transferable rule To identify a teratogen, find the one malformation that belongs to only one agent. Ignore the shared features that every candidate agent can produce.
Unchecked attributeAlcohol use: shares microcephaly and growth restriction, but has no association with cleft lip or palate, and none of the facial triad is described.
True-fact-wrong-slotCocaine use: causes preterm delivery, abruption and growth restriction, but no congenital defects.
Class-vs-memberLisinopril: a named teratogen, but it produces renal failure and Potter sequence, not clefting or digit hypoplasia.
True-fact-wrong-slotUntreated syphilis: symptomatic cases show snuffles, hepatomegaly and a maculopapular rash, none present here.
Unchecked attributeDown syndrome: hypotonia and a soft murmur fit, but Down syndrome gives upslanting palpebral fissures with epicanthal folds, a flat facial profile and a single palmar crease. These fissures are short.
True-fact-wrong-slotTrisomy 13 syndrome: it causes cleft lip and palate, holoprosencephaly, small eyes, scalp defects and extra digits, none of which this newborn has.
Unchecked attributeFragile X syndrome: the long face, large ears, prominent jaw and large testes appear later in childhood and after puberty; this newborn has a small jaw.
Unchecked attributeKlinefelter syndrome (seminiferous tubule dysgenesis): boys with 47,XXY look normal at birth; small testes, tall stature and gynecomastia appear at puberty.
Salient decoyCongenital toxoplasmosis: growth restriction fits, but it brings chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, scattered intracranial calcifications and an enlarged liver and spleen, not a facial pattern.

edits.html:
Primary Amenorrhea

pelvic ultrasound first · uterus present or absent, then read the FSH · Turner, agenesis, androgen insensitivityIs there a uterus, and if so is the FSH high or low; if not, is there pubic hair?

Source vignette Pt – 15 yo, no menses, distressed at looking younger than peers; no headache or visual change; mother and grandmother menarche at 13; height below the 3rd percentile, weight 20th · Exam – no breast development, normal external genitalia, Tanner 2 pubic hair; urine beta-hCG negative · Imaging – pelvic ultrasonography shows a prepubertal uterus with small ovaries · Labs – FSH 60 (normal under 40), LH 52 (normal 5–25) · Q – the next step in management, then the underlying cause; options spanned hormone measurements, imaging, karyotype and reassurance
The decision point

Primary amenorrhea is no menarche by 15 with secondary sexual characteristics, or by 13 without them. The first step is pelvic ultrasonography. The obstruction can sit anywhere from the hypothalamus and pituitary to the ovary, uterus and vagina. Imaging is the only test that answers the anatomical half of that chain in one move. Every hormonal test is interpretable only once you know whether there is a uterus. Uterus present → read the FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone). High FSH with high LH (luteinizing hormone) is primary ovarian insufficiency. With short stature, that is Turner syndrome: gonadal dysgenesis from loss of an X. Turner syndrome gives streak ovaries and absent oestrogen, while intact adrenals still produce pubic hair. Uterus absent → read the pubic hair. Pubic hair present means the androgen receptor works, so the diagnosis is 46,XX Müllerian agenesis. Absent pubic hair means it does not, so the diagnosis is 46,XY complete androgen insensitivity.

Defining criteria Primary amenorrhea – no menarche by age 15 with secondary sexual characteristics, or by age 13 without them · First step – pelvic ultrasonography, to establish whether a uterus is present before any hormone is measured · Uterus present, FSH high – primary ovarian insufficiency; with short stature, Turner syndrome (45,X on karyotype, FISH if mosaicism is suspected) · Uterus present, FSH low or inappropriately normal – central: MRI for a hypothalamic or pituitary lesion, or GnRH deficiency, Cushing syndrome, functional hypothalamic amenorrhea · Uterus absent – serum testosterone: female-range with normal pubic hair is Müllerian agenesis (46,XX); male-range with absent pubic and axillary hair is complete androgen insensitivity (46,XY)
Primary amenorrhea – the two-step algorithmanatomy first, then the gonadotropins
StepFindingConclusionConfirms, then
Before step 1: urine hCGNegativePregnancy excludedThen the ultrasound
1. Pelvic ultrasoundUterus presentGo to the FSHAnatomy only; the FSH picks the branch
1. Pelvic ultrasoundUterus absentGo to the testosterone and the pubic hairAnatomy only; the karyotype settles the branch
2a. FSH high± short staturePrimary ovarian insufficiency → karyotype → Turner if 45,X45,X karyotype, FISH if mosaicism is suspected; then echocardiogram and renal ultrasound
2a. FSH low or normal± anosmia, weight loss, athlete, cushingoidCentral: MRI, or functional, Kallmann or CushingMRI shows a sellar lesion, or is normal with anosmia in Kallmann; check TSH and prolactin
2b. Testosterone female-rangePubic hair presentMüllerian agenesis (46,XX) → evaluate the renal tract46,XX karyotype; then renal ultrasound
2b. Testosterone male-rangePubic hair absentComplete androgen insensitivity (46,XY)46,XY karyotype; then gonadectomy, usually after puberty, for tumor risk
Pertinent positives & negatives Height below the 3rd percentile – the key Turner clue; almost all patients develop short stature, often the only feature besides amenorrhea · No breast development with Tanner 2 pubic hair – oestrogen absent, adrenal androgens intact; the dissociation that points at the ovary rather than the axis · FSH 60 and LH 52 – loss of oestrogen negative feedback; hypergonadotropic hypogonadism · Prepubertal uterus with small ovaries – streak gonads; the uterus is present but was never stimulated · No headache or visual change – argues against a sellar mass, which is the central branch · Normal external genitalia – the genital tubercle is unaffected in every diagnosis on this list · Negative beta-hCG – pregnancy must be excluded before anything else
Decision spine Is the definition met? – No menarche by 13 without secondary characteristics → yes · What is the first test? – Pelvic ultrasound; anatomy before hormones · Is there a uterus? – Yes → read the FSH · Is the FSH high or low? – High → ovarian failure, not a central cause · Is she short? – Below the 3rd percentile → Turner · What confirms it? – Karyotype showing 45,X, with FISH for mosaicism if normal
Scenario bank
  1. 15 yo with no menarche, no breast development, Tanner 2 pubic hair, height below the 3rd percentile, normal external genitalia and a negative urine beta-hCG → Pelvic ultrasonography → establish the anatomy before measuring hormones
  2. 14 yo with primary amenorrhea and no secondary sexual characteristics in whom ultrasonography has confirmed a uterus → FSH level measurement → it separates central (low or normal) from peripheral (high) causes
  3. 15 yo with primary amenorrhea, no breast development and short stature; ultrasound shows a prepubertal uterus with small ovaries and FSH is 60 with LH 52 → Turner syndrome → 45,X on karyotype
  4. 16 yo distance runner with primary amenorrhea, Tanner 4 breast and pubic hair, normal external genitalia; ultrasound shows normal ovaries and no uterus → Müllerian agenesis → failure of paramesonephric duct development
  5. 16 yo with primary amenorrhea, Tanner 4 breast development, absent pubic and axillary hair, tall stature and no uterus on ultrasound → Complete androgen insensitivity syndrome → 46,XY with male-range testosterone
  6. 15 yo with primary amenorrhea, a uterus on ultrasound, FSH 3 and LH 2, normal weight and normal sense of smell → MRI of the brain → a low FSH points centrally
  7. 16 yo newly diagnosed with Müllerian agenesis → Renal ultrasonography → renal tract anomalies are commonly associated
  8. 17 yo gymnast training twice daily with a BMI of 16, primary amenorrhea, a uterus present, and low FSH and LH → Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea → energy deficit suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis
  9. Why girls with Turner syndrome develop pubic hair but no breast development → Adrenarche is intact while ovarian estrogen production fails → the adrenal glands are unaffected by loss of an X chromosome
Test order A 17-hydroxyprogesterone, a testosterone, a karyotype and an MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) are each the right move in some branch of this algorithm. Each is uninterpretable until the ultrasound has shown whether there is a uterus, so ordering it first is one step too early. Reassurance is right for a girl under 15 who has secondary sexual characteristics. It is wrong here because the definition is already met and her height is below the 3rd percentile.
Pearls Ultrasound first, always – every hormone in this workup is uninterpretable until you know whether there is a uterus · Uterus present → FSH. Uterus absent → pubic hair. These two questions, in that order, resolve almost every case of primary amenorrhea · High FSH means ovarian failure; low FSH means a central cause – the gonadotropins tell you which end of the axis to investigate · Turner patients have pubic hair, because adrenarche is adrenal and the adrenals are normal; pubic hair without breast development points to ovarian failure · Müllerian agenesis and androgen insensitivity both present with an absent uterus and differ in pubic hair · Müllerian agenesis obliges a renal ultrasound – the ducts develop alongside the urinary tract, so anomalies travel together · An athlete with amenorrhea can still have a structural cause; functional hypothalamic amenorrhea never explains missing anatomy
Pairs with Part I Abnormal Uterine Bleeding covers the opposite complaint on the same axis, too much bleeding rather than none, and shares the immature-axis physiology. Part II Puberty covers the staging vocabulary this brief uses throughout. Ask: is there a uterus, and if so is the FSH high or low?
Transferable rule When a workup has an anatomical branch and a hormonal branch, image first. A hormone measured before you know the anatomy produces a number you cannot interpret.
Sequencing trap17-hydroxyprogesterone: real in the amenorrhea workup for congenital adrenal hyperplasia, but indicated only once a uterus is confirmed and with suggestive features.
Uniform-answer doubtReassurance and observation: the definition is already met, and height below the 3rd percentile is itself a finding.
Unchecked attributeAndrogen insensitivity: requires an absent uterus; she has one.
Mirror twinDevelopmental failure of the urogenital sinus: produces a vaginal dimple with a uterus present, the mirror image of Müllerian agenesis.
Salient decoyAbnormal GnRH pulsatility: twice-daily training is a real risk factor, but central causes give low gonadotropins and cannot remove a uterus.

edits.html:
Genital Ulcers

painless vs painful ulcers · syphilis vs herpes vs chancroid · test for syphilis, herpes and HIV · penicillinDoes the ulcer hurt, and are there vesicles or suppurating nodes?

Source vignette Pt – 17 yo F, 5 days of a nontender vulvar lesion; three male partners, condoms used inconsistently; afebrile, normal vital signs · Exam – 2 cm ulcer with raised borders on the right labium majus · Q – the most likely causal organism; options were organism classes: gram-negative bacillus, gram-negative diplococcus, obligate intracellular bacterium, protozoan, spirochete and virus
The decision point

A single painless genital ulcer with a firm, raised border and no systemic signs is a primary syphilis chancre. The cause is Treponema pallidum, a spirochete. Genital herpes and chancroid both cause painful ulcers. HSV (herpes simplex virus) starts as grouped vesicles that break into shallow ulcers. Chancroid causes deep ulcers, often with tender suppurative inguinal nodes.

A chancre can also be multiple or painful, and the exam alone often misleads. Test every genital ulcer for syphilis and HSV, and test for HIV. Early in primary syphilis the RPR (rapid plasma reagin) can still be nonreactive. Darkfield microscopy or a molecular test of the ulcer exudate detects the spirochete directly.

Genital ulcer in a sexually active patient: the differential
DiagnosisUlcerNodes and courseThe NBME tell
Primary syphilis: Treponema pallidum, a spirocheteUsually single, painless, clean base, firm raised borderPainless, rubbery inguinal nodes; heals in weeks even untreated, and secondary syphilis can followPainless ulcer with an indurated, raised border; no vesicles
Genital herpes: HSV-2 or HSV-1, a virusPainful grouped vesicles on a red base that break into shallow ulcers, then crustTender inguinal nodes; a first episode can bring fever and dysuria; recursVesicles first, painful, often multiple
Chancroid: Haemophilus ducreyi, a gram-negative bacillusOne or more deep, painful ulcers with ragged, undermined edges and a purulent baseTender suppurative inguinal nodes (buboes) that can rupture; rare in the United StatesPainful ulcer with a suppurating node
Lymphogranuloma venereum: Chlamydia trachomatis L1 to L3, an obligate intracellular bacteriumSmall papule or ulcer that heals on its own and often goes unnoticedTender, usually unilateral inguinal or femoral nodes; proctocolitis after rectal exposureThe nodes, not the ulcer, bring the patient in
Discharge infections: N. gonorrhoeae (gram-negative diplococcus), C. trachomatis (obligate intracellular), Trichomonas vaginalis (protozoan)No ulcerCervicitis, urethritis and pelvic inflammatory disease; trichomoniasis gives a frothy, malodorous dischargeDischarge without an ulcer
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Nontreponemal test (RPR or VDRL, Venereal Disease Research Laboratory) plus a treponemal testFirstBoth reactiveSyphilis; a nonreactive nontreponemal test does not exclude early primary syphilis
HSV NAAT (nucleic acid amplification test, usually PCR, polymerase chain reaction) of a lesion swabFirstPositiveGenital herpes
HIV testScreenReactiveCo-infection; test everyone with a genital ulcer
Darkfield microscopy or PCR of ulcer exudateConfirmsMotile spirochetes or T. pallidum DNAPrimary syphilis, including before serology turns reactive
H. ducreyi culture on special mediaBy branchPositive in under 80%Chancroid; probable when ulcers are painful and syphilis and HSV tests are negative
Tzanck smearSkipInsensitive and nonspecificReplaced by HSV NAAT
Scenario bank
  1. 17 yo F, 5 days of a nontender vulvar lesion; three male partners, condoms used inconsistently; afebrile, normal vital signs; 2 cm ulcer with raised borders on the right labium majus → Spirochete → Treponema pallidum, primary syphilis chancre
  2. 18 yo F, 3 days of painful vulvar sores beginning a week after a new partner; dysuria, T 38.3 C; clusters of small vesicles and shallow ulcers on a red base on both labia; tender bilateral inguinal nodes → Genital herpes → HSV NAAT of a lesion; acyclovir or valacyclovir for 7 to 10 days
  3. 19 yo F, 1 week of two deep, painful vulvar ulcers with ragged, undermined edges and a purulent base; a tender, fluctuant left inguinal node; syphilis serology and HSV NAAT negative → Haemophilus ducreyi → chancroid; azithromycin 1 g orally once or ceftriaxone 250 mg IM (intramuscular) once
  4. 17 yo F, 6 days of a painless vulvar ulcer with a firm, raised border; nonreactive RPR; rubbery, nontender inguinal nodes; no vesicles → Darkfield microscopy of the ulcer exudate → primary syphilis; the RPR can be nonreactive this early
  5. 16 yo F, 1 week of a painless labial ulcer with a raised, indurated border; RPR and treponemal antibody test reactive; no rash; no drug allergies; negative pregnancy test → Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM once → primary syphilis; also test for HIV
  6. 20 yo F at 14 weeks of gestation with a painless vulvar ulcer; RPR and treponemal antibody test reactive; hives after amoxicillin as a child → Penicillin desensitization, then benzathine penicillin G → penicillin is the only recommended treatment in pregnancy
  7. 17 yo F given benzathine penicillin G for primary syphilis 6 hours ago; now T 38.6 C, headache and myalgia; no hives, wheeze or hypotension → Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction → antipyretics; not a penicillin allergy
  8. 18 yo F, 2 weeks of a tender, enlarging left inguinal node mass; a small painless vulvar bump 3 weeks ago that healed on its own; no current ulcer → Lymphogranuloma venereum → Chlamydia trachomatis L1 to L3; doxycycline for 21 days
Management Primary syphilis – benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM (intramuscular) once for adults and adolescents; children get 50,000 units/kg, up to 2.4 million units · Penicillin allergy, not pregnant – doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 14 days · Pregnancy – penicillin only; desensitize a patient with penicillin allergy, then treat · Genital herpes, first episode – oral acyclovir, valacyclovir or famciclovir for 7 to 10 days · Chancroid – azithromycin 1 g orally once or ceftriaxone 250 mg IM once
Organism classes Spirochete – Treponema pallidum: painless chancre · Virus – herpes simplex virus: painful vesicles, then ulcers · Gram-negative bacillus – Haemophilus ducreyi: painful ulcer, suppurative nodes · Obligate intracellular bacterium – Chlamydia trachomatis: cervicitis, or lymphogranuloma venereum with prominent nodes · Gram-negative diplococcus – Neisseria gonorrhoeae: cervicitis and discharge · Protozoan – Trichomonas vaginalis: frothy, malodorous discharge
Pearls In the United States, most genital ulcers in young, sexually active patients are genital herpes or syphilis · Treat presumptively for syphilis when the ulcer looks like a chancre, before results return · The Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction is fever, headache and myalgia within 24 hours of treating syphilis; it is not a penicillin allergy · How NBME framed it: every option was an organism class, so the ulcer had to be named as syphilis and then matched to spirochete.
Pairs with Part II Fever and Rash in a Child covers secondary syphilis. Ask: is there a rash on the palms and soles? Part I Cervicitis and Pelvic Inflammatory Disease covers gonorrhea and chlamydia. Ask: is there a discharge instead of an ulcer?
Transferable rule For a genital ulcer, ask first whether it hurts. A painless, indurated ulcer is primary syphilis until proven otherwise. A painful ulcer is herpes when vesicles came first and chancroid when the inguinal nodes suppurate.
Unchecked attributeGram-negative bacillus: Haemophilus ducreyi causes a genital ulcer, but the chancroid ulcer is painful and comes with tender suppurative nodes.
Unchecked attributeVirus: HSV (herpes simplex virus) is the most common cause of genital ulcers, but its lesions are painful and start as grouped vesicles.
True-fact-wrong-slotObligate intracellular bacterium: Chlamydia trachomatis is common in sexually active adolescents, but it causes cervicitis, and its lymphogranuloma venereum strains cause only a small transient ulcer.
Salient decoyGram-negative diplococcus: multiple partners suggest gonorrhea, but gonorrhea causes cervicitis and discharge, not an ulcer.
True-fact-wrong-slotProtozoan: Trichomonas vaginalis causes a frothy, malodorous discharge with itching, not an ulcer.

edits.html:
Preventive Care: Ranking Interventions

rank by magnitude of benefit · smoking cessation first · blood pressure, statin, glucose · organ-specific exceptionsWhich option has the largest mortality benefit, and is the outcome limited to one organ?

Source vignette Pt – 58 yo M smoker with hypertension, diabetes and hyperlipidemia · Q – the intervention that most reduces mortality; options spanned smoking cessation, a statin and lisinopril
The decision point

When every option is guideline-supported, rank them by magnitude of benefit. Smoking cessation reduces all-cause mortality more than any drug on the list. It cuts CV (cardiovascular) risk substantially within 1–2 years and approaches never-smoker risk over ~15 years.

Ranking preventive interventions – why each loses
ChoiceLegitimate claimWhy it loses
Smoking cessation – Largest mortality benefit of any intervention
LisinoprilDiabetic + HTN → ACE-I preferred, especially with albuminuriaBP only mildly elevated, no proteinuria – real but smaller
StatinDiabetic 40–75 → indicated regardless of LDLTrue indication, but ~25% relative risk reduction – cessation dwarfs it
↑ HCTZBP above goalMarginal, and worsens glucose and lipids in a diabetic
↑ MetforminA1c above targetGlycemic control reduces microvascular complications; weak macrovascular effect (UKPDS)
Scenario bank
  1. 58 yo M smoker with hypertension, diabetes and hyperlipidemia; which most reduces mortality → Smoking cessation
  2. 58 yo M who has already quit; which intervention is next → A statin
  3. 58 yo M asking how soon quitting helps → Cardiovascular risk falls within 1 to 2 years
  4. 58 yo M ready to quit within the month → Varenicline plus behavioral support
  5. 58 yo M who is not ready to quit → Motivational interviewing
  6. 58 yo M with 30 pack-years who quit 5 years ago → Annual low-dose CT screening
The hierarchy to bank For macrovascular outcomes, the order of benefit is smoking cessation > BP (blood pressure) control > statin > glycemic control. If the patient smokes and smoking cessation is an option, choose it. The exception is an outcome limited to a specific organ. For risk of nephropathy progression, choose an ACE-I (angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor) and BP control. For microvascular complications, choose glycemic (A1c) control. Lifestyle advice ranks low when vague ("recommend exercise") and high when specific and high-magnitude (smoking or alcohol cessation).

edits.html:
Elder Abuse

reasonable suspicion is enough · findings that build suspicion · reporting pathways · capacity determines whether to reportIs the suspicion reasonable, and is the victim a competent adult or a cognitively impaired elder?

The decision point

Reasonable suspicion → report to Adult Protective Services. You do not need proof, and you do not investigate first. Confounders such as warfarin (easy bruising) and dementia (unreliable historian) are real but irrelevant to the decision to report. Adult Protective Services investigates; you do not adjudicate.

Scenario bank
  1. 82 yo F with bruises in multiple stages of healing and a vague mechanism → Report now, on suspicion alone → proof is not required, and confirming it is not the physician's job
  2. 82 yo F on warfarin with easy bruising and an implausible history → Report to Adult Protective Services → anticoagulation explains bruising, not the implausible history; suspicion alone obligates the report
  3. 82 yo F with dementia who denies abuse while her caregiver is present → Interview her alone
  4. 34 yo F disclosing intimate partner violence, fully competent, who declines reporting → Support and safety planning, respecting her autonomy
  5. 6 yo M with a spiral femur fracture and an inconsistent history → Mandatory report to child protective services
  6. 82 yo F with suspected abuse; who investigates → Adult Protective Services → the physician reports suspicion; APS investigates
The findings that build suspicion Bruises in multiple stages of healing (the single most tested physical finding, as in child abuse) · implausible or vague mechanism · caregiver who cannot explain the injuries · patient who becomes uncomfortable and minimizes when asked alone · risk profile: dementia, dependency, caregiver stress. Interview technique: separate the patient from the caregiver, ask direct nonjudgmental questions, and do not confront the suspected abuser.
Reporting pathways
SituationPath
Elder / dependent adult abuseAPS – report on suspicion, mandated in most states
Child abuseCPS – report on suspicion, no parental consent needed
Intimate partner violence in a competent adultNOT reportable without consent in most states → safety assessment, safety plan, resources, document
Gunshot / stab wounds, certain infectionsReportable regardless
The asymmetry rule Capacity determines whether to report. Report abuse of children and cognitively impaired elders over anyone's objection. For a competent adult experiencing IPV (intimate partner violence), offer support and respect autonomy. Once abuse is suspected, never "document and re-ask at the next visit". Doing so sends a dependent patient back into the home you suspect.

edits.html:
Adolescent Confidentiality

the exceptions · services protected without parental consent · CRAFFT and brief counseling · encouraging self-disclosureWhat would have to be true to break confidentiality, and is any of it present?

Source vignette Pt – 16 yo M, well, discloses weekend marijuana use during the confidential portion of the visit · Q – the most appropriate next step; options spanned confidential counseling with CRAFFT screening, informing his parents and ordering a urine drug screen
The decision point

A minor discloses substance use during a confidential interview. In this case, keep it confidential and counsel him directly. Substance use is a confidential service in essentially every state, and nothing he describes meets an exception. Confidentiality is what makes honest disclosure possible at all; adolescents who don't expect it don't disclose.

Set the frame before he talks by saying "what you tell me stays between us, unless someone's safety is at risk". Then screen with CRAFFT (Car, Relax, Alone, Forget, Family/Friends, Trouble), deliver brief counseling, and encourage him to tell his parents himself. Encouraging voluntary disclosure is not the same as disclosing.

Defining criteria Suicidal or homicidal intent – harm to self or others; break confidentiality · Physical or sexual abuse – including statutory abuse by partner age; break confidentiality and report · Imminent danger – specific and serious; imminence is the word that decides · Not an exception – vagueness, a parent asking, an embarrassing diagnosis, or risky behavior that is not imminently lethal
Adolescent confidentiality – what is protected
Confidential without parental consent
STI diagnosis and treatment (all 50 states)
Contraception
Pregnancy care (abortion varies – many states require notification or consent)
Substance use evaluation and treatment
Mental health services (age and state vary)
Emancipated / mature minors: married, military, parenting, self-supporting, court-declared → consent as adults
Distractors "Inform his parents": parental authority is the higher principle for most care, but the confidential-services carve-outs exist to override it (trump-card inversion) · "Tell him you can't promise confidentiality": this sounds true but is harmful; frame confidentiality as conditional, naming the specific exceptions, not as a blanket refusal · "Refer to a substance-use program": escalating before you have screened severity is a sequencing trap; occasional use gets brief counseling, not a program · "Order a urine drug screen": he already told you. Testing to confirm a disclosure is redundant, and a non-consented screen is its own ethics violation.
Mnemonic HEEADSSS (Home, Education and employment, Eating, Activities, Drugs, Sexuality, Suicide and depression, Safety) is the adolescent psychosocial history, asked privately.
Scenario bank
  1. 16 yo M discloses weekend marijuana use, otherwise well → Confidential counseling, CRAFFT, encourage self-disclosure to parents
  2. 16 yo M discloses use and says he's been thinking about killing himself → Break confidentiality – safety exception
  3. 16 yo M who drives after drinking → Maintain confidentiality and counsel about the driving → escalate only if he describes an imminent plan to drive impaired
  4. 15 yo F requesting contraception, doesn't want her mother told → Provide it confidentially
  5. 15 yo F at 15 weeks, sexual partner is 24 years old → Report it → the age gap converts this to statutory abuse
  6. 17 yo M with chlamydia → Treat confidentially; partner notification is a public-health obligation and does not breach his confidentiality
  7. 17 yo F, married, needs surgery → She is emancipated and consents herself
  8. 16 yo M whose mother calls to ask what was discussed → Decline to disclose; redirect to encouraging the conversation at home
  9. 14 yo M with an appendectomy needed → Parental consent required → surgical care is not a confidential service
  10. 16 yo M, opioid use with withdrawal symptoms and IV track marks → Severity now warrants treatment referral, still discussed with him first
  11. 16 yo M in a state where billing goes to the parent's insurance → Address the practical confidentiality limit up front; this is the real-world failure point
Paired pearls Set the frame before the disclosure; confidentiality cannot be promised retroactively · CRAFFT (Car, Relax, Alone, Forget, Family/Friends, Trouble) is the validated adolescent screen; ≥2 is positive · emergency care never waits for consent · Management almost always includes "encourage him to tell his parents", which preserves confidentiality and the family relationship.
Pairs with Elder Abuse above covers the same axis in the opposite direction. There, impaired capacity forces reporting over the patient's wishes. Here, a minor with a confidential service forces confidentiality over the parent's wishes. Both turn on who holds decisional authority for this specific decision, not on who is older.
Transferable rule Maintain confidentiality unless the disclosure satisfies a named exception (harm to self, harm to others, abuse). Do not weigh how serious the behavior sounds; without a named exception, confidentiality holds no matter how alarming the disclosure.
